Without loss of generality, we may assume \( 0 < \varepsilon  \leq  {\bar{\varepsilon }}_{0} \) , where \( {\bar{\varepsilon }}_{0} \) is the sufficiently small (universal) positive constant in Lemma 7.4.2.

(i) This is analog of no local collapsing theorem II (Theorem 3.4.2). In comparison with the no local collapsing theorem II, this statement gives \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing property no matter how big the time is and it also allows the solution to be modified by surgery.

Let \( \eta \left( { \geq  {10}}\right) \) be the universal constant in the definition of the canonical neighborhood assumption. Recall that we had removed every component which has positive sectional curvature in our surgery procedure. By the same argument as in the first part of the proof of Lemma 7.4.2, the canonical neighborhood assumption of the solution implies the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing on the scales less than \( \frac{1}{2\eta }\widetilde{r}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) for some positive constant \( \kappa \) depending only on \( {C}_{1}\left( \varepsilon \right) \) and \( {C}_{2}\left( \varepsilon \right) \) (in the definition of the canonical neighborhood assumption). So we may assume \( \frac{1}{2\eta }\widetilde{r}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  \leq  {r}_{0} \leq  \sqrt{\frac{{t}_{0}}{2}} \) , and study the scales \( \rho ,\frac{1}{2\eta }\widetilde{r}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  \leq  \rho  \leq  {r}_{0} \) . Let \( x \in  {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0}, A{r}_{0}}\right) \) and assume that the solution satisfies

\[
\left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  {\rho }^{-2}
\]

for those points in \( P\left( {x,{t}_{0},\rho , - {\rho }^{2}}\right)  \triangleq  \left\{  {\left( {y, t}\right)  \mid  y \in  {B}_{t}\left( {x,\rho }\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {\rho }^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) for which the solution is defined. We want to bound the ratio \( {\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,\rho }\right) }\right) /{\rho }^{3} \) from below.

Recall that a space-time curve is called admissible if it stays in the region unaffected by surgery, and a space-time curve on the boundary of the set of admissible curves is called a barely admissible curve. Consider any barely admissible curve \( \gamma \) , parametrized by \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\gamma },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  ,{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2} \leq  {t}_{\gamma } \leq  {t}_{0} \) , with \( \gamma \left( {t}_{0}\right)  = x \) . The same proof for the assertion (7.4.2) (in the proof of Lemma 7.4.2) shows that for arbitrarily large \( L > 0 \) (to be determined later), one can find a sufficiently small \( \bar{\delta }\left( {L,{t}_{0},\widetilde{r}\left( {t}_{0}\right) ,\widetilde{r}\left( \frac{{t}_{0}}{2}\right) ,\varepsilon }\right)  > 0 \) such that when each \( \delta \) -cutoff in \( \left\lbrack  {\frac{{t}_{0}}{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) satisfies \( \delta  \leq  \bar{\delta }\left( {L,{t}_{0},\widetilde{r}\left( {t}_{0}\right) ,\widetilde{r}\left( \frac{{t}_{0}}{2}\right) ,\varepsilon }\right) \) , there holds

(7.5.1)

\[
{\int }_{{t}_{\gamma }}^{{t}_{0}}\sqrt{{t}_{0} - t}\left( {{R}_{ + }\left( {\gamma \left( t\right) , t}\right)  + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\left( t\right) \right| }^{2}}\right) {dt} \geq  L{r}_{0}.
\]

From now on, we assume that each \( \delta \) -cutoff of the solution in the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\frac{{t}_{0}}{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) satisfies \( \delta  \leq  \bar{\delta }\left( {L,{t}_{0},\widetilde{r}\left( {t}_{0}\right) ,\widetilde{r}\left( \frac{{t}_{0}}{2}\right) ,\varepsilon }\right) \) .

Let us scale the solution, still denoted by \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) , to make \( {r}_{0} = 1 \) and the time as \( {t}_{0} = 1 \) . By the maximum principle, it is easy to see that the (rescaled) scalar curvature satisfies

\[
R \geq   - \frac{3}{2t}
\]

on \( (0,1\rbrack \) . Let us consider the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{2},1}\right\rbrack \) and define a function of the form

\[
h\left( {y, t}\right)  = \phi \left( {{d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0}, y}\right)  - A\left( {{2t} - 1}\right) }\right) \left( {\bar{L}\left( {y,\tau }\right)  + 2\sqrt{\tau }}\right)
\]

where \( \tau  = 1 - t,\phi \) is the function of one variable chosen in the proof of Theorem 3.4.2 which is equal to one on \( \left( {-\infty ,\frac{1}{20}}\right) \) , rapidly increasing to infinity on \( \left( {\frac{1}{20},\frac{1}{10}}\right) \) , and satisfies \( 2\frac{{\left( {\phi }^{\prime }\right) }^{2}}{\phi } - {\phi }^{\prime \prime } \geq  \left( {{2A} + {300}}\right) {\phi }^{\prime } - C\left( A\right) \phi \) for some constant \( C\left( A\right)  <  + \infty \) , and \( \bar{L} \) is the function defined by

\[
\bar{L}\left( {q,\tau }\right)  = \inf \left\{  {2\sqrt{\tau }{\int }_{0}^{\tau }\sqrt{s}\left( {R + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\right| }^{2}}\right) {ds} \mid  \left( {\gamma \left( s\right) , s}\right) , s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\tau }\right\rbrack  }\right.
\]

\[
\text{ is a space-time curve with }\left. {\gamma \left( 0\right)  = x\text{ and }\gamma \left( \tau \right)  = q}\right\}  \text{ . }
\]

Note that

(7.5.2)

\[
\bar{L}\left( {y,\tau }\right)  \geq  2\sqrt{\tau }{\int }_{0}^{\tau }\sqrt{s}{Rds}
\]

\[
\geq   - 4{\tau }^{2}
\]

\[
>  - 2\sqrt{\tau }
\]

since \( R \geq   - 3 \) and \( 0 < \tau  \leq  \frac{1}{2} \) . This says \( h \) is positive for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{2},1}\right\rbrack \) . Also note that

(7.5.3)

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial \tau }\bar{L} + \bigtriangleup \bar{L} \leq  6
\]

as long as \( \bar{L} \) is achieved by admissible curves. Then as long as the shortest \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesics from \( \left( {{x}_{0},0}\right) \) to \( \left( {y,\tau }\right) \) are admissible, there holds at \( y \) and \( t = 1 - \tau \) ,

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \bigtriangleup }\right) h \geq  \left( {{\phi }^{\prime }\left\lbrack  {\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \bigtriangleup }\right) {d}_{t} - {2A}}\right\rbrack   - {\phi }^{\prime \prime }}\right)  \cdot  \left( {\bar{L} + 2\sqrt{\tau }}\right)
\]

\[
- \left( {6 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau }}}\right) \phi  - 2\langle \nabla \phi ,\nabla \bar{L}\rangle
\]

Firstly, we may assume the constant \( L \) in (7.5.1) is not less than \( 2\exp \left( {C\left( A\right)  + {100}}\right) \) . We claim that Lemma 3.4.1(i) is applicable for \( d = {d}_{t}\left( {\cdot ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) at \( y \) and \( t = 1 - \tau \) (with \( \tau  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{2}}\right\rbrack \) ) whenever \( \bar{L}\left( {y,\tau }\right) \) is achieved by admissible curves and satisfies the estimate

\[
\bar{L}\left( {y,\tau }\right)  \leq  3\sqrt{\tau }\exp \left( {C\left( A\right)  + {100}}\right) .
\]

Indeed, since the solution is defined on the whole neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{r}_{0}, - {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) \) with \( {r}_{0} = 1 \) and \( {t}_{0} = 1 \) , the point \( {x}_{0} \) at the time \( t = 1 - \tau \) lies on the region unaffected by surgery. Note that \( R \geq   - 3 \) for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{2},1}\right\rbrack \) . When \( \bar{L}\left( {y,\tau }\right) \) is achieved by admissible curves and satisfies \( \bar{L}\left( {y,\tau }\right)  \leq  3\sqrt{\tau }\exp \left( {\bar{C}\left( A\right)  + {100}}\right) \) , the estimate (7.5.1) implies that the point \( y \) at the time \( t = 1 - \tau \) does not lie in the collars of the gluing caps. Thus any minimal geodesic (with respect to the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) with \( t = 1 - \tau \) ) connecting \( {x}_{0} \) and \( y \) also lies in the region unaffected by surgery; otherwise the geodesic is not minimal. Then from the proof of Lemma 3.4.1(i), we see that it is applicable.

Assuming the minimum of \( h \) at a time, say \( t = 1 - \tau \) , is achieved at a point, say \( y \) , and assuming \( \bar{L}\left( {y,\tau }\right) \) is achieved by admissible curves and satisfies \( \bar{L}\left( {y,\tau }\right)  \leq \; 3\sqrt{\tau }\exp \left( {C\left( A\right)  + {100}}\right) \) , we have

\[
\left( {\bar{L} + 2\sqrt{\tau }}\right) \nabla \phi  =  - \phi \nabla \bar{L},
\]

and then by the computations and estimates in the proof of Theorem 3.4.2,

\[
\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \bigtriangleup }\right) h
\]

\[
\geq  \left( {{\phi }^{\prime }\left\lbrack  {\left( {\frac{\partial }{\partial t} - \bigtriangleup }\right) {d}_{t} - {2A}}\right\rbrack   - {\phi }^{\prime \prime } + 2\frac{{\left( {\phi }^{\prime }\right) }^{2}}{\phi }}\right)  \cdot  \left( {\bar{L} + 2\sqrt{\tau }}\right)  - \left( {6 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau }}}\right) \phi
\]

\[
\geq   - C\left( A\right) h - \left( {6 + \frac{1}{\sqrt{\tau }}}\right) \frac{h}{\left( 2\sqrt{\tau } - 4{\tau }^{2}\right) },
\]

at \( y \) and \( t = 1 - \tau \) . Here we used (7.5.2) and Lemma 3.4.1(i).

As before, denoting by \( {h}_{\min }\left( \tau \right)  = \mathop{\min }\limits_{z}h\left( {z,1 - \tau }\right) \) , we obtain

(7.5.4)

\[
\frac{d}{d\tau }\left( {\log \left( \frac{{h}_{\min }\left( \tau \right) }{\sqrt{\tau }}\right) }\right)  \leq  C\left( A\right)  + \frac{6\sqrt{\tau } + 1}{{2\tau } - 4{\tau }^{2}\sqrt{\tau }} - \frac{1}{2\tau }
\]

\[
\leq  C\left( A\right)  + \frac{50}{\sqrt{\tau }}
\]

as long as the associated shortest \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesics are admissible with \( \bar{L} \leq  3\sqrt{\tau }\exp (C\left( A\right)  + \) 100). On the other hand, by definition, we have

(7.5.5)

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\tau  \rightarrow  {0}^{ + }}}\frac{{h}_{\min }\left( \tau \right) }{\sqrt{\tau }} \leq  \phi \left( {{d}_{1}\left( {{x}_{0}, x}\right)  - A}\right)  \cdot  2 = 2.
\]

The combination of (7.5.4) and (7.5.5) gives the following assertion:

Let \( \tau  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{2}}\right\rbrack \) . If for each \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\tau }\right\rbrack  ,\inf \left\{  {\bar{L}\left( {y, s}\right)  \mid  {d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0}, y}\right)  \leq  A\left( {{2t} - 1}\right)  + }\right. \; \left. {\frac{1}{10}\text{ with }s = 1 - t}\right\} \) is achieved by admissible curves, then we have

(7.5.6)

\[
\inf \left\{  {\bar{L}\left( {y,\tau }\right)  \mid  {d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0}, y}\right)  \leq  A\left( {{2t} - 1}\right)  + \frac{1}{10}\text{ with }\tau  = 1 - t}\right\}
\]

\[
\leq  2\sqrt{\tau }\exp \left( {C\left( A\right)  + {100}}\right) .
\]

Note again that \( R \geq   - 3 \) for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{2},1}\right\rbrack \) . By combining with (7.5.1), we know that any barely admissible curve \( \gamma \) , parametrized by \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\tau }\right\rbrack  ,0 \leq  \tau  \leq  \frac{1}{2} \) , with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = x \) , satisfies

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\tau }\sqrt{s}\left( {R + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\right| }^{2}}\right) {ds} \geq  \frac{7}{4}\exp \left( {C\left( A\right)  + {100}}\right) ,
\]

by assuming \( L \geq  2\exp \left( {C\left( A\right)  + {100}}\right) \) .

Since \( \left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  {\rho }^{-2} \) on \( P\left( {x,{t}_{0},\rho , - {\rho }^{2}}\right) \) with \( \rho  \geq  \frac{1}{2\eta }\widetilde{r}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) (and \( {t}_{0} = 1 \) ) and \( \bar{\delta }\left( {L,{t}_{0},\widetilde{r}\left( {t}_{0}\right) ,\widetilde{r}\left( \frac{{t}_{0}}{2}\right) ,\varepsilon }\right)  > 0 \) is sufficiently small, the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {x,1,\rho , - {\rho }^{2}}\right) \) around the point \( \left( {x,1}\right) \) is contained in the region unaffected by the surgery. Thus as \( \tau  = 1 - t \) is sufficiently close to zero, \( \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\tau }}\inf \bar{L} \) can be bounded from above by a small positive constant and then the infimum \( \inf \left\{  {\bar{L}\left( {y,\tau }\right)  \mid  {d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0}, y}\right)  \leq  }\right. \; A\left( {{2t} - 1}\right)  + \frac{1}{10} \) with \( \tau  = 1 - t\} \) is achieved by admissible curves.

Hence we conclude that for each \( \tau  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{2}}\right\rbrack \) , any minimizing curve \( {\gamma }_{\tau } \) of \( \inf \left\{  {\bar{L}\left( {y,\tau }\right)  \mid  {d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0}, y}\right)  \leq  A\left( {{2t} - 1}\right)  + \frac{1}{10}\text{ with }\tau  = 1 - t}\right\} \) is admissible and satisfies

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\tau }\sqrt{s}\left( {R + {\left| {\dot{\gamma }}_{\tau }\right| }^{2}}\right) {ds} \leq  \exp \left( {C\left( A\right)  + {100}}\right) .
\]

Now we come back to the unrescaled solution. It then follows that the Li-Yau-Perelman distance \( l \) from \( \left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) \) satisfies the following estimate

(7.5.7)

\[
\min \left\{  {l\left( {y,{t}_{0} - \frac{1}{2}{r}_{0}^{2}}\right)  \mid  y \in  {B}_{{t}_{0} - \frac{1}{2}{r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{10}{r}_{0}}\right) }\right\}   \leq  \exp \left( {C\left( A\right)  + {100}}\right) ,
\]

by noting the (parabolic) scaling invariance of the Li-Yau-Perelman distance.

By the assumption that \( \left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) on \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{r}_{0}, - {r}_{0}^{2}}\right) \) , exactly as before, for any \( q \in  {B}_{{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) , we can choose a path \( \gamma \) parametrized by \( \tau  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{r}_{0}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) with \( \gamma \left( 0\right)  = x,\gamma \left( {r}_{0}^{2}\right)  = q \) , and \( \gamma \left( {\frac{1}{2}{r}_{0}^{2}}\right)  = y \in  {B}_{{t}_{0} - \frac{1}{2}{r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{10}{r}_{0}}\right) \) , where \( {\left. \gamma \right| }_{\left\lbrack  0,\frac{1}{2}{r}_{0}^{2}\right\rbrack  } \) achieves the minimum \( \min \left\{  {l\left( {y,{t}_{0} - \frac{1}{2}{r}_{0}^{2}}\right)  \mid  y \in  {B}_{{t}_{0} - \frac{1}{2}{r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{1}{10}{r}_{0}}\right) }\right\} \) and \( {\left. \gamma \right| }_{\left\lbrack  \frac{1}{2}{r}_{0}^{2},{r}_{0}^{2}\right\rbrack  } \) is a suitable curve satisfying \( {\left. \gamma \right| }_{\left\lbrack  \frac{1}{2}{r}_{0}^{2},{r}_{0}^{2}\right\rbrack  }\left( \tau \right)  \in  {B}_{{t}_{0} - \tau }\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) , for each \( \tau  \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{2}{r}_{0}^{2},{r}_{0}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) , so that the \( \mathcal{L} \) -length of \( \gamma \) is uniformly bounded from above by a positive constant (depending only on \( A \) ) multiplying \( {r}_{0} \) . This implies that the Li-Yau-Perelman distance from \( \left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) \) to the ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) is uniformly bounded by a positive constant \( L\left( A\right) \) (depending only on \( A \) ). Now we can choose the constant \( L \) in (7.5.1) by

\[
L = \max \{ {2L}\left( A\right) ,2\exp \left( {C\left( A\right)  + {100}}\right) \} .
\]

Thus every shortest \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic from \( \left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) \) to the ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) is necessarily admissible. By combining with the assumption that \( {\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq  {A}^{-1}{r}_{0}^{3} \) , we conclude that Perelman’s reduced volume of the ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) satisfies the estimate

(7.5.8)

\[
{\widetilde{V}}_{{r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  = {\int }_{{B}_{{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }{\left( 4\pi {r}_{0}^{2}\right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,{r}_{0}^{2}}\right) }\right) d{V}_{{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( q\right)
\]

\[
\geq  c\left( A\right)
\]

for some positive constant \( c\left( A\right) \) depending only on \( A \) .

We can now argue as in the last part of the proof of Lemma 7.4.2 to get a lower bound estimate for the volume of the ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,\rho }\right) \) . The union of all shortest \( \mathcal{L} \) - geodesics from \( \left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) \) to the ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) , defined by

\[
C{B}_{{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right)  = \{ \left( {y, t}\right)  \mid  \left( {y, t}\right) \text{ lies in a shortest }\mathcal{L}\text{ -geodesic from }
\]

\[
\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) \text{ to a point in }\left. {{B}_{{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right\}  \text{ , }
\]

forms a cone-like subset in space-time with vertex \( \left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Denote by \( B\left( t\right) \) the intersection of the cone-like subset \( C{B}_{{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) with the time-slice at \( t \) . Perelman’s reduced volume of the subset \( B\left( t\right) \) is given by

\[
{\widetilde{V}}_{{t}_{0} - t}\left( {B\left( t\right) }\right)  = {\int }_{B\left( t\right) }{\left( 4\pi \left( {t}_{0} - t\right) \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,{t}_{0} - t}\right) }\right) d{V}_{t}\left( q\right) .
\]

Since the cone-like subset \( C{B}_{{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) lies entirely in the region unaffected by surgery, we can apply Perelman's Jacobian comparison Theorem 3.2.7 and the estimate (7.5.8) to conclude that

(7.5.9)

\[
{\widetilde{V}}_{{t}_{0} - t}\left( {B\left( t\right) }\right)  \geq  {\widetilde{V}}_{{r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
\geq  c\left( A\right)
\]

for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {r}_{0}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) .

As before, denoting by \( \xi  = {\rho }^{-1}{\text{ Vol }}_{{t}_{0}}{\left( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( x,\rho \right) \right) }^{\frac{1}{3}} \) , we only need to get a positive lower bound for \( \xi \) . Of course we may assume \( \xi  < 1 \) . Consider \( \widetilde{B}\left( {{t}_{0} - \xi {\rho }^{2}}\right) \) , the subset at the time-slice \( \left\{  {t = {t}_{0} - \xi {\rho }^{2}}\right\} \) where every point can be connected to \( \left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) \) by an admissible shortest \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic. Perelman’s reduced volume of \( \widetilde{B}\left( {{t}_{0} - \xi {\rho }^{2}}\right) \) is given by

\[
\text{ (7.5.10) }{\widetilde{V}}_{\xi {\rho }^{2}}\left( {\widetilde{B}\left( {{t}_{0} - \xi {\rho }^{2}}\right) }\right)
\]

\[
= {\int }_{\widetilde{B}\left( {{t}_{0} - \xi {\rho }^{2}}\right) }{\left( 4\pi \xi {\rho }^{2}\right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,\xi {\rho }^{2}}\right) }\right) d{V}_{{t}_{0} - \xi {\rho }^{2}}\left( q\right)
\]

\[
= {\int }_{\overrightarrow{B}\left( {{t}_{0} - \xi {\rho }^{2}}\right)  \cap  \mathcal{L}{\exp }_{\left\{  \left| v\right|  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right\}  }\left( {\xi {\rho }^{2}}\right) }{\left( 4\pi \xi {\rho }^{2}\right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,\xi {\rho }^{2}}\right) }\right) d{V}_{{t}_{0} - \xi {\rho }^{2}}\left( q\right)
\]

\[
+ {\int }_{\widetilde{B}\left( {{t}_{0} - \xi {\rho }^{2}}\right)  \smallsetminus  \mathcal{L}{\exp }_{\left\{  \left| v\right|  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right\}  }\left( {\xi {\rho }^{2}}\right) }{\left( 4\pi \xi {\rho }^{2}\right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,\xi {\rho }^{2}}\right) }\right) d{V}_{{t}_{0} - \xi {\rho }^{2}}\left( q\right) .
\]

Note that the whole region \( P\left( {x,{t}_{0},\rho , - {\rho }^{2}}\right) \) is unaffected by surgery because \( \rho  \geq \; \frac{1}{2\eta }\widetilde{r}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) and \( \bar{\delta }\left( {L,{t}_{0},\widetilde{r}\left( {t}_{0}\right) ,\widetilde{r}\left( \frac{{t}_{0}}{2}\right) ,\varepsilon }\right)  > 0 \) is sufficiently small. Then exactly as before, there is a universal positive constant \( {\xi }_{0} \) such that when \( 0 < \xi  \leq  {\xi }_{0} \) , there holds

\[
\mathcal{L}{\exp }_{\left\{  \left| v\right|  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right\}  }\left( {\xi {\rho }^{2}}\right)  \subset  {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,\rho }\right)
\]

and the first term on RHS of (7.5.10) can be estimated by

(7.5.11)

\[
{\int }_{\bar{B}\left( {{t}_{0} - \xi {\rho }^{2}}\right)  \cap  \mathcal{L}{\exp }_{\left\{  \left| v\right|  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{ - }\frac{1}{2}\right\}  }{\left( \xi {\rho }^{2}\right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,\xi {\rho }^{2}}\right) }\right) d{V}_{{t}_{0} - \xi {\rho }^{2}}\left( q\right) }
\]

\[
\leq  {e}^{C\xi }{\left( 4\pi \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}{\xi }^{\frac{3}{2}}
\]

for some universal constant \( C \) ; while the second term on RHS of (7.5.10) can be estimated by

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
The argument is by contradiction, so we suppose that there is a \( T < {T}_{0} \) as in the statement of the proposition. Then the geometric limit flow on \( ( - T,0\rbrack \) is complete of non-negative curvature and with the curvature locally bounded in time. First suppose that the scalar curvature is bounded by, say \( Q < \infty \) . Fix \( {T}^{\prime } < T \) . The Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( {T}^{\prime }\right) }\right) \) is complete of non-negative curvature with the scalar curvature, and hence the norm of the Riemann curvature, bounded by \( Q \) . Thus, for any \( A < \infty \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the norm of the Riemann curvature of \( {Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( {-{T}^{\prime }}\right) \) on \( {B}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n}, - T, A}\right) \) is bounded above by \( {2Q} \) . Also, arguing as in the proof of Theorem 11.1 we see that any point \( y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) with \( R\left( {y, - {T}^{\prime }}\right)  > 4 \) has a \( \left( {{2C},{2\epsilon }}\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. Hence, applying Lemma 11.2 as in the argument in the proof of Corollary 11.3 shows that for all \( n \) sufficiently large, every point in \( {B}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n}, - {T}^{\prime }, A}\right) \) has a uniform size parabolic neighborhood on which the Riemann curvature is uniformly bounded, where both the time interval in the parabolic neighborhood and the curvature bound on this neighborhood depend only on \( C \) and the curvature bound on \( Q \) for the limit flow. According to Hamilton's result (Proposition 5.14) this implies that, by passing to a further subsequence, we can extend the limit flow backward beyond \( - {T}^{\prime } \) a uniform amount of time, say \( {2\delta } \) . Taking \( {T}^{\prime } > T - \delta \) then gives the desired extension under the condition that the scalar curvature is bounded on \( ( - T,0\rbrack \) .

It remains to show that, provided that \( T < {T}_{0} \) , the scalar curvature of the limit flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) , - T < t \leq  0 \) , is bounded. To establish this we need a couple of preliminary results.

Suppose that the assertion is false. Then there exists a sequence of positive numbers \( {h}_{j} \rightarrow  0 \) , a sequence of Ricci flows with surgery \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) and a sequence of points \( {x}_{j} \) with the following properties:

(i) The flow \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) has surgery parameters \( \varepsilon ,\widehat{r},{h}_{j},\widehat{\delta } \) . It is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{j}}\right) \) and goes singular as \( t \rightarrow  {T}_{j} \) .

(ii) The point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \) lies on an \( {4\varepsilon } \) -horn and \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right)  = {h}_{j}^{-2} \) .

(iii) The parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j},{\widehat{\delta }}^{-1}{h}_{j}, - {\widehat{\delta }}^{-1}{h}_{j}^{2}}\right) \) contains points modified by surgery, or it is not a \( \widehat{\delta } \) -neck.

By Definition 10.1, we have \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {4\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) whenever scal \( \geq  {\widehat{r}}^{-2} \) . Since \( {h}_{j} \rightarrow  0 \) , it follows that \( \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{x \in  {B}_{g\left( {T}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, A{h}_{j}}\right) }}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{T}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {\left( 1 + 2\eta A\right) }^{-2}{h}_{j}^{-2} \) . In particular, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( A \) ), then

\[
\mathop{\inf }\limits_{{x \in  {B}_{g\left( {T}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, A{h}_{j}}\right) }}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{T}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {10}{\left( \widehat{\delta }\widehat{r}\right) }^{-2}.
\]

We claim that for each \( A > 1 \) there exists a constant \( Q\left( A\right) \) (depending on \( A \) , but not on \( j \) ) such that \( \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  {B}_{g\left( {T}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, A{h}_{j}}\right) }}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{T}_{j}}\right)  \leq  Q\left( A\right) {h}_{j}^{-2} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. The proof of this statement is analogous to Claim 2 in Theorem 12.1 in [33]. Indeed, if no such constant \( Q\left( A\right) \) exists, then we can find a sequence of points \( \left( {{y}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \) (lying on the same horn as \( \left. \left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \right) \) such that the blow-up limit around \( \left( {{y}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \) is a piece of nonflat metric cone. Since the flow \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) satisfies the Canonical Neighborhood Assumption with accuracy \( {4\varepsilon } \) , the point \( \left( {{y}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \) either lies on a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck or on a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap. The second case can easily be ruled out, so \( \left( {{y}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \) must lie on a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck. In particular, there exists a small parabolic neighborhood of \( \left( {{y}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \) that is free of surgeries. In view of Proposition 10.3, the blow-up limit around \( \left( {{y}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \) is weakly PIC2. Hence, Proposition 6.5 implies that the limit cannot be a piece of a nonflat metric cone. This proves the claim.

In particular, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( A \) ), then the distance of the point \( {x}_{j} \) from either end of the horn is at least \( A{h}_{j} \) .

We now continue with the proof of Proposition 11.1. Let us fix a number \( A > 1 \) . Since the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \) lies on a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -horn, no point in \( {B}_{g\left( {T}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, A{h}_{j}}\right) \) can lie on a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap. Hence, the Canonical Neighborhood Assumption implies that every point in \( {B}_{g\left( {T}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, A{h}_{j}}\right) \) lies on a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck. Using Shi’s estimate, we obtain bounds for all the covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor in \( {B}_{g\left( {T}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\frac{1}{2}A{h}_{j}}\right) \) . Note that these bounds may depend on \( A \) , but are independent of \( j \) . We now pass to the limit, sending \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) first and \( A \rightarrow  \infty \) second. In the limit, we obtain a complete manifold with two ends that, by Proposition 10.3, is uniformly PIC and weakly PIC2. By the Cheeger-Gromoll splitting theorem, the limit is isometric to a product \( X \times  \mathbb{R} \) ; moreover, the cross-section \( X \) is compact and is nearly isometric to \( {S}^{n - 1} \) . Since every point in \( {B}_{g\left( {T}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, A{h}_{j}}\right) \) lies on a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck, we conclude that, for each \( A > 1 \) , the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j}, A{h}_{j}, - \frac{3{h}_{j}^{2}}{4}}\right) \) is free of surgeries if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( A \) ). After rescaling and passing to the limit, we obtain a solution to the Ricci flow that is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-\frac{1}{2},0}\right\rbrack \) and that splits off a line. Now, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( A) \) , then no point in \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j}, A{h}_{j}, - \frac{{h}_{j}^{2}}{2}}\right) \) can lie on a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap. Hence, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( A \) ), then every point in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j}, A{h}_{j}, - \frac{{h}_{j}^{2}}{2}}\right) \) lies on a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck. This allows us to extend the limit solution backward in time to the interval \( \left\lbrack  {-1,0}\right\rbrack \) . Repeating this argument, we can extend the limit solution backwards in time, so that it is defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-1,0}\right\rbrack  ,\left\lbrack  {-\frac{3}{2},0}\right\rbrack  ,\left\lbrack  {-2,0}\right\rbrack \) , etc. To summarize, we produce a limit solution that is ancient, uniformly PIC, weakly PIC2, and splits as a product of a line with a manifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n - 1} \) . By Theorem 6.4, the limiting solution is a family of standard cylinders. Therefore, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j},{\widehat{\delta }}^{-1}{h}_{j}, - {\widehat{\delta }}^{-1}{h}_{j}^{2}}\right) \) is free of surgeries, and \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j},{\widehat{\delta }}^{-1}{h}_{j}, - {\widehat{\delta }}^{-1}{h}_{j}^{2}}\right) \) is a \( \widehat{\delta } \) -neck. This contradicts (iii).

Step 2: Suppose that \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) is a point in space-time satisfying \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \; + {Q}_{j} \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) . The pointwise curvature derivative estimate implies that scal \( \leq \; 8{r}_{0}^{-2} \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},\frac{{r}_{0}}{100\eta }, - \frac{{r}_{0}^{2}}{100\eta }}\right) \) . Using Proposition 10.4, we conclude that \( \left| {{D}^{m}R}\right|  \leq  C\left( {n, m,\eta }\right) {r}_{0}^{-m - 2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Moreover, Proposition 10.9 implies \( {\operatorname{vol}}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq  \kappa {r}_{0}^{n} \) for some uniform constant \( \kappa \) that is independent of \( j \) .

Step 3: We next prove a long-range curvature estimate. Given any \( \rho  > 0 \) , we put

\[
\mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) }}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{t}_{j}}\right) .
\]

The pointwise curvature derivative estimate implies that \( \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  \leq  {16} \) for \( 0 < \; \rho  < \frac{1}{100\eta }. \)

We claim that \( \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \) for all \( \rho  > 0 \) . Suppose this is false. Let

\[
{\rho }^{ * } = \sup \{ \rho  \geq  0 : \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \}  < \infty .
\]

By definition of \( {\rho }^{ * } \) , we have an upper bound for the curvature in the geodesic ball \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) for each \( \rho  < {\rho }^{ * } \) . Using the results in Step 2, we obtain bounds for all the covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor in the geodesic ball \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) for each \( \rho  < {\rho }^{ * } \) . Moreover, the noncollapsing estimate in Step 2 gives a lower bound for the volume. We rescale around \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) and pass to the limit as \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) . In the limit, we obtain an incomplete manifold \( \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) that is weakly PIC2 (cf. [31, Th. 5.6]).

By definition of \( {\rho }^{ * } \) , there exists a sequence of points \( {y}_{j} \) such that

\[
{\rho }_{j} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {Q}_{j}^{\frac{1}{2}}{d}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{y}_{j}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }^{ * }\;\text{ and }\;{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty .
\]

Let \( {\gamma }_{j} : \left\lbrack  {0,{\rho }_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) be a unit-speed geodesic such that \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( 0\right)  = {x}_{j} \) and \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {{\rho }_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  = {y}_{j} \) , and let \( {\gamma }_{\infty } : \left\lbrack  {0,{\rho }^{ * }}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) denote the limit of \( {\gamma }_{j} \) . Using the estimate \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {4\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) we obtain for \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {{\rho }^{ * } - \frac{1}{100\eta },{\rho }^{ * }}\right) \) ,

\[
{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {{\gamma }_{\infty }\left( s\right) }\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {s{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {\left( 2\eta \left( {\rho }^{ * } - s\right) \right) }^{-2} \geq  {100}.
\]

Let us consider a real number \( \bar{s} \in  \left\lbrack  {{\rho }^{ * } - \frac{1}{100\eta },{\rho }^{ * }}\right) \) such that \( {64}{C}_{1}\eta \left( {{\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}}\right)  \leq  \bar{s} \) . We claim that \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) lies at the center of a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ). Indeed, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood Assumption implies that the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap. Furthermore, the Canonical Neighborhood is contained in a geodesic ball around \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) of radius \( 8{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , and the scalar curvature is at most \( 8{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) at each point in the Canonical Neighborhood. Since \( \mathbb{M}\left( \bar{s}\right)  < \infty \) , we obtain \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  = \infty \) ; consequently, \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {16}{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Hence, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood does not contain the point \( {y}_{j} \) . We next observe that \( {32}{C}_{1}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}{\left( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  {64}{C}_{1}\eta \left( {{\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}}\right)  \leq  \bar{s} \) . This implies \( {16}{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Hence, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood does not contain the point \( {x}_{j} \) . If the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) is a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap, then the geodesic \( {\gamma }_{j} \) must enter and exit this \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap, but this is impossible since \( {\gamma }_{j} \) minimizes length. To summarize, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ), then the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck. In particular, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ), then we have \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  C\left( n\right) \varepsilon {\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) . \)

Passing to the limit as \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) , we conclude that \( \left| {D{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}}\right|  \leq  C\left( n\right) \varepsilon {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at the point \( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \) . Integrating this estimate along \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) gives \( {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {{\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) }\right)  \geq \; {\left( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \left( {\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}\right) \right) }^{-2} \) . Moreover, since \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies at the center of a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck for \( j \) sufficiently large, the point \( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \) must lie on a strong \( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) .

As in \( \left\lbrack  {{33},§{12.1}}\right\rbrack \) , there is a sequence of rescalings that converges to a piece of a nonflat metric cone in the limit. Let us fix a point on this metric cone. In view of the preceding discussion, this point must lie on a strong \( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \) -neck. This gives a locally defined solution to the Ricci flow that is weakly PIC2 and that, at the final time, is a piece of nonflat metric cone. This contradicts Proposition 6.5.

Step 4: We now dilate the manifold \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) around the point \( {x}_{j} \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) . By Step 3, we have uniform bounds for the curvature at bounded distance. Using the results in Step 2, we obtain bounds for all the covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor at bounded distance. Using these estimates together with the noncollapsing estimate in Step 2, we conclude that the rescaled manifolds converge in the Cheeger-Gromov sense to a complete limit manifold \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) . Since \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) has \( \left( {f,\theta }\right) \) -pinched curvature, the curvature tensor of \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) is weakly PIC2 and satisfies \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \varnothing \mathrm{{id}} \in \) PIC. Using the Canonical Neighborhood Assumption, we conclude that every point in \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) with scalar curvature greater than 4 has a neighborhood that is either a strong \( {8\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {8\varepsilon } \) -cap.

We claim that \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) has bounded curvature. Indeed, if there is a sequence of points in \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) with curvature going to infinity, then \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) contains a sequence of necks with radii converging to 0 , contradicting Proposition 6.9. This shows that \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) has bounded curvature.

Step 5: We now extend the limit \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time. By Step 4, the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) is bounded from above by a constant \( \Lambda  > 4 \) . We claim that, given any \( A > 1 \) , the parabolic neighborhood

\[
P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right)
\]

is free of surgeries if \( j \) is sufficiently large. To prove this, fix \( A > 1 \) and suppose that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) contains points modified by surgery. Let \( {s}_{j} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }}\right\rbrack \) be the largest number such that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is free of surgeries. The pointwise curvature derivative estimate gives

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{\left. P\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\right) \right) }\operatorname{scal} \leq  {2\Lambda }{Q}_{j}
\]

if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Since the scalar curvature is greater than \( \frac{1}{2}{h}_{j}^{-2} \) at each point modified by surgery, we deduce that \( \frac{1}{2}{h}_{j}^{-2} \leq  {2\Lambda }{Q}_{j} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. In particular, \( {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1} \leq  \frac{1}{10\eta }{h}_{j}^{2} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Since \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \rightarrow  0 \) ,

Proposition 10.5 implies that the parabolic neighborhood

\[
P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right)
\]

is, after dilating by the factor \( {h}_{j} \) , arbitrarily close to a piece of the standard solution when \( j \) is sufficiently large. Using Corollary 9.3, we conclude that \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap when \( j \) is sufficiently large. If \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on an \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, then this neck is actually a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, since we are assuming that each \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \) -neck on which we perform surgery has a large backward parabolic neighborhood that is free of surgeries (cf. Definition 10.1). Moreover, Corollary 9.3 implies that \( \left| {D\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . Therefore, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of Theorem 10.10, and this contradicts statement (iii). Thus, given any \( A > 1 \) , the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is free of surgeries if \( j \) is sufficiently large.

Let \( {\tau }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }}  - \frac{1}{200\eta \Lambda } \) . In view of the preceding discussion, we may extend \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time to a complete solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfies \( {\Lambda }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  {2\Lambda } \) .

We now repeat this process. Suppose that we can extend \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time to a complete solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m},0}\right\rbrack \) , and satisfies \( {\Lambda }_{m} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } < \infty \) . Let \( {\tau }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{200\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} \) . We claim that we can extend the solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) backward to the interval \( \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack \) , and \( {\Lambda }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m} \) .

Indeed, if this is not possible, then there exists a number \( A > 1 \) with the property that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{100\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) contains points modified by surgery for \( j \) sufficiently large. Let \( {s}_{j} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{{100\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}}}\right\rbrack \) be the largest number such that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is free of surgeries. The pointwise curvature derivative estimate gives

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{\left. P\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}\right) \right) }\operatorname{scal} \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m}{Q}_{j}
\]

if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Let us choose \( {\alpha }_{m} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{n - 1}{2}}\right) \) so that \( \frac{{\alpha }_{m}}{{K}_{\text{ stnd }}\left( {1 - \frac{2{\alpha }_{m}}{n - 1}}\right) } \geq \; 8{\Lambda }_{m}\left( {\frac{1}{{100\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} - {\tau }_{m}}\right) \) . If \( \left( {{s}_{j} - {\tau }_{m}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1} \geq  {\alpha }_{m}{h}_{j}^{2} \) for \( j \) sufficiently large, then Proposition 10.5 together with the lower bound for the scalar curvature on the standard solution (cf. Theorem 9.1) gives

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) }}\operatorname{scal} \geq  \frac{1}{2{K}_{\text{ stnd }}\left( {1 - \frac{2{\alpha }_{m}}{n - 1}}\right) }{h}_{j}^{-2}
\]

\[
\geq  \frac{{\alpha }_{m}}{2{K}_{\text{ stnd }}\left( {1 - \frac{2{\alpha }_{m}}{n - 1}}\right) }{\left( {s}_{j} - {\tau }_{m}\right) }^{-1}{Q}_{j}
\]

\[
\geq  4{\Lambda }_{m}{Q}_{j}
\]

for \( j \) sufficiently large, which is impossible. Consequently, \( \left( {{s}_{j} - {\tau }_{m}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1} \leq  {\alpha }_{m}{h}_{j}^{2} \) for \( j \) sufficiently large. Since \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \rightarrow  0 \) , Proposition 10.5 implies that the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is, after dilating by the factor \( {h}_{j} \) , arbitrarily close to a piece of the standard solution when \( j \) is sufficiently large. Using Corollary 9.3, we conclude that \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap when \( j \) is sufficiently large. If \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on an \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, then this neck is actually a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, since we are assuming that each \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \) -neck on which we perform surgery has a large backward parabolic neighborhood that is free of surgeries (cf. Definition 10.1). Moreover, Corollary 9.3 implies that \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . Therefore, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of Theorem 10.10, and this contradicts statement (iii). Thus, we may extend the flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) backward to the interval \( \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack \) , where \( {\tau }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{200\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} \) , and we have \( {\Lambda }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m}. \)

Let \( {\tau }^{ * } = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\tau }_{m} \leq   - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda } \) . Using a standard diagonal sequence argument, we obtain a complete, smooth limit flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined on the interval \( \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) and that has bounded curvature for each \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) .

Step 6: We next show that \( {\tau }^{ * } =  - \infty \) . Indeed, if \( {\tau }^{ * } >  - \infty \) , it follows that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {\tau }_{m + 1}}\right)  = 0 \) , hence \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\Lambda }_{m} = \infty \) . Arguing as in Step 6 in the proof of Theorem 7.2, we can show that the limit flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) has bounded curvature. This contradicts the fact that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\Lambda }_{m} = \infty \) . Thus, \( {\tau }^{ * } =  - \infty \) . Hence, if we dilate the flow \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) around the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) , then (after passing to a subsequence) the rescaled flows converge to an ancient solution that is complete, has bounded curvature, is weakly PIC2, and satisfies \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \oslash \) id \( \in \) PIC. By Proposition 10.9, the limiting ancient solution is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed for some \( \kappa  > 0 \) that depends only on the initial data. By Corollary 6.22, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck with center at \( {x}_{j} \) ; or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap; or a closed manifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) ; or a quotient neck. Recall that we have discarded all connected components that are diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) (see Definition 10.1). Hence, the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) cannot be a closed manifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) . If the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) is a quotient neck, then Theorem A. 1 in [6] implies that the underlying manifold contains a nontrivial incompressible \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional space form, contrary to our assumption. Consequently, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck with center at \( {x}_{j} \) or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap. Finally, Corollary 6.20 implies that \( \left| {D\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\mathrm{{scal}}}^{2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . In summary, we have shown that the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of Theorem 10.10. This contradicts statement (iii). This completes the proof of Theorem 10.10.

(Perelman [104]). For any \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , let \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) ,0 \leq  t <  + \infty \) , be a solution to the Ricci flow with surgery, constructed by Theorem 7.4.3 with normalized initial data.

(i) Given \( w > 0, r > 0,\xi  > 0 \) , one can find \( T = T\left( {w, r,\xi ,\varepsilon }\right)  <  + \infty \) such that if the geodesic ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0}, r\sqrt{{t}_{0}}}\right) \) at some time \( {t}_{0} \geq  T \) has volume at least \( w{r}^{3}{t}_{0}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and the sectional curvature at least \( - {r}^{-2}{t}_{0}^{-1} \) , then the curvature at \( {x}_{0} \) at time \( t = {t}_{0} \) satisfies

(7.6.5)

\[
\left| {{2t}{R}_{ij} + {g}_{ij}}\right|  < \xi
\]

(ii) Given in addition \( 1 \leq  A < \infty \) and allowing \( T \) to depend on \( A \) , we can ensure (7.6.5) for all points in \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}}\right) \) .

(iii) The same is true for all points in the forward parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},{Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}, A{r}^{2}{t}_{0}}\right)  \triangleq  \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  \mid  x \in  {B}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},{Ar}\sqrt{{t}_{0}}}\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0},{t}_{0} + A{r}^{2}{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  }\right\}  . \)

\[

\[

Since we only need to consider the scale of the curvature less than \( \widetilde{r}{\left( \bar{t}\right) }^{-2} \) , the present situation is much easier than that of Proposition 7.4.1.

Firstly as before, we need to get a local curvature estimate.

For each adjusted \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , let \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) be the maximal subinterval of \( \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}{\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) so that for each sufficiently large \( \alpha \) and then sufficiently large \( \beta \) , the canonical neighborhood statement holds for any \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) in \( P\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},{t}^{\prime } - \bar{t}}\right)  = \{ \left( {x, t}\right)  \mid  x \in \; {B}_{t}\left( {\bar{x},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },\bar{t}}\right\rbrack  \} \) with \( R\left( {y, t}\right)  \geq  4\bar{Q} \) , where \( \eta \) is the universal positive constant in the definition of canonical neighborhood assumption. We want to show

(7.5.13)

\[
{t}^{\prime } = \bar{t} - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}{\bar{Q}}^{-1}.
\]

Consider the scalar curvature \( R \) at the point \( \bar{x} \) over the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . If there is a time \( \widetilde{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) satisfying \( R\left( {\bar{x},\widetilde{t}}\right)  \geq  4\bar{Q} \) , we let \( \widetilde{t} \) be the first of such time from \( \bar{t} \) . Since the chosen point \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) does not satisfy the canonical neighborhood statement, we know \( R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{r}{\left( \bar{t}\right) }^{-2} \) . Recall from our designed surgery procedure that if there is a cutoff surgery at a point \( x \) at a time \( t \) , the scalar curvature at \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) is at least \( {\left( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2}\widetilde{r}{\left( t\right) }^{-2} \) . Then for each fixed \( \alpha \) , for \( \beta \) large enough, the solution \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) around the point \( \bar{x} \) over the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\widetilde{t} - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}{\bar{Q}}^{-1},\widetilde{t}}\right\rbrack \) is well defined and satisfies the following curvature estimate

\[
R\left( {\bar{x}, t}\right)  \leq  8\bar{Q},
\]

for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\widetilde{t} - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}{\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) (or \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) if there is no such time \( \widetilde{t} \) ). By the assumption that \( {t}_{0} > 2{r}_{0}^{2} \) , we have

\[
\bar{t}R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  \geq  \frac{{t}_{0}}{2}R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)
\]

\[
\geq  {r}_{0}^{2}\left( {{K}_{1}{r}_{0}^{-2}}\right)
\]

\[
= {K}_{1} \rightarrow   + \infty \text{ . }
\]

Thus by using the pinching assumption and the gradient estimates in the canonical neighborhood assumption, we further have

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {30}\bar{Q},
\]

for all \( x \in  {B}_{t}\left( {\bar{x},\frac{1}{10}{\eta }^{-1}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\widetilde{t} - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}{\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) (or \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) ) and all sufficiently large \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) . Observe that Lemma 3.4.1 (ii) is applicable for \( {d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},\bar{x}}\right) \) with \( t \in \; \left\lbrack  {\widetilde{t} - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}{\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) (or \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) ) since any minimal geodesic, with respect to the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) , connecting \( {x}_{0} \) and \( \bar{x} \) lies in the region unaffected by surgery; otherwise the geodesic is not minimal. After having obtained the above curvature estimate, we can argue as deriving (7.2.2) and (7.2.3) in the proof of Theorem 7.2.1 to conclude that any point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) , with \( \widetilde{t} - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}{\bar{Q}}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) (or \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) ) and \( {d}_{t}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , satisfies

\[
{d}_{t}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  {d}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x},{x}_{0}}\right)  + \frac{1}{2}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},
\]

for all sufficiently large \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) . Then by combining with the choice of the points \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , we prove \( {t}^{\prime } = \bar{t} - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}{\bar{Q}}^{-1} \) (i.e., the canonical neighborhood statement holds for any point \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}{\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) with \( R\left( {y, t}\right)  \geq  4\bar{Q} \) ) for all sufficiently large \( \alpha \) and then sufficiently large \( \beta \) .

Now it follows from the gradient estimates in the canonical neighborhood assumption that the scalar curvatures of the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) satisfy

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {40}
\]

for those \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  P\left( {\bar{x},0,\frac{1}{10}{\eta }^{-1}, - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}}\right)  \triangleq  \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {\bar{x},\frac{1}{10}{\eta }^{-1}}\right) ,{t}^{\prime } \in  }\right. \; \left. \left\lbrack  {-\frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack  \right\} \) , for which the rescaled solution is defined. (Here \( {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) denotes the geodesic ball in the rescaled solution at time \( {t}^{\prime } \) ). Note again that \( R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{r}{\left( \bar{t}\right) }^{-2} \) and recall from our designed surgery procedure that if there is a cutoff surgery at a point \( x \) at a time \( t \) , the scalar curvature at \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) is at least \( {\left( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2}\widetilde{r}{\left( t\right) }^{-2} \) . Then for each fixed sufficiently large \( \alpha \) , for \( \beta \) large enough, the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) is defined on the whole parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {\bar{x},0,\frac{1}{10}{\eta }^{-1}, - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}}\right) \) . More generally, for arbitrarily fixed \( 0 < \widetilde{K} <  + \infty \) , there is a positive integer \( {\alpha }_{0} \) so that for each \( \alpha  \geq  {\alpha }_{0} \) we can

find \( {\beta }_{0} > 0 \) (depending on \( \alpha \) ) such that if \( \beta  \geq  {\beta }_{0} \) and \( \left( {y,0}\right) \) is a point on the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) with \( \widetilde{R}\left( {y,0}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{K} \) and \( {\widetilde{d}}_{0}\left( {y,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{K} \) , we have estimate

(7.5.14)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {40}\widetilde{K}
\]

for \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  P\left( {y,0,\frac{1}{10}{\eta }^{-1}{\widetilde{K}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}{\widetilde{K}}^{-1}}\right)  \triangleq  \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {y,}\right) }\right. \; \left. {\left. {\frac{1}{10}{\eta }^{-1}{\widetilde{K}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\rbrack  ,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {-\frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}{\widetilde{K}}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) . In particular, the rescaled solution is defined on the whole parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {y,0,\frac{1}{10}{\eta }^{-1}{\widetilde{K}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}{\widetilde{K}}^{-1}}\right) \) .

Next, we want to show the curvature of the rescaled solutions at the new times zero (after shifting) stay uniformly bounded at bounded distances from \( \bar{x} \) for some subsequences of \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) . Let \( {\alpha }_{m},{\beta }_{m} \rightarrow   + \infty \) be chosen so that the estimate (7.5.14) holds with \( \widetilde{K} = m \) . For all \( \rho  \geq  0 \) , set

\[
M\left( \rho \right)  = \sup \left\{  {\widetilde{R}\left( {x,0}\right)  \mid  m \geq  1,{d}_{0}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  \rho \text{ in the rescaled solutions }{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}}\right\}
\]

and

\[
{\rho }_{0} = \sup \{ \rho  \geq  0 \mid  M\left( \rho \right)  <  + \infty \} .
\]

Clearly the estimate (7.5.14) yields \( {\rho }_{0} > 0 \) . As we consider the unshifted time \( \bar{t} \) , by combining with the assumption that \( {t}_{0} > 2{r}_{0}^{2} \) , we have

(7.5.15)

\[
\bar{t}R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  \geq  \frac{{t}_{0}}{2}R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)
\]

\[
\geq  {r}_{0}^{2}\left( {{K}_{1}{r}_{0}^{-2}}\right)
\]

\[
= {K}_{1} \rightarrow   + \infty \text{ . }
\]

It then follows from the pinching assumption that we only need to show \( {\rho }_{0} =  + \infty \) . As before, we argue by contradiction. Suppose we have a sequence of points \( {y}_{m} \) in the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) with \( {\widetilde{d}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{y}_{m}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} <  + \infty \) and \( \widetilde{R}\left( {{y}_{m},0}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) . Denote by \( {\gamma }_{m} \) a minimizing geodesic segment from \( \bar{x} \) to \( {y}_{m} \) and denote by \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) the open geodesic balls centered at \( \bar{x} \) of radius \( {\rho }_{0} \) of the rescaled solutions. By applying the assertion in statement (i), we have uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing at the points \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) . By combining with the local curvature estimate (7.5.14) and Hamilton's compactness theorem, we can assume that, after passing to a subsequence, the marked sequence \( \left( {{\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}},\bar{x}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a marked (noncomplete) manifold \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) and the geodesic segments \( {\gamma }_{m} \) converge to a geodesic segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {B}_{\infty } \) emanating from \( {x}_{\infty } \) . Moreover, by the pinching assumption and the estimate (7.5.15), the limit has nonnegative sectional curvature.

Then exactly as before, we consider the tubular neighborhood along \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \)

\[
V = \mathop{\bigcup }\limits_{{{q}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{\infty }}}{B}_{\infty }\left( {{q}_{0},{4\pi }{\left( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {q}_{0}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)
\]

and the completion \( {\bar{B}}_{\infty } \) of \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }}\right) \) with \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {\bar{B}}_{\infty } \) the limit point of \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) . As before, by the choice of the points \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , we know that the limiting metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty } \) is cylindrical at any point \( {q}_{0} \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) which is sufficiently close to \( {y}_{\infty } \) . Then by the same reason as before the metric space \( \bar{V} = V \cup  \left\{  {y}_{\infty }\right\} \) has nonnegative curvature in Alexandrov sense, and we have a three-dimensional nonflat tangent cone \( {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V} \) at \( {y}_{\infty } \) . Pick \( z \in  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V} \) with distance one from the vertex and it is nonflat around \( z \) . By definition \( B\left( {z,\frac{1}{2}}\right) \left( { \subset  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V}}\right) \) is the Gromov-Hausdoff convergent limit of the scalings of a sequence of balls \( {B}_{\infty }\left( {{z}_{k},{\sigma }_{k}}\right) \left( { \subset  \left( {V,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }}\right) }\right) \) with \( {\sigma }_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) . Since the estimate (7.5.14) survives on \( \left( {V,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }}\right) \) for all \( \widetilde{K} <  + \infty \) , we know that this convergence is actually in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology and over some time interval. Since the limit \( B\left( {z,\frac{1}{2}}\right) \left( { \subset  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{V}}\right) \) is a piece of a nonnegatively curved nonflat metric cone, we get a contradiction with Hamilton's strong maximum Principle (Theorem 2.2.1) as before. Hence we have proved that a subsequence of the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) has uniformly bounded curvatures at bounded distance from \( \bar{x} \) at the new times zero.

Further, by the uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing at the points \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) and the estimate (7.5.14) again, we can take a \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) , defined on a space-time subset which contains the time slice \( \{ t = 0\} \) and is relatively open in \( {M}_{\infty } \times  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) , for the subsequence of the rescaled solutions. The limit is a smooth solution to the Ricci flow, and is complete at \( t = 0 \) , as well as has nonnegative sectional curvature by the pinching assumption and the estimate (7.5.15). Thus by repeating the same argument as in the Step 4 of the proof Proposition 7.4.1, we conclude that the curvature of the limit at \( t = 0 \) is bounded.

Finally we try to extend the limit backwards in time to get an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. Since the curvature of the limit is bounded at \( t = 0 \) , it follows from the estimate (7.5.14) that the limit is a smooth solution to the Ricci flow defined at least on a backward time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-a,0}\right\rbrack \) for some positive constant \( a \) . Let \( \left( {{t}_{\infty },0}\right\rbrack \) be the maximal time interval over which we can extract a smooth limiting solution. It suffices to show \( {t}_{\infty } =  - \infty \) . If \( {t}_{\infty } >  - \infty \) , there are only two possibilities: either there exist surgeries in finite distance around the time \( {t}_{\infty } \) or the curvature of the limiting solution becomes unbounded as \( t \searrow  {t}_{\infty } \) .

Let \( c > 0 \) be a positive constant much smaller than \( \frac{1}{100}{\eta }^{-1} \) . Note again that the infimum of the scalar curvature is nondecreasing in time. Then we can find some point \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and some time \( t = {t}_{\infty } + \theta \) with \( 0 < \theta  < \frac{c}{3} \) such that \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty } + \theta }\right)  \leq  2 \) .

Consider the (unrescaled) scalar curvature \( R \) of \( {g}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) at the point \( \bar{x} \) over the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . Since the scalar curvature \( {R}_{\infty } \) of the limit on \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{3},0}\right\rbrack \) is uniformly bounded by some positive constant \( C \) , we have the curvature estimate

\[
R\left( {\bar{x}, t}\right)  \leq  {2C}\bar{Q}
\]

for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) and all sufficiently large \( m \) . For each fixed \( m \) and \( {\alpha }_{m} \) , we may require the chosen \( {\beta }_{m} \) to satisfy

\[
{\left( {\bar{\delta }}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\right) }^{-2}{\left( \widetilde{r}\left( \frac{{t}_{0}^{{\alpha }_{m}}}{2}\right) \right) }^{-2} \geq  m\widetilde{r}{\left( {t}_{0}^{{\alpha }_{m}}\right) }^{-2} \geq  m\bar{Q}.
\]

When \( m \) is large enough, we observe again that Lemma 3.4.1 (ii) is applicable for \( {d}_{t}\left( {{x}_{0},\bar{x}}\right) \) with \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . Then by repeating the argument as in the derivation of (7.2.1),(7.2.2) and (7.2.3), we deduce that for all sufficiently large \( m \) , the canonical neighborhood statement holds for any \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{\theta }{2}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) . \)

Let \( \left( {{y}_{m},\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{m}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) be a sequence of associated points and times in the (unrescaled) solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) so that after rescaling, the sequence converges to \( \left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty } + \theta }\right) \) in the limit. Clearly \( \frac{\theta }{2} \leq  {\theta }_{m} \leq  {2\theta } \) for all sufficiently large \( m \) . Then by the argument as in the derivation of (7.5.13), we know that for all sufficiently large \( m \) , the solution \( {g}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) at \( {y}_{m} \) is defined on the whole time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{m} - }\right. }\right. \; \left. {\left. {\frac{1}{20}{\eta }^{-1}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + {\theta }_{m}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right\rbrack \) and satisfies the curvature estimate

\[
R\left( {{y}_{m}, t}\right)  \leq  8\bar{Q}
\]

there; moreover the canonical neighborhood statement holds for any \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) with \( R\left( {y, t}\right)  \geq  4\bar{Q} \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{y}_{m},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{3}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) .

We now consider the rescaled sequence \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) with the marked points replaced by \( {y}_{m} \) and the times replaced by \( {s}_{m} \in  \left\lbrack  {\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{4}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1},\bar{t} + \left( {{t}_{\infty } + \frac{c}{4}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right\rbrack \) . As before the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality implies the rescaling limit around \( \left( {{y}_{m},{s}_{m}}\right) \) agrees with the original one. Then the arguments in previous paragraphs imply the limit is well-defined and smooth on a space-time open neighborhood of the maximal time slice \( \left\{  {t = {t}_{\infty }}\right\} \) . Particularly this excludes the possibility of existing surgeries in finite distance around the time \( {t}_{\infty } \) . Moreover, the limit at \( t = {t}_{\infty } \) also has bounded curvature. By using the gradient estimates in the canonical neighborhood assumption on the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{y}_{m},\bar{t},\frac{1}{10}{K}_{1}^{\frac{1}{2}}{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{t}_{\infty } - \frac{c}{3}}\right) {\bar{Q}}^{-1}}\right) \) , we see that the second possibility is also impossible. Hence we have proved a subsequence of the rescaled solutions converges to an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution.

Therefore we have proved the canonical neighborhood statement (ii).

(iii) This is analogous to Theorem 7.2.1. We also argue by contradiction. Suppose for some \( A <  + \infty \) and sequences of positive numbers \( {K}_{2}^{\alpha } \rightarrow   + \infty ,{\bar{r}}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  0 \) there exists a sequence of times \( {t}_{0}^{\alpha } \) such that for any sequences \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } > 0 \) with \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \rightarrow  0 \) for fixed \( \alpha \) , we have sequences of solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) to the Ricci flow with surgery and sequences of points \( {x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \) , of positive constants \( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \) with \( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  {\bar{r}}^{\alpha }\sqrt{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }} \) which satisfy the assumptions, but for all \( \alpha ,\beta \) there hold

(7.5.16)

\[
R\left( {{x}^{\alpha \beta },{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\right)  > {K}_{2}^{\alpha }{\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2}\text{ , for some }{x}^{\alpha \beta } \in  {B}_{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\left( {{x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }, A{r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }}\right) .
\]

We may assume that \( {\bar{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  {\bar{\delta }}_{4A}\left( {t}_{0}^{\alpha }\right) \) for all \( \alpha ,\beta \) , where \( {\bar{\delta }}_{4A}\left( {t}_{0}^{\alpha }\right) \) is chosen so that the statements (i) and (ii) hold on \( {B}_{{t}_{0}^{\alpha }}\left( {{x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta },{4A}{r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }}\right) \) . Let \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) be the rescaled solutions of \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) around the origins \( {x}_{0}^{\alpha \beta } \) with factor \( {\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2} \) and shift the times \( {t}_{0}^{\alpha } \) to zero. Then by applying the statement (ii), we know that the regions, where the scalar curvature of the rescaled solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) is at least \( {K}_{1}\left( { = {K}_{1}\left( {4A}\right) }\right) \) , are canonical neighborhood regions. Note that canonical \( \varepsilon \) -neck neighborhoods are strong. Also note that the pinching assumption and the assertion

\[
{t}_{0}^{\alpha }{\left( {r}_{0}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{-2} \geq  {\left( {\bar{r}}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} \rightarrow   + \infty ,\text{ as }\alpha  \rightarrow   + \infty ,
\]

imply that any subsequent limit of the rescaled solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) must have nonnegative sectional curvature. Thus by the above argument in the proof of the statement (ii) (or the argument in Step 2 of the proof of Theorem 7.1.1), we conclude that there exist subsequences \( \alpha  = {\alpha }_{m},\beta  = {\beta }_{m} \) such that the curvatures of the rescaled solutions \( {\widehat{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) stay uniformly bounded at distances from the origins \( {x}_{0}^{{\alpha }_{m}{\beta }_{m}} \) not exceeding \( {2A} \) . This contradicts (7.5.16) for \( m \) sufficiently large. This proves the statements (iii).

Clearly for fixed \( A \) , after defining the \( {\bar{\delta }}_{A}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) for each \( {t}_{0} \) , one can adjust the \( {\bar{\delta }}_{A}\left( {t}_{0}\right) \) so that it is nonincreasing in \( {t}_{0} \) .

Therefore we have completed the proof of the theorem.

From now on we redefine the function \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) \) so that it is also less than \( {\bar{\delta }}_{2\left( {t + 1}\right) }\left( {2t}\right) \) and then the above theorem always holds for \( A \in  \left\lbrack  {1,2\left( {{t}_{0} + 1}\right) }\right\rbrack \) . Particularly, we still

have

\[
\widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right)  \leq  \bar{\delta }\left( t\right)  = \min \left\{  {\frac{1}{2{e}^{2}\log \left( {1 + t}\right) },{\delta }_{0}}\right\}  ,
\]

which tends to zero as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) . We may also require that \( \widetilde{r}\left( t\right) \) tends to zero as \( t \rightarrow   + \infty \) .

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose we have a solution to the Ricci Flow on a compact three- manifold, and suppose \( R \) becomes unbounded in some finite time \( T \) . Then there exists a sequence of dilations of the solution which converges to \( {S}^{3} \) or \( {S}^{2} \times  {R}^{1} \) or \( {\sum }^{2} \times  {R}^{1} \) (where \( {\sum }^{2} \) is the "cigar" soliton) or to a quotient of one of these solutions by a finite group of isometries acting freely (these quotients are the space forms \( {S}^{3}/\gamma , R{P}^{2} \times  {R}^{1} \) , and \( R{P}^{2} \times  {R}^{1} \) and \( {S}^{2} \times  {S}_{r}^{1}, R{P}^{2} \times  {S}_{r}^{1} \) and \( {\sum }^{2} \times  {S}_{r}^{1} \) for circles \( {S}_{r}^{1} \) of any radius \( r \) ), except possibly for the case of a Type I singularity where the injectivity radius times the square root of the maximum curvature goes to zero.

Proof. When we get an injectivity radius estimate valid for finite time we can always for a singularity model of Type I or II. First consider Type I. If the sectional curvature ever becomes positive everywhere, it becomes round and our limit is \( {S}^{3} \) or \( {S}^{3}/\gamma \) . Otherwise in Type I we get a limit which is an ancient solution with bounded non-negative sectional curvature which splits as a product of a surface with \( {R}^{1} \) . For the surface, if \( \left( {T - t}\right) R \leq  C \) it must be a round sphere or projective plane by Theorem 26.1. Otherwise we can take a backwards limit as \( t \rightarrow   - \infty \) to get a Type II limit, which must be the cigar \( {\sum }^{2} \) . Since a limit of a limit is also a limit, we get \( {\sum }^{2} \times  {R}^{1} \) or \( {\sum }^{2} \times  {S}^{1} \) as a limit of the three-manifold solution.

In order to take this backward limit we need an injectivity radius estimate on the surface in terms of the maximum curvature \( R \) at the current time. Since \( R > 0 \) this is easy. There are three cases. If the surface is compact and oriented, it is \( {S}^{2} \) and the result follows from a theorem for positive sectional curvature in even dimensions of Klingenberg ([9], 5.9). If it is compact but not oriented, it is \( R{P}^{2} \) and the double cover can be handled as before. If it is not compact, it is diffeomorphic to \( {R}^{2} \) and we can use the estimate for complete noncompact manifolds of positive sectional curvature.

If the limit is Type II, it must be a Ricci soliton of weakly positive sectional curvature from our pinching result in Theorem 24.4. If the sectional curvature is not strictly positive, it splits as a product of a surface soliton, which must be \( {\sum }^{2} \) , with a flat factor \( {R}^{2} \) or \( {S}^{1} \) (of any radius). Even if it does not split, we know the asymptotic curvature ratio is infinite

\[
A = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{s \rightarrow  \infty }}R{s}^{2} = \infty
\]

by Theorem 20.2, and by Theorem 22.3 since the dimension \( n = 3 \) is odd, we can do dimension reduction to find a limit of a limit which splits as a product with \( {R}^{1} \) of an ancient solution with bounded positive curvature on a surface. Again a limit of a limit is a limit, and we can classify the surface as a round \( {S}^{2} \) (not \( R{P}^{2} \) because it is oriented) or \( {\sum }^{2} \) . This finishes the proof of the Theorem.
