Type I: We consider a maximal solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) \) on \( M \times  \lbrack 0, T) \) with \( T <  + \infty \) and

\[
\Omega \overset{\Delta }{ = }\mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  T}}\left( {T - t}\right) {K}_{\max }\left( t\right)  <  + \infty .
\]

First we note that \( \Omega  > 0 \) . Indeed by the evolution equation of curvature,

\[
\frac{d}{dt}{K}_{\max }\left( t\right)  \leq  \text{ Const } \cdot  {K}_{\max }^{2}\left( t\right) .
\]

This implies that

\[
{K}_{\max }\left( t\right)  \cdot  \left( {T - t}\right)  \geq  \text{ Const } > 0,
\]

because

\[
\mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  T}}{K}_{\max }\left( t\right)  =  + \infty .
\]

Thus \( \Omega \) must be positive.

Choose a sequence of points \( {x}_{k} \) and times \( {t}_{k} \) such that \( {t}_{k} \rightarrow  T \) and

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}\left( {T - {t}_{k}}\right) \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }\right|  = \Omega .
\]

Denote by

\[
{\epsilon }_{k} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\left| \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x}_{k},{t}_{k}\right) \right| }}.
\]

We translate in time so that \( {t}_{k} \) becomes 0, dilate in space by the factor \( {\epsilon }_{k} \) and dilate in time by \( {\epsilon }_{k}^{2} \) to get

\[
{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\left( k\right) }\left( {\cdot ,\widetilde{t}}\right)  = {\epsilon }_{k}^{-2}{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{k} + {\epsilon }_{k}^{2}\widetilde{t}}\right) ,\;\widetilde{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{k}/{\epsilon }_{k}^{2},\left( {T - {t}_{k}}\right) /{\epsilon }_{k}^{2}}\right) .
\]

Then

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial \widetilde{t}}{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\left( k\right) }\left( {\cdot ,\widetilde{t}}\right)  = {\epsilon }_{k}^{-2}\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot , t}\right)  \cdot  {\epsilon }_{k}^{2}
\]

\[
=  - 2{R}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{k} + {\epsilon }_{k}^{2}\widetilde{t}}\right)
\]

\[
=  - 2{\widetilde{R}}_{ij}^{\left( k\right) }\left( {\cdot ,\widetilde{t}}\right) ,
\]

where \( {\widetilde{R}}_{ij}^{\left( k\right) } \) is the Ricci curvature of the metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\left( k\right) } \) . So \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\left( k\right) }\left( {\cdot ,\widetilde{t}}\right) \) is still a solution to the Ricci flow which exists on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{k}/{\epsilon }_{k}^{2},\left( {T - {t}_{k}}\right) /{\epsilon }_{k}^{2}}\right) \) , where

\[
{t}_{k}/{\epsilon }_{k}^{2} = {t}_{k}\left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }\right|  \rightarrow   + \infty
\]

and

\[
\left( {T - {t}_{k}}\right) /{\epsilon }_{k}^{2} = \left( {T - {t}_{k}}\right) \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }\right|  \rightarrow  \Omega .
\]

For any \( \epsilon  > 0 \) we can find a time \( \tau  < T \) such that for \( t \in  \lbrack \tau , T) \) ,

\[
\left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  \left( {\Omega  + \epsilon }\right) /\left( {T - t}\right)
\]

by the assumption. Then for \( \widetilde{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {\tau  - {t}_{k}}\right) /{\epsilon }_{k}^{2},\left( {T - {t}_{k}}\right) /{\epsilon }_{k}^{2}}\right) \) , the curvature of \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\left( k\right) }\left( {\cdot ,\widetilde{t}}\right) \) is bounded by

\[
\left| {\widetilde{R}{m}^{\left( k\right) }}\right|  = {\epsilon }_{k}^{2}\left| {Rm}\right|
\]

\[
\leq  \left( {\Omega  + \epsilon }\right) /\left( {\left( {T - t}\right) \left| {{Rm}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }\right| }\right)
\]

\[
= \left( {\Omega  + \epsilon }\right) /\left( {\left( {T - {t}_{k}}\right) \left| {{Rm}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }\right|  + \left( {{t}_{k} - t}\right) \left| {{Rm}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }\right| }\right)
\]

\[
\rightarrow  \left( {\Omega  + \epsilon }\right) /\left( {\Omega  - \widetilde{t}}\right) ,\;\text{ as }k \rightarrow   + \infty .
\]

This implies that \( \left\{  \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \right\} \) is a sequence of (almost) maximum points. And then by the injectivity radius condition and Hamilton's compactness theorem 4.1.5, there exists a subsequence of the metrics \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\left( k\right) }\left( \widetilde{t}\right) \) which converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a limit metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\left( \infty \right) }\left( \widetilde{t}\right) \) on a limiting manifold \( \widetilde{M} \) with \( \widetilde{t} \in  \left( {-\infty ,\Omega }\right) \) such that \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\left( \infty \right) }\left( \widetilde{t}\right) \) is a complete solution of the Ricci flow and its curvature satisfies the bound

\[
\left| {\widetilde{R}{m}^{\left( \infty \right) }}\right|  \leq  \Omega /\left( {\Omega  - \widetilde{t}}\right)
\]

everywhere on \( \widetilde{M} \times  \left( {-\infty ,\Omega }\right) \) with the equality somewhere at \( \widetilde{t} = 0 \) .

Type II(a): We consider a maximal solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) \) on \( M \times  \lbrack 0, T) \) with

\[
T <  + \infty \text{ and }\;\mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  T}}\left( {T - t}\right) {K}_{\max }\left( t\right)  =  + \infty .
\]

Let \( {T}_{k} < T <  + \infty \) with \( {T}_{k} \rightarrow  T \) , and \( {\gamma }_{k} \nearrow  1 \) , as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) . Pick points \( {x}_{k} \) and times \( {t}_{k} \) such that, as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) ,

\[
\left( {{T}_{k} - {t}_{k}}\right) \left| {{Rm}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }\right|  \geq  {\gamma }_{k}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  M, t \leq  {T}_{k}}}\left( {{T}_{k} - t}\right) \left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \rightarrow   + \infty .
\]

\[
{\epsilon }_{k} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{\left| \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x}_{k},{t}_{k}\right) \right| }}
\]

and dilate the solution as before to get

\[
{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\left( k\right) }\left( {\cdot ,\widetilde{t}}\right)  = {\epsilon }_{k}^{-2}{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{k} + {\epsilon }_{k}^{2}\widetilde{t}}\right) ,\;\widetilde{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{k}/{\epsilon }_{k}^{2},\left( {{T}_{k} - {t}_{k}}\right) /{\epsilon }_{k}^{2}}\right) ,
\]

\[

\]

\[
\left| {\widetilde{R}{m}^{\left( \infty \right) }}\right|  \leq  1
\]

everywhere on \( \widetilde{M} \times  \left( {-\infty , + \infty }\right) \) and the equality holds somewhere at \( \widetilde{t} = 0 \) .

Type II(b): We consider a maximal solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) \) on \( M \times  \lbrack 0, T) \) with

\[

\]

\]

where \( {\epsilon }_{k} = 1/\sqrt{\left| \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x}_{k},{t}_{k}\right) \right| } \) .

\[
{t}_{k}\left( {{T}_{k} - {t}_{k}}\right) \left| {{Rm}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }\right|  \geq  {\gamma }_{k}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  M, t \leq  {T}_{k}}}t\left( {{T}_{k} - t}\right) \left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|
\]

\[
\geq  {\gamma }_{k}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  M, t \leq  {T}_{k}/2}}t\left( {{T}_{k} - t}\right) \left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|
\]

\[
\geq  \frac{{T}_{k}}{2}{\gamma }_{k}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  M, t \leq  {T}_{k}/2}}t\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|
\]

we have

\[
\frac{{t}_{k}}{{\epsilon }_{k}^{2}} = {t}_{k}\left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }\right|  \geq  \frac{{\gamma }_{k}}{2}\left( \frac{{T}_{k}}{{T}_{k} - {t}_{k}}\right) \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  M, t \leq  {T}_{k}/2}}t\left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \rightarrow   + \infty ,
\]

\[
\frac{\left( {T}_{k} - {t}_{k}\right) }{{\epsilon }_{k}^{2}} = \left( {{T}_{k} - {t}_{k}}\right) \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }\right|  \geq  \frac{{\gamma }_{k}}{2}\left( \frac{{T}_{k}}{{t}_{k}}\right) \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  M, t \leq  {T}_{k}/2}}t\left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \rightarrow   + \infty ,
\]

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial \widetilde{t}}{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\left( k\right) }\left( {\cdot ,\widetilde{t}}\right)  =  - 2{\widetilde{R}}_{ij}^{\left( k\right) }\left( {\cdot ,\widetilde{t}}\right)
\]

\[

\[
= {\epsilon }_{k}^{2}\left| {Rm}\right|

\[

\[

\]

\[
= \frac{{t}_{k}\left( {{T}_{k} - {t}_{k}}\right) \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }\right| }{{\gamma }_{k}\left( {1 + \widetilde{t}/\left( {{t}_{k}\left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }\right| }\right) }\right) \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k}\left( {{T}_{k} - {t}_{k}}\right) \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }\right| \rbrack \left( {1 - \widetilde{t}/\left( {\left( {{T}_{k} - {t}_{k}}\right) \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }\right| }\right) }\right) }\right\rbrack  }
\]

\[

\]

Hence \( \left\{  \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \right\} \) is again a sequence of (almost) maximum points. \[
\left| {\widetilde{R}{m}^{\left( \infty \right) }}\right|  \leq  1
\]

everywhere on \( \widetilde{M} \times  \left( {-\infty , + \infty }\right) \) with the equality somewhere at \( \widetilde{t} = 0 \) .

Type III(a): We consider a maximal solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) \) on \( M \times  \lbrack 0, T) \) with \( T =  + \infty \) and

\[
\mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  T}}t{K}_{\max }\left( t\right)  = A \in  \left( {0, + \infty }\right) .
\]

Choose a sequence of \( {x}_{k} \) and \( {t}_{k} \) such that \( {t}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) and

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}{t}_{k}\left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }\right|  = A.
\]

Set \( {\epsilon }_{k} = 1/\sqrt{\left| \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x}_{k},{t}_{k}\right) \right| } \) and dilate the solution as before to get

\[
{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\left( k\right) }\left( {\cdot ,\widetilde{t}}\right)  = {\epsilon }_{k}^{-2}{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{k} + {\epsilon }_{k}^{2}\widetilde{t}}\right) ,\;\widetilde{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{k}/{\epsilon }_{k}^{2}, + \infty }\right)
\]

which is still a solution to the Ricci flow. Also, for arbitrarily fixed \( \epsilon  > 0 \) , there exists a sufficiently large positive constant \( \tau \) such that for \( t \in  \lbrack \tau , + \infty ) \) ,

\[
\left| {\widetilde{R}{m}^{\left( k\right) }}\right|  = {\epsilon }_{k}^{2}\left| {Rm}\right|
\]

\[
\leq  {\epsilon }_{k}^{2}\left( \frac{A + \epsilon }{t}\right)
\]

\[
= {\epsilon }_{k}^{2}\left( \frac{A + \epsilon }{{t}_{k} + {\epsilon }_{k}^{2}\widetilde{t}}\right)
\]

\[
= \left( {A + \epsilon }\right) /\left( {{t}_{k}\left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }\right|  + \widetilde{t}}\right) ,\;\text{ for }\widetilde{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {\tau  - {t}_{k}}\right) /{\epsilon }_{k}^{2}, + \infty }\right) .
\]

\[
\left( {A + \epsilon }\right) /\left( {{t}_{k}\left| {{Rm}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }\right|  + \widetilde{t}}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {A + \epsilon }\right) /\left( {A + \widetilde{t}}\right) ,\;\text{ as }k \rightarrow   + \infty
\]

and

\[
\left( {\tau  - {t}_{k}}\right) /{\epsilon }_{k}^{2} \rightarrow   - A,\;\text{ as }k \rightarrow   + \infty .
\]

Hence \( \left\{  \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \right\} \) is a sequence of (almost) maximum points. And then as before, there exists a subsequence of the metrics \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\left( k\right) }\left( \widetilde{t}\right) \) which converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a limit \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\left( \infty \right) }\left( \widetilde{t}\right) \) on a limiting manifold \( \widetilde{M} \) and \( \widetilde{t} \in  \left( {-A, + \infty }\right) \) such that \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\left( \infty \right) }\left( \widetilde{t}\right) \) is a complete solution of the Ricci flow and its curvature satisfies

\[
\left| {\widetilde{R}{m}^{\left( \infty \right) }}\right|  \leq  A/\left( {A + \widetilde{t}}\right)
\]

everywhere on \( \widetilde{M} \times  \left( {-A, + \infty }\right) \) with the equality somewhere at \( \widetilde{t} = 0 \) . C

\lim \left( {T - {t}_{j}}\right) R\left( {{P}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  = \Omega .
\]

For each of these solutions, let \( {P}_{j} \) be the origin 0, translate in time so that \( {t}_{j} \) becomes 0, dilate in space by a factor \( \lambda \) so that \( R\left( {{P}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) becomes 1 at the origin at \( t = 0 \) , and dilate in time by \( {\lambda }^{2} \) so it is still a solution to the Ricci Flow. The dilated solutions exist on a time interval

\[
- {A}_{j} \leq  t < {\Omega }_{j}
\]

where

\[
{\Omega }_{j} = \left( {T - {t}_{j}}\right) M\left( {t}_{j}\right)  \rightarrow  \Omega
\]

and

\[
{A}_{j} = {t}_{j}{\Omega }_{j}/\left( {T - {t}_{j}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty .
\]

Moreover, they satisfy curvature bounds. For any \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) we can find a time \( \tau  < T \) such that for \( \tau  \leq  t < T \) we have

\[
\left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  \left( {\Omega  + \varepsilon }\right) /\left( {T - t}\right)
\]

by assumption, before dilation. After dilation this becomes a curvature bound

\[
\left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  \left( {\Omega  + \varepsilon }\right) /\left( {{\Omega }_{j} - t}\right)
\]

for times \( - {\theta }_{j} \leq  t < {\Omega }_{j} \) where

\[
{\theta }_{j} = \left( {{t}_{j} - \tau }\right) {\Omega }_{j}/\left( {T - {t}_{j}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty .
\]

Consequently the limit exists on the time interval \( - \infty  < t < \Omega \) and satisfies

\[
\left| {Rm}\right|  \leq  \Omega /\left( {\Omega  - t}\right)
\]

everywhere, while \( \left| {{Rm}\left( {0,0}\right) }\right|  = 1 \) .

For Type II(a), we have to be a little more subtle. We start by picking a sequence \( {T}_{j} < T < \infty \) with \( {T}_{j} \rightarrow  T \) . If the manifold is compact we can pick points \( {P}_{j} \) and \( {t}_{j} \) where

\[
\left( {{T}_{j} - {t}_{j}}\right) \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{P}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) }\right|  = \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{P, t < {T}_{j}}}\left( {{T}_{j} - t}\right) \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {P, t}\right) }\right|
\]

as the latter goes to zero as \( t \nearrow  {T}_{j} \) . If the manifold is not compact, we can take \( {\gamma }_{j} \nearrow  1 \) and find \( {P}_{j} \) and \( {t}_{j} \) so that at least

\[
\left( {{T}_{j} - {t}_{j}}\right) \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{P}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) }\right|  \geq  {\gamma }_{j}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{P, t \leq  {T}_{j}}}\left( {{T}_{j} - t}\right) \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {P, t}\right) }\right|
\]

Now pick \( {P}_{j} \) to be the origin \( {O}_{j} \) , translate in time so \( {t}_{j} \) becomes zero, dilate in space by a factor \( \lambda \) so \( R\left( {{P}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) becomes 1 at the origin at \( t = 0 \) , and dilate time by \( {\lambda }^{2} \) so that we still have a solution to the Ricci Flow. The dilated solution exists for \( {A}_{j} \leq  t < {\Omega }_{j} \) where

\[
{\Omega }_{j} = \left( {{T}_{j} - {t}_{j}}\right) \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{P}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) }\right|  \rightarrow  \infty
\]

and

\[
{A}_{j} = \frac{{t}_{j}}{{T}_{j} - {t}_{j}}{\Omega }_{j} = {t}_{j}\left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{P}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) }\right|  \rightarrow  \infty
\]

also. To see \( {\Omega }_{j} \rightarrow  \infty \) for Type II(a) where \( T < \infty \) , note that \( {T}_{j} \nearrow  T,{P}_{j} \) and \( {t}_{j} \) are chosen maximally and

\[
\lim \sup \left( {T - t}\right) \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {P, t}\right) }\right|  = \infty \text{ . }
\]

To see \( {A}_{j} \rightarrow  \infty \) for Type II(a), use the fact that \( {\Omega }_{j} \rightarrow  \infty \) forces \( {t}_{j} \rightarrow  T \) and \( \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{P}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) }\right|  \rightarrow  \infty \) . We also get a bound on curvature. We have for \( 0 \leq  t \leq  {T}_{j} \)

\[
\left( {{T}_{j} - t}\right) \left| {{Rm}\left( {P, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {\Gamma }_{j}\left( {{T}_{j} - {t}_{j}}\right) \left| {{Rm}\left( {{P}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) }\right|
\]

where \( {\Gamma }_{j} = 1/{\gamma }_{j} \rightarrow  1 \) also, before dilation. After dilation this becomes for \( - {A}_{j} \leq  t \leq  {\Omega }_{j} \)

\[
\left( {{\Omega }_{j} - t}\right) \left| {{Rm}\left( {P, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {\Gamma }_{j}{\Omega }_{j}.
\]

Write this as

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {P, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {\Gamma }_{j}{\Omega }_{j}/\left( {{\Omega }_{j} - t}\right) .
\]

As \( j \rightarrow  \infty ,{\Gamma }_{j} \rightarrow  1 \) and \( {\Omega }_{j}/\left( {{\Omega }_{j} - t}\right)  \rightarrow  1 \) for any fixed \( t \) . Hence the limit exists and satisfies

\[
\left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {P, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  1
\]

everywhere for \( - \infty  < t <  + \infty \) , while \( \left| {{Rm}\left( {0,0}\right) }\right|  = 1 \) .

For type II(b), we again choose a sequence \( {T}_{j} \nearrow  T = \infty \) , but now we pick \( {P}_{j} \) and \( {t}_{j} \) so that

\[
{t}_{j}\left( {{T}_{j} - {t}_{j}}\right) \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{P}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) }\right|  \geq  {\gamma }_{j}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{P, t \leq  {T}_{j}}}t\left( {{T}_{j} - t}\right) \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {P, t}\right) }\right|
\]

where again \( {\gamma }_{j} \nearrow  1 \) . Pick \( {P}_{j} \) to be the origin \( {O}_{j} \) , translate in time so \( {t}_{j} \) becomes zero, dilate in space by a factor \( \lambda \) so that \( R\left( {{P}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) becomes 1 at the origin at \( t = 0 \) , and dilate time by \( {\lambda }^{2} \) so it is still a solution of the Ricci Flow. Suppose \( {T}_{j} \) dilates to \( {\Omega }_{j} \) and 0 dilates to \( - {A}_{j} \) . The solution now exists after dilation on a time interval \( - {A}_{j} < t < {\Omega }_{j} \) where by dilation invariance

\[
\frac{{A}_{j}{\Omega }_{j}}{{A}_{j} + {\Omega }_{j}} = \frac{{t}_{j}\left( {{T}_{j} - {t}_{j}}\right) }{{T}_{j}}\left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{P}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) }\right|  \rightarrow  \infty
\]

since by assumption

\[
\lim \sup t\left| {{Rm}\left( {P, t}\right) }\right|  = \infty \text{ . }
\]

This forces \( {A}_{j} \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( {\Omega }_{j} \rightarrow  \infty \) as well since

\[
\frac{xy}{x + y} = \frac{1}{1/x + 1/y}
\]

Before dilation we have an estimate for \( 0 \leq  t \leq  {T}_{j} \)

\[
t\left( {{T}_{j} - t}\right) \left| {{Rm}\left( {P, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {\Gamma }_{j}{t}_{j}\left( {{T}_{j} - {t}_{j}}\right) \left| {{Rm}\left( {{P}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) }\right|
\]

where again \( {\Gamma }_{j} = 1/{\gamma }_{j} \rightarrow  1 \) . After dilation this becomes for \( - {A}_{j} \leq  t \leq  {\Omega }_{j} \)

\[
\left( {t + {A}_{j}}\right) \left( {{\Omega }_{j} - t}\right) \left| {{Rm}\left( {P, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {\Gamma }_{j}{A}_{j}{\Omega }_{j}.
\]

Write this as

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {P, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  \frac{{\Gamma }_{j}{A}_{j}{\Omega }_{j}}{\left( {t + {A}_{j}}\right) \left( {{\Omega }_{j} - t}\right) }.
\]

As \( j \rightarrow  \infty ,{\Gamma }_{j} \rightarrow  1 \) and \( {A}_{j}{\Omega }_{j}/\left( {t + {A}_{j}}\right) \left( {{\Omega }_{j} - t}\right)  \rightarrow  1 \) also for any fixed \( t \) . Hence the limit exists and satisfies

\[
\left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {P, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  1
\]

everywhere for \( - \infty  < t < \infty \) while \( \left| {{Rm}\left( {0,0}\right) }\right|  = 1 \) .

Finally we come to Type III, where \( T = \infty \) and

\[
A = \lim \sup {tM}\left( t\right)  < \infty \text{ . }
\]

First we claim \( A > 0 \) . Indeed if \( t\left| {{Rm}\left( {P, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  \varepsilon \) for large \( t \) then the diameter \( L \) satisfies an estimate

\[
\frac{dL}{dt} \leq  {C\varepsilon L}
\]

for a constant \( C \) independent of \( \varepsilon \) and \( L \) . This makes \( L \) grow at most like \( {t}^{C\varepsilon } \) while \( \left| {Rm}\right| \) falls off at least like \( 1/t \) . If \( {C\varepsilon } < 1/2 \) we see that \( {L}^{2}M \rightarrow  0 \) , which means that after rescaling the curvature collapses with bounded diameter. By a well-known result of Gromov the manifold is nilpotent; more to the point the injectivity radius bound we assumed would fail. Thus \( A > 0 \) .

Now pick a sequence of points \( {P}_{j} \) and times \( {t}_{j} \) so that \( {t}_{j} \rightarrow  \infty \) and

\[
\lim {t}_{j}\left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{P}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) }\right|  = A.
\]

Choose \( {P}_{j} \) to be the origin \( {O}_{j} \) , translate in time so \( {t}_{j} \) becomes \( {O}_{j} \) , dilate in space by a factor \( \lambda \) so that \( \left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{P}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) }\right| \) becomes 1 at the origin at time \( t = 0 \) , and dilate in time by a factor \( {\lambda }^{2} \) so we still have a solution of the Ricci Flow. After dilation the solution will exist for times \( - {A}_{j} \leq  t < \infty \) where time 0 dilates to

\[
{A}_{j} = {t}_{j}\left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {{P}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) }\right|  \rightarrow  A.
\]

Moreover for any \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) we can find a time \( \tau  < \infty \) such that for \( t \geq  \tau \)

\[
t\left| {\operatorname{Rm}\left( {P, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  A + \varepsilon
\]

by hypothesis, before dilation. After dilation this becomes a bound

\[
\left( {t + A}\right) \left| {{Rm}\left( {P, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  A + \varepsilon
\]

for time \( t \geq   - {\theta }_{j} \) where

\[
{\theta }_{j} = \left( {{t}_{j} - \tau }\right) {A}_{j}/{t}_{j} \rightarrow  A
\]

since \( {t}_{j} \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( {A}_{j} \rightarrow  A > 0 \) while \( \tau \) is fixed. Hence we get a limit which satisfies

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {P, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  A/\left( {t + A}\right)
\]

on \( - A < t < \infty \) while \( \left| {{Rm}\left( {0,0}\right) }\right|  = 1 \) . This completes the proof of the Theorem.

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vanishing Asymptotic Volume Ratio for Nonflat Ancient Solutions
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \( M \) be an \( n \) -dimensional complete noncompact Riemannian manifold. Suppose \( {g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) , x \in  M \) and \( t \in  \left( {-\infty , T}\right) \) with \( T > 0 \) , is a nonflat ancient solution of the Ricci flow with nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature. Then the asymptotic volume ratio of the solution metric satisfies

\[
{\nu }_{M}\left( t\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{r \rightarrow   + \infty }}\frac{{\operatorname{Vol}}_{t}\left( {{B}_{t}\left( {O, r}\right) }\right) }{{r}^{n}} = 0
\]

for each \( t \in  \left( {-\infty , T}\right) \) .

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
The proof is by induction on the dimension. When the dimension is two, the lemma is valid by Theorem 6.2.2. For dimension \( \geq  3 \) , we argue by contradiction.

Suppose the lemma is valid for dimensions \( \leq  n - 1 \) and suppose \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) for some \( n \) -dimensional nonflat ancient solution with nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature at some time \( {t}_{0} \leq  0 \) . Fixing a point \( {x}_{0} \in  M \) , we consider the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio

\[
A = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty }}R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right) .
\]

We divide the proof into three cases.

Case 1: \( A =  + \infty \) .

By Lemma 6.1.3, there exist sequences of points \( {x}_{k} \in  M \) divergent to infinity, of radii \( {r}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) , and of positive constants \( {\delta }_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) such that

(i) \( R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{k}}\right) R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) \) for all \( x \) in the ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) \) of radius \( {r}_{k} \) around \( {x}_{k} \) ,

(ii) \( {r}_{k}^{2}R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) ,

(iii) \( {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right) /{r}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) .

By scaling the solution around the points \( {x}_{k} \) with factor \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) \) , and shifting the time \( {t}_{0} \) to the new time zero, we get a sequence of rescaled solutions

\[
{g}_{k}\left( s\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0} + \frac{s}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right)
\]

to the Ricci flow. Since the ancient solution has nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature, there holds the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality (Corollary 2.5.5). Thus the rescaled solutions satisfy

\[
{R}_{k}\left( {x, s}\right)  \leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{k}}\right)
\]

for all \( s \leq  0 \) and \( x \in  {B}_{{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{k}\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) \) . Since \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) , it follows from the standard volume comparison and Theorem 4.2.2 that the injectivity radii of the rescaled solutions \( {g}_{k} \) at the points \( {x}_{k} \) and the new time zero is uniformly bounded below by a positive number. Then by Hamilton's compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), after passing to a subsequence, \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( s\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) will converge to a solution \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( s\right) , O}\right) \) to the Ricci flow with

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {y, s}\right)  \leq  1\text{ , for all }s \leq  0\text{ and }y \in  \widetilde{M}\text{ , }
\]

and

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {O,0}\right)  = 1\text{ . }
\]

Since the metric is shrinking, by (ii) and (iii), we get

\[
R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0} + \frac{s}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) }^{2}\left( {{x}_{0},{x}_{k}}\right)  \geq  R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }^{2}\left( {{x}_{0},{x}_{k}}\right)
\]

which tends to \( + \infty \) , as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) , for all \( s \leq  0 \) . Thus by Proposition 6.1.2, for each \( s \leq  0,\left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( s\right) }\right) \) splits off a line. We now consider the lifting of the solution \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( s\right) }\right) , s \leq  0 \) , to its universal cover and denote it by \( \left( {\widetilde{\widetilde{M}},\widetilde{\widetilde{g}}\left( s\right) }\right) , s \leq  0 \) . Clearly we still have

\[
{\nu }_{\widetilde{M}}\left( 0\right)  > 0\text{ and }{\nu }_{\widetilde{\widetilde{M}}}\left( 0\right)  > 0\text{ . }
\]

By applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle and the de Rham decomposition theorem, the universal cover \( \widetilde{\widetilde{M}} \) splits isometrically as \( X \times  \mathbb{R} \) for some \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) - dimensional nonflat (complete) ancient solution \( X \) with nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature. These imply that \( {\nu }_{X}\left( 0\right)  > 0 \) , which contradicts the induction hypothesis.

Case 2: \( 0 < A <  + \infty \) .

Take a sequence of points \( {x}_{k} \) divergent to infinity such that

\[
R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow  A,\text{ as }k \rightarrow   + \infty .
\]

Consider the rescaled solutions \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( s\right) }\right) \) (around the fixed point \( {x}_{0} \) ), where

\[
{g}_{k}\left( s\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0} + \frac{s}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) , s \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack .
\]

Then there is a constant \( C > 0 \) such that

(6.3.1)

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} {R}_{k}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  C/{d}_{k}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0},0}\right) , \\  {R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},0}\right)  = 1, \\  {d}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0},0}\right)  \rightarrow  \sqrt{A} > 0, \end{array}\right.
\]

where \( {d}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,{x}_{0},0}\right) \) is the distance function from the point \( {x}_{0} \) in the metric \( {g}_{k}\left( 0\right) \) .

Since \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) , it is a basic result in Alexandrov space theory (see for example Theorem 7.6 of [20]) that a subsequence of \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( s\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) converges in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense to an \( n \) -dimensional metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) with vertex \( {x}_{0} \) .

By (6.3.1), the standard volume comparison and Theorem 4.2.2, we know that the injectivity radius of \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) at \( {x}_{k} \) is uniformly bounded from below by a positive number \( {\rho }_{0} \) . After taking a subsequence, we may assume \( {x}_{k} \) converges to a point \( {x}_{\infty } \) in \( M \smallsetminus  \left\{  {x}_{0}\right\} \) . Then by Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), we can take a subsequence such that the metrics \( {g}_{k}\left( s\right) \) on the metric balls \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k},\frac{1}{2}{\rho }_{0}}\right) \left( { \subset  M}\right. \) with respect to the metric \( {g}_{k}\left( 0\right) ) \) converge in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a solution of the Ricci flow on a ball \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{\infty },\frac{1}{2}{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) . Clearly the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) limit has nonnegative curvature operator and it is a piece of the metric cone at the time \( s = 0 \) . By (6.3.1), we have

(6.3.2)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right)  = 1
\]

Let \( x \) be any point in the limiting ball \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{\infty },\frac{1}{2}{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) and \( {e}_{1} \) be any radial direction at \( x \) . Clearly \( \widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{1}}\right)  = 0 \) . Recall that the evolution equation of the Ricci tensor in frame coordinates is

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\widetilde{R}}_{ab} = \widetilde{\bigtriangleup }{\widetilde{R}}_{ab} + 2{\widetilde{R}}_{acbd}{\widetilde{R}}_{cd}.
\]

Since the curvature operator is nonnegative, by applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle (Theorem 2.2.1) to the above equation, we deduce that the null space of Ric is invariant under parallel translation. In particular, all radial directions split off locally and isometrically. While by (6.3.2), the piece of the metric cone is nonflat. This gives a contradiction.

Case 3: \( A = 0 \) .

The gap theorem as was initiated by Mok-Siu-Yau [93] and established by Greene-Wu [49, 50], Eschenberg-Shrader-Strake [45], and Drees [44] shows that a complete noncompact \( n \) -dimensional (except \( n = 4 \) or 8) Riemannian manifold with nonnegative sectional curvature and the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio \( A = 0 \) must be flat. So the present case is ruled out except in dimension \( n = 4 \) or 8 . Since in our situation the asymptotic volume ratio is positive and the manifold is the solution of the Ricci flow, we can give an alternative proof for all dimensions as follows.

We claim the sectional curvature of \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is positive everywhere. Indeed, by Theorem 2.2.2, the image of the curvature operator is just the restricted holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) of the manifold. If the sectional curvature vanishes for some two-plane, then the holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) cannot be \( {so}\left( n\right) \) . We observe the manifold is not Einstein since it is noncompact, nonflat and has nonnegative curvature operator. If \( \mathcal{G} \) is irreducible, then by Berger’s Theorem [7], \( \mathcal{G} = u\left( \frac{n}{2}\right) \) . Thus the manifold is Kähler with bounded and nonnegative bisectional curvature and with curvature decay faster than quadratic. Then by the gap theorem obtained by Chen and the second author in [31], this Kähler manifold must be flat. This contradicts the assumption. Hence the holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) is reducible and the universal cover of \( M \) splits isometrically as \( {\widetilde{M}}_{1} \times  {\widetilde{M}}_{2} \) nontrivially. Clearly the universal cover of \( M \) has positive asymptotic volume ratio. So \( {\widetilde{M}}_{1} \) and \( {\widetilde{M}}_{2} \) still have positive asymptotic volume ratio and at least one of them is nonflat. By the induction hypothesis, this is also impossible. Thus our claim is proved.

Now we know that the sectional curvature of \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is positive everywhere. Choose a sequence of points \( {x}_{k} \) divergent to infinity such that

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  = \sup \left\{  {R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \mid  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right) }\right\}  , \\  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq  k, \\  R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  = {\varepsilon }_{k} \rightarrow  0. \end{array}\right.
\]

Consider the rescaled metric

\[
{g}_{k}\left( 0\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right)
\]

as before. Then

(6.3.3)

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} {R}_{k}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  {\varepsilon }_{k}/{d}_{k}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0},0}\right) ,\;\text{ for }{d}_{k}\left( {x,{x}_{0},0}\right)  \geq  \sqrt{{\varepsilon }_{k}}, \\  {d}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0},0}\right)  = \sqrt{{\varepsilon }_{k}} \rightarrow  0. \end{array}\right.
\]

As in Case 2, the rescaled marked solutions \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) will converge in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense to a metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) . And by the virtue of Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), up to a subsequence, the convergence is in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology in \( \widetilde{M} \smallsetminus  \left\{  {x}_{0}\right\} \) . We next claim the metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) is isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) .

Indeed, let us write the metric cone \( \widetilde{M} \) as a warped product \( {\mathbb{R}}_{ + }{ \times  }_{r}{X}^{n - 1} \) for some \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional manifold \( {X}^{n - 1} \) . By (6.3.3), the metric cone must be flat and \( {X}^{n - 1} \) is isometric to a quotient of the round sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{n - 1} \) by fixed point free isometries in the standard metric. To show \( \widetilde{M} \) is isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) , we only need to verify that \( {X}^{n - 1} \) is simply connected.

Let \( \varphi \) be the Busemann function of \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) with respect to the point \( {x}_{0} \) . Since \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) has nonnegative sectional curvature, it is easy to see that for any small \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there is a \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) such that

\[
\left( {1 - \varepsilon }\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \varphi \left( x\right)  \leq  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  M \smallsetminus  {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) . The strict positivity of the sectional curvature of the manifold \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) implies that the square of the Busemann function is strictly convex (and exhausting). Thus every level set \( {\varphi }^{-1}\left( a\right) \) , with \( a > \inf \{ \varphi \left( x\right)  \mid  x \in  M\} \) , of the Busemann function \( \varphi \) is diffeomorphic to the \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{n - 1} \) . In particular, \( {\varphi }^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {a,\frac{3}{2}a}\right\rbrack  \right) \) is simply connected for \( a > \inf \{ \varphi \left( x\right)  \mid  x \in  M\} \) since \( n \geq  3 \) .

Consider an annulus portion \( \left\lbrack  {1,2}\right\rbrack   \times  {X}^{n - 1} \) of the metric cone \( \widetilde{M} = {\mathbb{R}}_{ + }{ \times  }_{r}{X}^{n - 1} \) . It is the limit of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) , where

\[
{M}_{k} = \left\{  {x \in  M\left| {\;\frac{1}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }} \leq  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{2}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right. }\right\}  .
\]

It is clear that

\[
{\varphi }^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }},\frac{2\left( {1 - \varepsilon }\right) }{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right\rbrack  \right)  \subset  {M}_{k} \subset  {\varphi }^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {\frac{1 - \varepsilon }{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }},\frac{2}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right\rbrack  \right)
\]

for \( k \) large enough. Thus any closed loop in \( \left\{  \frac{3}{2}\right\}   \times  {X}^{n - 1} \) can be shrunk to a point by a homotopy in \( \left\lbrack  {1,2}\right\rbrack   \times  {X}^{n - 1} \) . This shows that \( {X}^{n - 1} \) is simply connected. Hence we have proven that the metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) is isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . Consequently,

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow   + \infty }}\frac{{\operatorname{Vol}}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{r}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right)  \smallsetminus  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{\sigma r}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right) }\right) }{{\left( \frac{r}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) }^{n}} = {\alpha }_{n}\left( {1 - {\sigma }^{n}}\right)
\]

for any \( r > 0 \) and \( 0 < \sigma  < 1 \) , where \( {\alpha }_{n} \) is the volume of the unit ball in the Euclidean space \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . Finally, by combining with the monotonicity of the Bishop-Gromov volume comparison, we conclude that the manifold \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is flat and isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . This contradicts the assumption.

Therefore, we have proved the lemma. Ⓡ

Finally we would like to include an alternative simpler argument, inspired by Ni [98], for the above Case 2 and Case 3 to avoid the use of the gap theorem, holonomy groups, and asymptotic cone structure.

Alternative Proof for Case 2 and Case 3. Let us consider the situation of \( 0 \leq \; A <  + \infty \) in the above proof. Observe that \( {\nu }_{M}\left( t\right) \) is nonincreasing in time \( t \) by using Lemma 3.4.1(ii) and the fact that the metric is shrinking in \( t \) . Suppose \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) , then the solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed for \( t \leq  {t}_{0} \) for some uniform \( \kappa  > 0 \) . By combining with Theorem 6.2.1, there exist a sequence of points \( {q}_{k} \) and a sequence of times \( {t}_{k} \rightarrow   - \infty \) such that the scalings of \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) around \( {q}_{k} \) with factor \( {\left| {t}_{k}\right| }^{-1} \) and with the times \( {t}_{k} \) shifting to the new time zero converge to a nonflat gradient shrinking soliton \( \bar{M} \) in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology. This gradient soliton also has maximal volume growth (i.e. \( {\nu }_{\bar{M}}\left( t\right)  > 0 \) ) and satisfies the Li-Yau-Hamilton estimate (Corollary 2.5.5). If the curvature of the shrinking soliton \( \bar{M} \) at the time -1 is bounded, then we see from the proof of Theorem 6.2.2 that by using the equations (6.2.24)-(6.2.26), the scalar curvature has a positive lower bound everywhere on \( \bar{M} \) at the time -1 . In particular, this implies the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio \( A = \infty \) for the soliton at the time -1 , which reduces to Case 1 and arrives at a contradiction by the dimension reduction argument. On the other hand, if the scalar curvature is unbounded, then by Lemma 6.1.4, the Li-Yau-Hamilton estimate (Corollary 2.5.5) and Lemma 6.1.2, we can do the same dimension reduction as in Case 1 to arrive at a contradiction also. 0

The following lemma is a local and space-time version of Lemma 6.1.4 on picking local (almost) maximum curvature points. We formulate it from Perelman's arguments in the section 10 of [103].

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: Given \( \epsilon  > 0,\kappa  > 0 \) and a function \( \phi \) as above, one can find \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) with the following property. If \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) ,0 \leq  t \leq  T \) is a solution to the Ricci flow on a closed three-manifold \( M \) , which has \( \phi \) -almost nonnegative curvature and is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales \( < {r}_{0} \) , then for any point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{0} \geq  1 \) and \( Q = R\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) , the solution in \( \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  : {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  < }\right. \; \left. {{\left( \epsilon Q\right) }^{-1},{t}_{0} - {\left( \epsilon Q\right) }^{-1} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{0}}\right\} \) is , after scaling by the factor \( Q \) , \( \epsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of some ancient solution, satisfying the assumptions in 11.1.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
An argument by contradiction. Take a sequence of \( {r}_{0} \) converging to zero, and consider the solutions \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) , such that the conclusion does not hold for some \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) ; moreover, by tampering with the condition \( {t}_{0} \geq  1 \) a little bit, choose among all such \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) , in the solution under consideration, the one with nearly the smallest curvature \( Q \) . (More precisely, we can choose \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) in such a way that the conclusion of the theorem holds for all \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) , satisfying \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  > {2Q},{t}_{0} - H{Q}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{0} \) , where \( H \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( {r}_{0} \rightarrow  0 \) ) Our goal is to show that the sequence of blow-ups of such solutions at such points with factors \( Q \) would converge, along some subsequence of \( {r}_{0} \rightarrow  0 \) , to an ancient solution, satisfying 11.1.

Claim 1. For each \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{0} - H{Q}^{-1} \leq  \bar{t} \leq  {t}_{0} \) we have \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4\bar{Q} \) whenever \( \bar{t} - c{\bar{Q}}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  c{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , where \( \bar{Q} = Q + R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) and \( c = c\left( \kappa \right)  > 0 \) is a small constant.

Proof of Claim 1. Use the fact (following from the choice of \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) and the description of the ancient solutions) that for each \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) with \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  > \; {2Q} \) and \( {t}_{0} - H{Q}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{0} \) we have the estimates \( \left| {{R}_{t}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  C{R}^{2}\left( {x, t}\right) \) , \( \left| {\nabla R}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C{R}^{\frac{3}{2}}\left( {x, t}\right) . \)

Claim 2. There exists \( c = c\left( \kappa \right)  > 0 \) and for any \( A > 0 \) there exist \( D = D\left( A\right)  < \infty ,{\rho }_{0} = {\rho }_{0}\left( A\right)  > 0 \) , with the following property. Suppose that \( {r}_{0} < {\rho }_{0} \) , and let \( \gamma \) be a shortest geodesic with endpoints \( \bar{x}, x \) in \( {g}_{ij}\left( \bar{t}\right) \) , for some \( \bar{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - H{Q}^{-1},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , such that \( R\left( {y,\bar{t}}\right)  > {2Q} \) for each \( y \in  \gamma \) . Let \( z \in  \gamma \) satisfy \( {cR}\left( {z,\bar{t}}\right)  > R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  = \bar{Q} \) . Then \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {\bar{x}, z}\right)  \geq  A{\bar{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) whenever \( R\left( {x,\bar{t}}\right)  \geq  D\bar{Q} \) .

Proof of Claim 2. Note that from the choice of \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) and the description of the ancient solutions it follows that an appropriate parabolic (backward in time) neighborhood of a point \( y \in  \gamma \) at \( t = \bar{t} \) is \( \epsilon \) -close to the evolving round cylinder, provided \( {c}^{-1}\bar{Q} \leq  R\left( {y,\bar{t}}\right)  \leq  {cR}\left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) for an appropriate \( c = c\left( \kappa \right) \) . Now assume that the conclusion of the claim does not hold, take \( {r}_{0} \) to zero, \( R\left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) - to infinity, and consider the scalings around \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with factors \( \bar{Q} \) . We can imagine two possibilities for the behavior of the curvature along \( \gamma \) in the scaled metric: either it stays bounded at bounded distances from \( \bar{x} \) , or not. In the first case we can take a limit (for a subsequence) of the scaled metrics along \( \gamma \) and get a nonnegatively curved almost cylindrical metric, with \( \gamma \) going to infinity. Clearly, in this case the curvature at any point of the limit does not exceed \( {c}^{-1} \) ; therefore, the point \( z \) must have escaped to infinity, and the conclusion of the claim stands.

In the second case, we can also take a limit along \( \gamma \) ; it is a smooth non-negatively curved manifold near \( \bar{x} \) and has cylindrical shape where curvature is large; the radius of the cylinder goes to zero as we approach the (first) singular point, which is located at finite distance from \( \bar{x} \) ; the region beyond the first singular point will be ignored. Thus, at \( t = \bar{t} \) we have a metric, which is a smooth metric of nonnegative curvature away from a single singular point \( o \) . Since the metric is cylindrical at points close to \( o \) , and the radius of the cylinder is at most \( \epsilon \) times the distance from \( o \) , the curvature at \( o \) is nonnegative in Aleksandrov sense. Thus, the metric near \( o \) must be cone-like. In other words, the scalings of our metric at points \( {x}_{i} \rightarrow  o \) with factors \( R\left( {{x}_{i},\bar{t}}\right) \) converge to a piece of nonnegatively curved non-flat metric cone. Moreover, using claim 1, we see that we actually have the convergence of the solutions to the Ricci flow on some time interval, and not just metrics at \( t = \bar{t} \) . Therefore, we get a contradiction with the strong maximum principle of Hamilton [H 2].

Now continue the proof of theorem, and recall that we are considering scalings at \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) with factor \( Q \) . It follows from claim 2 that at \( t = {t}_{0} \) the curvature of the scaled metric is bounded at bounded distances from \( {x}_{0} \) . This allows us to extract a smooth limit at \( t = {t}_{0} \) (of course, we use the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing assumption here). The limit has bounded nonnegative curvature (if the curvatures were unbounded, we would have a sequence of cylindrical necks with radii going to zero in a complete manifold of nonnegative curvature). Therefore, by claim 1, we have a limit not only at \( t = {t}_{0} \) , but also in some interval of times smaller than \( {t}_{0} \) .

We want to show that the limit actually exists for all \( t < {t}_{0} \) . Assume that this is not the case, and let \( {t}^{\prime } \) be the smallest value of time, such that the blowup limit can be taken on \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) . From the differential Harnack inequality of Hamilton [H 3] we have an estimate \( {R}_{t}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq   - R\left( {x, t}\right) {\left( t - {t}^{\prime }\right) }^{-1} \) , therefore, if \( \widetilde{Q} \) denotes the maximum of scalar curvature at \( t = {t}_{0} \) , then \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{Q}\frac{{t}_{0} - {t}^{\prime }}{t - {t}^{\prime }} \) . Hence by lemma 8.3(b) \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x, y}\right)  + C \) for all \( t \) , where \( C = \; {10n}\left( {{t}_{0} - {t}^{\prime }}\right) \sqrt{\widetilde{Q}} \) .

The next step is needed only if our limit is noncompact. In this case there exists \( D > 0 \) , such that for any \( y \) satisfying \( d = {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0}, y}\right)  > D \) , one can find \( x \) satisfying \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x, y}\right)  = d,{\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  > \frac{3}{2}d \) . We claim that the scalar curvature \( R\left( {y, t}\right) \) is uniformly bounded for all such \( y \) and all \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) . Indeed, if \( R\left( {y, t}\right) \) is large, then the neighborhood of \( \left( {y, t}\right) \) is like in an ancient solution; therefore,(long) shortest geodesics \( \gamma \) and \( {\gamma }_{0} \) , connecting at time \( t \) the point \( y \) to \( x \) and \( {x}_{0} \) respectively, make the angle close to 0 or \( \pi \) at \( y \) ; the former case is ruled out by the assumptions on distances, if \( D > {10C} \) ; in the latter case, \( x \) and \( {x}_{0} \) are separated at time \( t \) by a small neighborhood of \( y \) , with diameter of order \( R{\left( y, t\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , hence the same must be true at time \( {t}_{0} \) , which is impossible if \( R\left( {y, t}\right) \) is too large.

Thus we have a uniform bound on curvature outside a certain compact set, which has uniformly bounded diameter for all \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) . Then claim 2 gives a uniform bound on curvature everywhere. Hence, by claim 1, we can extend our blow-up limit past \( {t}^{\prime } \) - a contradiction.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: (cf. Theorem I.12.1) Given \( \epsilon ,\kappa ,\sigma  > 0 \) and a function \( \Phi \) as above, one can find \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) with the following property. Let \( g\left( \cdot \right) \) be a Ricci flow solution on a three-manifold \( M \) , defined for \( 0 \leq  t \leq  T \) with \( T \geq  1 \) . We suppose that for each \( t, g\left( t\right) \) is complete, and the sectional curvature is bounded on compact time intervals. Suppose that the Ricci flow has \( \Phi \) -almost nonnegative curvature and is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales less than \( \sigma \) . Then for any point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{0} \geq  1 \) and \( Q = R\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) , the solution in \( \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  : {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  < {\left( \epsilon Q\right) }^{-1},{t}_{0} - {\left( \epsilon Q\right) }^{-1} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{0}}\right\} \) is, after scaling by the factor \( Q \) , \( \epsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of a \( \kappa \) -solution.
