knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
We give a proof which differs in some points from the proof in [51] but which has the same ingredients. We first outline the argument.

Suppose that the theorem is false. Then for some \( \epsilon ,\kappa ,\sigma  > 0 \) , we have a sequence of such \( \Phi \) -nonnegatively curved 3-dimensional Ricci flows \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) defined on intervals \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) , and sequences \( {r}_{k} \rightarrow  0,{\widehat{x}}_{k} \in  {M}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k} \geq  1 \) such that \( {M}_{k} \) is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales \( < \sigma \) and \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right)  \geq  {r}_{k}^{-2} \) , but the \( {Q}_{k} \) -rescaled solution in \( {B}_{{\left( \epsilon {Q}_{k}\right) }^{-1/2}}\left( {\widehat{x}}_{k}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{\widehat{t}}_{k} - {\left( \epsilon {Q}_{k}\right) }^{-1},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) is not \( \epsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of any \( \kappa \) -solution.

We note that if the statement were false for \( \epsilon \) then it would also be false for any smaller \( \epsilon \) . Because of this, somewhat paradoxically, we will begin the argument with a given \( \epsilon \) but will allow ourselves to make \( \epsilon \) small enough later so that the argument works. To be clear, we will eventually get a contradiction using a fixed (small) value of \( \epsilon \) , but as the proof goes along we will impose some upper bounds on this value in order for the proof to work. (If we tried to list all of the constraints at the beginning of the argument then they would look unmotivated.)

The goal is to get a contradiction based on the "bad" points \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) . In a sense, the method of proof of Theorem 52.7 is an induction on the curvature scale. For example, if we were to make the additional assumption in the theorem that \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  R\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) for all \( x \in  M \) and \( t \leq  {t}_{0} \) then the theorem would be very easy to prove. We would just take a convergent subsequence of the rescaled solutions, based at \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) , to get a \( \kappa \) -solution; this would give a contradiction. This simple argument can be considered to be the first step in a proof by induction on curvature scale. In the proof of Theorem 52.7 one effectively proves the result at a given curvature scale inductively by assuming that the result is true at higher curvature scales.

The actual proof consists of four steps. Step 1 consists of replacing the sequence \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) by another sequence of "bad" points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) which have the property that points near \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) with distinctly higher scalar curvature are "good" points. It then suffices to get a contradiction based on the existence of the sequence \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) .

In steps 2-4 one uses the points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) to build up a \( \kappa \) -solution, whose existence then contradicts the "badness" of the points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . More precisely, let \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) be the result of rescaling \( {g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) \) by \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . We will show that the sequence of pointed flows \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) accumulates on a \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) , thereby obtaining a contradiction.

In step 2 one takes a pointed limit of the manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{k},{x}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) in order to construct what will become the final time slice of the \( \kappa \) -solution, \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) . In order to take this limit, it is necessary to show that the manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{k},{x}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) have uniformly bounded curvature on distance balls of a fixed radius. If this were not true then for some radius, a subsequence of the manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{k},{x}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) would have curvatures that asymptotically blowup on the ball of that radius. One shows that geometrically, the curvature blowup is due to the asymptotic formation of a cone-like point at the blowup radius. Doing a further rescaling at this cone-like point, one obtains a Ricci flow solution that ends on a part of a nonflat metric cone. This gives a contradiction as in the case \( 0 < \mathcal{R} < \infty \) of Theorem 41.2.

Thus one can construct the pointed limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) . The goal now is to show that \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) is the final time slice of a \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) . In step 3 one shows that \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) extends backward to a Ricci flow solution on some time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - \Delta ,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , and that the time slices have bounded nonnegative curvature. In step 4 one shows that the Ricci flow solution can be extended all the way to time \( \left( {-\infty ,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , thereby constructing a \( \kappa \) -solution

Step 1: Adjusting the choice of basepoints.

We first modify the points \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) slightly in time to points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) so that in the given Ricci flow solution, there are no other "bad" points with much larger scalar curvature in a earlier time interval whose length is large compared to \( R{\left( {x}_{k},{t}_{k}\right) }^{-1} \) . (The phrase "nearly the smallest curvature \( Q \) " in [51, Proof of Theorem 12.1] should read "nearly the largest curvature \( Q \) ". This is clear from the sentence in parentheses that follows.) The proof of the next lemma is by pointpicking, as in Appendix H.

Lemma 52.9. We can find \( {H}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty ,{x}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) , and \( {t}_{k} \geq  \frac{1}{2} \) such that \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) , and for all \( k \) the conclusion of Theorem 52.7 fails at \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , but holds for any \( \left( {y, t}\right)  \in \; {M}_{k} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - {H}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) for which \( R\left( {y, t}\right)  \geq  {2R}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) .

Proof. Choose \( {H}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) such that \( {H}_{k}{\left( R\left( {\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}\right) \right) }^{-1} \leq  \frac{1}{10} \) for all \( k \) . For each \( k \) , initially set \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  = \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) . Put \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) and look for a point in \( {M}_{k} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - {H}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) at which Theorem 52.7 fails, and the scalar curvature is at least \( {2R}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . If such a point exists, replace \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) by this point; otherwise do nothing. Repeat this until the second alternative occurs. This process must terminate with a new choice of \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) satisfying the lemma.

Hereafter we use this modified sequence \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . Let \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) be the result of rescaling \( {g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) \) by \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . We use \( {\bar{R}}_{k} \) to denote its scalar curvature; in particular, \( {\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  = 1 \) . Note that the rescaled time interval of Lemma 52.9 has duration \( {H}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) ; this is what we want in order to try to extract an ancient solution.

Step 2: For every \( \rho  < \infty \) , the scalar curvature \( {\bar{R}}_{k} \) is uniformly bounded on the \( \rho \) -balls \( B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) (the argument for this is essentially equivalent to [51, Pf. of Claim 2 of Theorem I.12.1]). Before proceeding, we need some bounds which come from our choice of basepoints, and the derivative bounds inherited (by approximation) from \( \kappa \) -solutions.

Lemma 52.10. There is a constant \( C = C\left( \kappa \right) \) so that for any \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in a Ricci flow solution, if \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  > 0 \) and the solution in \( {B}_{t}\left( {x,{\left( \epsilon R\left( x, t\right) \right) }^{-1/2}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {t - {\left( \epsilon R\left( x, t\right) \right) }^{-1}, t}\right\rbrack \) is \( \epsilon \) -close to a corresponding subset of a \( \kappa \) -solution then \( \left| {\nabla {R}^{-1/2}}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C \) and \( \left| {{\partial }_{t}{R}^{-1}}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C \) .

Proof. This follows from the compactness in Theorem 46.1.

Note that the same value of \( C \) in Lemma 52.10 also works for smaller \( \epsilon \) .

Lemma 52.11. (cf. Claim 1 of I.12.1) For each \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{k} - \frac{1}{2}{H}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1} \leq  \bar{t} \leq  {t}_{k} \) , we have \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4{\bar{Q}}_{k} \) whenever \( \bar{t} - c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1/2} \) , where \( {\bar{Q}}_{k} = {Q}_{k} + \left| {{R}_{k}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) }\right| \) and \( c = c\left( \kappa \right)  > 0 \) is a small constant.

Proof. If \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  2{Q}_{k} \) then there is nothing to show. If \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  > 2{Q}_{k} \) , consider a spacetime curve \( \gamma \) that goes linearly from \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to \( \left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) , and then goes from \( \left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) to \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) along a minimizing geodesic. If there is a point on \( \gamma \) with curvature \( 2{Q}_{k} \) , let \( p \) be the nearest such point to \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) . If not, put \( p = \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) . From the conclusion of Lemma 52.9, we can apply Lemma 52.10 along \( \gamma \) from \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to \( p \) . The claim follows from integrating the ensuing derivative bounds along \( \gamma \) .

Lemma 52.12. In terms of the rescaled solution \( {\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) \) , for each \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{k} - \frac{1}{2}{H}_{k} \leq  \bar{t} \leq  {t}_{k} \) , we have \( {\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4{\widetilde{Q}}_{k} \) whenever \( \bar{t} - c{\widetilde{Q}}_{k}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  c{\widetilde{Q}}_{k}^{-1/2} \) , where \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{k} = 1 + \left| {{\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) }\right| . \)

Proof. This is just the rescaled version of Lemma 52.11.

For all \( \rho  \geq  0 \) , put

(52.13)

\[
D\left( \rho \right)  = \sup \left\{  {{\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {x,{t}_{k}}\right)  \mid  k \geq  1, x \in  B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) }\right\}  ,
\]

and let \( {\rho }_{0} \) be the supremum of the \( \rho \) ’s for which \( D\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \) . Note that \( {\rho }_{0} > 0 \) , in view of Lemma 52.12 (taking \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  = \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) ). Suppose that \( {\rho }_{0} < \infty \) . After passing to a subsequence if necessary, we can find a sequence \( {y}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) with \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k},{y}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} \) and \( \bar{R}\left( {{y}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) . Let \( {\eta }_{k} \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) be a minimizing geodesic segment from \( {x}_{k} \) to \( {y}_{k} \) . Let \( {z}_{k} \in  {\eta }_{k} \) be the point on \( {\eta }_{k} \) closest to \( {y}_{k} \) at which \( \bar{R}\left( {{z}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  = 2 \) , and let \( {\gamma }_{k} \) be the subsegment of \( {\eta }_{k} \) running from \( {y}_{k} \) to \( {z}_{k} \) . By Lemma 52.12 the length of \( {\gamma }_{k} \) is bounded away from zero independent of \( k \) . Due to the \( \Phi \) -pinching (see (52.4)), for all \( \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) , we have a uniform bound on \( \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| \) on the balls \( B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) . The injectivity radius is also controlled in \( B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right) \) , in view of the curvature bounds and the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing. Therefore after passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the pointed sequence \( \left( {B\left( {{x}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) converges in the pointed Gromov-Hausdorff topology (i.e. for all \( \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) we have the usual Gromov-Hausdorff convergence) to a pointed \( {C}^{1} \) -Riemannian manifold \( \left( {Z,{\bar{g}}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) , the segments \( {\eta }_{k} \) converge to a segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\eta }_{\infty } \subset  Z \) emanating from \( {x}_{\infty } \) , and \( {\gamma }_{k} \) converges to \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {\eta }_{\infty } \) . Let \( \bar{Z} \) denote the completion of \( \left( {Z,{\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) , and \( {y}_{\infty } \in  \bar{Z} \) the limit point of \( {\eta }_{\infty } \) . Note that by Lemma 52.9 and part 4 of Corollary 42.1, the Riemannian structure near \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) may be chosen to be many times differentiable. (Alternatively, this follows from Lemma 52.12 and the Shi estimates of Appendix D.) In particular the scalar curvature \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty } \) is defined, differentiable, and satisfies the bound in Lemma 52.10 near \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) .

Lemma 52.14. 1. There is a function \( c : \left( {0,\infty }\right)  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) depending only on \( \kappa \) , with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}c\left( t\right)  = \; \infty \) , such that if \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) then \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) d{\left( {y}_{\infty }, w\right) }^{2} > c\left( \epsilon \right) \) .

2. There is a function \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } : \left( {0,\infty }\right)  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \cup  \{ \infty \} \) depending only on \( \kappa \) , with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}{\epsilon }^{\prime }\left( t\right)  = 0 \) , such that if \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) and \( d\left( {{y}_{\infty }, w}\right) \) is sufficiently small then the pointed manifold \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( 2{\epsilon }^{\prime }\left( \epsilon \right) \) -close to a round cylinder in the \( {C}^{2} \) topology.

Proof. It follows from Lemma 52.9 that for all \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) , the pointed Riemannian manifold \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( {2\epsilon } \) -close to (a time slice of) a pointed \( \kappa \) -solution. From the definition of pointed closeness, there is an embedded region around \( w \) , large on the scale defined by \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) \) , which is close to the corresponding subset of a pointed \( \kappa \) -solution. This gives a lower bound on the distance \( {\rho }_{0} - d\left( {w,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) to the point of curvature blowup, thereby proving part 1 of the lemma.

We know that \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( {2\epsilon } \) -close to a pointed \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {N,\star , h\left( t\right) }\right) \) in the pointed \( {C}^{2} \) -topology. By Lemma 52.10, we know \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) \) tends to \( \infty \) as \( d\left( {w,{x}_{\infty }}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} \) , for \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) . In particular, \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {d}^{2}\left( {w,{x}_{\infty }}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) . From part 1 above, we can choose \( \epsilon \) small enough in order to make \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {d}^{2}\left( {w,{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) large enough to apply Proposition 49.1. Hence the pointed manifold \( \left( {N,\star , R\left( \star \right) h\left( t\right) }\right) \) is \( {\epsilon }^{\prime \prime }\left( \epsilon \right) \) -close to a round cylinder, where \( {\epsilon }^{\prime \prime } : \left( {0,\infty }\right)  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) is a function with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}{\epsilon }^{\prime \prime }\left( t\right)  = 0 \) . The lemma follows.

Note that the function \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \) in Lemma 52.14 is independent of the particular manifold \( Z \) that arises in our proof.

From part 2 of Lemma 52.14, if \( \epsilon \) is small and \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) is sufficiently close to \( {y}_{\infty } \) then \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( {C}^{2} \) -close to a round cylinder. The cross-section of the cylinder has diameter approximately \( \pi {\left( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) /2\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) . If we form the union of the balls \( B\left( {w,{2\pi }{\left( {R}_{\infty }\left( w\right) /2\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) , as \( w \) ranges over such points in \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) , then we obtain a connected Riemannian manifold \( W \) . By adding in the point \( {y}_{\infty } \) , we get a metric space \( \bar{W} \) which is locally complete, and geodesic near \( {y}_{\infty } \) . As the original manifolds \( {M}_{k} \) had \( \Phi \) -almost nonnegative curvature, it follows from Lemma 52.5 that \( W \) is nonnegatively curved. Furthermore, \( {y}_{\infty } \) cannot be an interior point of any geodesic segment in \( \bar{W} \) , since such a geodesic would have to pass through a cylindrical region near \( {y}_{\infty } \) twice. The usual proof of the Toponogov triangle comparison inequality now applies near \( {y}_{\infty } \) since minimizers remain in the smooth nonnegatively curved part of \( \bar{W} \) . Then \( \bar{W} \) has nonnegative curvature in the Alexandrov sense.

This implies that blowups of \( \left( {\bar{W},{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) converge to the tangent cone \( {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{W} \) . As \( \bar{W} \) is three-dimensional, so is \( {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{W} \) [12, Corollary 7.11]. It will be \( {C}^{2} \) -smooth away from the vertex and nowhere flat, by part 2 of Lemma 52.14. Pick \( z \in  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{W} \) such that \( d\left( {z,{y}_{\infty }}\right)  = 1 \) . Then for any \( \delta  < \frac{1}{2} \) , the ball \( B\left( {z,\delta }\right)  \subset  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{W} \) is the Gromov-Hausdorff limit of a sequence of rescaled balls \( B\left( {{\widehat{z}}_{k},{\widehat{r}}_{k}}\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) where \( {\widehat{r}}_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) , whose center points \( \left( {{\widehat{z}}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) satisfy the conclusions of Theorem 52.7. Applying Lemma 52.12 and Appendix B, if \( \delta  = \delta \left( \kappa \right) \) is taken small enough then we get the curvature bounds needed to extract a limiting Ricci flow solution whose time zero slice is isometric to \( B\left( {z,\delta }\right) \) . Now we can apply the reasoning from the \( 0 < \mathcal{R} < \infty \) case of Theorem 41.2 to get a contradiction. This completes step 2.

Step 3: The sequence of pointed flows \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) ,\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }\right) \) accumulates on a pointed Ricci flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) ,\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) which is defined on a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) with \( {t}^{\prime } < {t}_{0} \) . By step 2, we know that the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) at \( y \in  {M}_{k} \) is bounded by a function of the distance from \( y \) to \( {x}_{k} \) . Lemma 52.12 extends this curvature control to a backward parabolic neighborhood centered at \( y \) whose radius depends only on \( d\left( {y,{x}_{k}}\right) \) . Thus we can conclude, using \( \Phi \) -pinching (52.4) and Shi’s estimates (Appendix D), that all derivatives of the curvature \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) are controlled as a function of the distance from \( {x}_{k} \) , which means that the sequence of pointed manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) accumulates to a smooth manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) .

From Lemma 52.5, \( {M}_{\infty } \) has nonnegative sectional curvature. We claim that \( {M}_{\infty } \) has bounded curvature. If not then there is a sequence of points \( {q}_{k} \in  {M}_{\infty } \) so that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}\bar{R}\left( {q}_{k}\right)  = \; \infty \) and \( \bar{R}\left( q\right)  \leq  2\bar{R}\left( {q}_{k}\right) \) for \( q \in  B\left( {{y}_{k},{A}_{k}\bar{R}{\left( {q}_{k}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) , where \( {A}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) ; compare [33, Lemma 22.2]. Lemma 52.9 implies that for large \( k \) , a rescaled neighborhood of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{q}_{k}}\right) \) is \( \epsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of a time slice of a \( \kappa \) -solution. As in the proof of Theorem 46.1, we obtain a sequence of neck-like regions in \( {M}_{\infty } \) with smaller and smaller cross-sections, which contradicts the existence of the Sharafutdinov retraction.

By Lemma 52.12 again, we now get curvature control on \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) for a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - \Delta ,{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) for some \( \Delta  > 0 \) , and hence we can extract a subsequence which converges to a pointed Ricci flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - \Delta ,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , which has nonnegative curvature and bounded curvature on compact time intervals.

Step 4: Getting an ancient solution. Let \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) be the maximal time interval on which we can extract a limiting solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) with bounded curvature on compact time intervals. Suppose that \( {t}^{\prime } >  - \infty \) . By Lemma 52.12 the maximum of the scalar curvature on the time slice \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) must tend to infinity as \( t \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime } \) . From the trace Harnack inequality, \( {R}_{t} + \frac{R}{t - {t}^{\prime }} \geq  0 \) , and so

(52.15)

\[
{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  Q\frac{{t}_{0} - {t}^{\prime }}{t - {t}^{\prime }},
\]

where \( Q \) is the maximum of the scalar curvature on \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) . Combining this with Corollary 27.16, we get

(52.16)

\[
\frac{d}{dt}{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \geq  \text{ const. }\sqrt{Q\frac{{t}_{0} - {t}^{\prime }}{t - {t}^{\prime }}}.
\]

Since the right hand side is integrable on \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , and using the fact that distances are nonincreasing in time (since \( \mathrm{{Rm}} \geq  0 \) ), it follows that there is a constant \( C \) such that

(52.17)

\[
\left| {{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  - {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x, y}\right) }\right|  < C
\]

for all \( x, y \in  {M}_{\infty }, t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) .

If \( {M}_{\infty } \) is compact then by (52.17) the diameter of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is bounded independent of \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) . Since the minimum of the scalar curvature is increasing in time, it is also bounded independent of \( t \) . Now the argument in Step 2 shows that the curvature is bounded everywhere independent of \( t \) . (We can apply the argument of Step 2 to the time- \( t \) slice because the main ingredient was Lemma 52.9, which holds for rescaled time \( t \) .)

We may therefore assume \( {M}_{\infty } \) is noncompact. To be consistent with the notation of I.12.1, we now relabel the basepoint \( \left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) \) as \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Since nonnegatively curved manifolds are asymptotically conical (see Appendix G), there is a constant \( D \) such that if \( y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) , and \( {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {y,{x}_{0}}\right)  > D \) , then there is a point \( x \in  {M}_{\infty } \) such that

(52.18)

\[
{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x, y}\right)  = {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {y,{x}_{0}}\right) \;\text{ and }\;{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq  \frac{3}{2}{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {y,{x}_{0}}\right) ;
\]

by (52.17) the same conditions hold at all times \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , up to error \( C \) . If for some such \( y \) , and some \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) the scalar curvature were large, then \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {y, t}\right) ,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( {y, t}\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) would be \( {2\epsilon } \) -close to a \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {N, h\left( \cdot \right) ,\left( {z,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) . When \( \epsilon \) is small we could use Proposition 49.1 to see that \( y \) lies in a neck region \( U \) in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) of diameter \( \approx  R{\left( y, t\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \ll  1 \) .

We claim that \( U \) separates \( {x}_{0} \) from \( x \) in the sense that \( {x}_{0} \) and \( x \) belong to disjoint components of \( {M}_{\infty } - U \) , where \( {x}_{0}, y \) , and \( x \) satisfy (52.18). To see this, we recall that if \( {M}_{\infty } \) has more than one end then it splits isometrically, in which case the claim is clear. If \( {M}_{\infty } \) has one end then we consider an exhaustion of \( {M}_{\infty } \) by totally convex compact sets \( {C}_{t} \) as in Section 46. One of the sets \( {C}_{t} \) will have boundary consisting of an approximate 2-sphere cross-section in the neck region \( U \) , giving the separation.

(For another argument, suppose that \( U \) does not separate \( {x}_{0} \) from \( x \) . Since \( {\widetilde{Z}}_{y}\left( {{x}_{0}, x}\right)  > \frac{\pi }{2} \) (from Proposition 49.1), the segments \( \overline{y{x}_{0}} \) and \( \overline{yx} \) must exit \( U \) by different ends. If \( {x}_{0} \) and \( x \) can be joined by a curve avoiding \( U \) then there is a nonzero element of \( {\mathrm{H}}^{1}\left( {{M}_{\infty },\mathbb{Z}}\right) \) . The corresponding infinite cyclic cover of \( {M}_{\infty } \) will then isometrically split off a line and its quotient \( {M}_{\infty } \) will be compact, which is a contradiction. We thank one of the referees for this argument.)

Obviously, at time \( {t}_{0} \) the set \( U \) still separates \( {x}_{0} \) from \( x \) . Since \( {\bar{g}}_{\infty } \) has nonnegative curvature, we have \( {\operatorname{diam}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( U\right)  \leq  {\operatorname{diam}}_{t}\left( U\right)  \ll  1 \) . Since \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) has bounded geometry, there cannot be topologically separating subsets of arbitrarily small diameter. Thus there must be a uniform upper bound on \( R\left( {y, t}\right) \) and the curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is uniformly bounded (in space and time) outside a set of uniformly bounded diameter. Repeating the reasoning from Step 2, we get uniform bounds everywhere. This contradicts our assumption that the curvature blows up as \( t \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime } \) .

It remains to show that the ancient solution is a \( \kappa \) -solution. The only remaining point is to show that it is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed at all scales. This follows from the fact that the original Ricci flow solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) were \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales less than the fixed number \( \sigma \) .

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
Induction on dimension. In dimension two the statement is vacuous, as we have just shown. Now let \( n \geq  3 \) , suppose that \( \mathcal{V} > 0 \) for some \( t = {t}_{0} \) , and consider the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio \( \mathcal{R} = \; \lim \sup R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) {d}^{2}\left( x\right) \) as \( d\left( x\right)  \rightarrow  \infty .(d\left( x\right) \) denotes the distance, at time \( {t}_{0} \) , from \( x \) to some fixed point \( {x}_{0} \) ) If \( \mathcal{R} = \infty \) , then we can find a sequence of points \( {x}_{k} \) and radii \( {r}_{k} > 0 \) , such that \( {r}_{k}/d\left( {x}_{k}\right)  \rightarrow  0, R\left( {x}_{k}\right) {r}_{k}^{2} \rightarrow  \infty \) , and \( R\left( x\right)  \leq  {2R}\left( {x}_{k}\right) \) whenever \( x \in  B\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) \) . Taking blow-up limit of \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) \) at \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) \) with factors \( R\left( {x}_{k}\right) \) , we get a smooth non-flat ancient solution, satisfying the assumptions of 11.1, which splits off a line (this follows from a standard argument based on the Aleksandrov-Toponogov concavity). Thus, we can do dimension reduction in this case (cf. [H 4,§22]).

If \( 0 < \mathcal{R} < \infty \) , then a similar argument gives a blow-up limit in a ball of finite radius; this limit has the structure of a non-flat metric cone. This is ruled out by Hamilton's strong maximum principle for nonnegative curvature operator.

Finally, if \( \mathcal{R} = 0 \) , then (in dimensions three and up) it is easy to see that the metric is flat.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
Consider any sequence of three-dimensional ancient \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solutions and marking points \( \left( {{x}_{k},0}\right) \) with \( R\left( {{x}_{k},0}\right)  = 1 \) . By Theorem 6.4.3(i), the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality and Hamilton's compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), we can extract a \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) converging subsequence such that the limit \( \left( {\bar{M},{\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) , with \( - \infty  < t \leq  0 \) , is an ancient solution to the Ricci flow with nonnegative curvature operator and \( {\kappa }_{{0}^{ - }} \) noncollapsed on all scales. Since any ancient \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solution satisfies the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality, it implies that the scalar curvature \( \bar{R}\left( {x, t}\right) \) of the limit \( \left( {\bar{M},{\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) is pointwise nondecreasing in time. Thus it remains to show that the limit solution has bounded curvature at \( t = 0 \) .

Obviously we may assume the limiting manifold \( \bar{M} \) is noncompact. By pulling back the limiting solution to its orientable cover, we can assume that the limiting manifold \( \bar{M} \) is orientable. We now argue by contradiction. Suppose the scalar curvature \( \bar{R} \) of the limit at \( t = 0 \) is unbounded.

By applying Lemma 6.1.4, we can choose a sequence of points \( {x}_{j} \in  \bar{M}, j = \; 1,2,\ldots \) , divergent to infinity such that the scalar curvature \( \bar{R} \) of the limit satisfies

\[
\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)  \geq  j\text{ and }\bar{R}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  4\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)
\]

for all \( j = 1,2,\ldots \) , and \( x \in  {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{j}, j/\sqrt{\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) }}\right) \) . Then from the fact that the limiting scalar curvature \( \bar{R}\left( {x, t}\right) \) is pointwise nondecreasing in time, we have

(6.4.20)

\[
\bar{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)
\]

for all \( j = 1,2,\ldots , x \in  {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{j}, j/\sqrt{\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) }}\right) \) and \( t \leq  0 \) . By combining with Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5) and the \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -noncollapsing, we know that a subsequence of the rescaled solutions

\[
\left( {\bar{M},\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) {\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t/\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) }\right) ,{x}_{j}}\right) ,\;j = 1,2,\ldots ,
\]

converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a nonflat smooth solution of the Ricci flow. Then Proposition 6.1.2 implies that the new limit at the new time \( \{ t = 0\} \) must split off a line. By pulling back the new limit to its universal cover and applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle, we deduce that the pull-back of the new limit on the universal cover splits off a line for all time \( t \leq  0 \) . Thus by combining with Theorem 6.2.2 and the argument in the proof of Lemma 6.4.1, we further deduce that the new limit is either the round cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) or the round \( {\mathbb{{RP}}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Since \( \bar{M} \) is orientable, the new limit must be \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Moreover, since \( \left( {\bar{M},{\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x,0}\right) }\right) \) has nonnegative curvature operator and the points \( \left\{  {x}_{j}\right\} \) are going to infinity and \( \bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) , this gives a contradiction to Proposition 6.1.1. So we have proved that the limit \( \left( {\bar{M},{\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) has uniformly bounded curvature. \( \square \)

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Suppose that \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) , is a complete ancient solution to the Ricci flow that is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on all scales, is weakly PIC2, and satisfies \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \varnothing \) id \( \in \) PIC for some uniform constant \( \theta  > 0 \) . Moreover, suppose that \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) satisfies the Harnack inequality

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\operatorname{scal} + 2\langle \nabla \operatorname{scal}, v\rangle  + 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {v, v}\right)  \geq  0
\]

for every tangent vector \( v \) . Then \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) has bounded curvature.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
Since \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) satisfies the Harnack inequality, it suffices to show that \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) has bounded curvature. The proof is by contradiction. Suppose that \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) has unbounded curvature.

By the strict maximum principle, we can find a real number \( \delta  > 0 \) with the property that the scalar curvature \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is strictly positive for \( t \in  ( - \delta ,0\rbrack \) .

Consequently, \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is strictly PIC for \( t \in  ( - \delta ,0\rbrack \) . We distinguish two cases:

Case 1: Suppose first that \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is strictly PIC2. In this case, \( M \) is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) by the soul theorem (cf. [10]). By a standard point-picking argument, there exists a sequence of points \( {x}_{j} \in  M \) such that \( {Q}_{j} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \; \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)  \geq  {j}^{4} \) and

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  {B}_{g\left( 0\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{2j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) }}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  4{Q}_{j}.
\]

Since \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) satisfies the Harnack inequality, we obtain

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{\left( {x, t}\right)  \in  {B}_{g\left( 0\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{2j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-4{j}^{2}{Q}_{j}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4{Q}_{j}.
\]

Using Shi's interior derivative estimate, we obtain bounds for all the derivatives of curvature on \( {B}_{g\left( 0\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, j{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{j}^{2}{Q}_{j}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . We now dilate the flow \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) around the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) . Using the noncollapsing assumption and the curvature derivative estimates, we conclude that, after passing to a subsequence, the rescaled flows converge in the Cheeger-Gromov sense to a smooth nonflat ancient solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) . The limit \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is complete, has bounded curvature, is weakly PIC2, and satisfies \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \oslash  \mathrm{{id}} \in \) PIC. By Proposition 6.8, the manifold \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) splits off a line. By Corollary 6.7, universal cover of \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is isometric to a family of shrinking cylinders \( {S}^{n - 1} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Therefore, \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is isometric to a quotient \( \left( {{S}^{n - 1}/\Gamma }\right)  \times  \mathbb{R} \) . If \( \Gamma \) is nontrivial, then a result of Hamilton implies that \( M \) contains a nontrivial incompressible \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional space form \( {S}^{n - 1}/\Gamma \) (cf. [6, Th. A.2]), but this is impossible since \( M \) is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . Thus, \( \Gamma \) is trivial, and \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is isometric to a standard cylinder \( {S}^{n - 1} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Consequently, \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) contains a sequence of necks with radii converging to 0 . This contradicts Proposition 6.9.

Case 2: Suppose finally that \( \left( {M, g\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is not strictly PIC2. By Proposition 6.6, the universal cover of \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) is isometric to a product \( \left( {X,{g}_{X}\left( t\right) }\right)  \times  \mathbb{R} \) for each \( t \in  ( - \delta ,0\rbrack \) . Clearly, \( \left( {X,{g}_{X}\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  ( - \delta ,0\rbrack \) , is a complete solution to the Ricci flow of dimension \( n - 1 \) , which is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on all scales, weakly PIC2, and uniformly PIC1. By assumption, \( \left( {X,{g}_{X}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) has unbounded curvature. Using a point-picking lemma, we can construct a sequence of points \( {x}_{j} \in  X \) such that \( {Q}_{j} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)  \geq  {j}^{4} \) and

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  {B}_{{g}_{X}\left( 0\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{2j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) }}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  4{Q}_{j}.
\]

As in Case 1, the Harnack inequality and Shi's interior derivative estimate give bounds for all the derivatives of curvature on \( {B}_{{g}_{X}\left( 0\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, j{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{j}^{2}{Q}_{j}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . We now dilate the manifold \( \left( {X,{g}_{X}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) around the point \( {x}_{j} \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) . Passing to the limit as \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) , we obtain a smooth nonflat limit that is uniformly PIC1 and that must split off a line by Proposition 6.8. This is a contradiction.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
Suppose that the assertion is false. Then there exists a time \( \tau  \in \; \left( {0,{t}_{0}}\right) \) with the property that the universal cover of \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) does not split off a line. Since \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is strictly PIC, we conclude that \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is locally irreducible. In view of Berger's holonomy classification theorem, there are four possible cases:

Case 1: Suppose first that \( {\operatorname{Hol}}^{0}\left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right)  = {SO}\left( n\right) \) . If we fix an arbitrary pair of real numbers \( \lambda ,\mu  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) , then Theorem 9.13 in [5] implies that the set of all orthonormal four-frames \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\} \) satisfying

\[
{R}_{g\left( \tau \right) }\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{3},{e}_{1},{e}_{3}}\right)  + {\lambda }^{2}{R}_{g\left( \tau \right) }\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{4},{e}_{1},{e}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
+ {\mu }^{2}{R}_{g\left( \tau \right) }\left( {{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{2},{e}_{3}}\right)  + {\lambda }^{2}{\mu }^{2}{R}_{g\left( \tau \right) }\left( {{e}_{2},{e}_{4},{e}_{2},{e}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
- {2\lambda \mu }{R}_{g\left( \tau \right) }\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right)  = 0
\]

is invariant under parallel transport. Since \( {\operatorname{Hol}}^{0}\left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right)  = {SO}\left( n\right) \) , we conclude that

\[
{R}_{g\left( \tau \right) }\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{3},{e}_{1},{e}_{3}}\right)  + {\lambda }^{2}{R}_{g\left( \tau \right) }\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{4},{e}_{1},{e}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
+ {\mu }^{2}{R}_{g\left( \tau \right) }\left( {{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{2},{e}_{3}}\right)  + {\lambda }^{2}{\mu }^{2}{R}_{g\left( \tau \right) }\left( {{e}_{2},{e}_{4},{e}_{2},{e}_{4}}\right)
\]

\[
- {2\lambda \mu }{R}_{g\left( \tau \right) }\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right)  > 0
\]

for all orthonormal four-frames \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2},{e}_{3},{e}_{4}}\right\} \) and all \( \lambda ,\mu  \in  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) . In other words, the curvature tensor of \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) lies in the interior of the PIC2 cone.

Let \( \Omega \) be a bounded open neighborhood of the point \( {p}_{0} \) with smooth boundary. Let us choose a smooth function \( f : \bar{\Omega } \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) with the property that \( f > 0 \) in \( \Omega , f = 0 \) on \( \partial \Omega \) , and \( {R}_{g\left( \tau \right) } - \frac{1}{2}f \) id \( \oslash \) id \( \in \) PIC2. Let \( F \) : \( \bar{\Omega } \times  \left\lbrack  {\tau ,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) denote the solution of the linear heat equation with respect to the evolving metric \( g\left( t\right) \) with initial data \( F\left( {\cdot ,\tau }\right)  = f \) and Dirichlet boundary condition \( F = 0 \) on \( \partial \Omega  \times  \left\lbrack  {\tau ,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) . Let \( S \mathrel{\text{ := }} {R}_{g\left( t\right) } - \frac{1}{2}F\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) id \( \oslash \) id. Then \( {D}_{t}S = {\Delta S} + Q\left( S\right)  + {2F}\operatorname{Ric}\left( S\right)  \oslash  \operatorname{id} + \left( {n - 1}\right) {F}^{2}\operatorname{id} \oslash  \operatorname{id} \) . Using the maximum principle, we conclude that \( {R}_{g\left( t\right) } - \frac{1}{2}F\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) id \( \oslash \) id \( \in \) PIC2 at each point in \( \Omega  \times  \left\lbrack  {\tau ,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) . Since \( F\left( {{p}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  > 0 \) , the curvature tensor at \( \left( {{p}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) lies in the interior of the PIC2 cone, contrary to our assumption.

Case 2: Suppose that \( n = {2m} \) and \( {\operatorname{Hol}}^{0}\left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right)  = U\left( m\right) \) . In this case, the universal cover of \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is a Kähler manifold. This is impossible since \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is strictly PIC.

Case 3: Suppose next that \( n = {4m} \geq  8 \) and \( {\operatorname{Hol}}^{0}\left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right)  = \operatorname{Sp}\left( m\right) \) . \( \mathrm{{Sp}}\left( 1\right) \) . In this case, the universal cover of \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is a quaternionic Kähler manifold. In particular, \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is an Einstein manifold. Since \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is strictly PIC, we conclude that the universal cover of \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is a round sphere (cf. [4]). This is impossible.

Case 4: Suppose finally that \( {\operatorname{Hol}}^{0}\left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right)  \neq  {SO}\left( n\right) \) and \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is locally symmetric. In this case, \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is an Einstein manifold, for otherwise the eigenspaces of the Ricci tensor give a splitting of the tangent bundle into parallel subbundles, which is impossible since \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is locally irreducible. Since \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is strictly PIC, it follows that the universal cover of \( \left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right) \) is a round sphere (cf. [4]). This contradicts the fact that \( {\operatorname{Hol}}^{0}\left( {M, g\left( \tau \right) }\right)  \neq  {SO}\left( n\right) \) . This completes the proof of Theorem 6.6.

Suppose that the assertion is false. Then there exists a sequence of positive numbers \( {h}_{j} \rightarrow  0 \) , a sequence of Ricci flows with surgery \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) and a sequence of points \( {x}_{j} \) with the following properties:

(i) The flow \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) has surgery parameters \( \varepsilon ,\widehat{r},{h}_{j},\widehat{\delta } \) . It is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{j}}\right) \) and goes singular as \( t \rightarrow  {T}_{j} \) .

(ii) The point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \) lies on an \( {4\varepsilon } \) -horn and \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right)  = {h}_{j}^{-2} \) .

(iii) The parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j},{\widehat{\delta }}^{-1}{h}_{j}, - {\widehat{\delta }}^{-1}{h}_{j}^{2}}\right) \) contains points modified by surgery, or it is not a \( \widehat{\delta } \) -neck.

By Definition 10.1, we have \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {4\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) whenever scal \( \geq  {\widehat{r}}^{-2} \) . Since \( {h}_{j} \rightarrow  0 \) , it follows that \( \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{x \in  {B}_{g\left( {T}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, A{h}_{j}}\right) }}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{T}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {\left( 1 + 2\eta A\right) }^{-2}{h}_{j}^{-2} \) . In particular, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( A \) ), then

\[
\mathop{\inf }\limits_{{x \in  {B}_{g\left( {T}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, A{h}_{j}}\right) }}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{T}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {10}{\left( \widehat{\delta }\widehat{r}\right) }^{-2}.
\]

We claim that for each \( A > 1 \) there exists a constant \( Q\left( A\right) \) (depending on \( A \) , but not on \( j \) ) such that \( \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  {B}_{g\left( {T}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, A{h}_{j}}\right) }}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{T}_{j}}\right)  \leq  Q\left( A\right) {h}_{j}^{-2} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. The proof of this statement is analogous to Claim 2 in Theorem 12.1 in [33]. Indeed, if no such constant \( Q\left( A\right) \) exists, then we can find a sequence of points \( \left( {{y}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \) (lying on the same horn as \( \left. \left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \right) \) such that the blow-up limit around \( \left( {{y}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \) is a piece of nonflat metric cone. Since the flow \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) satisfies the Canonical Neighborhood Assumption with accuracy \( {4\varepsilon } \) , the point \( \left( {{y}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \) either lies on a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck or on a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap. The second case can easily be ruled out, so \( \left( {{y}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \) must lie on a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck. In particular, there exists a small parabolic neighborhood of \( \left( {{y}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \) that is free of surgeries. In view of Proposition 10.3, the blow-up limit around \( \left( {{y}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \) is weakly PIC2. Hence, Proposition 6.5 implies that the limit cannot be a piece of a nonflat metric cone. This proves the claim.

In particular, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( A \) ), then the distance of the point \( {x}_{j} \) from either end of the horn is at least \( A{h}_{j} \) .

We now continue with the proof of Proposition 11.1. Let us fix a number \( A > 1 \) . Since the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j}}\right) \) lies on a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -horn, no point in \( {B}_{g\left( {T}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, A{h}_{j}}\right) \) can lie on a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap. Hence, the Canonical Neighborhood Assumption implies that every point in \( {B}_{g\left( {T}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, A{h}_{j}}\right) \) lies on a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck. Using Shi’s estimate, we obtain bounds for all the covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor in \( {B}_{g\left( {T}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\frac{1}{2}A{h}_{j}}\right) \) . Note that these bounds may depend on \( A \) , but are independent of \( j \) . We now pass to the limit, sending \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) first and \( A \rightarrow  \infty \) second. In the limit, we obtain a complete manifold with two ends that, by Proposition 10.3, is uniformly PIC and weakly PIC2. By the Cheeger-Gromoll splitting theorem, the limit is isometric to a product \( X \times  \mathbb{R} \) ; moreover, the cross-section \( X \) is compact and is nearly isometric to \( {S}^{n - 1} \) . Since every point in \( {B}_{g\left( {T}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, A{h}_{j}}\right) \) lies on a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck, we conclude that, for each \( A > 1 \) , the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j}, A{h}_{j}, - \frac{3{h}_{j}^{2}}{4}}\right) \) is free of surgeries if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( A \) ). After rescaling and passing to the limit, we obtain a solution to the Ricci flow that is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-\frac{1}{2},0}\right\rbrack \) and that splits off a line. Now, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( A) \) , then no point in \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j}, A{h}_{j}, - \frac{{h}_{j}^{2}}{2}}\right) \) can lie on a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap. Hence, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( A \) ), then every point in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j}, A{h}_{j}, - \frac{{h}_{j}^{2}}{2}}\right) \) lies on a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck. This allows us to extend the limit solution backward in time to the interval \( \left\lbrack  {-1,0}\right\rbrack \) . Repeating this argument, we can extend the limit solution backwards in time, so that it is defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-1,0}\right\rbrack  ,\left\lbrack  {-\frac{3}{2},0}\right\rbrack  ,\left\lbrack  {-2,0}\right\rbrack \) , etc. To summarize, we produce a limit solution that is ancient, uniformly PIC, weakly PIC2, and splits as a product of a line with a manifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n - 1} \) . By Theorem 6.4, the limiting solution is a family of standard cylinders. Therefore, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j},{\widehat{\delta }}^{-1}{h}_{j}, - {\widehat{\delta }}^{-1}{h}_{j}^{2}}\right) \) is free of surgeries, and \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{T}_{j},{\widehat{\delta }}^{-1}{h}_{j}, - {\widehat{\delta }}^{-1}{h}_{j}^{2}}\right) \) is a \( \widehat{\delta } \) -neck. This contradicts (iii).

Moreover, there exists a diffeomorphism \( F : \Omega  \rightarrow  {B}^{n} \) and an \( {\varepsilon }_{0} \) -isometry \( f : \partial \Omega  \rightarrow  {S}^{n - 1} \) with the property that \( {\left. knowledge_statements.proof_latex: By the soul theorem (cf. [10]), \( M \) is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . By the solution of the Schoenflies conjecture in dimension \( n \geq  5,\sum \) bounds a compact domain \( \Omega \) that is diffeomorphic to \( {B}^{n} \) . Let us choose a diffeomorphism \( F : \Omega  \rightarrow \; {B}^{n} \) , and let \( f : \partial \Omega  \rightarrow  {S}^{n - 1} \) be an \( {\varepsilon }_{0} \) -isometry. Without loss of generality, we may assume that the map \( {\left. F\right| }_{\partial \Omega } \circ  {f}^{-1} : {S}^{n - 1} \rightarrow  {S}^{n - 1} \) is orientation-preserving. We claim that the map \( {\left. F\right| }_{\partial \Omega } \circ  {f}^{-1} : {S}^{n - 1} \rightarrow  {S}^{n - 1} \) is isotopic to the identity. To prove this, let \( z \) denote the height function on the neck \( N \) , so that \( \{ z = 0\}  = \sum \) and \( \{ z \in  \lbrack  - {10},0)\}  \subset  \Omega \) . Moreover, let \( \varphi \left( z\right)  = {e}^{-\frac{1}{z}} \) for \( z \in  \left( {0,\frac{1}{10}}\right\rbrack \) . Let us define a modified metric \( \widetilde{g} \) as follows. The metric \( \widetilde{g} \) agrees with \( g \) inside \( \Omega \) . In the region \( \left\{  {z \in  \left( {0,\frac{1}{20}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , we change the metric conformally by \( \widetilde{g} = {e}^{-{2\varphi }}g \) . In the region \( \left\{  {z \in  \left( {\frac{1}{20},\frac{1}{10}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , we define \( \widetilde{g} = {e}^{-{2\varphi }}\left( {\chi \left( z\right) g + \left( {1 - \chi \left( z\right) }\right) \bar{g}}\right) \) , where \( \bar{g} \) denotes the standard metric on the cylinder and \( \chi  : \left( {\frac{1}{20},\frac{1}{10}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \left\lbrack  {0,1}\right\rbrack \) is a smooth cutoff function satisfying \( \chi \left( z\right)  = 1 \) for \( z \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{20},\frac{1}{18}}\right\rbrack \) and \( \chi \left( z\right)  = 0 \) for \( z \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{12},\frac{1}{10}}\right\rbrack \) . Since the original metric \( g \) is strictly PIC2, the modified metric \( \widetilde{g} \) will be strictly PIC2 in the region \( \left\{  {z \in  \left( {0,\frac{1}{10}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) . Moreover, the surgically modified metric \( \widetilde{g} \) is rotationally symmetric for \( z \in  \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{12},\frac{1}{10}}\right\rbrack \) . Consequently, we can extend \( \widetilde{g} \) by gluing in a rotationally symmetric cap. This can be done in such a way that the glued metric is strictly PIC2. To summarize, we obtain a closed manifold that is obtained by gluing two balls, and that admits a metric that is strictly PIC2. If the map \( {\left. F\right| }_{\partial \Omega } \circ  {f}^{-1} \) is not isotopic to the identity, then this glued manifold is an exotic sphere, that contradicts the fact that exotic spheres do not admit metrics that are strictly PIC2 (cf. [8]).

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
(Canonical neighborhood theorem). For any \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) one can find positive constants \( {C}_{1} = {C}_{1}\left( \varepsilon \right) \) and \( {C}_{2} = {C}_{2}\left( \varepsilon \right) \) with the following property. Suppose we have a three-dimensional nonflat (compact or noncompact) ancient \( \kappa \) - solution \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) . Then either the ancient solution is the round \( {\mathbb{{RP}}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) , or every point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) has an open neighborhood \( B \) , with \( {B}_{t}\left( {x, r}\right)  \subset  B \subset  {B}_{t}\left( {x,{2r}}\right) \) for some \( 0 < r < {C}_{1}R{\left( x, t\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , which falls into one of the following three categories:

(a) \( B \) is an evolving \( \varepsilon \) -neck (in the sense that it is the slice at the time \( t \) of the parabolic region \( \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  B,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {t - {\varepsilon }^{-2}R{\left( x, t\right) }^{-1}, t}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) which is, after scaling with factor \( R\left( {x, t}\right) \) and shifting the time \( t \) to zero, \( \varepsilon \) -close (in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  {\varepsilon }^{-1}\right\rbrack  } \) topology) to the subset \( \left( {{\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{I}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{\varepsilon }^{-2},0}\right\rbrack \) of the evolving standard round cylinder with scalar curvature 1 and length \( 2{\varepsilon }^{-1} \) to \( \mathbb{I} \) at the time zero), or

(b) \( B \) is an evolving \( \varepsilon \) -cap (in the sense that it is the time slice at the time \( t \) of an evolving metric on \( {\mathbb{B}}^{3} \) or \( {\mathbb{{RP}}}^{3} \smallsetminus  {\mathbb{B}}^{3} \) such that the region outside some suitable compact subset of \( {\mathbb{B}}^{3} \) or \( {\mathbb{{RP}}}^{3} \smallsetminus  {\mathbb{B}}^{3} \) is an evolving \( \varepsilon \) -neck), or

(c) \( B \) is a compact manifold (without boundary) with positive sectional curvature (thus it is diffeomorphic to the round three-sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) or a metric quotient of \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3}) \)

furthermore, the scalar curvature of the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution on \( B \) at time \( t \) is between \( {C}_{2}^{-1}R\left( {x, t}\right) \) and \( {C}_{2}R\left( {x, t}\right) \) , and the volume of \( B \) in case (a) and case (b) satisfies

\[
{\left( {C}_{2}R\left( x, t\right) \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}} \leq  {\operatorname{Vol}}_{t}\left( B\right)  \leq  \varepsilon {r}^{3}.
\]

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
As before, we first consider the easy case that the curvature operator has a nontrivial null vector somewhere at some time. By pulling back the solution to its universal cover and applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle and Theorem 6.2.2, we deduce that the universal cover is the evolving round cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Then exactly as before, by the argument in the proof of Lemma 6.4.1, we conclude that the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is isometric to the round \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R},{\mathbb{{RP}}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) , or the twisted product \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2}\widetilde{ \times  }\mathbb{R} \) where \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) flips both \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) and \( \mathbb{R} \) . Clearly each point of the round cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) or the twisted product \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2}\widetilde{ \times  }\mathbb{R} \) has a neighborhood falling into the category (a) or (b) (over \( {\mathbb{{RP}}}^{3} \smallsetminus  \overline{{\mathbb{B}}^{3}} \) ).

We now assume that the curvature operator of the nonflat ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is positive everywhere. Then the manifold is orientable by the Cheeger-Gromoll theorem [23] for the noncompact case or the Synge theorem [22] for the compact case.

Without loss of generality, we may assume \( \varepsilon \) is suitably small, say \( 0 < \varepsilon  < \frac{1}{100} \) . If the nonflat ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is noncompact, the conclusions follow immediately from the combination of Corollary 6.4.5 and Theorem 6.4.3(i). Thus we may assume the nonflat ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is compact. By Proposition 6.4.2, either the compact ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is isometric to a metric quotient of the round \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) , or it is \( {\kappa }_{{0}^{ - }} \) noncollapsed on all scales for the universal positive constant \( {\kappa }_{0} \) . Clearly each point of a metric quotient of the round \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) has a neighborhood falling into category (c). Thus we may further assume the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is also \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -noncollapsing.

We argue by contradiction. Suppose that for some \( \varepsilon  \in  \left( {0,\frac{1}{100}}\right) \) , there exist a sequence of compact orientable ancient \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}}\right) \) with positive curvature operator, a sequence of points \( \left( {{x}_{k},0}\right) \) with \( {x}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) and sequences of positive constants \( {C}_{1k} \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( {C}_{2k} = \omega \left( {4{C}_{1k}^{2}}\right) \) , with the function \( \omega \) given in Theorem 6.4.3, such that for every radius \( r,0 < r < {C}_{1k}R{\left( {x}_{k},0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , any open neighborhood \( B \) , with \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k}, r}\right)  \subset  B \subset  {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k},{2r}}\right) \) , does not fall into one of the three categories (a),(b) and (c), where in the case (a) and case (b), we require the neighborhood \( B \) to satisfy the volume estimate

\[
{\left( {C}_{2k}R\left( {x}_{k},0\right) \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}} \leq  {\operatorname{Vol}}_{0}\left( B\right)  \leq  \varepsilon {r}^{3}.
\]

By Theorem 6.4.3(i) and the choice of the constants \( {C}_{2k} \) we see that the diameter of each \( {M}_{k} \) at \( t = 0 \) is at least \( {C}_{1k}R{\left( {x}_{k},0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) ; otherwise we can choose suitable \( r \in  \left( {0,{C}_{1k}R{\left( {x}_{k},0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) and \( B = {M}_{k} \) , which falls into the category (c) with the scalar curvature between \( {C}_{2k}^{-1}R\left( {x,0}\right) \) and \( {C}_{2k}R\left( {x,0}\right) \) on \( B \) . Now by scaling the ancient \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solutions along the points \( \left( {{x}_{k},0}\right) \) with factors \( R\left( {{x}_{k},0}\right) \) , it follows from Corollary 6.4.4 that a sequence of the ancient \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solutions converge in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a noncompact orientable ancient \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solution.

If the curvature operator of the noncompact limit has a nontrivial null vector somewhere at some time, it follows exactly as before by using the argument in the proof of Lemma 6.4.1 that the orientable limit is isometric to the round \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) , or the twisted product \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) where \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) flips both \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) and \( \mathbb{R} \) . Then for \( k \) large enough, a suitable neighborhood \( B \) (for suitable \( r \) ) of the point \( \left( {{x}_{k},0}\right) \) would fall into the category (a) or (b) (over \( {\mathbb{{RP}}}^{3} \smallsetminus  {\mathbb{B}}^{3} \) ) with the desired volume estimate. This is a contradiction.

If the noncompact limit has positive sectional curvature everywhere, then by using Corollary 6.4.5 and Theorem 6.4.3(i) for the noncompact limit we see that for \( k \) large enough, a suitable neighborhood \( B \) (for suitable \( r \) ) of the point \( \left( {{x}_{k},0}\right) \) would fall into category (a) or (b) (over \( {\mathbb{B}}^{3} \) ) with the desired volume estimate. This is also a contradiction.

Finally, the statement on the curvature estimate in the neighborhood \( B \) follows directly from Theorem 6.4.3(i). 0

We first consider the easy case that the curvature operator of the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution has a nontrivial null vector somewhere at some time. Let us pull back the solution to its universal cover. By applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle and Theorem 6.2.2, we see that the universal cover is the evolving round cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Thus in this case, by the argument in the proof of Lemma 6.4.1, we conclude that the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is either isometric to the round cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) or one of its \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) metric quotients (i.e., \( {\mathbb{{RP}}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) , or the twisted product \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) where \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) flips both \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) , or \( \mathbb{R} \) ).

We then assume that the curvature operator of the nonflat ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is positive everywhere. Firstly we want to show \( {M}_{\varepsilon } \) is compact. We argue by contradiction. Suppose there exists a sequence of points \( {z}_{k}, k = 1,2,\ldots \) , going to infinity (with respect to the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( 0\right) \) ) such that each \( {z}_{k} \) is not the center of any evolving \( \varepsilon \) -neck. For an arbitrarily fixed point \( {z}_{0} \in  M \) , it follows from Theorem 6.4.3(i) that

\[
0 < R\left( {{z}_{0},0}\right)  \leq  R\left( {{z}_{k},0}\right)  \cdot  \omega \left( {R\left( {{z}_{k},0}\right) {d}_{0}^{2}\left( {{z}_{k},{z}_{0}}\right) }\right)
\]

which implies that

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}R\left( {{z}_{k},0}\right) {d}_{0}^{2}\left( {{z}_{k},{z}_{0}}\right)  =  + \infty .
\]

Since the sectional curvature of the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is positive everywhere, the underlying manifold is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) , and in particular, orientable. Then as before, by Proposition 6.1.2, Theorem 6.2.2 and Corollary 6.4.4, we conclude that \( {z}_{k} \) is the center of an evolving \( \varepsilon \) -neck for \( k \) sufficiently large. This is a contradiction, so we have proved that \( {M}_{\varepsilon } \) is compact.

Again, we notice that \( M \) is diffeomorphic to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{3} \) since the curvature operator is positive. According to the resolution of the Schoenflies conjecture in three-dimensions, every approximately round two-sphere cross-section through the center of an evolving \( \varepsilon \) -neck divides \( M \) into two parts such that one of them is diffeomorphic to the three-ball \( {\mathbb{B}}^{3} \) . Let \( \varphi \) be the Busemann function on \( M \) , it is a standard fact that \( \varphi \) is convex and proper. Since \( {M}_{\varepsilon } \) is compact, \( {M}_{\varepsilon } \) is contained in a compact set \( K = {\varphi }^{-1}\left( {( - \infty , A\rbrack }\right) \) for some large \( A \) . We note that each point \( x \in  M \smallsetminus  {M}_{\varepsilon } \) is the center of an \( \varepsilon \) -neck. It is clear that there is an \( \varepsilon \) -neck \( N \) lying entirely outside \( K \) . Consider a point \( x \) on one of the boundary components of the \( \varepsilon \) -neck \( N \) . Since \( x \in  M \smallsetminus  {M}_{\varepsilon } \) , there is an \( \varepsilon \) -neck adjacent to the initial \( \varepsilon \) -neck, producing a longer neck. We then take a point on the boundary of the second \( \varepsilon \) -neck and continue. This procedure can either terminate when we get into \( {M}_{\varepsilon } \) or go on infinitely to produce a semi-infinite (topological) cylinder. The same procedure can be repeated for the other boundary component of the initial \( \varepsilon \) -neck. This procedure will give a maximal extended neck \( \widetilde{N} \) . If \( \widetilde{N} \) never touches \( {M}_{\varepsilon } \) , the manifold will be diffeomorphic to the standard infinite cylinder, which is a contradiction. If both ends of \( \widetilde{N} \) touch \( {M}_{\varepsilon } \) , then there is a geodesic connecting two points of \( {M}_{\varepsilon } \) and passing through \( N \) . This is impossible since the function \( \varphi \) is convex. So we conclude that one end of \( \widetilde{N} \) will touch \( {M}_{\varepsilon } \) and the other end will tend to infinity to produce a semi-infinite (topological) cylinder. Thus we can find an approximately round two-sphere cross-section which encloses the whole set \( {M}_{\varepsilon } \) and touches some point \( {x}_{0} \in  \partial {M}_{\varepsilon } \) . We next want to show that \( R{\left( {x}_{0},0\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \cdot  \operatorname{diam}\left( {M}_{\varepsilon }\right) \) is bounded from above by some positive constant \( C = C\left( \varepsilon \right) \) depending only on \( \varepsilon \) .

Suppose not; then there exists a sequence of nonflat noncompact three-dimensional ancient \( \kappa \) -solutions with positive curvature operator such that for the above chosen points \( {x}_{0} \in  \partial {M}_{\varepsilon } \) there would hold

(6.4.21)

\[
R{\left( {x}_{0},0\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \cdot  \operatorname{diam}\left( {M}_{\varepsilon }\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty .
\]

By Proposition 6.4.2, we know that the ancient solutions are \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -noncollapsed on all scales for some universal positive constant \( {\kappa }_{0} \) . Let us dilate the ancient solutions around the points \( {x}_{0} \) with the factors \( R\left( {{x}_{0},0}\right) \) . By Corollary 6.4.4, we can extract a convergent subsequence. From the choice of the points \( {x}_{0} \) and (6.4.21), the limit has at least two ends. Then by Toponogov's splitting theorem the limit is isometric to \( X \times  \mathbb{R} \) for some nonflat two-dimensional ancient \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solution \( X \) . Since \( M \) is orientable, we conclude from Theorem 6.2.2 that limit must be the evolving round cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . This contradicts the fact that each chosen point \( {x}_{0} \) is not the center of any evolving \( \varepsilon \) -neck. Therefore we have proved

\[
\operatorname{diam}\left( {M}_{\varepsilon }\right)  \leq  C{Q}^{-\frac{1}{2}}
\]

for some positive constant \( C = C\left( \varepsilon \right) \) depending only on \( \varepsilon \) , where \( Q = R\left( {{x}_{0},0}\right) \) .

Finally by combining this diameter estimate with Theorem 6.4.3(i), we immediately deduce

\[
{\widetilde{C}}^{-1}Q \leq  R\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{C}Q,\text{ whenever }x \in  {M}_{\varepsilon },
\]

for some positive constant \( \widetilde{C} \) depending only on \( \varepsilon \) . \( \square \)
