We first consider the case that the sectional curvature of the nonflat gradient shrinking soliton is not strictly positive. Let us pull back the soliton to its universal cover. Then the pull-back metric is again a nonflat ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. By Hamilton's strong maximum principle (Theorem 2.2.1), we know that the pull-back solution splits as the metric product of a two-dimensional nonflat ancient \( \kappa \) -solution and \( \mathbb{R} \) . Since the two-dimensional nonflat ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is simply connected, it follows from Theorem 6.2.2 that it must be the round sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) . Thus, the gradient shrinking soliton must be \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R}/\Gamma \) , a metric quotient of the round cylinder.

For each \( \sigma  \in  \Gamma \) and \( \left( {x, s}\right)  \in  {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) , we write \( \sigma \left( {x, s}\right)  = \left( {{\sigma }_{1}\left( {x, s}\right) ,{\sigma }_{2}\left( {x, s}\right) }\right)  \in \; {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Since \( \sigma \) sends lines to lines, and sends cross spheres to cross spheres, we have \( {\sigma }_{2}\left( {x, s}\right)  = {\sigma }_{2}\left( {y, s}\right) \) , for all \( x, y \in  {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) . This says that \( {\sigma }_{2} \) reduces to a function of \( s \) alone on \( \mathbb{R} \) . Moreover, for any \( \left( {x, s}\right) ,\left( {{x}^{\prime },{s}^{\prime }}\right)  \in  {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) , since \( \sigma \) preserves the distances between cross spheres \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \{ s\} \) and \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \left\{  {s}^{\prime }\right\} \) , we have \( \left| {{\sigma }_{2}\left( {x, s}\right)  - {\sigma }_{2}\left( {{x}^{\prime },{s}^{\prime }}\right) }\right|  = \left| {s - {s}^{\prime }}\right| \) . So the projection \( {\Gamma }_{2} \) of \( \Gamma \) to the second factor \( \mathbb{R} \) is an isometry subgroup of \( \mathbb{R} \) . If the metric quotient \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R}/\Gamma \) were compact, it would not be \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on sufficiently large scales as \( t \rightarrow   - \infty \) . Thus the metric quotient \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R}/\Gamma \) is noncompact. It follows that \( {\Gamma }_{2} = \{ 1\} \) or \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) . In particular, there is a \( \Gamma \) -invariant cross sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) in the round cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Denote it by \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \{ 0\} \) . Then \( \Gamma \) acts on the round two-sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \{ 0\} \) isometrically without fixed points. This implies \( \Gamma \) is either \( \{ 1\} \) or \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) . Hence we conclude that the gradient shrinking soliton is either the round cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) , or \( {\mathbb{{RP}}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) , or the twisted product \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) where \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) flips both \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) and \( \mathbb{R} \) .

We next consider the case that the gradient shrinking soliton is compact and has strictly positive sectional curvature everywhere. By the proof of Theorem 5.2.1 (see also Remark 5.2.8) we see that the compact gradient shrinking soliton is getting round and tends to a space form (with positive constant curvature) as the time approaches the maximal time \( t = 0 \) . Since the shape of a gradient shrinking Ricci soliton does not change up to reparametrizations and homothetical scalings, the gradient shrinking soliton has to be the round three-sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) or a metric quotient of \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) .

Finally we want to exclude the case that the gradient shrinking soliton is non-compact and has strictly positive sectional curvature everywhere.

Suppose there is a (complete three-dimensional) noncompact \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed gradient shrinking soliton \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) , - \infty  < t < 0 \) , with bounded and positive sectional curvature at each \( t \in  \left( {-\infty ,0}\right) \) and satisfying the equation (6.4.1). Then as in (6.2.25), we have

(6.4.2)

\[
{\nabla }_{i}R = 2{R}_{ij}{\nabla }_{j}f
\]

Fix some \( t < 0 \) , say \( t =  - 1 \) , and consider a long shortest geodesic \( \gamma \left( s\right) ,0 \leq  s \leq  \bar{s} \) . Let \( {x}_{0} = \gamma \left( 0\right) \) and \( X\left( s\right)  = \dot{\gamma }\left( s\right) \) . Let \( U\left( 0\right) \) be any unit vector orthogonal to \( \dot{\gamma }\left( 0\right) \) and translate \( U\left( 0\right) \) along \( \gamma \left( s\right) \) to get a parallel vector field \( U\left( s\right) ,0 \leq  s \leq  \bar{s} \) , on \( \gamma \) . Set

\[
\widetilde{U}\left( s\right)  = \left\{  \begin{array}{lll} {sU}\left( s\right) , & \text{ for } & 0 \leq  s \leq  1, \\  U\left( s\right) , & \text{ for } & 1 \leq  s \leq  \bar{s} - 1 \\  \left( {\bar{s} - s}\right) U\left( s\right) , & \text{ for } & \bar{s} - 1 \leq  s \leq  \bar{s}. \end{array}\right.
\]

It follows from the second variation formula of arclength that

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\left( {{\left| \dot{\widetilde{U}}\left( s\right) \right| }^{2} - R\left( {X,\widetilde{U}, X,\widetilde{U}}\right) }\right) {ds} \geq  0.
\]

Since the curvature of the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( {-1}\right) \) is bounded, we clearly have

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}R\left( {X, U, X, U}\right) {ds} \leq  \text{ const. }
\]

and then

(6.4.3)

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) {ds} \leq  \text{ const.. }
\]

Moreover, since the curvature of the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( {-1}\right) \) is positive, it follows from the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality that for any unit vector field \( Y \) along \( \gamma \) and orthogonal to \( X\left( { = \dot{\gamma }\left( s\right) }\right) \) , we have

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}{\left| \operatorname{Ric}\left( X, Y\right) \right| }^{2}{ds} \leq  {\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) \operatorname{Ric}\left( {Y, Y}\right) {ds}
\]

\[
\leq  \text{ const. } \cdot  {\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) {ds}
\]

\[
\leq  \text{ const. }
\]

and then

(6.4.4)

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\left| {\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, Y}\right) }\right| {ds} \leq  \text{ const. } \cdot  \left( {\sqrt{\bar{s}} + 1}\right) .
\]

From (6.4.1) we know

\[
{\nabla }_{X}{\nabla }_{X}f + \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  - \frac{1}{2} = 0
\]

and by integrating this equation we get

\[
X\left( {f\left( {\gamma \left( \bar{s}\right) }\right) }\right)  - X\left( {f\left( {\gamma \left( 0\right) }\right) }\right)  + {\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) {ds} - \frac{1}{2}\bar{s} = 0.
\]

Thus by (6.4.3) we deduce

(6.4.5)

\[
\frac{\bar{s}}{2} - \text{ const. } \leq  \langle X,\nabla f\left( {\gamma \left( \bar{s}\right) }\right) \rangle  \leq  \frac{\bar{s}}{2} + \text{ const. }
\]

Similarly by integrating (6.4.1) and using (6.4.4) we can deduce

(6.4.6)

\[
\left| {\langle Y,\nabla f\left( {\gamma \left( \bar{s}\right) }\right) \rangle }\right|  \leq  \text{ const. } \cdot  \left( {\sqrt{\bar{s}} + 1}\right) .
\]

These two inequalities tell us that at large distances from the fixed point \( {x}_{0} \) the function \( f \) has no critical point, and its gradient makes a small angle with the gradient of the distance function from \( {x}_{0} \) .

Now from (6.4.2) we see that at large distances from \( {x}_{0}, R \) is strictly increasing along the gradient curves of \( f \) , in particular

\[
\bar{R} = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{{d}_{\left( -1\right) }\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty }}R\left( {x, - 1}\right)  > 0.
\]

Let us choose a sequence of points \( \left( {{x}_{k}, - 1}\right) \) where \( R\left( {{x}_{k}, - 1}\right)  \rightarrow  \bar{R} \) . By the noncol-lapsing assumption we can take a limit along this sequence of points of the gradient soliton and get an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution defined on \( - \infty  < t < 0 \) . By Proposition 6.1.2, we deduce that the limiting ancient \( \kappa \) -solution splits off a line. Since the soliton has positive sectional curvature, we know from Gromoll-Meyer [52] that it is orientable. Then it follows from Theorem 6.2.2 that the limiting solution is the shrinking round infinite cylinder with scalar curvature \( \bar{R} \) at time \( t =  - 1 \) . Since the limiting solution exists on \( \left( {-\infty ,0}\right) \) , we conclude that \( \bar{R} \leq  1 \) . Hence

\[
R\left( {x, - 1}\right)  < 1
\]

when the distance from \( x \) to the fixed \( {x}_{0} \) is large enough on the gradient shrinking soliton.

Let us consider the level surface \( \{ f = a\} \) of \( f \) . The second fundamental form of the level surface is given by

\[
{h}_{ij} = \left\langle  {{\nabla }_{i}\left( \frac{\nabla f}{\left| \nabla f\right| }\right) ,{e}_{j}}\right\rangle
\]

\[
= {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f/\left| {\nabla f}\right| ,\;i, j = 1,2,
\]

where \( \left\{  {{e}_{1},{e}_{2}}\right\} \) is an orthonormal basis of the level surface. By (6.4.1), we have

\[
{\nabla }_{{e}_{i}}{\nabla }_{{e}_{i}}f = \frac{1}{2} - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {{e}_{i},{e}_{i}}\right)  \geq  \frac{1}{2} - \frac{R}{2} > 0,\;i = 1,2,
\]

since for a three-manifold the positivity of sectional curvature is equivalent to \( R \geq \) 2Ric. It then follows from the first variation formula that

(6.4.7)

\[
\frac{d}{da}\operatorname{Area}\{ f = a\}  = {\int }_{\{ f = a\} }\operatorname{div}\left( \frac{\nabla f}{\left| \nabla f\right| }\right)
\]

\[
\geq  {\int }_{\{ f = a\} }\frac{1}{\left| \nabla f\right| }\left( {1 - R}\right)
\]

\[
> {\int }_{\{ f = a\} }\frac{1}{\left| \nabla f\right| }\left( {1 - \bar{R}}\right)
\]

\[
\geq  0
\]

for \( a \) large enough. We conclude that Area \( \{ f = a\} \) strictly increases as \( a \) increases. From (6.4.5) we see that for \( s \) large enough

\[
\left| {\frac{df}{ds} - \frac{s}{2}}\right|  \leq  \text{ const., }
\]

and then

\[
\left| {f - \frac{{s}^{2}}{4}}\right|  \leq  \text{ const. } \cdot  \left( {s + 1}\right) .
\]

Thus we get from (6.4.7)

\[
\frac{d}{da}\operatorname{Area}\{ f = a\}  > \frac{1 - \bar{R}}{2\sqrt{a}}\operatorname{Area}\{ f = a\}
\]

for \( a \) large enough. This implies that

\[
\log \operatorname{Area}\{ f = a\}  > \left( {1 - \bar{R}}\right) \sqrt{a} - \text{ const. }
\]

for \( a \) large enough. But it is clear from (6.4.7) that Area \( \{ f = a\} \) is uniformly bounded from above by the area of the round sphere of scalar curvature \( \bar{R} \) for all large \( a \) . Thus we deduce that \( \bar{R} = 1 \) . So

(6.4.8)

\[
\text{ Area }\{ f = a\}  < {8\pi }
\]

for a large enough.

Denote by \( X \) the unit normal vector to the level surface \( \{ f = a\} \) . By using the Gauss equation and (6.4.1), the intrinsic curvature of the level surface \( \{ f = a\} \) can be computed as

(6.4.9) intrinsic curvature

\[
= {R}_{1212} + \det \left( {h}_{ij}\right)
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{2}\left( {R - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) }\right)  + \frac{\det \left( {\operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) }\right) }{{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}
\]

\[
\leq  \frac{1}{2}\left( {R - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) }\right)  + \frac{1}{4{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}{\left( \operatorname{tr}\left( \operatorname{Hess}\left( f\right) \right) \right) }^{2}
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{2}\left( {R - 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) }\right)  + \frac{1}{4{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}{\left( 1 - \left( R - \operatorname{Ric}\left( X, X\right) \right) \right) }^{2}
\]

\[
= \frac{1}{2}\left\lbrack  {1 - \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right)  - \left( {1 - R + \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) }\right)  + \frac{{\left( 1 - R + \operatorname{Ric}\left( X, X\right) \right) }^{2}}{2{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2}}}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
< \frac{1}{2}
\]

for sufficiently large \( a \) , since \( \left( {1 - R + \operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) }\right)  > 0 \) and \( \left| {\nabla f}\right| \) is large when \( a \) is large. Thus the combination of (6.4.8) and (6.4.9) gives a contradiction to the Gauss-Bonnet formula.

Therefore we have proved the lemma.

Let \( {g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) , x \in  M \) and \( t \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) , be a nonflat ancient \( \kappa \) -solution for some \( \kappa  > 0 \) . For an arbitrary point \( \left( {p,{t}_{0}}\right)  \in  M \times  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) , we define as in Chapter 3 that

\[
\tau  = {t}_{0} - t,\;\text{ for }t < {t}_{0},
\]

\[
l\left( {q,\tau }\right)  = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{\tau }}\inf \left\{  {{\int }_{0}^{\tau }\sqrt{s}\left( {R\left( {\gamma \left( s\right) ,{t}_{0} - s}\right)  + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\left( s\right) \right| }_{{g}_{ij}\left( {{t}_{0} - s}\right) }^{2}}\right) {ds} \mid  }\right.
\]

\[
\gamma  : \left\lbrack  {0,\tau }\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M\text{ with }\left. {\gamma \left( 0\right)  = p,\gamma \left( \tau \right)  = q}\right\}  ,
\]

\[
\text{ and }\widetilde{V}\left( \tau \right)  = {\int }_{M}{\left( 4\pi \tau \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,\tau }\right) }\right) d{V}_{{t}_{0} - \tau }\left( q\right) \text{ . }
\]

Recall from (6.2.1) that for each \( \tau  > 0 \) we can find \( q = q\left( \tau \right) \) such that \( l\left( {q,\tau }\right)  \leq  \frac{3}{2} \) . In view of Lemma 6.4.1, we may assume that the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is not a gradient shrinking Ricci soliton. Thus by (the proof of) Theorem 6.2.1, the scalings of \( {g}_{ij}\left( {{t}_{0} - \tau }\right) \) at \( q\left( \tau \right) \) with factor \( {\tau }^{-1} \) converge along a subsequence of \( \tau  \rightarrow   + \infty \) to a nonflat gradient shrinking soliton with nonnegative curvature operator which is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on all scales. We now show that the limit has bounded curvature.

Denote the limiting nonflat gradient shrinking soliton by \( \left( {\bar{M},{\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) with \( - \infty  < \; t \leq  0 \) . Note that there holds the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality (Theorem 2.5.4) on any ancient \( \kappa \) -solution and in particular, the scalar curvature of the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is pointwise nondecreasing in time. This implies that the scalar curvature of the limiting soliton \( \left( {\bar{M},{\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) is still pointwise nondecreasing in time. Thus we only need to show that the limiting soliton has bounded curvature at \( t = 0 \) .

We argue by contradiction. By lifting to its orientable cover, we may assume that \( \bar{M} \) is orientable. Suppose the curvature of the limiting soliton is unbounded at \( t = 0 \) . Of course in this case the limiting soliton \( \bar{M} \) is noncompact. Then by applying Lemma 6.1.4, we can choose a sequence of points \( {x}_{j}, j = 1,2,\ldots \) , divergent to infinity such that the scalar curvature \( \bar{R} \) of the limit satisfies

\[
\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)  \geq  j\text{ and }\bar{R}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  4\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{j}, j/\sqrt{\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) }}\right) \) and \( j = 1,2,\ldots \) Since the scalar curvature is nondecreasing in time, we have

(6.4.10)

\[
\bar{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) ,
\]

for all \( x \in  {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{j}, j/\sqrt{\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) }}\right) \) , all \( t \leq  0 \) and \( j = 1,2,\ldots \) By combining with Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5) and the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing, we know that a subsequence of the rescaled solutions

\[
\left( {\bar{M},\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) {\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t/\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) }\right) ,{x}_{j}}\right) ,\;j = 1,2,\ldots ,
\]

converges in the \( {C}_{\text{ loc }}^{\infty } \) topology to a nonflat smooth solution of the Ricci flow. Then Proposition 6.1.2 implies that the new limit at the new time \( \{ t = 0\} \) must split off a line. By pulling back the new limit to its universal cover and applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle, we deduce that the pull-back of the new limit on the universal cover splits off a line for all time \( t \leq  0 \) . Thus by combining with Theorem 6.2.2 and the argument in the proof of Lemma 6.4.1, we further deduce that the new limit is either the round cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) or the round \( {\mathbb{{RP}}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Since \( \bar{M} \) is orientable, the new limit must be \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Since \( \left( {\bar{M},{\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x,0}\right) }\right) \) has nonnegative curvature operator and the points \( \left\{  {x}_{j}\right\} \) going to infinity and \( \bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) , this gives a contradiction to Proposition 6.1.1. So we have proved that the limiting gradient shrinking soliton has bounded curvature at each time.

Hence by Lemma 6.4.1, the limiting gradient shrinking soliton is either the round three-sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) or its metric quotients, or the infinite cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) or one of its \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) quotients. If the asymptotic gradient shrinking soliton is the round three-sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) or its metric quotients, it follows from Lemma 5.2.4 and Proposition 5.2.5 that the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution must be round. Thus in the following we may assume the asymptotic gradient shrinking soliton is the infinite cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) or a \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) quotient of \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) .

We now come back to consider the original ancient \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) . By rescaling, we can assume that \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  1 \) for all \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) satisfying \( {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x, p}\right)  \leq  2 \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - 1,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) . We will argue as in the proof of Theorem 3.3.2 (Perelman’s no local collapsing theorem I) to obtain a positive lower bound for \( {\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {p,1}\right) }\right) \) .

Denote by \( \xi  = {\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}{\left( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( p,1\right) \right) }^{\frac{1}{3}} \) . For any \( v \in  {T}_{p}M \) we can find an \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic \( \gamma \left( \tau \right) \) , starting at \( p \) , with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\tau  \rightarrow  {0}^{ + }}}\sqrt{\tau }\dot{\gamma }\left( \tau \right)  = v \) . It follows from the \( \mathcal{L} \) -geodesic equation (3.2.1) that

\[
\frac{d}{d\tau }\left( {\sqrt{\tau }\dot{\gamma }}\right)  - \frac{1}{2}\sqrt{\tau }\nabla R + 2\operatorname{Ric}\left( {\sqrt{\tau }\dot{\gamma }, \cdot  }\right)  = 0.
\]

By integrating as before we see that for \( \tau  \leq  \xi \) with the property \( \gamma \left( \sigma \right)  \in  {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {p,1}\right) \) as long as \( \sigma  < \tau \) , there holds

\[
\left| {\sqrt{\tau }\dot{\gamma }\left( \tau \right)  - v}\right|  \leq  {C\xi }\left( {\left| v\right|  + 1}\right)
\]

where \( C \) is some positive constant depending only on the dimension. Without loss of generality, we may assume \( {C\xi } \leq  \frac{1}{4} \) and \( \xi  \leq  \frac{1}{100} \) . Then for \( v \in  {T}_{p}M \) with \( \left| v\right|  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) and for \( \tau  \leq  \xi \) with the property \( \gamma \left( \sigma \right)  \in  {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {p,1}\right) \) as long as \( \sigma  < \tau \) , we have

\[
{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {p,\gamma \left( \tau \right) }\right)  \leq  {\int }_{0}^{\tau }\left| {\dot{\gamma }\left( \sigma \right) }\right| {d\sigma }
\]

\[
< \frac{1}{2}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}{\int }_{0}^{\tau }\frac{d\sigma }{\sqrt{\sigma }}
\]

\[
= 1\text{ . }
\]

This shows

(6.4.11)

\[
\mathcal{L}\exp \left\{  {\left| v\right|  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\}  \left( \xi \right)  \subset  {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {p,1}\right) .
\]

We decompose Perelman’s reduced volume \( \widetilde{V}\left( \xi \right) \) as

(6.4.12)

\[
\widetilde{V}\left( \xi \right)  = {\int }_{\mathcal{L}\exp \left\{  {\left| v\right|  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\}  \left( \xi \right) }
\]

\[
+ {\int }_{M \smallsetminus  \mathcal{L}\exp \left\{  {\left| v\right|  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\}  \left( \xi \right) }{\left( 4\pi \xi \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,\xi }\right) }\right) d{V}_{{t}_{0} - \xi }\left( q\right) .
\]

By using (6.4.11) and the metric evolution equation of the Ricci flow, the first term on the RHS of (6.4.12) can be estimated by

\[
{\int }_{\mathcal{L}\exp \left\{  {\left| v\right|  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\}  \left( \xi \right) }{\left( 4\pi \xi \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,\xi }\right) }\right) d{V}_{{t}_{0} - \xi }\left( q\right)
\]

\[
\leq  {\int }_{{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {p,1}\right) }{\left( 4\pi \xi \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}{e}^{3\xi }d{V}_{{t}_{0}}\left( q\right)
\]

\[
= {\left( 4\pi \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}{e}^{3\xi }{\xi }^{\frac{3}{2}}
\]

\[
< {\xi }^{\frac{3}{2}}\text{ , }
\]

while by using Theorem 3.2.7 (Perelman's Jacobian comparison theorem), the second term on the RHS of (6.4.12) can be estimated by

(6.4.13)

\[
{\int }_{M \smallsetminus  \mathcal{L}\exp \left\{  {\left| v\right|  \leq  \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\}  \left( \xi \right) }{\left( 4\pi \xi \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,\xi }\right) }\right) d{V}_{{t}_{0} - \xi }\left( q\right)
\]

\[
\leq  {\int }_{\left\{  \left| v\right|  > \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right\}  }{\left( 4\pi \tau \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}{\left. \exp \left( -l\left( \tau \right) \right) \mathcal{J}\left( \tau \right) \right| }_{\tau  = 0}{dv}
\]

\[
= {\left( 4\pi \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}{\int }_{\left\{  \left| v\right|  > \frac{1}{4}{\xi }^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right\}  }\exp \left( {-{\left| v\right| }^{2}}\right) {dv}
\]

\[
< {\xi }^{\frac{3}{2}}
\]

since \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\tau  \rightarrow  {0}^{ + }}}{\tau }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\mathcal{J}\left( \tau \right)  = 1 \) and \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{\tau  \rightarrow  {0}^{ + }}}l\left( \tau \right)  = {\left| v\right| }^{2} \) by (3.2.18) and (3.2.19) respectively. Thus we obtain

(6.4.14)

\[
\widetilde{V}\left( \xi \right)  < 2{\xi }^{\frac{3}{2}}.
\]

On the other hand, we recall that there exist a sequence \( {\tau }_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) and a sequence of points \( q\left( {\tau }_{k}\right)  \in  M \) with \( l\left( {q\left( {\tau }_{k}\right) ,{\tau }_{k}}\right)  \leq  \frac{3}{2} \) so that the scalings of the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution at \( q\left( {\tau }_{k}\right) \) with factor \( {\tau }_{k}^{-1} \) converge to either round \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) or one of its \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) quotients. For sufficiently large \( k \) , we construct a path \( \gamma  : \;\left\lbrack  {0,2{\tau }_{k}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  M \) , connecting \( p \) to any given point \( q \in  M \) , as follows: the first half path \( {\left. \gamma \right| }_{\left\lbrack  0,{\tau }_{k}\right\rbrack  } \) connects \( p \) to \( q\left( {\tau }_{k}\right) \) such that

\[
l\left( {q\left( {\tau }_{k}\right) ,{\tau }_{k}}\right)  = \frac{1}{2\sqrt{{\tau }_{k}}}{\int }_{0}^{{\tau }_{k}}\sqrt{\tau }\left( {R + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\left( \tau \right) \right| }^{2}}\right) {d\tau } \leq  2,
\]

and the second half path \( {\left. \gamma \right| }_{\left\lbrack  {\tau }_{k},2{\tau }_{k}\right\rbrack  } \) is a shortest geodesic connecting \( q\left( {\tau }_{k}\right) \) to \( q \) with respect to the metric \( {g}_{ij}\left( {{t}_{0} - {\tau }_{k}}\right) \) . Note that the rescaled metric \( {\tau }_{k}^{-1}{g}_{ij}\left( {{t}_{0} - \tau }\right) \) over the domain \( {B}_{{t}_{0} - {\tau }_{k}}\left( {q\left( {\tau }_{k}\right) ,\sqrt{{\tau }_{k}}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - 2{\tau }_{k},{t}_{0} - {\tau }_{k}}\right\rbrack \) is sufficiently close to the round

\( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) or its \( {\mathbb{Z}}_{2} \) quotients. Then there is a universal positive constant \( \beta \) such that

\[
l\left( {q,2{\tau }_{k}}\right)  \leq  \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2{\tau }_{k}}}\left( {{\int }_{0}^{{\tau }_{k}} + {\int }_{{\tau }_{k}}^{2{\tau }_{k}}}\right) \sqrt{\tau }\left( {R + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\left( \tau \right) \right| }^{2}}\right) {d\tau }
\]

\[
\leq  \sqrt{2} + \frac{1}{2\sqrt{2{\tau }_{k}}}{\int }_{{\tau }_{k}}^{2{\tau }_{k}}\sqrt{\tau }\left( {R + {\left| \dot{\gamma }\left( \tau \right) \right| }^{2}}\right) {d\tau }
\]

\[
\leq  \beta
\]

for all \( q \in  {B}_{{t}_{0} - {\tau }_{k}}\left( {q\left( {\tau }_{k}\right) ,\sqrt{{\tau }_{k}}}\right) \) . Thus

\[
\widetilde{V}\left( {2{\tau }_{k}}\right)  = {\int }_{M}{\left( 4\pi \left( 2{\tau }_{k}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}\exp \left( {-l\left( {q,2{\tau }_{k}}\right) }\right) d{V}_{{t}_{0} - 2{\tau }_{k}}\left( q\right)
\]

\[
\geq  {e}^{-\beta }{\int }_{{B}_{{t}_{0} - {\tau }_{k}}\left( {q\left( {\tau }_{k}\right) ,\sqrt{{\tau }_{k}}}\right) }{\left( 4\pi \left( 2{\tau }_{k}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{3}{2}}d{V}_{{t}_{0} - 2{\tau }_{k}}\left( q\right)
\]

\[
\geq  \widetilde{\beta }
\]

for some universal positive constant \( \widetilde{\beta } \) . Here we have used the curvature estimate (6.2.6). By combining with the monotonicity of Perelman's reduced volume (Theorem 3.2.8) and (6.4.14), we deduce that

\[
\widetilde{\beta } \leq  \widetilde{V}\left( {2{\tau }_{k}}\right)  \leq  \widetilde{V}\left( \xi \right)  < 2{\xi }^{\frac{3}{2}}.
\]

This proves

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {p,1}\right) }\right)  \geq  {\kappa }_{0} > 0
\]

for some universal positive constant \( {\kappa }_{0} \) . So we have proved that the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is also an ancient \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solution. \( \square \)

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
Let \( {g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) \) be a nonflat ancient \( \kappa \) -solution defined on \( M \times  \left( {-\infty , T}\right) \) (for some \( T > 0 \) ), where \( M \) is a two-dimensional manifold. Note that the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution satisfies the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality (Corollary 2.5.5). In particular by Corollary 2.5.8, the scalar curvature of the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution is pointwise nondecreasing in time. Moreover by the strong maximum principle, the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution has strictly positive curvature everywhere.

By the above Theorem 6.2.1, we know that the scalings of the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution along a sequence of points \( {q}_{k} \) in \( M \) and a sequence of times \( {t}_{k} \rightarrow   - \infty \) converge to a nonflat gradient shrinking soliton \( \left( {\bar{M},{\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) with \( - \infty  < t \leq  0 \) .

We first show that the limiting gradient shrinking soliton \( \left( {\bar{M},{\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) has uniformly bounded curvature. Clearly, the limiting soliton has nonnegative curvature and is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on all scales, and its scalar curvature is still pointwise nondecreasing in time. Thus we only need to show that the limiting soliton has bounded curvature at \( t = 0 \) . We argue by contradiction. Suppose the curvature of the limiting soliton is unbounded at \( t = 0 \) . Of course in this case the limiting soliton \( \bar{M} \) is noncompact. Then by applying Lemma 6.1.4, we can choose a sequence of points \( {x}_{j}, j = 1,2,\ldots \) , divergent to infinity such that the scalar curvature \( \bar{R} \) of the limit satisfies

\[
\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)  \geq  j\text{ and }\bar{R}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  4\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)
\]

for all \( j = 1,2,\ldots \) , and \( x \in  {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{j}, j/\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) }}\right) \) . And then by the nondecreasing (in time) of the scalar curvature, we have

\[
\bar{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) ,
\]

for all \( j = 1,2,\ldots , x \in  {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{j}, j/\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) }}\right) \) and \( t \leq  0 \) . By combining with Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5) and the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing, we know that a subsequence of the rescaling solutions

\[
\left( {\bar{M},\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) {\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t/\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) }\right) ,{x}_{j}}\right) ,\;j = 1,2,\ldots ,
\]

converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a nonflat smooth solution of the Ricci flow. Then Proposition 6.1.2 implies that the new (two-dimensional) limit must be flat. This arrives at a contradiction. So we have proved that the limiting gradient shrinking soliton has uniformly bounded curvature.

We next show that the limiting soliton is compact. Suppose the limiting soliton is (complete and) noncompact. By the strong maximum principle we know that the limiting soliton also has strictly positive curvature everywhere. After a shift of the time, we may assume that the limiting soliton satisfies the following equation

(6.2.24)

\[
{\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f + {\bar{R}}_{ij} + \frac{1}{2t}{\bar{g}}_{ij} = 0,\;\text{ on } - \infty  < t < 0,
\]

everywhere for some function \( f \) . Differentiating the equation (6.2.24) and switching the order of differentiations, as in the derivation of (1.1.14), we get

(6.2.25)

\[
{\nabla }_{i}\bar{R} = 2{\bar{R}}_{ij}{\nabla }_{j}f.
\]

Fix some \( t < 0 \) , say \( t =  - 1 \) , and consider a long shortest geodesic \( \gamma \left( s\right) ,0 \leq  s \leq  \bar{s} \) . Let \( {x}_{0} = \gamma \left( 0\right) \) and \( X\left( s\right)  = \dot{\gamma }\left( s\right) \) . Let \( V\left( 0\right) \) be any unit vector orthogonal to \( \dot{\gamma }\left( 0\right) \) and translate \( V\left( 0\right) \) along \( \gamma \left( s\right) \) to get a parallel vector field \( V\left( s\right) ,0 \leq  s \leq  \bar{s} \) on \( \gamma \) . Set

\[
\widehat{V}\left( s\right)  = \left\{  \begin{array}{ll} {sV}\left( s\right) , & \text{ for }0 \leq  s \leq  1, \\  V\left( s\right) , & \text{ for }1 \leq  s \leq  \bar{s} - 1, \\  \left( {\bar{s} - s}\right) V\left( s\right) , & \text{ for }\bar{s} - 1 \leq  s \leq  \bar{s}. \end{array}\right.
\]

It follows from the second variation formula of arclength that

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\left( {{\left| \dot{\widehat{V}}\left( s\right) \right| }^{2} - \bar{R}\left( {X,\widehat{V}, X,\widehat{V}}\right) }\right) {ds} \geq  0.
\]

Thus we clearly have

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\bar{R}\left( {X,\widehat{V}, X,\widehat{V}}\right) {ds} \leq  \text{ const., }
\]

and then

(6.2.26)

\[
{\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) {ds} \leq  \text{ const.. }
\]

By integrating the equation (6.2.24) we get

\[
X\left( {f\left( {\gamma \left( \bar{s}\right) }\right) }\right)  - X\left( {f\left( {\gamma \left( 0\right) }\right) }\right)  + {\int }_{0}^{\bar{s}}\operatorname{Ric}\left( {X, X}\right) {ds} - \frac{1}{2}\bar{s} = 0
\]

and then by (6.2.26), we deduce

\[
\frac{d}{ds}\left( {f \circ  \gamma \left( s\right) }\right)  \geq  \frac{s}{2} - \text{ const. },
\]

\[
\text{ and }f \circ  \gamma \left( s\right)  \geq  \frac{{s}^{2}}{4} - \text{ const. } \cdot  s - \text{ const. }
\]

for \( s > 0 \) large enough. Thus at large distances from the fixed point \( {x}_{0} \) the function \( f \) has no critical points and is proper. It then follows from the Morse theory that any two high level sets of \( f \) are diffeomorphic via the gradient curves of \( f \) . Since by (6.2.25),

\[
\frac{d}{ds}\bar{R}\left( {\eta \left( s\right) , - 1}\right)  = \langle \nabla \bar{R},\dot{\eta }\left( s\right) \rangle
\]

\[
= 2{\bar{R}}_{ij}{\nabla }_{i}f{\nabla }_{j}f
\]

\[
\geq  0
\]

for any integral curve \( \eta \left( s\right) \) of \( \nabla f \) , we conclude that the scalar curvature \( \bar{R}\left( {x, - 1}\right) \) has a positive lower bound on \( \bar{M} \) , which contradicts the Bonnet-Myers Theorem. So we have proved that the limiting gradient shrinking soliton is compact.

By Proposition 5.1.10, the compact limiting gradient shrinking soliton has constant curvature. This says that the scalings of the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) along a sequence of points \( {q}_{k} \in  M \) and a sequence of times \( {t}_{k} \rightarrow   - \infty \) converge in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) topology to the round \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) or the round \( {\mathbb{{RP}}}^{2} \) . In particular, by looking at the time derivative of the volume and the Gauss-Bonnet theorem, we know that the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) exists on a maximal time interval \( \left( {-\infty , T}\right) \) with \( T <  + \infty \) .

Consider the scaled entropy of Hamilton [60]

\[
E\left( t\right)  = {\int }_{M}R\log \left\lbrack  {R\left( {T - t}\right) }\right\rbrack  d{V}_{t}
\]

We compute

(6.2.27)

\[
\frac{d}{dt}E\left( t\right)  = {\int }_{M}\log \left\lbrack  {R\left( {T - t}\right) }\right\rbrack  {\Delta Rd}{V}_{t} + {\int }_{M}\left\lbrack  {{\Delta R} + {R}^{2} - \frac{R}{\left( T - t\right) }}\right\rbrack  d{V}_{t}
\]

\[
= {\int }_{M}\left\lbrack  {-\frac{{\left| \nabla R\right| }^{2}}{R} + {R}^{2} - {rR}}\right\rbrack  d{V}_{t}
\]

\[
= {\int }_{M}\left\lbrack  {-\frac{{\left| \nabla R\right| }^{2}}{R} + {\left( R - r\right) }^{2}}\right\rbrack  d{V}_{t}
\]

where \( r = {\int }_{M}{Rd}{V}_{t}/{\operatorname{Vol}}_{t}\left( M\right) \) and we have used \( {\operatorname{Vol}}_{t}\left( M\right)  = \left( {{\int }_{M}{Rd}{V}_{t}}\right)  \cdot  \left( {T - t}\right) \) (by the Gauss-Bonnet theorem).

For a smooth function \( f \) on the surface \( M \) , one can readily check

\[
{\int }_{M}{\left( \Delta f\right) }^{2} = 2{\int }_{M}{\left| {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f - \frac{1}{2}\left( \Delta f\right) {g}_{ij}\right| }^{2} + {\int }_{M}R{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2},
\]

\[
{\int }_{M}\frac{{\left| \nabla R + R\nabla f\right| }^{2}}{R} = {\int }_{M}\frac{{\left| \nabla R\right| }^{2}}{R} - 2{\int }_{M}R\left( {\Delta f}\right)  + {\int }_{M}R{\left| \nabla f\right| }^{2},
\]

and then

\[
{\int }_{M}\frac{{\left| \nabla R\right| }^{2}}{R} + {\int }_{M}\left( {\Delta f}\right) \left( {{\Delta f} - {2R}}\right)
\]

\[
= 2{\int }_{M}{\left| {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f - \frac{1}{2}\left( \Delta f\right) {g}_{ij}\right| }^{2} + {\int }_{M}\frac{{\left| \nabla R + R\nabla f\right| }^{2}}{R}.
\]

By choosing \( {\Delta f} = R - r \) , we get

\[
{\int }_{M}\frac{{\left| \nabla R\right| }^{2}}{R} - {\int }_{M}{\left( R - r\right) }^{2}
\]

\[
= 2{\int }_{M}{\left| {\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f - \frac{1}{2}\left( \Delta f\right) {g}_{ij}\right| }^{2} + {\int }_{M}\frac{{\left| \nabla R + R\nabla f\right| }^{2}}{R} \geq  0.
\]

If the equality holds, then we have

\[
{\nabla }_{i}{\nabla }_{j}f - \frac{1}{2}\left( {\Delta f}\right) {g}_{ij} = 0
\]

i.e., \( \nabla f \) is conformal. By the Kazdan-Warner identity [77], it follows that

\[
{\int }_{M}\nabla R \cdot  \nabla f = 0
\]

so

\[
0 =  - {\int }_{M}{R\Delta f}
\]

\[
=  - {\int }_{M}{\left( R - r\right) }^{2}.
\]

Hence we have proved the following inequality due to Chow [37]

(6.2.28)

\[
{\int }_{M}\frac{{\left| \nabla R\right| }^{2}}{R} \geq  {\int }_{M}{\left( R - r\right) }^{2}
\]

and the equality holds if and only if \( R \equiv  r \) .

The combination (6.2.27) and (6.2.28) shows that the scaled entropy \( E\left( t\right) \) is strictly decreasing along the Ricci flow unless we are on the round sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) or its quotient \( {\mathbb{{RP}}}^{2} \) . Moreover the convergence result in Theorem 5.1.11 shows that the scaled entropy \( E \) has its minimum value at the constant curvature metric (round \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \) or round \( {\mathbb{{RP}}}^{2} \) ). We had shown that the scalings of the nonflat ancient \( \kappa \) -solution along a sequence of times \( {t}_{k} \rightarrow   - \infty \) converge to the constant curvature metric. Then \( E\left( t\right) \) has its minimal value at \( t =  - \infty \) , so it was constant all along, hence the ancient \( \kappa \) -solution must have constant curvature for each \( t \in  \left( {-\infty , T}\right) \) . This proves the theorem.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
(Justification of the canonical neighborhood assumption). Given any small \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there exist decreasing sequences \( 0 < {\widetilde{r}}_{j} < \varepsilon ,{\kappa }_{j} > 0 \) , and \( 0 < {\widetilde{\delta }}_{j} < {\varepsilon }^{2}, j = 1,2,\cdots \) , with the following property. Define the positive function \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) \) on \( \lbrack 0, + \infty ) \) by \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right)  = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{j} \) for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {j - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, j{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) \) . Suppose there is a surgically modified solution, defined on \( \lbrack 0, T) \) with \( T <  + \infty \) , to the Ricci flow which satisfies the following:

(1) it starts on a compact orientable three-manifold with normalized initial metric, and

(2) it has only a finite number of surgeries such that each surgery at a time \( t \in  \left( {0, T}\right) \) is a \( \delta \left( t\right) \) -cutoff surgery with

\[
0 < \delta \left( t\right)  \leq  \min \{ \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) ,\bar{\delta }\left( t\right) \} .
\]

Then on each time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\left( {j - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, j{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack  \bigcap \lbrack 0, T), j = 1,2,\cdots \) , the solution satisfies the \( {\kappa }_{j} \) -noncollapsing condition on all scales less than \( \varepsilon \) and the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) with \( r = {\widetilde{r}}_{j} \) .

Here and in the following, we call a (three-dimensional) surgically modified solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) ,0 \leq  t < T,\kappa \) -noncollapsed at \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) on the scales less than \( \rho \) (for some \( \kappa  > 0,\rho  > 0 \) ) if it satisfies the following property: whenever \( r < \rho \) and

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {r}^{-2}
\]

for all those \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}, r, - {r}^{2}}\right)  = \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {B}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) ,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {r}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , for which the solution is defined, we have

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) }\right)  \geq  \kappa {r}^{3}.
\]

The proof of the proposition is by induction: having constructed our sequences for \( 1 \leq  j \leq  m \) , we make one more step, defining \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m + 1} \) , \( {\kappa }_{m + 1},{\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) , and redefining \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) . In view of the previous lemma, we only need to define \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m + 1} \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) .

In Theorem 7.1.1 we have obtained the canonical neighborhood structure for smooth solutions. When adapting the arguments in the proof of Theorem 7.1.1 to the present surgical solutions, we will encounter the new difficulty of how to take a limit for the surgically modified solutions. The idea to overcome the difficulty consists of two parts. The first part, due to Perelman [104], is to choose \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) small enough to push the surgical regions to infinity in space. (This is the reason why we need to redefine \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) .) The second part is to show that solutions are smooth on some small, but uniform, time intervals (on compact subsets) so that we can apply Hamilton's compactness theorem, since we only have curvature bounds; otherwise Shi's interior derivative estimate may not be applicable. In fact, the second part is more crucial. That is just concerned with the question of whether the surgery times accumulate or not. Our argument will use the canonical neighborhood characterization of the standard solution in Lemma 7.3.5.

We now start to prove the proposition by contradiction. Suppose for sequence of positive numbers \( {r}^{\alpha } \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) , satisfying \( {r}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  0 \) as \( \alpha  \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  \frac{1}{\alpha  \cdot  \beta }\left( { \rightarrow  0}\right) \) , there exist sequences of solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) to the Ricci flow with surgery, where each of them has only a finite number of cutoff surgeries and has a compact orientable normalized three-manifold as initial data, so that the following two assertions hold:

(i) each \( \delta \) -cutoff at a time \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) satisfies \( \delta  \leq  {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) ; and

(ii) the solutions satisfy the statement of the proposition on \( \left\lbrack  {0, m{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) , but violate the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) on \( \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) .

For each solution \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) , we choose \( \bar{t} \) (depending on \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) ) to be the nearly first time for which the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) is violated. More precisely, we choose \( \bar{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) so that the canonical neighborhood assumption with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) and with accuracy parameter \( \varepsilon \) is violated at some \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , however the canonical neighborhood assumption with accuracy parameter \( {2\varepsilon } \) holds on \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . After passing to subsequences, we may assume each \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) is less than the \( \widetilde{\delta } \) in Lemma 7.4.2 with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) when \( \alpha \) is fixed. Then by Lemma 7.4.2 we have uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing on all scales less than \( \varepsilon \) on \( \left\lbrack  {0,\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) with some \( \kappa  > 0 \) independent of \( \alpha ,\beta \) .

Slightly abusing notation, we will often drop the indices \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) .

Let \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) be the rescaled solutions around \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with factors \( R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \left( { \geq  {r}^{-2} \rightarrow   + \infty }\right) \) and shift the times \( \bar{t} \) to zero. We hope to take a limit of the rescaled solutions for subsequences of \( \alpha ,\beta  \rightarrow  \infty \) and show the limit is an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution, which will give the desired contradiction. We divide our arguments into the following six steps.

Step 1. Let \( \left( {y,\widehat{t}}\right) \) be a point on the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) with \( \widetilde{R}\left( {y,\widehat{t}}\right)  \leq  A \) (for some \( A \geq  1 \) ) and \( \widehat{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {-\left( {\bar{t} - \left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) ,0}\right\rbrack \) . Then we have estimate

(7.4.14)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10A}
\]

for those \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {y,\widehat{t},\frac{1}{2}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-1}}\right)  \triangleq \; \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {y,\frac{1}{2}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {\widehat{t} - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-1},\widehat{t}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , for which the rescaled solution is defined.

Indeed, as in the first step of the proof of Theorem 7.1.1, this follows directly from the gradient estimates (7.3.4) in the canonical neighborhood assumption with parameter \( {2\varepsilon } \) .

Step 2. In this step, we will prove three time extension results.

Assertion 1. For arbitrarily fixed \( \alpha ,0 < A <  + \infty ,1 \leq  C <  + \infty \) and \( 0 \leq  B < \frac{1}{2}{\varepsilon }^{2}{\left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{C}^{-1} \) , there is a \( {\beta }_{0} = {\beta }_{0}\left( {\varepsilon , A, B, C}\right) \) (independent of \( \alpha \) ) such that if \( \beta  \geq  {\beta }_{0} \) and the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) on the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) is defined on a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack \) with \( 0 \leq  b \leq  B \) and the scalar curvature satisfies

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C,\;\text{ on }{\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack  ,
\]

then the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) on the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) is also defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{C}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) .

Before giving the proof, we make a simple observation: once a space point in the Ricci flow with surgery is removed by surgery at some time, then it never appears for later time; if a space point at some time \( t \) cannot be defined before the time \( t \) , then either the point lies in a gluing cap of the surgery at time \( t \) or the time \( t \) is the initial time of the Ricci flow.

Proof of Assertion 1. Firstly we claim that there exists \( {\beta }_{0} = {\beta }_{0}\left( {\varepsilon , A, B, C}\right) \) such that when \( \beta  \geq  {\beta }_{0} \) , the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) on the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) can be defined before the time \( - b \) (i.e., there are no surgeries interfering in \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-b - {\epsilon }^{\prime }, - b}\right\rbrack \) for some \( \left. {{\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0}\right) \) .

We argue by contradiction. Suppose not, then there is some point \( \widetilde{x} \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) such that the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) at \( \widetilde{x} \) cannot be defined before the time \( - b \) . By the above observation, there is a surgery at the time \( - b \) such that the point \( \widetilde{x} \) lies in the instant gluing cap.

Let \( \widetilde{h}\left( { = R{\left( \bar{x},\bar{t}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}h}\right) \) be the cut-off radius at the time \( - b \) for the rescaled solution. Clearly, there is a universal constant \( D \) such that \( {D}^{-1}\widetilde{h} \leq  \widetilde{R}{\left( \widetilde{x}, - b\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  D\widetilde{h} \) .

By Lemma 7.3.4 and looking at the rescaled solution at the time \( - b \) , the gluing cap and the adjacent \( \delta \) -neck, of radius \( \widetilde{h} \) , constitute a \( {\left( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \) -cap \( \mathcal{K} \) . For any fixed small positive constant \( {\delta }^{\prime } \) (much smaller than \( \varepsilon \) ), we see that

\[
{\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{R}{\left( \widetilde{x}, - b\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \subset  \mathcal{K}
\]

when \( \beta \) large enough. We first verify the following

CLAIM 1. For any small constants \( 0 < \widetilde{\theta } < 1,{\delta }^{\prime } > 0 \) , there exists a \( \beta \left( {{\delta }^{\prime },\varepsilon ,\widetilde{\theta }}\right)  > 0 \) such that when \( \beta  \geq  \beta \left( {{\delta }^{\prime },\varepsilon ,\widetilde{\theta }}\right) \) , we have

(i) the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) over \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \cap  \left\lbrack  {-b, - b + \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2}}\right\rbrack \)

(ii) the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) in the \( {\left( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \) -cap \( \mathcal{K} \) evolved by the Ricci flow on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \cap  \left\lbrack  {-b, - b + \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) is, after scaling with factor \( {\widetilde{h}}^{-2} \) , \( {\delta }^{\prime } \) -close (in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  {\delta }^{\prime  - 1}\right\rbrack  } \) topology) to the corresponding subset of the standard solution.

This claim essentially follows from Lemma 7.3.6. Indeed, suppose there is a surgery at some time \( \widetilde{\widetilde{t}} \in  \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \cap  \left( {-b, - b + \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) which removes some point \( \widetilde{\widetilde{x}} \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) . We assume \( \widetilde{\widetilde{t}} \in  ( - b,0\rbrack \) is the first time with that property.

Then by Lemma 7.3.6, there is a \( \bar{\delta } = \bar{\delta }\left( {{\delta }^{\prime },\varepsilon ,\widetilde{\theta }}\right) \) such that if \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } < \bar{\delta } \) , then the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) in the \( {\left( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \) -cap \( \mathcal{K} \) evolved by the Ricci flow on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,\widetilde{\widetilde{t}}}\right) \) is, after scaling with factor \( {\widetilde{h}}^{-2},{\delta }^{\prime } \) -close to the corresponding subset of the standard solution. Note that the metrics for times in \( \lbrack  - b,\widetilde{\widetilde{t}}) \) on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) are equivalent. By Lemma 7.3.6, the solution on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) keeps looking like a cap for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-b,\widetilde{\widetilde{t}}}\right\rbrack \) . On the other hand, by the definition, the surgery is always done along the middle two-sphere of a \( \delta \) -neck with \( \delta  < {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) . Then for \( \beta \) large, all the points in \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) are removed (as a part of a capped horn) at the time \( \widetilde{\widetilde{t}} \) . But \( \widetilde{x} \) (near the tip of the cap) exists past the time \( \widetilde{\widetilde{t}} \) . This is a contradiction. Hence we have proved that \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \cap  \left\lbrack  {-b, - b + \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) .

The \( {\delta }^{\prime } \) -closeness of the solution on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}h}\right)  \times  \left( {\left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \cap  \left\lbrack  {-b, - b + \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2}}\right\rbrack  }\right) \) with the corresponding subset of the standard solution follows from Lemma 7.3.6. Then we have proved Claim 1.

We next verify the following

CLAIM 2. There is \( \widetilde{\theta } = \widetilde{\theta }\left( {CB}\right) ,0 < \widetilde{\theta } < 1 \) , such that \( b \leq  \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2} \) when \( \beta \) large.

Note from Proposition 7.3.3, there is a universal constant \( {D}^{\prime } > 0 \) such that the standard solution satisfies the following curvature estimate

\[
R\left( {y, s}\right)  \geq  \frac{2{D}^{\prime }}{1 - s}.
\]

We choose \( \widetilde{\theta } = {D}^{\prime }/2\left( {{D}^{\prime } + {CB}}\right) \) . Then for \( \beta \) large enough, the rescaled solution satisfies

(7.4.15)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  \frac{{D}^{\prime }}{1 - \left( {t + b}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{-2}}{\widetilde{h}}^{-2}
\]

on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right)  \times  \left( {\left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \cap  \left\lbrack  {-b, - b + \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2}}\right\rbrack  }\right) \) .

Suppose \( b \geq  \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2} \) . Then by combining with the assumption \( \widetilde{R}\left( {\widetilde{x}, t}\right)  \leq  C \) for \( t = \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2} - b \) , we have

\[
C \geq  \frac{{D}^{\prime }}{1 - \left( {t + b}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{-2}}{\widetilde{h}}^{-2},
\]

and then

\[
1 \geq  \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) \left( {1 + \frac{{D}^{\prime }}{CB}}\right) .
\]

This is a contradiction. Hence we have proved Claim 2.

The combination of the above two claims shows that there is a positive constant \( 0 < \widetilde{\theta } = \widetilde{\theta }\left( {CB}\right)  < 1 \) such that for any small \( {\delta }^{\prime } > 0 \) , there is a positive \( \beta \left( {{\delta }^{\prime },\varepsilon ,\widetilde{\theta }}\right) \) such that when \( \beta  \geq  \beta \left( {{\delta }^{\prime },\varepsilon ,\widetilde{\theta }}\right) \) , we have \( b \leq  \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2} \) and the rescaled solution in the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack \) is, after scaling with factor \( {\widetilde{h}}^{-2},{\delta }^{\prime } \) -close (in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  {\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\right\rbrack  } \) topology) to the corresponding subset of the standard solution.

By (7.4.15) and the assumption \( \widetilde{R} \leq  C \) on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack \) , we know that the cut-off radius \( \widetilde{h} \) at the time \( - b \) for the rescaled solution satisfies

\[
\widetilde{h} \geq  \sqrt{\frac{{D}^{\prime }}{C}}.
\]

Let \( {\delta }^{\prime } > 0 \) be much smaller than \( \varepsilon \) and \( \min \left\{  {{A}^{-1}, A}\right\} \) . Since \( {\widetilde{d}}_{0}\left( {\widetilde{x},\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  A \) , it follows that there is constant \( C\left( \widetilde{\theta }\right) \) depending only on \( \widetilde{\theta } \) such that \( {\widetilde{d}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  C\left( \widetilde{\theta }\right) A \ll \; {\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h} \) . We now apply Lemma 7.3.5 with the accuracy parameter \( \varepsilon /2 \) . Let \( C\left( {\varepsilon /2}\right) \) be the positive constant in Lemma 7.3.5. Without loss of generality, we may assume the positive constant \( {C}_{1}\left( \varepsilon \right) \) in the canonical neighborhood assumption is larger than \( {4C}\left( {\varepsilon /2}\right) \) . When \( {\delta }^{\prime }\left( { > 0}\right) \) is much smaller than \( \varepsilon \) and \( \min \left\{  {{A}^{-1}, A}\right\} \) , the point \( \bar{x} \) at the time \( \bar{t} \) has a neighborhood which is either a \( \frac{3}{4}\varepsilon \) -cap or a \( \frac{3}{4}\varepsilon \) -neck.

Since the canonical neighborhood assumption with accuracy parameter \( \varepsilon \) is violated at \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , the neighborhood of the point \( \bar{x} \) at the new time zero for the rescaled solution must be a \( \frac{3}{4}\varepsilon \) -neck. By Lemma 7.3.5 (b), we know the neighborhood is the slice at the time zero of the parabolic neighborhood

\[
P\left( {\bar{x},0,\frac{4}{3}{\varepsilon }^{-1}\widetilde{R}{\left( \bar{x},0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \min \left\{  {\widetilde{R}{\left( \bar{x},0\right) }^{-1}, b}\right\}  }\right)
\]

(with \( \widetilde{R}\left( {\bar{x},0}\right)  = 1 \) ) which is \( \frac{3}{4}\varepsilon \) -close (in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  \frac{4}{3}{\varepsilon }^{-1}\right\rbrack  } \) topology) to the corresponding subset of the evolving standard cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) over the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-\min \{ b,1\} ,0}\right\rbrack \) with scalar curvature 1 at the time zero. If \( b \geq  1 \) , the \( \frac{3}{4}\varepsilon \) -neck is strong, which is a contradiction. While if \( b < 1 \) , the \( \frac{3}{4}\varepsilon \) -neck at time \( - b \) is contained in the union of the gluing cap and the adjacent \( \delta \) -neck where the \( \delta \) -cutoff surgery took place. Since \( \varepsilon \) is small (say \( \varepsilon  < 1/{100} \) ), it is clear that the point \( \bar{x} \) at time \( - b \) is the center of an \( \varepsilon \) -neck which is entirely contained in the adjacent \( \delta \) -neck. By the proof of Lemma 7.3.2, the adjacent \( \delta \) -neck approximates an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. This implies the point \( \bar{x} \) at the time \( \bar{t} \) has a strong \( \varepsilon \) -neck, which is also a contradiction.

For each \( \ell \) , the limit has nonnegative sectional curvature and has bounded curvature at each time slice. Moreover by the gradient estimate in canonical neighborhood assumption with accuracy parameter \( {2\varepsilon } \) , the limit has bounded curvature on each subinterval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \subset  \left( {-{t}_{\ell },0}\right\rbrack \) . Denote by \( \widetilde{Q} \) the scalar curvature upper bound of the limit at time zero \( \left( {\widetilde{Q}\text{ is independent of }}\right. \ell ) \) . Then we can apply Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality (Corollary 2.5.5) to get

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\ell }^{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \frac{{t}_{\ell }}{t + {t}_{\ell }}\widetilde{Q}
\]

where \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\ell }^{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right) \) are the scalar curvatures of the limits \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\ell }^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) . Hence by the definition of convergence and the above curvature estimates, we can find a subsequence of the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) which converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a smooth limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) on the maximal time interval \( \left( {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) .

We need to show \( - {t}_{\max } =  - \infty \) . Suppose \( - {t}_{\max } >  - \infty \) , there are only the following two possibilities: either

(1) The curvature of the limiting solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) becomes unbounded as \( t \searrow   - {t}_{\max } \) ; or

(2) For each small constant \( \theta  > 0 \) and each large integer \( {k}_{0} > 0 \) , there is some \( k \geq \; {k}_{0} \) such that the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) has a surgery time \( {T}_{k} \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \theta ,0}\right\rbrack \) and a surgery point \( {x}_{k} \) lying in a gluing cap at the times \( {T}_{k} \) so that \( {d}_{{T}_{k}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},\bar{x}}\right) \) is uniformly bounded from above by a constant independent of \( \theta \) and \( {k}_{0} \) .

We next claim that the possibility (1) always occurs. Suppose not; then the curvature of the limiting solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) is bounded on \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left( {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) by some positive constant \( \widehat{C} \) . In particular, for any \( A > 0 \) , there is a sufficiently large integer \( {k}_{1} > 0 \) such that any rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) with \( k \geq  {k}_{1} \) on the geodesic ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) and its scalar curvature is bounded by \( 2\widehat{C} \) there. (Here, without loss of generality, we may assume that the upper bound \( \widehat{C} \) is so large that \( - {t}_{\max } + \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1} < 0 \) .) By Assertion 1 in Step 2, for \( k \) large enough, the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) over \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) can be defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) and has the scalar curvature \( \widetilde{R} \leq  {10}\widehat{C} \) on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . So we can extract a smooth limit from the sequence to get the limiting solution which is defined on a larger time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . This contradicts the definition of the maximal time \( - {t}_{\max } \) .

It remains to exclude the possibility (1).

By using Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality (Corollary 2.5.5) again, we have

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \frac{{t}_{\max }}{t + {t}_{\max }}\widetilde{Q}.
\]

So we only need to control the curvature near \( - {t}_{\max } \) . Exactly as in Step 4 in the proof of Theorem 7.1.1, it follows from Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality that

(7.4.16)

\[
{\widetilde{d}}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  {\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  {\widetilde{d}}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)  + {30}{t}_{\max }\sqrt{\widetilde{Q}}
\]

for any \( x, y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and \( t \in  \left( {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) .

Since the infimum of the scalar curvature is nondecreasing in time, we have some point \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and some time \( - {t}_{\max } < {t}_{\infty } <  - {t}_{\max } + \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1} \) such that \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty }}\right)  < \; 5/4 \) . By (7.4.16), there is a constant \( {\widetilde{A}}_{0} > 0 \) such that \( {\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {\bar{x},{y}_{\infty }}\right)  \leq  {\widetilde{A}}_{0}/2 \) for all \( t \in  \left( {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) .

Now we come back to the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) . Clearly, for arbitrarily given small \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) , when \( k \) large enough, there is a point \( {y}_{k} \) in the underlying manifold of \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) at time 0 satisfying the following properties

(7.4.17)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {{y}_{k},{t}_{\infty }}\right)  < \frac{3}{2},\;{\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {\bar{x},{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  {\widetilde{A}}_{0}
\]

for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . By the definition of convergence, we know that for any fixed \( {A}_{0} \geq  2{\widetilde{A}}_{0} \) , for \( k \) large enough, the rescaled solution over \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{A}_{0}}\right) \) is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\infty },0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfies

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \frac{2{t}_{\max }}{t + {t}_{\max }}\widetilde{Q}
\]

on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{A}_{0}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\infty },0}\right\rbrack \) . Then by Assertion 2 of Step 2, we have proved that there is a sufficiently large integer \( {\bar{k}}_{0} \) such that when \( k \geq  {\bar{k}}_{0} \) , the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) at \( {y}_{k} \) can be defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) , and satisfy

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {{y}_{k}, t}\right)  \leq  {15}
\]

for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack \) .

We now prove a statement analogous to Assertion 4 (i) of Step 3.

Assertion 5. For the above rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) and \( {\bar{k}}_{0} \) , we have that for any \( L > 0 \) , there is a positive constant \( \omega \left( L\right) \) such that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) satisfy

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \omega \left( L\right)
\]

for all \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) with \( {\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {x,{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  L \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack \) , and for all \( k \geq  {\bar{k}}_{0} \) .

Proof of Assertion 5. We slightly modify the argument in the proof of Assertion 4 (i). Let

\[
M\left( \rho \right)  = \sup \left\{  {\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \mid  {\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {x,{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  \rho }\right. \text{ and }t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
\text{ in the rescaled solutions }\left. {{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}}, k \geq  {\bar{k}}_{0}}\right\}
\]

and

\[
{\rho }_{0} = \sup \{ \rho  > 0 \mid  M\left( \rho \right)  <  + \infty \} .
\]

Note that the estimate (7.4.14) implies that \( {\rho }_{0} > 0 \) . We only need to show \( {\rho }_{0} =  + \infty \) .

We argue by contradiction. Suppose \( {\rho }_{0} <  + \infty \) . Then, after passing to a subsequence, there is a sequence \( \left( {{\widetilde{y}}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) in the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) with \( {t}_{k} \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack \) and \( {\widetilde{d}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},{\widetilde{y}}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} <  + \infty \) such that \( \widetilde{R}\left( {{\widetilde{y}}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) . Denote by \( {\gamma }_{k} \) a minimizing geodesic segment from \( {y}_{k} \) to \( {\widetilde{y}}_{k} \) at the time \( {t}_{k} \) and denote by \( {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) the open geodesic ball centered at \( {y}_{k} \) of radius \( {\rho }_{0} \) on the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{k}}\right) \) .

For any \( 0 < \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) with \( \rho \) near \( {\rho }_{0} \) , by applying Assertion 3 as before, we get that the rescaled solutions on the balls \( {B}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},\rho }\right) \) are defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - \frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}M{\left( \rho \right) }^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) for all large \( k \) . By Step 1 and Shi’s derivative estimate, we further know that the covariant derivatives and higher order derivatives of the curvatures on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},\rho  - \frac{\left( {\rho }_{0} - \rho \right) }{2}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - \frac{1}{32}{\eta }^{-1}M{\left( \rho \right) }^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) are also uniformly bounded. Then by the uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing property and Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), after passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the marked sequence \( \left( {{\widetilde{B}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{k}}\right) ,{y}_{k}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a marked (noncomplete) manifold \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty },{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) and the geodesic segments \( {\gamma }_{k} \) converge to a geodesic segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {B}_{\infty } \) emanating from \( {y}_{\infty } \) .

Clearly, the limit also has nonnegative sectional curvature by the pinching assumption. Then by repeating the same argument as in the proof of Assertion 4 (i) in the rest, we derive a contradiction with Hamilton's strong maximum principle. This proves Assertion 5.

We then apply the second estimate of (7.4.17) and Assertion 5 to conclude that for any large constant \( 0 < A <  + \infty \) , there is a positive constant \( C\left( A\right) \) such that for any small \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) , the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) satisfy

(7.4.18)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C\left( A\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , and for all sufficiently large \( k \) . Then by applying Assertion 1 in Step 2, we conclude that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) on the geodesic balls \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) are also defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime } - }\right. \; \left. {\frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) for all sufficiently large \( k \) . Furthermore, by the gradient estimates as in Step 1, we have

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10C}\left( A\right)
\]

for \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime } - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . Since \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) is arbitrarily small and the positive constant \( C\left( A\right) \) is independent of \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \) , we conclude that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) are defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - }\right. \; \left. {\frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfy

(7.4.19)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10C}\left( A\right) ,
\]

for \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) , and for all sufficiently large \( k \) .

Now, by taking convergent subsequences from the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) , we see that the limit solution is defined smoothly on a space-time open subset of \( {M}_{\infty } \times \; ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) containing \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) . By Step 4, we see that the limiting metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , - {t}_{\max }}\right) \) at time \( - {t}_{\max } \) has bounded curvature. Then by combining with the canonical neighborhood assumption of accuracy \( {2\varepsilon } \) , we conclude that the curvature of the limit is uniformly bounded on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) . So we have excluded the possibility (1).

Hence we have proved a subsequence of the rescaled solutions converges to an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution.

Finally by combining with the canonical neighborhood theorem (Theorem 6.4.6), we see that \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) has a canonical neighborhood with parameter \( \varepsilon \) , which is a contradiction. Therefore we have completed the proof of the proposition. 0

Then we can find positive numbers \( \widehat{r} \) and \( \widehat{\delta } \) with the following property: Suppose that we have a Ricci flow with surgery with parameters \( \varepsilon ,\widehat{r},\widehat{\delta }, h \) that is defined on some interval \( \lbrack 0, T) \) . Moreover, suppose that \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) is an arbitrary point in space-time satisfying \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {\left( 2\widehat{r}\right) }^{-2} \) . Then there exists a neighborhood \( B \) of \( {x}_{0} \) such that

\[
{B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},{\left( 2{C}_{1}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {x}_{0},{t}_{0}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \subset  B \subset  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},2{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {x}_{0},{t}_{0}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)
\]

and

\[
{\left( 2{C}_{2}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right)  \leq  2{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  B \) . Moreover, \( B \) is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck (in the sense of [35]) with center at \( {x}_{0} \) or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap. Finally, we have \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq \; {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) .
