We argue by contradiction. Suppose that the assertion is false. Then we can find a sequence of Ricci flows with surgery \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) and a sequence of points \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) in space-time with the following properties:

(i) The flow \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{j}}\right) \) and has surgery parameters \( \varepsilon ,{\widehat{r}}_{j},{h}_{j},{\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \) , where \( {\widehat{r}}_{j} \leq  \frac{1}{j} \) and \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \leq  \min \left\{  {\widetilde{\widetilde{\delta }}\left( {\widehat{r}}_{j}\right) ,\frac{1}{j}}\right\} \) . Here, \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( \cdot \right) \) is the function introduced in Proposition 10.9.

(ii) \( {Q}_{j} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {\left( 2{\widehat{r}}_{j}\right) }^{-2} \) .

(iii) The point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) does not satisfy the conclusion of Theorem 10.10.

Condition (iii) means that at least one of the following statements is true:

- There does not exist a neighborhood \( B \) of \( {x}_{j} \) with the property that \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{\left( 2{C}_{1}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \subset  B \subset  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},2{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) and \( {\left( 2{C}_{2}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \leq  \operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{t}_{j}}\right)  \leq  2{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) for all \( x \in  B \) , and such that \( B \) is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck (in the sense of [35]) with center at \( {x}_{j} \) or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap.

- \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  > {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) .

- \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  > {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) at \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) .

We will proceed in several steps:

Step 1: By Definition 10.1, we have \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {4\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq \; {4\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) for each point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in space-time satisfying \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  4{Q}_{j} \) . Moreover, by Proposition 10.9, the flow \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales less than \( \varepsilon \) for some uniform constant \( \kappa \) that may depend on the initial data, but it is independent of \( j \) .

Step 2: Suppose that \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) is a point in space-time satisfying \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \; + {Q}_{j} \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) . The pointwise curvature derivative estimate implies that scal \( \leq \; 8{r}_{0}^{-2} \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},\frac{{r}_{0}}{100\eta }, - \frac{{r}_{0}^{2}}{100\eta }}\right) \) . Using Proposition 10.4, we conclude that \( \left| {{D}^{m}R}\right|  \leq  C\left( {n, m,\eta }\right) {r}_{0}^{-m - 2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Moreover, Proposition 10.9 implies \( {\operatorname{vol}}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq  \kappa {r}_{0}^{n} \) for some uniform constant \( \kappa \) that is independent of \( j \) .

Step 3: We next prove a long-range curvature estimate. Given any \( \rho  > 0 \) , we put

\[
\mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) }}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{t}_{j}}\right) .
\]

The pointwise curvature derivative estimate implies that \( \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  \leq  {16} \) for \( 0 < \; \rho  < \frac{1}{100\eta }. \)

We claim that \( \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \) for all \( \rho  > 0 \) . Suppose this is false. Let

\[
{\rho }^{ * } = \sup \{ \rho  \geq  0 : \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \}  < \infty .
\]

By definition of \( {\rho }^{ * } \) , we have an upper bound for the curvature in the geodesic ball \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) for each \( \rho  < {\rho }^{ * } \) . Using the results in Step 2, we obtain bounds for all the covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor in the geodesic ball \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) for each \( \rho  < {\rho }^{ * } \) . Moreover, the noncollapsing estimate in Step 2 gives a lower bound for the volume. We rescale around \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) and pass to the limit as \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) . In the limit, we obtain an incomplete manifold \( \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) that is weakly PIC2 (cf. [31, Th. 5.6]).

By definition of \( {\rho }^{ * } \) , there exists a sequence of points \( {y}_{j} \) such that

\[
{\rho }_{j} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {Q}_{j}^{\frac{1}{2}}{d}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{y}_{j}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }^{ * }\;\text{ and }\;{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty .
\]

Let \( {\gamma }_{j} : \left\lbrack  {0,{\rho }_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) be a unit-speed geodesic such that \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( 0\right)  = {x}_{j} \) and \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {{\rho }_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  = {y}_{j} \) , and let \( {\gamma }_{\infty } : \left\lbrack  {0,{\rho }^{ * }}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) denote the limit of \( {\gamma }_{j} \) . Using the estimate \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {4\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) we obtain for \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {{\rho }^{ * } - \frac{1}{100\eta },{\rho }^{ * }}\right) \) ,

\[
{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {{\gamma }_{\infty }\left( s\right) }\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {s{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {\left( 2\eta \left( {\rho }^{ * } - s\right) \right) }^{-2} \geq  {100}.
\]

Let us consider a real number \( \bar{s} \in  \left\lbrack  {{\rho }^{ * } - \frac{1}{100\eta },{\rho }^{ * }}\right) \) such that \( {64}{C}_{1}\eta \left( {{\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}}\right)  \leq  \bar{s} \) . We claim that \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) lies at the center of a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ). Indeed, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood Assumption implies that the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap. Furthermore, the Canonical Neighborhood is contained in a geodesic ball around \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) of radius \( 8{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , and the scalar curvature is at most \( 8{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) at each point in the Canonical Neighborhood. Since \( \mathbb{M}\left( \bar{s}\right)  < \infty \) , we obtain \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  = \infty \) ; consequently, \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {16}{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Hence, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood does not contain the point \( {y}_{j} \) . We next observe that \( {32}{C}_{1}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}{\left( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  {64}{C}_{1}\eta \left( {{\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}}\right)  \leq  \bar{s} \) . This implies \( {16}{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Hence, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood does not contain the point \( {x}_{j} \) . If the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) is a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap, then the geodesic \( {\gamma }_{j} \) must enter and exit this \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap, but this is impossible since \( {\gamma }_{j} \) minimizes length. To summarize, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ), then the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck. In particular, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ), then we have \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  C\left( n\right) \varepsilon {\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) . \)

Passing to the limit as \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) , we conclude that \( \left| {D{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}}\right|  \leq  C\left( n\right) \varepsilon {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at the point \( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \) . Integrating this estimate along \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) gives \( {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {{\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) }\right)  \geq \; {\left( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \left( {\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}\right) \right) }^{-2} \) . Moreover, since \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies at the center of a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck for \( j \) sufficiently large, the point \( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \) must lie on a strong \( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) .

As in \( \left\lbrack  {{33},§{12.1}}\right\rbrack \) , there is a sequence of rescalings that converges to a piece of a nonflat metric cone in the limit. Let us fix a point on this metric cone. In view of the preceding discussion, this point must lie on a strong \( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \) -neck. This gives a locally defined solution to the Ricci flow that is weakly PIC2 and that, at the final time, is a piece of nonflat metric cone. This contradicts Proposition 6.5.

Step 4: We now dilate the manifold \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) around the point \( {x}_{j} \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) . By Step 3, we have uniform bounds for the curvature at bounded distance. Using the results in Step 2, we obtain bounds for all the covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor at bounded distance. Using these estimates together with the noncollapsing estimate in Step 2, we conclude that the rescaled manifolds converge in the Cheeger-Gromov sense to a complete limit manifold \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) . Since \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) has \( \left( {f,\theta }\right) \) -pinched curvature, the curvature tensor of \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) is weakly PIC2 and satisfies \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \varnothing \mathrm{{id}} \in \) PIC. Using the Canonical Neighborhood Assumption, we conclude that every point in \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) with scalar curvature greater than 4 has a neighborhood that is either a strong \( {8\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {8\varepsilon } \) -cap.

We claim that \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) has bounded curvature. Indeed, if there is a sequence of points in \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) with curvature going to infinity, then \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) contains a sequence of necks with radii converging to 0 , contradicting Proposition 6.9. This shows that \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) has bounded curvature.

Step 5: We now extend the limit \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time. By Step 4, the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) is bounded from above by a constant \( \Lambda  > 4 \) . We claim that, given any \( A > 1 \) , the parabolic neighborhood

\[
P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right)
\]

is free of surgeries if \( j \) is sufficiently large. To prove this, fix \( A > 1 \) and suppose that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) contains points modified by surgery. Let \( {s}_{j} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }}\right\rbrack \) be the largest number such that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is free of surgeries. The pointwise curvature derivative estimate gives

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{\left. P\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\right) \right) }\operatorname{scal} \leq  {2\Lambda }{Q}_{j}
\]

if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Since the scalar curvature is greater than \( \frac{1}{2}{h}_{j}^{-2} \) at each point modified by surgery, we deduce that \( \frac{1}{2}{h}_{j}^{-2} \leq  {2\Lambda }{Q}_{j} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. In particular, \( {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1} \leq  \frac{1}{10\eta }{h}_{j}^{2} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Since \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \rightarrow  0 \) ,

Proposition 10.5 implies that the parabolic neighborhood

\[
P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right)
\]

is, after dilating by the factor \( {h}_{j} \) , arbitrarily close to a piece of the standard solution when \( j \) is sufficiently large. Using Corollary 9.3, we conclude that \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap when \( j \) is sufficiently large. If \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on an \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, then this neck is actually a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, since we are assuming that each \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \) -neck on which we perform surgery has a large backward parabolic neighborhood that is free of surgeries (cf. Definition 10.1). Moreover, Corollary 9.3 implies that \( \left| {D\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . Therefore, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of Theorem 10.10, and this contradicts statement (iii). Thus, given any \( A > 1 \) , the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is free of surgeries if \( j \) is sufficiently large.

Let \( {\tau }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }}  - \frac{1}{200\eta \Lambda } \) . In view of the preceding discussion, we may extend \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time to a complete solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfies \( {\Lambda }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  {2\Lambda } \) .

We now repeat this process. Suppose that we can extend \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time to a complete solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m},0}\right\rbrack \) , and satisfies \( {\Lambda }_{m} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } < \infty \) . Let \( {\tau }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{200\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} \) . We claim that we can extend the solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) backward to the interval \( \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack \) , and \( {\Lambda }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m} \) .

Indeed, if this is not possible, then there exists a number \( A > 1 \) with the property that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{100\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) contains points modified by surgery for \( j \) sufficiently large. Let \( {s}_{j} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{{100\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}}}\right\rbrack \) be the largest number such that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is free of surgeries. The pointwise curvature derivative estimate gives

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{\left. P\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}\right) \right) }\operatorname{scal} \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m}{Q}_{j}
\]

if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Let us choose \( {\alpha }_{m} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{n - 1}{2}}\right) \) so that \( \frac{{\alpha }_{m}}{{K}_{\text{ stnd }}\left( {1 - \frac{2{\alpha }_{m}}{n - 1}}\right) } \geq \; 8{\Lambda }_{m}\left( {\frac{1}{{100\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} - {\tau }_{m}}\right) \) . If \( \left( {{s}_{j} - {\tau }_{m}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1} \geq  {\alpha }_{m}{h}_{j}^{2} \) for \( j \) sufficiently large, then Proposition 10.5 together with the lower bound for the scalar curvature on the standard solution (cf. Theorem 9.1) gives

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) }}\operatorname{scal} \geq  \frac{1}{2{K}_{\text{ stnd }}\left( {1 - \frac{2{\alpha }_{m}}{n - 1}}\right) }{h}_{j}^{-2}
\]

\[
\geq  \frac{{\alpha }_{m}}{2{K}_{\text{ stnd }}\left( {1 - \frac{2{\alpha }_{m}}{n - 1}}\right) }{\left( {s}_{j} - {\tau }_{m}\right) }^{-1}{Q}_{j}
\]

\[
\geq  4{\Lambda }_{m}{Q}_{j}
\]

for \( j \) sufficiently large, which is impossible. Consequently, \( \left( {{s}_{j} - {\tau }_{m}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1} \leq  {\alpha }_{m}{h}_{j}^{2} \) for \( j \) sufficiently large. Since \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \rightarrow  0 \) , Proposition 10.5 implies that the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is, after dilating by the factor \( {h}_{j} \) , arbitrarily close to a piece of the standard solution when \( j \) is sufficiently large. Using Corollary 9.3, we conclude that \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap when \( j \) is sufficiently large. If \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on an \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, then this neck is actually a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, since we are assuming that each \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \) -neck on which we perform surgery has a large backward parabolic neighborhood that is free of surgeries (cf. Definition 10.1). Moreover, Corollary 9.3 implies that \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . Therefore, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of Theorem 10.10, and this contradicts statement (iii). Thus, we may extend the flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) backward to the interval \( \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack \) , where \( {\tau }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{200\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} \) , and we have \( {\Lambda }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m}. \)

Let \( {\tau }^{ * } = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\tau }_{m} \leq   - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda } \) . Using a standard diagonal sequence argument, we obtain a complete, smooth limit flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined on the interval \( \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) and that has bounded curvature for each \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) .

Step 6: We next show that \( {\tau }^{ * } =  - \infty \) . Indeed, if \( {\tau }^{ * } >  - \infty \) , it follows that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {\tau }_{m + 1}}\right)  = 0 \) , hence \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\Lambda }_{m} = \infty \) . Arguing as in Step 6 in the proof of Theorem 7.2, we can show that the limit flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) has bounded curvature. This contradicts the fact that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\Lambda }_{m} = \infty \) . Thus, \( {\tau }^{ * } =  - \infty \) . Hence, if we dilate the flow \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) around the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) , then (after passing to a subsequence) the rescaled flows converge to an ancient solution that is complete, has bounded curvature, is weakly PIC2, and satisfies \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \oslash \) id \( \in \) PIC. By Proposition 10.9, the limiting ancient solution is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed for some \( \kappa  > 0 \) that depends only on the initial data. By Corollary 6.22, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck with center at \( {x}_{j} \) ; or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap; or a closed manifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) ; or a quotient neck. Recall that we have discarded all connected components that are diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) (see Definition 10.1). Hence, the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) cannot be a closed manifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) . If the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) is a quotient neck, then Theorem A. 1 in [6] implies that the underlying manifold contains a nontrivial incompressible \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional space form, contrary to our assumption. Consequently, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck with center at \( {x}_{j} \) or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap. Finally, Corollary 6.20 implies that \( \left| {D\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\mathrm{{scal}}}^{2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . In summary, we have shown that the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of Theorem 10.10. This contradicts statement (iii). This completes the proof of Theorem 10.10.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
For any \( C < \infty \) the following holds. Suppose that \( X \) is a connected subset of a Riemannian three-manifold \( \left( {M, g}\right) \) . Suppose that every point of \( X \) is either the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck or is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap. Then one of the following holds (see FIG. 4):

(1) \( X \) is contained in a component of \( M \) that is the union of two \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -caps and is diffeomorphic to one of \( {S}^{3},\mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3}\# \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) .

(2) \( X \) is contained in a component of \( M \) that is a double \( C \) -capped \( \epsilon \) -tube. This component is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{3},\mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3}\# \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) .

(3) \( X \) is contained in a single \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap.

(4) \( X \) is contained in a \( C \) -capped \( \epsilon \) -tube.

(5) \( X \) is contained in an \( \epsilon \) -tube.

(6) \( X \) is contained in a component of \( M \) that is an \( \epsilon \) -fibration, which itself is a union of \( \epsilon \) -necks.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
We divide the proof into two cases: Case I: There is a point of \( X \) contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap. Case II: Every point of \( X \) is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck.

Case I: We begin the study of this case with a claim.

CLAIM A.22. It is not possible to have an infinite chain of \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -caps \( {C}_{0} \subset  {C}_{1} \subset  \cdots \) in \( M \) with the property that for each \( i \geq  1 \) , the closure of the core of \( {C}_{i} \) contains a point of the frontier of \( {C}_{i - 1} \)

Proof. We argue by contradiction. Suppose there is such an infinite chain. Fix a point \( {x}_{0} \in  {C}_{0} \) and let \( {Q}_{0} = R\left( {x}_{0}\right) \) . For each \( i \geq  1 \) let \( {x}_{i} \) be a point in the frontier of \( {C}_{i - 1} \) that is contained in the closure of the core of \( {C}_{i} \) . For each \( i \) let \( {N}_{i} \) be the \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( {C}_{i} \) that is the complement of the closure of its core. We orient the \( {s}_{{N}_{i}} \) -direction so that the core of \( {C}_{i} \) lies off the negative end of \( {N}_{i} \) . Let \( {S}_{i}^{\prime } \) be the boundary of the core of \( {C}_{i} \) . It is the central two-sphere of an \( \epsilon \) -neck \( {N}_{i}^{\prime } \) in \( {C}_{i} \) . We orient the \( s \) -direction of \( {N}_{i}^{\prime } \) so that the non-compact end of \( {C}_{i} \) lies off the positive end of \( {N}_{i}^{\prime } \) . We denote by \( {h}_{i - 1} \) the scale of \( {N}_{i - 1} \) and by \( {h}_{i}^{\prime } \) the scale of \( {N}_{i}^{\prime } \) . By Lemma A. 2 the ratio \( {h}_{i - 1}/{h}_{i}^{\prime } \) is between 0.99 and 1.01 . Suppose that \( {S}_{i}^{\prime } \) is disjoint from \( {C}_{i - 1} \) . Then one of the complementary components of \( {S}_{i}^{\prime } \) in \( M \) contains \( {C}_{i - i} \) , and of course, one of the complementary components of \( {S}_{i}^{\prime } \) is the core of \( {C}_{i} \) . These complementary components must be the same, for otherwise \( {C}_{i - 1} \) would be disjoint from the core of \( {C}_{i} \) and hence the intersection of \( {C}_{i - 1} \) and \( {C}_{i} \) would be contained in \( {N}_{i} \) . This cannot happen since \( {C}_{i - 1} \) is contained in \( {C}_{i} \) . Thus, if \( {S}_{i}^{\prime } \) is disjoint from \( {C}_{i - 1} \) , then the core of \( {C}_{i} \) contains \( {C}_{i - 1} \) . This means that the distance from \( {x}_{0} \) to the complement of \( {C}_{i} \) is greater than the distance of \( {x}_{0} \) to the complement of \( {C}_{i - 1} \) by an amount equal to the width of \( {N}_{i} \) . Since the scale of \( {N}_{i} \) is at least \( {C}^{-1/2}R{\left( {x}_{0}\right) }^{-1/2} \) (see (5) of Definition 9.72), it follows from Corollary A. 5 that this width is at least \( 2\left( {0.99}\right) {C}^{-1/2}R{\left( {x}_{0}\right) }^{-1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1} \) .

Next suppose that \( {S}_{i}^{\prime } \) is contained in \( {C}_{i - 1} \) . Then one of the complementary components \( A \) of \( {S}_{i}^{\prime } \) in \( M \) has closure contained in \( {C}_{i - 1} \) . This component cannot be the core of \( {C}_{i} \) since the closure of the core of \( {C}_{i} \) contains a point of the frontier of \( {C}_{i - 1} \) in \( M \) . Thus, \( A \) contains \( {N}_{i} \) . Of course, \( A \neq  {N}_{i} \) since the frontier of \( A \) in \( M \) is \( {S}_{i}^{\prime } \) whereas \( {N}_{i} \) has two components to its frontier in \( M \) . This means that \( {C}_{i} \) does not contain \( A \) , which is a contradiction since \( {C}_{i} \) contains \( {C}_{i - 1} \) and \( A \subset  {C}_{i - 1} \) .

Lastly, we suppose that \( {S}_{i}^{\prime } \) is neither contained in \( {C}_{i - 1} \) nor in its complement. Then \( {S}_{i}^{\prime } \) must meet \( {N}_{i - 1} \) . According to Proposition A. 11 the \( s \) -directions in \( {N}_{i - 1} \) and \( {N}_{i}^{\prime } \) either almost agree or are almost opposite. Let \( x \in  {S}_{i}^{\prime } \cap  \partial {N}_{i - 1} \) so that \( {s}_{{N}_{i}^{\prime }}\left( x\right)  = 0 \) . Move from \( x \) along the \( {s}_{{N}_{i}^{\prime }} \) -direction that moves into \( {N}_{i - 1} \) to a point \( {x}^{\prime } \) with \( \left| {{s}_{{N}_{i}}\left( {x}^{\prime }\right) }\right|  = \left( {0.05}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1} \) . According to Proposition A.11, \( \left( {0.94}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1} < {s}_{{N}_{i - 1}}\left( {x}^{\prime }\right)  < \left( {0.96}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1} \) . Let \( {S}^{\prime }\left( {x}^{\prime }\right) \) be the two-sphere in the neck structure for \( {N}_{i}^{\prime } \) through this point. According to Proposition A.11, \( {S}^{\prime }\left( {x}^{\prime }\right)  \subset  {N}_{i - 1} \) , and \( {S}^{\prime }\left( {x}^{\prime }\right) \) is isotopic in \( {N}_{i - 1} \) to its central two-sphere. One of the complementary components of \( {S}^{\prime }\left( {x}^{\prime }\right) \) in \( {C}_{i} \) , let us call it \( {A}^{\prime } \) , is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) . Also, one of the complementary components \( A \) of \( {S}^{\prime }\left( {x}^{\prime }\right) \) in \( M \) contains the core of \( {C}_{i - 1} \) . As before, since \( {C}_{i - 1} \subset  {C}_{i} \) , the complementary component \( A \) cannot meet \( {C}_{i} \) in \( {A}^{\prime } \) . This means that the \( {s}_{{N}_{i - 1}} \) - and \( {s}_{{N}_{i}^{\prime }} \) -directions almost line up along \( {S}^{\prime }\left( {x}^{\prime }\right) \) . This means that \( {S}^{\prime }\left( {x}^{\prime }\right)  = {s}_{{N}_{i}^{\prime }}^{-1}\left( {-\left( {0.05}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) . Since the diameter of \( {S}^{\prime }\left( {x}^{\prime }\right) \) is less than \( {2\pi }{h}_{i - 1} \) , and since \( {s}_{{N}_{i - 1}}\left( {x}^{\prime }\right)  \geq  \left( {0.94}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1} \) , it follows that \( {S}^{\prime }\left( {x}^{\prime }\right)  \subset  {S}_{{N}_{i - 1}}^{-1}\left( \left( {{0.9}{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \right) \) . Since the distance from \( {S}_{i}^{\prime } \) to the central two-sphere is at least \( \left( {0.99}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1}{h}_{i}^{\prime } \) , It follows from Corollary A. 5 that the central two-sphere of \( {N}_{i} \) is disjoint from \( {C}_{i - 1} \) and lies off the positive end of \( {N}_{i - 1} \) . This implies that the distance from \( {x}_{0} \) to the complement of \( {C}_{i} \) is greater than the distance from \( {x}_{0} \) to the complement of \( {C}_{i - 1} \) by an amount bounded below by the distance from the central two-sphere of \( {N}_{i} \) to its positive end. According to Corollary A. 5 this distance is at least \( \left( {0.99}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1}{h}_{i} \) , where \( {h}_{i} \) is the scale of \( {N}_{i} \) . But we know that \( {h}_{i} \geq  {C}^{-1/2}R{\left( {x}_{0}\right) }^{-1/2} \) .

Thus, all cases either lead to a contradiction or to the conclusion that the distance from \( {x}_{0} \) to the complement of \( {C}_{i} \) is at least a fixed positive amount (independent of \( i \) ) larger than the distance from \( {x}_{0} \) to the complement of \( {C}_{i - 1} \) . Since the diameter of any \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap is uniformly bounded, this contradicts the existence of an infinite chain \( {C}_{0} \subset  {C}_{1} \subset  \cdots \) contrary to the claim. This completes the proof of the claim.

Now let us turn to the proof of the proposition. We suppose first that there is a point \( {x}_{0} \in  X \) that is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap. Applying the previous claim, we can find a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap \( {C}_{0} \) containing \( {x}_{0} \) with the property that no point of \( X \) contained in the frontier of \( {C}_{0} \) is contained in the closure of the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap \( {C}_{1} \) that contains \( {C}_{0} \) .

There are three possibilities to examine:

(i) \( X \) is disjoint from the frontier of \( {C}_{0} \) .

(ii) \( X \) meets the frontier of \( {C}_{0} \) but every point of this intersection is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck.

(iii) There is a point of the intersection of \( X \) with the frontier of \( {C}_{0} \) that is contained in the core of \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap.

In the first case, since \( X \) is connected, it is contained in \( {C}_{0} \) . In the second case we let \( {N}_{1} \) be an \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at a point of the intersection of \( X \) with the frontier of \( {C}_{0} \) , and we replace \( {C}_{0} \) by \( {C}_{0} \cup  {N}_{1} \) and repeat the argument at the frontier of \( {C}_{0} \cup  {N}_{1} \) . We continue in this way creating \( {C}_{0} \) union a balanced chain of \( \epsilon \) -necks \( {C}_{0} \cup  {N}_{1} \cup  {N}_{2} \cup  \cdots  \cup  {N}_{k} \) . At each step it is possible that either there is no point of the frontier containing a point of \( X \) , in which case the union, which is a \( C \) -capped \( \epsilon \) -tube, contains \( X \) . Another possibility is that we can repeat the process forever creating a \( C \) -capped infinite \( \epsilon \) -tube. By Lemma A. 15 this union is a component of \( M \) and hence contains \( X \) .

We have shown that one of following holds:

(a) There is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap that contains \( X \) .

(b) There is a finite or infinite \( C \) -capped \( \epsilon \) -tube that contains \( X \) .

(c) There is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap or a finite \( C \) -capped \( \epsilon \) -tube \( \widetilde{C} \) containing a point of \( X \) and there is a point of the intersection of \( X \) with the frontier of \( \widetilde{C} \) that is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap.

In the first two cases we have established the proposition. Let us examine the third case in more detail. Let \( {N}_{0} \subset  {C}_{0} \) be the \( \epsilon \) -neck that is the complement of the closure of the core of \( {C}_{0} \) . First notice that by Lemma A. 20 the union \( {N}_{0} \cup  {N}_{1} \cup  \cdots  \cup  {N}_{k} \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) , with the two-spheres coming from the \( \epsilon \) -neck structure of each \( {N}_{i} \) being isotopic to the two-sphere factor in this product structure. It follows immediately that \( \widetilde{C} \) is diffeomorphic to \( {C}_{0} \) . Let \( {C}^{\prime } \) be a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap whose core contains a point of the intersection of \( X \) with the frontier of \( \widetilde{C} \) . We use the terminology ’the core of \( {\widetilde{C}}^{\prime } \) to mean \( \widetilde{C} \smallsetminus  {N}_{k} \) . Notice that if \( k = 0 \) , this is exactly the core of \( {C}_{0} \) . To complete the proof of the result we must show that the following hold:

CLAIM A.23. If \( {C}^{\prime } \) is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap whose core contains a point of the frontier of \( \widetilde{C} \) , then \( \widetilde{C} \cup  {C}^{\prime } \) is a component of \( M \) containing \( X \) .

Proof. We suppose that \( \widetilde{C} \) is the union of \( {C}_{0} \) and a balanced chain \( {N}_{0},\ldots ,{N}_{k} \) of \( \epsilon \) -necks. We orient this chain so that \( {C}_{0} \) lies off the negative end of each of the \( {N}_{i} \) . Let \( {S}^{\prime } \) be the boundary of the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) and let \( {N}^{\prime } \) be an \( \epsilon \) -neck contained in \( {C}^{\prime } \) whose central two-sphere is \( {S}^{\prime } \) . We orient the direction \( {s}_{{N}^{\prime }} \) so that the positive direction points away from the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) . The first step in proving this claim is to establish the following.

CLAIM A.24. Suppose that there is a two-sphere \( \sum  \subset  {N}^{\prime } \) contained in the closure of the positive half of \( {N}^{\prime } \) and also contained in \( \widetilde{C} \) . Suppose that \( \sum \) is isotopic in \( {N}^{\prime } \) to the central two-sphere \( {S}^{\prime } \) of \( {N}^{\prime } \) . Then \( \widetilde{C} \cup  {C}^{\prime } \) is a component of \( M \) , a component containing \( X \) .

Proof. \( \sum \) separates \( \widetilde{C} \) into two components: \( A \) , which has compact closure in \( \widetilde{C} \) , and \( B \) , containing the end of \( \widetilde{C} \) . The two-sphere \( \sum \) also divides \( {C}^{\prime } \) into two components. Since \( \sum \) is isotopic in \( {N}^{\prime } \) to \( {S}^{\prime } \) , the complementary component \( {A}^{\prime } \) of \( \sum \) in \( {C}^{\prime } \) with compact closure contains the closure of the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) . Of course, the frontier of \( A \) in \( M \) and the frontier of \( {A}^{\prime } \) in \( M \) are both equal to \( \sum \) . If \( A = {A}^{\prime } \) , then the closure of the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) is contained in the closure of \( A \) and hence is contained in \( \widetilde{C} \) , contradicting our assumption that \( {C}^{\prime } \) contains a point of the frontier of \( \widetilde{C} \) . Thus, \( A \) and \( {A}^{\prime } \) lie on opposite sides of their common frontier. This means that \( \bar{A} \cup  {\bar{A}}^{\prime } \) is a component of \( M \) . Clearly, this component is also equal to \( \widetilde{C} \cup  {C}^{\prime } \) . Since \( X \) is connected and this component contains a point \( {x}_{0} \) of \( X \) , it contains \( X \) . This completes the proof of Claim A.24.

Now we return to the proof of Claim A.23. We consider three cases.

First Subcase: \( {S}^{\prime } \subset  \widetilde{C} \) . In this case we apply Claim A. 24 to see that \( \widetilde{C} \cup  {C}^{\prime } \) is a component of \( M \) containing \( X \) .

Second Subcase: \( {S}^{\prime } \) is disjoint from \( \widetilde{C} \) . Let \( A \) be the complementary component of \( {S}^{\prime } \) in \( M \) containing \( \widetilde{C} \) . The intersection of \( A \) with \( {C}^{\prime } \) is either the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) or is a submanifold of \( {C}^{\prime } \) diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) . The first case is not possible since it would imply that the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) contains \( \widetilde{C} \) and hence contains \( {C}_{0} \) , contrary to the way we chose \( {C}_{0} \) . Thus, the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) and the complementary component \( A \) containing \( \widetilde{C} \) both have \( {S}^{\prime } \) as their frontier and they lie on opposite sides of \( {S}^{\prime } \) . Since the closure of the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) contains a point of the frontier of \( \widetilde{C} \) , it must be the case that \( {S}^{\prime } \) also contains a point of this frontier. By Proposition A.11, the neck \( {N}^{\prime } \subset  {C}^{\prime } \) meets \( {N}_{k} \) and there is a two-sphere \( \sum  \subset  {N}^{\prime } \cap  {N}_{k} \) isotopic in \( {N}^{\prime } \) to \( {S}^{\prime } \) and isotopic in \( {N}_{k} \) to the central two-sphere of \( {N}_{k} \) . Because \( {N}_{k} \subset  \widetilde{C} \) and \( \widetilde{C} \) is disjoint from the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) , we see that \( \sum \) is contained in the positive half of \( {N}^{\prime } \) . Applying Claim A. 24 we see that \( \widetilde{C} \cup  {C}^{\prime } \) is a component of \( M \) containing \( X \) .

Third Subcase: \( {S}^{\prime } \cap  \widetilde{C} \neq  \varnothing \) and \( {S}^{\prime } ⊄ \widetilde{C} \) . Clearly, in this case \( {S}^{\prime } \) contains a point of the frontier of \( \widetilde{C} \) in \( M \) , i.e., a point of the frontier of the positive end of \( {N}_{k} \) in \( M \) . Since \( {N}_{k} \cap  {N}^{\prime } \neq  \varnothing \) , by Lemma A. 2 the scales of \( {N}_{k} \) and \( {N}^{\prime } \) are within \( 1 \pm  {0.01} \) of each other, and hence the diameter of \( {S}^{\prime } \) is at most \( {2\pi } \) times the scale of \( {N}_{k} \) . Since the central two-sphere \( {S}^{\prime } \) of \( {N}^{\prime } \) contains a point in the frontier of the positive end of \( {N}_{k} \) , it follows from Lemma A. 5 that \( {S}^{\prime } \) is contained on the positive side of the central two-sphere of \( {N}_{k} \) and that the frontier of the positive end of \( {N}_{k} \) is contained in \( {N}^{\prime } \) . By Proposition A. 11 there is a two-sphere \( \sum \) in the neck structure for \( {N}^{\prime } \) that is contained in \( {N}_{k} \) and is isotopic in \( {N}_{k} \) to the central two-sphere from that neck structure. Let \( A \) be the complementary component of \( \sum \) in \( M \) that contains \( \widetilde{C} \smallsetminus  {N}_{k} \) . If the complementary component of \( \sum \) that contains \( {C}^{\prime } \smallsetminus  {N}^{\prime } \) is not \( A \) , then \( \widetilde{C} \cup  {C}^{\prime } \) is a component of \( M \) containing \( X \) . Suppose that \( A \) is also the complementary component of \( \sum \) in \( M \) that contains \( {C}^{\prime } \smallsetminus  {N}^{\prime } \) . Of course, \( A \) is contained in the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) . If \( k \geq  1 \) , we see that \( A \) and hence the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) contains \( \widetilde{C} \smallsetminus  {N}_{k} \) , which in turn contains the core of \( {C}_{0} \) . This contradicts our choice of \( {C}_{0} \) . If \( k = 0 \) , then \( {C}_{0} = A \cup  \left( {{N}_{0} \cap  \left( {M \smallsetminus  A}\right) }\right) \) . Of course, \( A \subset  {C}^{\prime } \) . Also, the frontier of \( {N}_{0} \cap  \left( {M \smallsetminus  A}\right) \) in \( M \) is the union of \( A \) and the frontier of the positive end of \( {N}_{0} \) in \( M \) . But we have already established that the frontier of the positive end of \( {N}_{0} \) in \( M \) is contained in \( {N}^{\prime } \) . Since \( A \subset  {C}^{\prime } \) , it follows that all of \( {C}_{0} \) is contained in \( {C}^{\prime } \) . On the other hand, there is a point of the frontier of \( {C}_{0} \) contained in the closure of the core of \( {C}^{\prime } \) . This then contradicts our choice of \( {C}_{0} \) .

This completes the analysis of all the cases and hence completes the proof of Claim A.23.

The last thing to do in this case in order to prove the proposition in Case I is to show that \( \widetilde{C} \cup  {C}^{\prime } \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{3},\mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) , or \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3}\# \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) . The reason for this is that \( \widetilde{C} \) is diffeomorphic to \( {C}_{0} \) ; hence \( \widetilde{C} \) either is diffeomorphic to an open three-ball or to a punctured \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) . Thus, the frontier of \( {C}^{\prime } \) in \( \widetilde{C} \) is a two-sphere that bounds either a compact three-ball or the complement of an open three-ball in \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) . Since \( {C}^{\prime } \) itself is diffeomorphic either to a three-ball or to a punctured \( \mathbb{R}{P}^{3} \) , the result follows.

Case II: Suppose that every point of \( X \) is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck. Then if the two-spheres of these necks separate \( M \) , it follows from Proposition A. 19 that \( X \) is contained in an \( \epsilon \) -tube in \( M \) .

It remains to consider the case when the two-spheres of these necks do not separate \( M \) . As in the case when the 2-spheres separate, we begin building a balanced chain of \( \epsilon \) -necks with each neck in the chain centered at a point of \( X \) . Either this construction terminates after a finite number of steps in a finite \( \epsilon \) -chain whose union contains \( X \) , or it can be continued infinitely often creating an infinite \( \epsilon \) -chain containing \( X \) or at some finite stage (possibly after reversing the indexing and the \( s \) -directions of the necks) we have a balanced \( \epsilon \) -chain \( {N}_{a} \cup  \cdots  \cup  {N}_{b - 1} \) and a point of the intersection of \( X \) with the frontier of the positive end of \( {N}_{b - 1} \) that is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck \( {N}_{b} \) with the property that \( {N}_{b} \) meets the negative end of \( {N}_{a} \) . Intuitively, the chain wraps around on itself like a snake eating its tail. If the intersection of \( {N}_{a} \cap  {N}_{b} \) contains a point \( x \) with \( {s}_{{N}_{a}}\left( x\right)  \geq   - \left( {0.9}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1} \) , then according to Proposition A. 11 the intersection of \( {N}_{a} \cap  {N}_{b} \) is diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{2} \times  \left( {0,1}\right) \) and the two-sphere in this product structure is isotopic in \( {N}_{a} \) to the central two-sphere of \( {N}_{a} \) and is isotopic in \( {N}_{b} \) to the central two-sphere of \( {N}_{b} \) . In this case it is clear that \( {N}_{a} \cup  \cdots  \cup  {N}_{b} \) is a component of \( M \) that is an \( \epsilon \) -fibration.

We examine the possibility that the intersection \( {N}_{a} \cap  {N}_{b} \) contains some points in the negative end of \( {N}_{a} \) but is contained in \( {s}_{{N}_{a}}^{-1}\left( \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1}, - \left( {0.9}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \right) \) . Set \( A = {s}_{{N}_{a}}^{-1}\left( \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1}, - \left( {0.8}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \right) \) . Notice that since \( X \) is connected and \( X \) contains a point in the frontier of the positive end of \( {N}_{a} \) (since we have added at least one neck at this end), it follows that \( X \) contains points in \( {s}_{{N}_{a}}^{-1}\left( s\right) \) for all \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {0,{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) . If there are no points of \( X \) in \( A \) , then we replace \( {N}_{a} \) by an \( \epsilon \) -neck \( {N}_{a}^{\prime } \) centered at a point of \( {s}_{{N}_{a}}^{-1}\left( {\left( {0.15}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1}}\right)  \cap  X \) . Clearly, by Lemma A. 5 \( {N}_{a}^{\prime } \) contains \( {s}_{{N}_{a}}^{-1}\left( {-\left( {0.8}\right) \epsilon  - 1,{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) and is disjoint from \( {s}_{{N}_{a}}^{-1}\left( \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1}, - \left( {0.9}\right) {\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \right. \) , so that \( {N}_{a}^{\prime },{N}_{a + 1},\ldots ,{N}_{b} \) is a chain of \( \epsilon \) -necks containing \( X \) . If there is a point of \( X \cap  A \) , then we let \( {N}_{b + 1} \) be a neck centered at this point. Clearly, \( {N}_{a} \cup  \cdots  \cup  {N}_{b + 1} \) is a component, \( {M}_{0} \) , of \( M \) containing \( X \) . The preimage in the universal covering of \( {M}_{0} \) is a chain of \( \epsilon \) -necks infinite in both directions. That is to say, the universal covering of \( {M}_{0} \) is an \( \epsilon \) -tube. Furthermore, each point in the universal cover of \( {M}_{0} \) is the center of an \( \epsilon \) -neck that is disjoint from all its non-trivial covering translates. Hence, the quotient \( {M}_{0} \) is an \( \epsilon \) -fibration.

We have now completed the proof of Proposition A.21.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
By supposition, for each \( b \) there is a point \( x \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) at which the strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood assumption fails for the parameter \( {r}_{a} \) . We call points at which this condition fails counterexample points. Of course, since \( {r}_{a} \leq  {r}_{i} \) and since the restriction of \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) },{g}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right) \) to \( {\mathbf{t}}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{i}}\right) \right) \) satisfies the hypothesis of the proposition, we see that any counterexample point \( x \) has \( \mathbf{t}\left( x\right)  \geq  {T}_{i} \) . Take a sequence \( {x}_{n} = {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) of counterexample points with \( \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n + 1}\right)  \leq  \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n}\right) \) for all \( n \) that minimizes \( \mathbf{t} \) among all counterexample points in the sense that for any \( \xi  > 0 \) and for any counterexample point \( x \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) eventually \( \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n}\right)  < \mathbf{t}\left( x\right)  + \xi \) . Let \( {t}^{\prime } = {t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{n \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n}\right) \) . Clearly, \( {t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{T}_{i},{T}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right) \) , and by construction the restriction of \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) },{G}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right) \) to \( {\mathbf{t}}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {0,{t}^{\prime }}\right) \right) \) satisfies the \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood assumption with parameter \( {r}_{a} \) . Since the surgery times are discrete, there is \( {t}^{\prime \prime } = {t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime \prime } \) with \( {t}^{\prime } < {t}^{\prime \prime } \leq  {T}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) and a diffeomorphism \( \psi  = {\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) } : {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime \prime }}\right)  \rightarrow  {\mathbf{t}}^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime \prime }}\right) \right) \) compatible with time and the vector field. We view \( {\psi }^{ * }{G}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) as a one-parameter family of metrics \( g\left( t\right)  = {g}_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( t\right) \) on \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime \prime }}\right) \) . By passing to a subsequence we can arrange that \( \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n}\right)  \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime \prime }}\right) \) for all \( n \) . Thus, for each \( n \) there are \( {y}_{n} = {y}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \in  {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) and \( {t}_{n} \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime \prime }}\right) \) with \( \psi \left( {{y}_{n},{t}_{n}}\right)  = {x}_{n} \) . Since \( {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) is a compact 3-manifold, by passing to a further subsequence we can assume that \( {y}_{n} \rightarrow  {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \in  {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) . Of course, \( {t}_{n} \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime } \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{n \rightarrow  \infty }}{x}_{n} = {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b,\right) } \) .

We claim that, for all \( b \) sufficiently large, the strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood assumption with parameter \( {r}_{a} \) fails at \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . Notice that since \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is the limit of a sequence where the strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -neighborhood assumption fails, the points in the sequence converging to \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) have scalar curvature at least \( {r}_{a}^{-2} \) . It follows that \( R\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right)  \geq  {r}_{a}^{-2} \) . Suppose that \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) satisfies the strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood assumption with parameter \( {r}_{a} \) . This means that there is a neighborhood \( U = {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) of \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \in  {M}_{{t}^{\prime }} \) which is a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood of \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . According to Definition 9.78 there are four possibilities. The first two we consider are that \( \left( {U, g\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) }\right) \) is an \( \epsilon \) -round component or a \( C \) -component. In either of these cases, since the defining inequalities given in Definition 9.76 and 9.75 are strong inequalities, all metrics on \( U \) sufficiently close to \( g\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \) in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) - topology satisfy these same inequalities. But as \( n \) tends to \( \infty \) , the metrics \( {\left. g\left( {t}_{n}\right) \right| }_{U} \) converge in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology to \( {\left. g\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) \right| }_{U} \) . Thus, in these two cases, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the metrics \( g\left( {t}_{n}\right) \) on \( U \) are \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood metrics of the same type as \( {\left. g\left( {t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }\right) \right| }_{U} \) . Hence, in either of these cases, for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood of the same type as \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) , contrary to our assumption about the sequence \( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) .

Now suppose that there is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap whose core contains \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . This is to say that \( \left( {U, g\left( {t}^{\prime }\right) }\right) \) is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap whose core contains \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . By Proposition 9.79, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( \left( {U, g\left( {t}_{n}\right) }\right) \) is also a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap with the same core. This core contains \( {y}_{n} \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, showing that \( {x}_{n} \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap for all \( n \) sufficiently large.

Now let us consider the remaining case when \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck. In this case we have an embedding

\[
{\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} : {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \times  \left( {{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } - {R}^{-1}\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) ,{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) }
\]

compatible with time and the vector field and a diffeomorphism \( {f}_{\left( a, b\right) } : {S}^{2} \times \; \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right)  \rightarrow  {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) such that

\[
{\left( {f}_{\left( a, b\right) } \times  \mathrm{{Id}}\right) }^{ * }{\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }}^{ * }\left( {R\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) {G}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right)
\]

is \( \epsilon \) -close in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology to the evolving product metric

\[
{h}_{0}\left( t\right)  \times  d{s}^{2}, - 1 < t \leq  0,
\]

where \( {h}_{0}\left( t\right) \) is a round metric of scalar curvature \( 1/\left( {1 - t}\right) \) on \( {S}^{2} \) and \( d{s}^{2} \) is the Euclidean metric on the interval. Here, there are two subcases to consider.

(i) \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} \) extends backward past \( {t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } - {R}^{-1}\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) .

(ii) There is a flow line through a point \( {y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \in  {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) that is defined on the interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } - {R}^{-1}\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) ,{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) but with the value of the flow line at \( {t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } - {R}^{-1}\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) an exposed point.

Let us consider the first subcase. The embedding \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} \) extends forward in time because of the diffeomorphism \( {\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) } : {M}_{{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime },{t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime \prime }}\right)  \rightarrow  {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) and, by assumption, \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} \) extends backward in time some amount. Thus, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, we can use these extensions of \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} \) to define an embedding \( {\psi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } : {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \times  \left( {\mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }\right)  - {R}^{-1}\left( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }\right) ,\mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }\right) \rbrack  \rightarrow  {\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right. \) compatible with time and the vector field. Furthermore, since the \( {\psi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) converge in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology to \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} \) as \( n \) tends to infinity, the Riemannian metrics \( {\left( {f}_{\left( a, b\right) } \times  \mathrm{{Id}}\right) }^{ * }{\psi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }^{ * }\left( {R\left( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }\right) {G}_{a, b}}\right) \) converge in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology to the pullback \( {\left( {f}_{\left( a, b\right) } \times  \mathrm{{Id}}\right) }^{ * }{\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }}^{ * }\left( {R\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) {G}_{a, b}}\right) \) . Clearly then, for fixed \( \left( {a, b}\right) \) and for all \( n \) sufficiently large the pullbacks of the rescalings of these metrics by \( R\left( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }\right) \) are within \( \epsilon \) in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  1/\epsilon \right\rbrack  } \) -topology of the standard evolving flow \( {h}_{0}\left( t\right)  \times  d{s}^{2}, - 1 < t \leq  0 \) , on the product of \( {S}^{2} \) with the interval. Under these identifications the points \( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) correspond to points

\[
\left( {{p}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) },{s}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }}\right)  \in  {S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right)
\]

where \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{n \rightarrow  \infty }}{s}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } = 0 \) . The last thing we do is to choose diffeomorphisms \( {\varphi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } : \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \) that are the identity near both ends, such that \( {\varphi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) carries 0 to \( {s}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) and such that the \( {\varphi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) converge to the identity in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology for fixed \( \left( {a, b}\right) \) as \( n \) tends to infinity. Then, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the composition

\[
{S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \overset{\operatorname{Id} \times  {\varphi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }}{ \rightarrow  }{S}^{2} \times  \left( {-{\epsilon }^{-1},{\epsilon }^{-1}}\right) \overset{{f}_{\left( a, b\right) }}{ \rightarrow  }U\overset{{\psi }_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) }}{ \rightarrow  }{\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) }
\]

is a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) . This shows that for any \( b \) for which the first subcase holds, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, there is a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{n,\left( {a, b}\right) } \) .

Now suppose that the second subcase holds for all \( b \) . Here, unlike all previous cases, we shall have to let \( b \) vary and we shall prove the result only for \( b \) sufficiently large. We shall show that for all \( b \) sufficiently large, \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap. This will establish the result by contradiction, for as we showed in the previous case, if \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap, then the same is true for the \( {x}_{n} \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, contrary to our assumption.

For the moment fix \( b \) . Set \( {\bar{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) } = {t}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } - {R}_{{G}_{\left( a, b\right) }}{\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) }^{-1} \) . Since, by supposition the embedding \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }} \) does not extend backwards past \( {\bar{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) , it must be the case that \( {\bar{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is a surgery time and furthermore that there is a surgery cap \( {\mathcal{C}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) at this time with the property that there is a point \( {y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \in  {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) such that \( {\psi }_{{U}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\left( {{y}_{\left( a, b\right) }, t}\right) \) converges to a point \( {z}_{\left( a, b\right) } \in  {\mathcal{C}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) as \( t \) tends to \( {\bar{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) from above. (See FIG. 1.) We denote by \( {p}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) the tip of \( {\mathcal{C}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) , and we denote by \( {\bar{h}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) the scale of the surgery at time \( {\bar{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) .

Since the statement that \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap is a scale invariant statement, we are free to replace \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{\left( a, b\right) },{G}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right) \) with \( \left( {{\widetilde{\mathcal{M}}}_{\left( a, b\right) },{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right) \) , which has been rescaled to make \( {\bar{h}}_{\left( a, b\right) } = 1 \) and shifted in time so that \( {\bar{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) } = 0 \) . We denote the new time function by \( \widetilde{\mathbf{t}} \) . (Notice that this rescaling and time-shifting is different from what we usually do. Normally, when we have a base point like \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) we rescale to make its scalar curvature 1 and we shift time to make it be at time 0 . Here we have rescaled based on the scale of the surgery cap rather than \( R\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) .) We set \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } = \; {R}_{{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) and we set \( {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } = \widetilde{\mathbf{t}}\left( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) . Since the initial time of the strong \( \epsilon \) -neck is zero, \( {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } = {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{-1} \) . We denote the flow line backward in time from \( {y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) by \( {y}_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( \widetilde{t}\right) ,0 \leq  \widetilde{t} \leq  {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } \) , so that \( {y}_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }\right)  = {y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . Since \( {U}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck, by our choice of \( \epsilon \) , it follows from Lemma A. 2 and rescaling that \( R\left( {\psi \left( {{y}_{\left( a, b\right) },\widetilde{t}}\right) }\right) \) is within \( \left( {0.01}\right) {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) of \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }/\left( {1 + {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( {{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } - \widetilde{t}}\right) }\right) \) for all \( t \in  \left( {0,{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) . By taking limits as \( t \) approaches 0, we see that \( {R}_{{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\left( {z}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) is within \( \left( {0.01}\right) {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) of \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }/2 \) . Let \( D \) be the universal constant given in Lemma 12.3, so that the scalar curvature at any point of the standard initial metric is at least \( {D}^{-1} \) and at most \( D \) . It follows from the third item in Theorem 13.2 that, since we have rescaled to make the surgery scale 1, for all \( b \) sufficiently large the scalar curvature on the surgery \( {\mathcal{C}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is at least \( {\left( 2D\right) }^{-1} \) and at most \( {2D} \) . \[
{\left( 2D\right) }^{-1} \leq  {R}_{\widetilde{G}\left( {a, b}\right) }\left( {z}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right)  \leq  {2D}.

\[
{\left( 5D\right) }^{-1} \leq  {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \leq  {5D}.

{d}_{0}\left( {{q}_{\left( a, b\right) },{p}_{0}}\right)  < \left( {1.15}\right) {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{-1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1} + \left( {1.05}\right) \left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right) .
\]

Since the standard flow has non-negative curvature, it is a distance nonincreasing flow. Therefore,

\[
{d}_{{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\left( {{q}_{\left( a, b\right) },{p}_{0}}\right)  < \left( {1.15}\right) {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{-1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1} + \left( {1.05}\right) \left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right) .
\]

Suppose that a point \( \left( {q,{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right) \) in the standard solution were the center of a \( {\beta \epsilon }/3 \) -neck, where \( \beta \) is the constant from Proposition 15.2. Of course, for all \( b \) sufficiently large, \( R\left( {q,{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }}\right)  > \left( {0.99}\right) {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . Since \( \beta  < 1/2 \) and \( \epsilon  < \sqrt{5D}\left( {{A}_{0} + 5}\right) /2 \) and \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \leq  {5D} \) , it follows from the above distance estimate that this neck would contain \( \left( {{p}_{0},{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right) \) . But this is impossible: since \( \left( {{p}_{0},{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right) \) is an isolated fixed point of an isometric \( {SO}\left( 3\right) \) -action on the standard flow, all the sectional curvatures at \( \left( {{p}_{0},{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right) \) are equal, and this is in contradiction with estimates on the sectional curvatures at any point of an \( \epsilon \) -neck given in Lemma A.2. We can then conclude from Theorem 12.32 that for all \( b \) sufficiently large, the point \( \left( {{p}_{0},{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right) \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C\left( {{\beta \epsilon }/3}\right) ,{\beta \epsilon }/3}\right) \) -cap \( {Y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) in the \( {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime } \) time-slice of the standard solution. Now note that for all \( b \) sufficiently large, the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{q}_{\left( a, b\right) },{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }}\right) \) is at least \( \left( {0.99}\right) {\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) , since the scalar curvature of \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is equal to \( {Q}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . This implies that the diameter of \( {Y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is at most

\[
\text{ (1.01) }{\widetilde{Q}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{-1/2}C\left( {{\beta \epsilon }/3}\right)  < \left( {1.1}\right) \sqrt{5D}C\left( {{\beta \epsilon }/3}\right) \text{ . }
\]

Since \( B\left( {{p}_{0},0, A}\right) \) contains \( B\left( {{p}_{0},{\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }, A/2}\right) \) , and since \( C > C\left( {{\beta \epsilon }/3}\right) \) , it follows from the definition of \( A \) , the above distance estimate, and the triangle inequality that for all \( b \) sufficiently large \( B\left( {{p}_{0},0, A}\right)  \times  \left\{  {\widetilde{t}}_{\left( a, b\right) }^{\prime }\right\} \) contains \( {Y}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) .

Since \( C > C\left( {{\beta \epsilon }/3}\right)  + 1 \) and since for \( b \) sufficiently large \( {\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) }^{ * }{\widetilde{G}}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) is arbitrarily close to the restriction of the standard solution metric, it follows from Theorem 12.32 and Proposition 9.79 that for all \( b \) sufficiently large, the image \( {\psi }_{\left( a, b\right) }\left( {Y}_{\left( a, b\right) }\right) \) is a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap whose core contains \( {x}_{\left( a, b\right) } \) . As we have already remarked, this contradicts the assumption that no \( {x}_{n} \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood.

This completes the proof in the last case and establishes Lemma 17.2.

Fix \( \rho  > 0 \) . Then for any \( \delta  > 0 \) there is an \( 0 < h = \; h\left( {\delta ,\rho }\right)  \leq  \min \left( {\rho  \cdot  \delta ,\rho /{2C}}\right) \) , implicitly depending on \( r \) and \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) which are fixed, such that for any generalized Ricci flow \( \left( {\mathcal{M}, G}\right) \) defined for \( 0 \leq  t < \; T < \infty \) satisfying Assumptions 11.18 and for any \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn \( \mathcal{H} \) of \( \left( {\Omega , g\left( T\right) }\right) \) with boundary contained in \( {\Omega }_{\rho /{2C}} \) , every point \( x \in  \mathcal{H} \) with \( R\left( {x, T}\right)  \geq  {h}^{-2} \) is the center of a strong \( \delta \) -neck in \( \left( {\widehat{\mathcal{M}},\widehat{G}}\right) \) contained in \( \mathcal{H} \) . Furthermore, there is a point \( y \in  \mathcal{H} \) with \( R\left( y\right)  = {h}^{-2} \) with the property that the central 2-sphere of the \( \delta \) -neck centered at \( y \) cuts off an end of the \( \mathcal{H} \) disjoint from \( {\Omega }_{\rho } \) . See FIG. 4.
