knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
The proof of the first statement is by contradiction. Fix \( \rho  > 0 \) and \( \delta  > 0 \) and suppose that there is no \( 0 < h \leq  \min \left( {\rho  \cdot  \delta ,\rho /{2C}}\right) \) as required. Then there is a sequence of generalized Ricci flows \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) defined for \( 0 \leq  t < {T}_{n} < \infty \) satisfying Assumptions 11.18 and points \( {x}_{n} \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) with \( \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n}\right)  = {T}_{n} \) contained in \( {2\epsilon } \) -horns \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) in \( {\Omega }_{n} \) with boundary contained in \( {\left( {\Omega }_{n}\right) }_{\rho /{2C}} \) with \( {Q}_{n} = R\left( {x}_{n}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) but such that no \( {x}_{n} \) is the center of a strong \( \delta \) -neck in \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) . Form the maximal extensions, \( \left( {{\widehat{\mathcal{M}}}_{n},{\widehat{G}}_{n}}\right) \) , to time \( T \) of the \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) .

CLAIM 11.32. The sequence \( \left( {{\widehat{\mathcal{M}}}_{n},{\widehat{G}}_{n},{x}_{n}}\right) \) satisfies the five hypotheses of Theorem 11.1.

Proof. By our assumptions, hypotheses (1) and (3) of Theorem 11.1 hold for this sequence. Also, we are assuming that any point \( y \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) with \( R\left( y\right)  \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. Since \( R\left( {x}_{n}\right)  = \; {Q}_{n} \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) this means that for all \( n \) sufficiently large, any point \( y \in  {\widehat{\mathcal{M}}}_{n} \) with \( R\left( y\right)  \geq  R\left( {x}_{n}\right) \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. This establishes hypothesis (2) in the statement of Theorem 11.1.

Next, we have:

CLAIM 11.33. For any \( A < \infty \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the ball \( B\left( {{x}_{n},0, A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2}}\right) \) is contained in the \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) and has compact closure in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) .

Proof. Any point \( z \in  \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) has scalar curvature at most \( {16}{C}^{2}{\rho }^{-2} \) and there is a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( z \) . This means that for all \( y \) with \( {d}_{{G}_{n}}\left( {z, y}\right)  < {\epsilon }^{-1}\rho /{2C} \) we have \( R\left( y\right)  \leq  {32}{C}^{2}{\rho }^{-2} \) . Hence, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( {d}_{{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n}, z}\right)  > {\epsilon }^{-1}\rho /{2C} \) , and thus \( {d}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n}, z}\right)  > {Q}_{n}^{1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1}\rho /{2C} \) . This implies that, given \( A < \infty \) , for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( z \notin  {B}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n},0, A}\right) \) . Since this is true for all \( z \in  \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) , it follows that for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( {B}_{{Q}_{n},{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n},0, A}\right)  \subset  {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) . Next, we must show that, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, this ball has compact closure. That is to say, we must show that for every \( A \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large the distance from \( {x}_{n} \) to the end of the horn \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) is greater than \( A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2} \) . If not, then since the curvature at the end of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) goes to infinity for each \( n \) , this sequence would violate Theorem 10.2.

Because \( B\left( {{x}_{n},0, A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2}}\right) \) is contained in a \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn, it is \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed on scales \( \leq  r \) for a universal \( \kappa  > 0 \) and \( r > 0 \) . Also, because every point in the horn is the center of a strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck, for every \( n \) sufficiently large and every \( y \in  B\left( {{x}_{n},0, A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2}}\right) \) the flow is defined on an interval through \( y \) defined for backward time \( R{\left( y\right) }^{-1} \) .

This completes the proof that all the hypotheses of Theorem 11.1 hold and establishes Claim 11.32.

We form a new sequence of generalized Ricci flows from the \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) by translating by \( - {T}_{n} \) , so that the final time-slice is at \( {\mathbf{t}}_{n} = 0 \) , where \( {\mathbf{t}}_{n} \) is the time function for \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) .

Theorem 11.1 implies that, after passing to a subsequence, there is a limit flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) ,\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right) }\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack  ) \) defined for some \( {t}_{0} > 0 \) for the sequence \( \left( {{Q}_{n}{\widehat{\mathcal{M}}}_{n},{Q}_{n}{\widehat{G}}_{n},{x}_{n}}\right) \) . Because of the curvature pinching toward positive assumption, by Theorem 5.33, the limit Ricci flow has non-negative sectional curvature. Of course, \( R\left( {x}_{\infty }\right)  = 1 \) so that the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is non-flat.

CLAIM 11.34. \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is isometric to the product \( \left( {{S}^{2}, h}\right)  \times  \left( {\mathbb{R}, d{s}^{2}}\right) \) , where \( h \) is a metric of non-negative curvature on \( {S}^{2} \) and \( d{s}^{2} \) is the usual Euclidean metric on the real line.

Proof. Because of the fact that the \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) have curvature pinched toward positive, and since \( {Q}_{n} \) tend to \( \infty \) as \( n \) tends to infinity, it follows that the geometric limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) has non-negative curvature. In \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) take a minimizing geodesic ray \( {\alpha }_{n} \) from \( {x}_{n} \) to the end of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) and a minimizing geodesic \( {\beta }_{n} \) from \( {x}_{n} \) to \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) . As we have seen, the lengths of both \( {\alpha }_{n} \) and \( {\beta }_{n} \) tend to \( \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) . By passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the \( {\alpha }_{n} \) converge to a minimizing geodesic ray \( \alpha \) in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) and that the \( {\beta }_{n} \) converge to a minimizing geodesic ray \( \beta \) in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) . Since, for all \( n \) , the union of \( {\alpha }_{n} \) and \( {\beta }_{n} \) forms a piecewise smooth ray in \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) meeting the central 2-sphere of a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{n} \) in a single point and at this point crossing from one side of this 2-sphere to the other, the union of \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) forms a proper, piecewise smooth map of \( \mathbb{R} \) to \( {M}_{\infty } \) that meets the central 2-sphere of a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{\infty } \) in a single point and crosses from one side to the other at the point. This means that \( {M}_{\infty } \) has at least two ends. Since \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) has non-negative curvature, according to Theorem 2.13, this implies that \( {M}_{\infty } \) is a product of a surface with \( \mathbb{R} \) . Since \( M \) has nonnegative curvature, the surface has non-negative curvature. Since \( M \) has positive curvature at least at one point, the surface is diffeomorphic to the 2-sphere.

According to Theorem 11.1, after passing to a subsequence there is a limit flow defined on some interval of the form \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) for \( {t}_{0} > 0 \) . Suppose that, after passing to a subsequence there is a limit flow defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T,0}\right\rbrack \) for some \( 0 < T < \infty \) . It follows that for any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-T,0}\right\rbrack \) , the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is of non-negative curvature and has two ends. Again by Theorem 2.13, this implies that for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-T,0}\right\rbrack \) the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is a Riemannian product of a metric of non-negative curvature on \( {S}^{2} \) with \( \mathbb{R} \) . Thus, by Corollary 4.19 the Ricci flow is a product of a Ricci flow \( \left( {{S}^{2}, h\left( t\right) }\right) \) with the trivial flow on \( \left( {\mathbb{R}, d{s}^{2}}\right) \) . It now follows from Corollary 4.14 that for every \( t \in  ( - T,0\rbrack \) the curvature of \( {g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) \) on \( {S}^{2} \) is positive.

Let \( {M}_{n} \) be the zero time-slice of \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) . Since \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) is the geometric limit of the \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{n}}\right) \) , there is an exhaustive sequence \( {x}_{\infty } \in \; {V}_{1} \subset  {V}_{2} \subset  \cdots \) of open subsets of \( {M}_{\infty } \) with compact closure and embeddings \( {\varphi }_{n} : {V}_{n} \rightarrow  {M}_{n} \) sending \( {x}_{\infty } \) to \( {x}_{n} \) such that \( {\varphi }_{n}^{ * }\left( {{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) converges in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology, uniformly on compact sets, to \( {g}_{\infty } \) .

CLAIM 11.35. For any \( z \in  {M}_{\infty } \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( z \in  {V}_{n} \) , so that \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) \) is defined. Furthermore, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, there is a backward flow line through \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) \) in the generalized Ricci flow \( \left( {{Q}_{n}{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\right) \) defined on the interval \( \left( {-T - \left( {{R}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}^{-1}\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) ,0}\right) /2}\right) ,0}\right) \) . The scalar curvature is bounded above on this entire flow line by \( R\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) ,0}\right) \) .

Proof. Of course, for any compact subset \( K \subset  {M}_{\infty } \) and any \( {t}^{\prime } < T \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( K \subset  {V}_{n} \) , and there is an embedding \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack   \subset \; {Q}_{n}{\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) compatible with time and the vector field. The map \( {\varphi }_{n} \) defines a map \( {Q}_{n}^{-1}{\varphi }_{n} : K \times  \left\lbrack  {-{Q}_{n}^{-1}{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) . Since the scalar curvature of the limit is positive, and hence bounded away from zero on the compact set \( K \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) and since \( {Q}_{n} \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \) tends to infinity, the following is true: For any compact subset \( K \subset  M \) and any \( {t}^{\prime } < T \) , for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the scalar curvature of \( {G}_{n} \) on the image \( {Q}_{n}^{-1}{\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{Q}_{n}^{-1}{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) is greater than \( {r}_{0}^{-2} \) , and hence for all \( n \) sufficiently large, every point in \( {Q}_{n}^{-1}{\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times \; \left\lbrack  {-{Q}_{n}^{-1}{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) . Since having a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood is invariant under rescaling, it follows that for all \( n \) sufficiently large, every point of \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood.

Next we claim that, for all \( n \) sufficiently large and for any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , the point \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck. We have already seen that for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. Of course, since \( {M}_{\infty } \) is non-compact, for \( n \) sufficiently large, the canonical neighborhood of \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) must either be a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap or a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck. We shall rule out the possibility of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap, at least for all \( n \) sufficiently large.

To do this, take \( K \) to be a neighborhood of \( \left( {z,0}\right) \) in the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) with the topology of \( {S}^{2} \times  I \) and with the metric being the product of a positively curved metric on \( {S}^{2} \) with the Euclidean metric on \( I \) . We take \( K \) to be sufficiently large to contain the \( {2C} \) -ball centered at \( \left( {z,0}\right) \) . Because the limit flow is the product of a positively curved flow on \( {S}^{2} \) with the trivial flow on \( \mathbb{R} \) , the flow is distance decreasing. Thus, for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) the subman-ifold \( K \times  \{ t\} \) contains the ball in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) centered at \( \left( {z, t}\right) \) of radius \( {2C} \) . For every \( n \) sufficiently large, consider the submanifolds \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) of \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) \) . Since the metrics \( {\varphi }_{n}^{ * }{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) \) are converging uniformly for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) to the product flow on \( K \) , for all \( n \) sufficiently large and any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , this submanifold contains the \( C \) -ball centered at \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) in \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) \) . Furthermore, the maximal curvature two-plane at any point of \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) is almost tangent to the \( {S}^{2} \) -direction of \( K \) . Hence, by Lemma A. 2 the central 2-sphere of any \( \epsilon \) -neck contained \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) is almost parallel to the \( {S}^{2} \) -factors in the product structure on \( K \) at every point. This implies that the central 2-sphere of any such \( \epsilon \) -neck is isotopic to the \( {S}^{2} \) -factor of \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) . Suppose that \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap \( \mathcal{C} \) . Then \( \mathcal{C} \) is contained in \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) . Consider the \( \epsilon \) -neck \( N \subset  \mathcal{C} \) that is the complement of the core of \( \mathcal{C} \) . Its central 2-sphere, \( \sum \) , is isotopic in \( K \) to the 2-sphere factor of \( K \) , but this is absurd since \( \sum \) bounds a 3-ball in the \( \mathcal{C} \) . This contradiction shows that for all \( n \) sufficiently large and all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , it is not possible for \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) to be contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap. The only other possibility is that for all \( n \) sufficiently large and all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) the point \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) \) .

Fix \( n \) sufficiently large. Since, for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , the point \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck, it follows from Definition 9.78 that for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) we have \( R\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right)  \leq  R\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) ,0}\right) \) (this follows from the fact that the partial derivative in the time-direction of the scalar curvature of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck of scale one is positive and bounded away from 0 \( ) \) . It also follows from Definition 9.78 that the flow near \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , - {t}^{\prime }}\right) \) extends backwards to time

\[
- {t}^{\prime } - {R}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}^{-1}\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( {z,{t}^{\prime }}\right) }\right)  <  - {t}^{\prime } - {R}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}^{-1}\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( {z,0}\right) }\right) ,
\]

with the same inequality for scalar curvature holding for all \( t \) in this extended interval. Applying this for \( {t}^{\prime } < T \) but sufficiently close to \( T \) establishes the last statement in the claim, and completes the proof of the claim.

Let \( {Q}_{0} \) be the upper bound of the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) . By the previous claim, \( {Q}_{0} \) is also an upper bound for the curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( {-{t}^{\prime }}\right) }\right) \) for any \( {t}^{\prime } < T \) . Applying Theorem 11.1 to the flows

\[
\left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) , - {t}^{\prime } - {Q}_{0}^{-1}/2 < t \leq   - {t}^{\prime },
\]

we conclude that there is \( {t}_{0} \) depending only on the bound of the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( {-{t}^{\prime }}\right) }\right) \) , and hence depending only on \( {Q}_{0} \) , such that, after passing to a subsequence the limit flow exists for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime } - {t}_{0}, - {t}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) . Since the limit flow already exists on \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , we conclude that, for this further subsequence, the limit flow exists on \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime } - {t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) . Now apply this with \( {t}^{\prime } = T - {t}_{0}/2 \) . This proves that if, after passing to a subsequence, there is a limit flow defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T,0}\right\rbrack \) , then, after passing to a further subsequence there is a limit flow defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T - {t}_{0}/2,0}\right\rbrack \) where \( {t}_{0} \) depends only on \( {Q}_{0} \) , and in particular, is independent of \( T \) . Repeating this argument with \( T + \left( {{t}_{0}/2}\right) \) replacing \( T \) , we pass to a further subsequence so that the limit flow is defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T - {t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) . Repeating this inductively, we can find a sequence of subsequences so that for the \( n \) subsequence the limit flow is defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T - n{t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) . Taking a diagonal subsequence produces a subsequence for which the limit is defined on \( ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) .

The limit flow is the product of a flow on \( {S}^{2} \) of positive curvature defined for \( t \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) and the trivial flow on \( \mathbb{R} \) . Now, invoking Hamilton’s result (Corollary 9.50), we see that the ancient solution of positive curvature on \( {S}^{2} \) must be a shrinking round \( {S}^{2} \) . This means that the limit flow is the product of the shrinking round \( {S}^{2} \) with \( \mathbb{R} \) , and implies that for all \( n \) sufficiently large there is a strong \( \delta \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{n} \) . This contradiction proves the existence of \( h \) as required.

Now let us establish the last statement in Theorem 11.31. The subset of \( \mathcal{H} \) consisting of all \( z \in  \mathcal{H} \) with \( R\left( z\right)  \leq  {\rho }^{-2} \) is compact (since \( R \) is a proper function), and disjoint from any \( \delta \) -neck of scale \( h \) since \( h < \rho /{2C} \) . On the other hand, for any point \( z \in  \mathcal{H} \) with \( R\left( z\right)  \leq  {\rho }^{-2} \) take a minimal geodesic from \( z \) to the end of \( \mathcal{H} \) . There must be a point \( y \) on this geodesic with \( R\left( y\right)  = {h}^{-2} \) . The \( \delta \) -neck centered at \( y \) is disjoint from \( z \) (since \( h < \rho /{2C} \) ) and hence this neck separates \( z \) from the end of \( \mathcal{H} \) . It now follows easily that there is a point \( y \in  \mathcal{H} \) with \( R\left( y\right)  = {h}^{-2} \) and such that the central 2-sphere of the \( \delta \) -neck centered at \( y \) divides \( \mathcal{H} \) into two pieces with the non-compact piece disjoint from \( {\Omega }_{\rho } \) .

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
(Justification of the canonical neighborhood assumption). Given any small \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there exist decreasing sequences \( 0 < {\widetilde{r}}_{j} < \varepsilon ,{\kappa }_{j} > 0 \) , and \( 0 < {\widetilde{\delta }}_{j} < {\varepsilon }^{2}, j = 1,2,\cdots \) , with the following property. Define the positive function \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) \) on \( \lbrack 0, + \infty ) \) by \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right)  = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{j} \) for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {j - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, j{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) \) . Suppose there is a surgically modified solution, defined on \( \lbrack 0, T) \) with \( T <  + \infty \) , to the Ricci flow which satisfies the following:

(1) it starts on a compact orientable three-manifold with normalized initial metric, and

(2) it has only a finite number of surgeries such that each surgery at a time \( t \in  \left( {0, T}\right) \) is a \( \delta \left( t\right) \) -cutoff surgery with

\[
0 < \delta \left( t\right)  \leq  \min \{ \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) ,\bar{\delta }\left( t\right) \} .
\]

Then on each time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\left( {j - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, j{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack  \bigcap \lbrack 0, T), j = 1,2,\cdots \) , the solution satisfies the \( {\kappa }_{j} \) -noncollapsing condition on all scales less than \( \varepsilon \) and the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) with \( r = {\widetilde{r}}_{j} \) .

Here and in the following, we call a (three-dimensional) surgically modified solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) ,0 \leq  t < T,\kappa \) -noncollapsed at \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) on the scales less than \( \rho \) (for some \( \kappa  > 0,\rho  > 0 \) ) if it satisfies the following property: whenever \( r < \rho \) and

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {r}^{-2}
\]

for all those \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}, r, - {r}^{2}}\right)  = \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {B}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) ,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {r}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , for which the solution is defined, we have

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) }\right)  \geq  \kappa {r}^{3}.
\]

The proof of the proposition is by induction: having constructed our sequences for \( 1 \leq  j \leq  m \) , we make one more step, defining \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m + 1} \) , \( {\kappa }_{m + 1},{\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) , and redefining \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) . In view of the previous lemma, we only need to define \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m + 1} \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) .

In Theorem 7.1.1 we have obtained the canonical neighborhood structure for smooth solutions. When adapting the arguments in the proof of Theorem 7.1.1 to the present surgical solutions, we will encounter the new difficulty of how to take a limit for the surgically modified solutions. The idea to overcome the difficulty consists of two parts. The first part, due to Perelman [104], is to choose \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) small enough to push the surgical regions to infinity in space. (This is the reason why we need to redefine \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) .) The second part is to show that solutions are smooth on some small, but uniform, time intervals (on compact subsets) so that we can apply Hamilton's compactness theorem, since we only have curvature bounds; otherwise Shi's interior derivative estimate may not be applicable. In fact, the second part is more crucial. That is just concerned with the question of whether the surgery times accumulate or not. Our argument will use the canonical neighborhood characterization of the standard solution in Lemma 7.3.5.

We now start to prove the proposition by contradiction. Suppose for sequence of positive numbers \( {r}^{\alpha } \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) , satisfying \( {r}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  0 \) as \( \alpha  \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  \frac{1}{\alpha  \cdot  \beta }\left( { \rightarrow  0}\right) \) , there exist sequences of solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) to the Ricci flow with surgery, where each of them has only a finite number of cutoff surgeries and has a compact orientable normalized three-manifold as initial data, so that the following two assertions hold:

(i) each \( \delta \) -cutoff at a time \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) satisfies \( \delta  \leq  {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) ; and

(ii) the solutions satisfy the statement of the proposition on \( \left\lbrack  {0, m{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) , but violate the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) on \( \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) .

For each solution \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) , we choose \( \bar{t} \) (depending on \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) ) to be the nearly first time for which the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) is violated. More precisely, we choose \( \bar{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) so that the canonical neighborhood assumption with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) and with accuracy parameter \( \varepsilon \) is violated at some \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , however the canonical neighborhood assumption with accuracy parameter \( {2\varepsilon } \) holds on \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . After passing to subsequences, we may assume each \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) is less than the \( \widetilde{\delta } \) in Lemma 7.4.2 with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) when \( \alpha \) is fixed. Then by Lemma 7.4.2 we have uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing on all scales less than \( \varepsilon \) on \( \left\lbrack  {0,\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) with some \( \kappa  > 0 \) independent of \( \alpha ,\beta \) .

Slightly abusing notation, we will often drop the indices \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) .

Let \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) be the rescaled solutions around \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with factors \( R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \left( { \geq  {r}^{-2} \rightarrow   + \infty }\right) \) and shift the times \( \bar{t} \) to zero. We hope to take a limit of the rescaled solutions for subsequences of \( \alpha ,\beta  \rightarrow  \infty \) and show the limit is an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution, which will give the desired contradiction. We divide our arguments into the following six steps.

Step 1. Let \( \left( {y,\widehat{t}}\right) \) be a point on the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) with \( \widetilde{R}\left( {y,\widehat{t}}\right)  \leq  A \) (for some \( A \geq  1 \) ) and \( \widehat{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {-\left( {\bar{t} - \left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) ,0}\right\rbrack \) . Then we have estimate

(7.4.14)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10A}
\]

for those \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {y,\widehat{t},\frac{1}{2}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-1}}\right)  \triangleq \; \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {y,\frac{1}{2}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {\widehat{t} - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-1},\widehat{t}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , for which the rescaled solution is defined.

Indeed, as in the first step of the proof of Theorem 7.1.1, this follows directly from the gradient estimates (7.3.4) in the canonical neighborhood assumption with parameter \( {2\varepsilon } \) .

Step 2. In this step, we will prove three time extension results.

Assertion 1. For arbitrarily fixed \( \alpha ,0 < A <  + \infty ,1 \leq  C <  + \infty \) and \( 0 \leq  B < \frac{1}{2}{\varepsilon }^{2}{\left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{C}^{-1} \) , there is a \( {\beta }_{0} = {\beta }_{0}\left( {\varepsilon , A, B, C}\right) \) (independent of \( \alpha \) ) such that if \( \beta  \geq  {\beta }_{0} \) and the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) on the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) is defined on a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack \) with \( 0 \leq  b \leq  B \) and the scalar curvature satisfies

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C,\;\text{ on }{\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack  ,
\]

then the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) on the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) is also defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{C}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) .

Before giving the proof, we make a simple observation: once a space point in the Ricci flow with surgery is removed by surgery at some time, then it never appears for later time; if a space point at some time \( t \) cannot be defined before the time \( t \) , then either the point lies in a gluing cap of the surgery at time \( t \) or the time \( t \) is the initial time of the Ricci flow.

Proof of Assertion 1. Firstly we claim that there exists \( {\beta }_{0} = {\beta }_{0}\left( {\varepsilon , A, B, C}\right) \) such that when \( \beta  \geq  {\beta }_{0} \) , the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) on the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) can be defined before the time \( - b \) (i.e., there are no surgeries interfering in \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-b - {\epsilon }^{\prime }, - b}\right\rbrack \) for some \( \left. {{\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0}\right) \) .

We argue by contradiction. Suppose not, then there is some point \( \widetilde{x} \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) such that the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) at \( \widetilde{x} \) cannot be defined before the time \( - b \) . By the above observation, there is a surgery at the time \( - b \) such that the point \( \widetilde{x} \) lies in the instant gluing cap.

Let \( \widetilde{h}\left( { = R{\left( \bar{x},\bar{t}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}h}\right) \) be the cut-off radius at the time \( - b \) for the rescaled solution. Clearly, there is a universal constant \( D \) such that \( {D}^{-1}\widetilde{h} \leq  \widetilde{R}{\left( \widetilde{x}, - b\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  D\widetilde{h} \) .

By Lemma 7.3.4 and looking at the rescaled solution at the time \( - b \) , the gluing cap and the adjacent \( \delta \) -neck, of radius \( \widetilde{h} \) , constitute a \( {\left( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \) -cap \( \mathcal{K} \) . For any fixed small positive constant \( {\delta }^{\prime } \) (much smaller than \( \varepsilon \) ), we see that

\[
{\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{R}{\left( \widetilde{x}, - b\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \subset  \mathcal{K}
\]

when \( \beta \) large enough. We first verify the following

CLAIM 1. For any small constants \( 0 < \widetilde{\theta } < 1,{\delta }^{\prime } > 0 \) , there exists a \( \beta \left( {{\delta }^{\prime },\varepsilon ,\widetilde{\theta }}\right)  > 0 \) such that when \( \beta  \geq  \beta \left( {{\delta }^{\prime },\varepsilon ,\widetilde{\theta }}\right) \) , we have

(i) the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) over \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \cap  \left\lbrack  {-b, - b + \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2}}\right\rbrack \)

(ii) the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) in the \( {\left( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \) -cap \( \mathcal{K} \) evolved by the Ricci flow on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \cap  \left\lbrack  {-b, - b + \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) is, after scaling with factor \( {\widetilde{h}}^{-2} \) , \( {\delta }^{\prime } \) -close (in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  {\delta }^{\prime  - 1}\right\rbrack  } \) topology) to the corresponding subset of the standard solution.

This claim essentially follows from Lemma 7.3.6. Indeed, suppose there is a surgery at some time \( \widetilde{\widetilde{t}} \in  \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \cap  \left( {-b, - b + \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) which removes some point \( \widetilde{\widetilde{x}} \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) . We assume \( \widetilde{\widetilde{t}} \in  ( - b,0\rbrack \) is the first time with that property.

Then by Lemma 7.3.6, there is a \( \bar{\delta } = \bar{\delta }\left( {{\delta }^{\prime },\varepsilon ,\widetilde{\theta }}\right) \) such that if \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } < \bar{\delta } \) , then the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) in the \( {\left( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta }\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}} \) -cap \( \mathcal{K} \) evolved by the Ricci flow on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,\widetilde{\widetilde{t}}}\right) \) is, after scaling with factor \( {\widetilde{h}}^{-2},{\delta }^{\prime } \) -close to the corresponding subset of the standard solution. Note that the metrics for times in \( \lbrack  - b,\widetilde{\widetilde{t}}) \) on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) are equivalent. By Lemma 7.3.6, the solution on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) keeps looking like a cap for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-b,\widetilde{\widetilde{t}}}\right\rbrack \) . On the other hand, by the definition, the surgery is always done along the middle two-sphere of a \( \delta \) -neck with \( \delta  < {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) . Then for \( \beta \) large, all the points in \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) are removed (as a part of a capped horn) at the time \( \widetilde{\widetilde{t}} \) . But \( \widetilde{x} \) (near the tip of the cap) exists past the time \( \widetilde{\widetilde{t}} \) . This is a contradiction. Hence we have proved that \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \cap  \left\lbrack  {-b, - b + \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2}}\right\rbrack \) .

The \( {\delta }^{\prime } \) -closeness of the solution on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}h}\right)  \times  \left( {\left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \cap  \left\lbrack  {-b, - b + \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2}}\right\rbrack  }\right) \) with the corresponding subset of the standard solution follows from Lemma 7.3.6. Then we have proved Claim 1.

We next verify the following

CLAIM 2. There is \( \widetilde{\theta } = \widetilde{\theta }\left( {CB}\right) ,0 < \widetilde{\theta } < 1 \) , such that \( b \leq  \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2} \) when \( \beta \) large.

Note from Proposition 7.3.3, there is a universal constant \( {D}^{\prime } > 0 \) such that the standard solution satisfies the following curvature estimate

\[
R\left( {y, s}\right)  \geq  \frac{2{D}^{\prime }}{1 - s}.
\]

We choose \( \widetilde{\theta } = {D}^{\prime }/2\left( {{D}^{\prime } + {CB}}\right) \) . Then for \( \beta \) large enough, the rescaled solution satisfies

(7.4.15)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  \frac{{D}^{\prime }}{1 - \left( {t + b}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{-2}}{\widetilde{h}}^{-2}
\]

on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right)  \times  \left( {\left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \cap  \left\lbrack  {-b, - b + \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2}}\right\rbrack  }\right) \) .

Suppose \( b \geq  \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2} \) . Then by combining with the assumption \( \widetilde{R}\left( {\widetilde{x}, t}\right)  \leq  C \) for \( t = \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2} - b \) , we have

\[
C \geq  \frac{{D}^{\prime }}{1 - \left( {t + b}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{-2}}{\widetilde{h}}^{-2},
\]

and then

\[
1 \geq  \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) \left( {1 + \frac{{D}^{\prime }}{CB}}\right) .
\]

This is a contradiction. Hence we have proved Claim 2.

The combination of the above two claims shows that there is a positive constant \( 0 < \widetilde{\theta } = \widetilde{\theta }\left( {CB}\right)  < 1 \) such that for any small \( {\delta }^{\prime } > 0 \) , there is a positive \( \beta \left( {{\delta }^{\prime },\varepsilon ,\widetilde{\theta }}\right) \) such that when \( \beta  \geq  \beta \left( {{\delta }^{\prime },\varepsilon ,\widetilde{\theta }}\right) \) , we have \( b \leq  \left( {1 - \widetilde{\theta }}\right) {\widetilde{h}}^{2} \) and the rescaled solution in the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h}}\right) \) on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack \) is, after scaling with factor \( {\widetilde{h}}^{-2},{\delta }^{\prime } \) -close (in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  {\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\right\rbrack  } \) topology) to the corresponding subset of the standard solution.

By (7.4.15) and the assumption \( \widetilde{R} \leq  C \) on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack \) , we know that the cut-off radius \( \widetilde{h} \) at the time \( - b \) for the rescaled solution satisfies

\[
\widetilde{h} \geq  \sqrt{\frac{{D}^{\prime }}{C}}.
\]

Let \( {\delta }^{\prime } > 0 \) be much smaller than \( \varepsilon \) and \( \min \left\{  {{A}^{-1}, A}\right\} \) . Since \( {\widetilde{d}}_{0}\left( {\widetilde{x},\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  A \) , it follows that there is constant \( C\left( \widetilde{\theta }\right) \) depending only on \( \widetilde{\theta } \) such that \( {\widetilde{d}}_{\left( -b\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  C\left( \widetilde{\theta }\right) A \ll \; {\left( {\delta }^{\prime }\right) }^{-1}\widetilde{h} \) . We now apply Lemma 7.3.5 with the accuracy parameter \( \varepsilon /2 \) . Let \( C\left( {\varepsilon /2}\right) \) be the positive constant in Lemma 7.3.5. Without loss of generality, we may assume the positive constant \( {C}_{1}\left( \varepsilon \right) \) in the canonical neighborhood assumption is larger than \( {4C}\left( {\varepsilon /2}\right) \) . When \( {\delta }^{\prime }\left( { > 0}\right) \) is much smaller than \( \varepsilon \) and \( \min \left\{  {{A}^{-1}, A}\right\} \) , the point \( \bar{x} \) at the time \( \bar{t} \) has a neighborhood which is either a \( \frac{3}{4}\varepsilon \) -cap or a \( \frac{3}{4}\varepsilon \) -neck.

Since the canonical neighborhood assumption with accuracy parameter \( \varepsilon \) is violated at \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , the neighborhood of the point \( \bar{x} \) at the new time zero for the rescaled solution must be a \( \frac{3}{4}\varepsilon \) -neck. By Lemma 7.3.5 (b), we know the neighborhood is the slice at the time zero of the parabolic neighborhood

\[
P\left( {\bar{x},0,\frac{4}{3}{\varepsilon }^{-1}\widetilde{R}{\left( \bar{x},0\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \min \left\{  {\widetilde{R}{\left( \bar{x},0\right) }^{-1}, b}\right\}  }\right)
\]

(with \( \widetilde{R}\left( {\bar{x},0}\right)  = 1 \) ) which is \( \frac{3}{4}\varepsilon \) -close (in the \( {C}^{\left\lbrack  \frac{4}{3}{\varepsilon }^{-1}\right\rbrack  } \) topology) to the corresponding subset of the evolving standard cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) over the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-\min \{ b,1\} ,0}\right\rbrack \) with scalar curvature 1 at the time zero. If \( b \geq  1 \) , the \( \frac{3}{4}\varepsilon \) -neck is strong, which is a contradiction. While if \( b < 1 \) , the \( \frac{3}{4}\varepsilon \) -neck at time \( - b \) is contained in the union of the gluing cap and the adjacent \( \delta \) -neck where the \( \delta \) -cutoff surgery took place. Since \( \varepsilon \) is small (say \( \varepsilon  < 1/{100} \) ), it is clear that the point \( \bar{x} \) at time \( - b \) is the center of an \( \varepsilon \) -neck which is entirely contained in the adjacent \( \delta \) -neck. By the proof of Lemma 7.3.2, the adjacent \( \delta \) -neck approximates an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. Indeed, let \( {t}_{\ell } \) be a sequence of positive numbers such that \( {t}_{\ell } \rightarrow  {t}_{\max } \) and there exist smooth limits \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\ell }^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) defined on \( \left( {-{t}_{\ell },0}\right\rbrack \) . For each \( \ell \) , the limit has nonnegative sectional curvature and has bounded curvature at each time slice. Moreover by the gradient estimate in canonical neighborhood assumption with accuracy parameter \( {2\varepsilon } \) , the limit has bounded curvature on each subinterval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack   \subset  \left( {-{t}_{\ell },0}\right\rbrack \) . Denote by \( \widetilde{Q} \) the scalar curvature upper bound of the limit at time zero \( \left( {\widetilde{Q}\text{ is independent of }}\right. \ell ) \) . Then we can apply Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality (Corollary 2.5.5) to get

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\ell }^{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \frac{{t}_{\ell }}{t + {t}_{\ell }}\widetilde{Q}
\]

where \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\ell }^{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right) \) are the scalar curvatures of the limits \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{\ell }^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) . Hence by the definition of convergence and the above curvature estimates, we can find a subsequence of the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) which converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a smooth limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) on the maximal time interval \( \left( {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) .

We need to show \( - {t}_{\max } =  - \infty \) . Suppose \( - {t}_{\max } >  - \infty \) , there are only the following two possibilities: either

(1) The curvature of the limiting solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) becomes unbounded as \( t \searrow   - {t}_{\max } \) ; or

(2) For each small constant \( \theta  > 0 \) and each large integer \( {k}_{0} > 0 \) , there is some \( k \geq \; {k}_{0} \) such that the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) has a surgery time \( {T}_{k} \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \theta ,0}\right\rbrack \) and a surgery point \( {x}_{k} \) lying in a gluing cap at the times \( {T}_{k} \) so that \( {d}_{{T}_{k}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},\bar{x}}\right) \) is uniformly bounded from above by a constant independent of \( \theta \) and \( {k}_{0} \) .

We next claim that the possibility (1) always occurs. Suppose not; then the curvature of the limiting solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , t}\right) }\right) \) is bounded on \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left( {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) by some positive constant \( \widehat{C} \) . In particular, for any \( A > 0 \) , there is a sufficiently large integer \( {k}_{1} > 0 \) such that any rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) with \( k \geq  {k}_{1} \) on the geodesic ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) and its scalar curvature is bounded by \( 2\widehat{C} \) there. (Here, without loss of generality, we may assume that the upper bound \( \widehat{C} \) is so large that \( - {t}_{\max } + \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1} < 0 \) .) By Assertion 1 in Step 2, for \( k \) large enough, the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) over \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) can be defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) and has the scalar curvature \( \widetilde{R} \leq  {10}\widehat{C} \) on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . So we can extract a smooth limit from the sequence to get the limiting solution which is defined on a larger time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1}{\widehat{C}}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . This contradicts the definition of the maximal time \( - {t}_{\max } \) .

It remains to exclude the possibility (1).

By using Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality (Corollary 2.5.5) again, we have

\[
{\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \frac{{t}_{\max }}{t + {t}_{\max }}\widetilde{Q}.
\]

So we only need to control the curvature near \( - {t}_{\max } \) . Exactly as in Step 4 in the proof of Theorem 7.1.1, it follows from Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality that

(7.4.16)

\[
{\widetilde{d}}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  {\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  {\widetilde{d}}_{0}\left( {x, y}\right)  + {30}{t}_{\max }\sqrt{\widetilde{Q}}
\]

for any \( x, y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and \( t \in  \left( {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) .

Since the infimum of the scalar curvature is nondecreasing in time, we have some point \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {M}_{\infty } \) and some time \( - {t}_{\max } < {t}_{\infty } <  - {t}_{\max } + \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1} \) such that \( {\widetilde{R}}_{\infty }\left( {{y}_{\infty },{t}_{\infty }}\right)  < \; 5/4 \) . By (7.4.16), there is a constant \( {\widetilde{A}}_{0} > 0 \) such that \( {\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {\bar{x},{y}_{\infty }}\right)  \leq  {\widetilde{A}}_{0}/2 \) for all \( t \in  \left( {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) .

Now we come back to the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) . Clearly, for arbitrarily given small \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) , when \( k \) large enough, there is a point \( {y}_{k} \) in the underlying manifold of \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) at time 0 satisfying the following properties

(7.4.17)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {{y}_{k},{t}_{\infty }}\right)  < \frac{3}{2},\;{\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {\bar{x},{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  {\widetilde{A}}_{0}
\]

for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) . By the definition of convergence, we know that for any fixed \( {A}_{0} \geq  2{\widetilde{A}}_{0} \) , for \( k \) large enough, the rescaled solution over \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{A}_{0}}\right) \) is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\infty },0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfies

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \frac{2{t}_{\max }}{t + {t}_{\max }}\widetilde{Q}
\]

on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x},{A}_{0}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{\infty },0}\right\rbrack \) . Then by Assertion 2 of Step 2, we have proved that there is a sufficiently large integer \( {\bar{k}}_{0} \) such that when \( k \geq  {\bar{k}}_{0} \) , the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) at \( {y}_{k} \) can be defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) , and satisfy

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {{y}_{k}, t}\right)  \leq  {15}
\]

for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack \) .

We now prove a statement analogous to Assertion 4 (i) of Step 3.

Assertion 5. For the above rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) and \( {\bar{k}}_{0} \) , we have that for any \( L > 0 \) , there is a positive constant \( \omega \left( L\right) \) such that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) satisfy

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  \omega \left( L\right)
\]

for all \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) with \( {\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {x,{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  L \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack \) , and for all \( k \geq  {\bar{k}}_{0} \) .

Proof of Assertion 5. We slightly modify the argument in the proof of Assertion 4 (i). Let

\[
M\left( \rho \right)  = \sup \left\{  {\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \mid  {\widetilde{d}}_{t}\left( {x,{y}_{k}}\right)  \leq  \rho }\right. \text{ and }t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
\text{ in the rescaled solutions }\left. {{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}}, k \geq  {\bar{k}}_{0}}\right\}
\]

and

\[
{\rho }_{0} = \sup \{ \rho  > 0 \mid  M\left( \rho \right)  <  + \infty \} .
\]

Note that the estimate (7.4.14) implies that \( {\rho }_{0} > 0 \) . We only need to show \( {\rho }_{0} =  + \infty \) .

We argue by contradiction. Suppose \( {\rho }_{0} <  + \infty \) . Then, after passing to a subsequence, there is a sequence \( \left( {{\widetilde{y}}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) in the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) with \( {t}_{k} \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{50}{\eta }^{-1},{t}_{\infty }}\right\rbrack \) and \( {\widetilde{d}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},{\widetilde{y}}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} <  + \infty \) such that \( \widetilde{R}\left( {{\widetilde{y}}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) . Denote by \( {\gamma }_{k} \) a minimizing geodesic segment from \( {y}_{k} \) to \( {\widetilde{y}}_{k} \) at the time \( {t}_{k} \) and denote by \( {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) the open geodesic ball centered at \( {y}_{k} \) of radius \( {\rho }_{0} \) on the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{k}}\right) \) .

For any \( 0 < \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) with \( \rho \) near \( {\rho }_{0} \) , by applying Assertion 3 as before, we get that the rescaled solutions on the balls \( {B}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},\rho }\right) \) are defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - \frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}M{\left( \rho \right) }^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) for all large \( k \) . By Step 1 and Shi’s derivative estimate, we further know that the covariant derivatives and higher order derivatives of the curvatures on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},\rho  - \frac{\left( {\rho }_{0} - \rho \right) }{2}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - \frac{1}{32}{\eta }^{-1}M{\left( \rho \right) }^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) are also uniformly bounded. Then by the uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing property and Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), after passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the marked sequence \( \left( {{\widetilde{B}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{k}}\right) ,{y}_{k}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a marked (noncomplete) manifold \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty },{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) and the geodesic segments \( {\gamma }_{k} \) converge to a geodesic segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {B}_{\infty } \) emanating from \( {y}_{\infty } \) .

Clearly, the limit also has nonnegative sectional curvature by the pinching assumption. Then by repeating the same argument as in the proof of Assertion 4 (i) in the rest, we derive a contradiction with Hamilton's strong maximum principle. This proves Assertion 5.

We then apply the second estimate of (7.4.17) and Assertion 5 to conclude that for any large constant \( 0 < A <  + \infty \) , there is a positive constant \( C\left( A\right) \) such that for any small \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) , the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) satisfy

(7.4.18)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C\left( A\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , and for all sufficiently large \( k \) . Then by applying Assertion 1 in Step 2, we conclude that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) on the geodesic balls \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) are also defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime } - }\right. \; \left. {\frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) for all sufficiently large \( k \) . Furthermore, by the gradient estimates as in Step 1, we have

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10C}\left( A\right)
\]

for \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime } - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . Since \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) is arbitrarily small and the positive constant \( C\left( A\right) \) is independent of \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \) , we conclude that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) are defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - }\right. \; \left. {\frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfy

(7.4.19)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10C}\left( A\right) ,
\]

for \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) , and for all sufficiently large \( k \) .

Now, by taking convergent subsequences from the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) , we see that the limit solution is defined smoothly on a space-time open subset of \( {M}_{\infty } \times \; ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) containing \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) . By Step 4, we see that the limiting metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , - {t}_{\max }}\right) \) at time \( - {t}_{\max } \) has bounded curvature. Then by combining with the canonical neighborhood assumption of accuracy \( {2\varepsilon } \) , we conclude that the curvature of the limit is uniformly bounded on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) . So we have excluded the possibility (1).

Hence we have proved a subsequence of the rescaled solutions converges to an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution.

Finally by combining with the canonical neighborhood theorem (Theorem 6.4.6), we see that \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) has a canonical neighborhood with parameter \( \varepsilon \) , which is a contradiction. Therefore we have completed the proof of the proposition. 0

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Vanishing Asymptotic Volume Ratio for Nonflat Ancient Solutions
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \( M \) be an \( n \) -dimensional complete noncompact Riemannian manifold. Suppose \( {g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) , x \in  M \) and \( t \in  \left( {-\infty , T}\right) \) with \( T > 0 \) , is a nonflat ancient solution of the Ricci flow with nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature. Then the asymptotic volume ratio of the solution metric satisfies

\[
{\nu }_{M}\left( t\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{r \rightarrow   + \infty }}\frac{{\operatorname{Vol}}_{t}\left( {{B}_{t}\left( {O, r}\right) }\right) }{{r}^{n}} = 0
\]

for each \( t \in  \left( {-\infty , T}\right) \) .

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
The proof is by induction on the dimension. When the dimension is two, the lemma is valid by Theorem 6.2.2. For dimension \( \geq  3 \) , we argue by contradiction.

Suppose the lemma is valid for dimensions \( \leq  n - 1 \) and suppose \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) for some \( n \) -dimensional nonflat ancient solution with nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature at some time \( {t}_{0} \leq  0 \) . Fixing a point \( {x}_{0} \in  M \) , we consider the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio

\[
A = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty }}R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right) .
\]

We divide the proof into three cases.

Case 1: \( A =  + \infty \) .

By Lemma 6.1.3, there exist sequences of points \( {x}_{k} \in  M \) divergent to infinity, of radii \( {r}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) , and of positive constants \( {\delta }_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) such that

(i) \( R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{k}}\right) R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) \) for all \( x \) in the ball \( {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{k}}\right) \) of radius \( {r}_{k} \) around \( {x}_{k} \) ,

(ii) \( {r}_{k}^{2}R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) ,

(iii) \( {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right) /{r}_{k} \rightarrow   + \infty \) .

By scaling the solution around the points \( {x}_{k} \) with factor \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) \) , and shifting the time \( {t}_{0} \) to the new time zero, we get a sequence of rescaled solutions

\[
{g}_{k}\left( s\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0} + \frac{s}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right)
\]

to the Ricci flow. Since the ancient solution has nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature, there holds the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality (Corollary 2.5.5). Thus the rescaled solutions satisfy

\[
{R}_{k}\left( {x, s}\right)  \leq  \left( {1 + {\delta }_{k}}\right)
\]

for all \( s \leq  0 \) and \( x \in  {B}_{{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\left( {{x}_{k},{r}_{k}\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) \) . Since \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) , it follows from the standard volume comparison and Theorem 4.2.2 that the injectivity radii of the rescaled solutions \( {g}_{k} \) at the points \( {x}_{k} \) and the new time zero is uniformly bounded below by a positive number. Then by Hamilton's compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), after passing to a subsequence, \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( s\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) will converge to a solution \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( s\right) , O}\right) \) to the Ricci flow with

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {y, s}\right)  \leq  1\text{ , for all }s \leq  0\text{ and }y \in  \widetilde{M}\text{ , }
\]

and

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {O,0}\right)  = 1\text{ . }
\]

Since the metric is shrinking, by (ii) and (iii), we get

\[
R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0} + \frac{s}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) }^{2}\left( {{x}_{0},{x}_{k}}\right)  \geq  R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }^{2}\left( {{x}_{0},{x}_{k}}\right)
\]

which tends to \( + \infty \) , as \( k \rightarrow   + \infty \) , for all \( s \leq  0 \) . Thus by Proposition 6.1.2, for each \( s \leq  0,\left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( s\right) }\right) \) splits off a line. We now consider the lifting of the solution \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( s\right) }\right) , s \leq  0 \) , to its universal cover and denote it by \( \left( {\widetilde{\widetilde{M}},\widetilde{\widetilde{g}}\left( s\right) }\right) , s \leq  0 \) . Clearly we still have

\[
{\nu }_{\widetilde{M}}\left( 0\right)  > 0\text{ and }{\nu }_{\widetilde{\widetilde{M}}}\left( 0\right)  > 0\text{ . }
\]

By applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle and the de Rham decomposition theorem, the universal cover \( \widetilde{\widetilde{M}} \) splits isometrically as \( X \times  \mathbb{R} \) for some \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) - dimensional nonflat (complete) ancient solution \( X \) with nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature. These imply that \( {\nu }_{X}\left( 0\right)  > 0 \) , which contradicts the induction hypothesis.

Case 2: \( 0 < A <  + \infty \) .

Take a sequence of points \( {x}_{k} \) divergent to infinity such that

\[
R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  \rightarrow  A,\text{ as }k \rightarrow   + \infty .
\]

Consider the rescaled solutions \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( s\right) }\right) \) (around the fixed point \( {x}_{0} \) ), where

\[
{g}_{k}\left( s\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0} + \frac{s}{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) , s \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack .
\]

Then there is a constant \( C > 0 \) such that

(6.3.1)

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} {R}_{k}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  C/{d}_{k}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0},0}\right) , \\  {R}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},0}\right)  = 1, \\  {d}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0},0}\right)  \rightarrow  \sqrt{A} > 0, \end{array}\right.
\]

where \( {d}_{k}\left( {\cdot ,{x}_{0},0}\right) \) is the distance function from the point \( {x}_{0} \) in the metric \( {g}_{k}\left( 0\right) \) .

Since \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) , it is a basic result in Alexandrov space theory (see for example Theorem 7.6 of [20]) that a subsequence of \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( s\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) converges in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense to an \( n \) -dimensional metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) with vertex \( {x}_{0} \) .

By (6.3.1), the standard volume comparison and Theorem 4.2.2, we know that the injectivity radius of \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) at \( {x}_{k} \) is uniformly bounded from below by a positive number \( {\rho }_{0} \) . After taking a subsequence, we may assume \( {x}_{k} \) converges to a point \( {x}_{\infty } \) in \( M \smallsetminus  \left\{  {x}_{0}\right\} \) . Then by Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), we can take a subsequence such that the metrics \( {g}_{k}\left( s\right) \) on the metric balls \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{k},\frac{1}{2}{\rho }_{0}}\right) \left( { \subset  M}\right. \) with respect to the metric \( {g}_{k}\left( 0\right) ) \) converge in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a solution of the Ricci flow on a ball \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{\infty },\frac{1}{2}{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) . Clearly the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) limit has nonnegative curvature operator and it is a piece of the metric cone at the time \( s = 0 \) . By (6.3.1), we have

(6.3.2)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right)  = 1
\]

Let \( x \) be any point in the limiting ball \( {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{\infty },\frac{1}{2}{\rho }_{0}}\right) \) and \( {e}_{1} \) be any radial direction at \( x \) . Clearly \( \widetilde{\operatorname{Ric}}\left( {{e}_{1},{e}_{1}}\right)  = 0 \) . Recall that the evolution equation of the Ricci tensor in frame coordinates is

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\widetilde{R}}_{ab} = \widetilde{\bigtriangleup }{\widetilde{R}}_{ab} + 2{\widetilde{R}}_{acbd}{\widetilde{R}}_{cd}.
\]

Since the curvature operator is nonnegative, by applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle (Theorem 2.2.1) to the above equation, we deduce that the null space of Ric is invariant under parallel translation. In particular, all radial directions split off locally and isometrically. While by (6.3.2), the piece of the metric cone is nonflat. This gives a contradiction.

Case 3: \( A = 0 \) .

The gap theorem as was initiated by Mok-Siu-Yau [93] and established by Greene-Wu [49, 50], Eschenberg-Shrader-Strake [45], and Drees [44] shows that a complete noncompact \( n \) -dimensional (except \( n = 4 \) or 8) Riemannian manifold with nonnegative sectional curvature and the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio \( A = 0 \) must be flat. So the present case is ruled out except in dimension \( n = 4 \) or 8 . Since in our situation the asymptotic volume ratio is positive and the manifold is the solution of the Ricci flow, we can give an alternative proof for all dimensions as follows.

We claim the sectional curvature of \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is positive everywhere. Indeed, by Theorem 2.2.2, the image of the curvature operator is just the restricted holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) of the manifold. If the sectional curvature vanishes for some two-plane, then the holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) cannot be \( {so}\left( n\right) \) . We observe the manifold is not Einstein since it is noncompact, nonflat and has nonnegative curvature operator. If \( \mathcal{G} \) is irreducible, then by Berger’s Theorem [7], \( \mathcal{G} = u\left( \frac{n}{2}\right) \) . Thus the manifold is Kähler with bounded and nonnegative bisectional curvature and with curvature decay faster than quadratic. Then by the gap theorem obtained by Chen and the second author in [31], this Kähler manifold must be flat. This contradicts the assumption. Hence the holonomy algebra \( \mathcal{G} \) is reducible and the universal cover of \( M \) splits isometrically as \( {\widetilde{M}}_{1} \times  {\widetilde{M}}_{2} \) nontrivially. Clearly the universal cover of \( M \) has positive asymptotic volume ratio. So \( {\widetilde{M}}_{1} \) and \( {\widetilde{M}}_{2} \) still have positive asymptotic volume ratio and at least one of them is nonflat. By the induction hypothesis, this is also impossible. Thus our claim is proved.

Now we know that the sectional curvature of \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is positive everywhere. Choose a sequence of points \( {x}_{k} \) divergent to infinity such that

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  = \sup \left\{  {R\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \mid  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right) }\right\}  , \\  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq  k, \\  R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0}}\right)  = {\varepsilon }_{k} \rightarrow  0. \end{array}\right.
\]

Consider the rescaled metric

\[
{g}_{k}\left( 0\right)  = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) g\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right)
\]

as before. Then

(6.3.3)

\[
\left\{  \begin{array}{l} {R}_{k}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  {\varepsilon }_{k}/{d}_{k}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0},0}\right) ,\;\text{ for }{d}_{k}\left( {x,{x}_{0},0}\right)  \geq  \sqrt{{\varepsilon }_{k}}, \\  {d}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{x}_{0},0}\right)  = \sqrt{{\varepsilon }_{k}} \rightarrow  0. \end{array}\right.
\]

As in Case 2, the rescaled marked solutions \( \left( {M,{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) will converge in the Gromov-Hausdorff sense to a metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) . And by the virtue of Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), up to a subsequence, the convergence is in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology in \( \widetilde{M} \smallsetminus  \left\{  {x}_{0}\right\} \) . We next claim the metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) is isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) .

Indeed, let us write the metric cone \( \widetilde{M} \) as a warped product \( {\mathbb{R}}_{ + }{ \times  }_{r}{X}^{n - 1} \) for some \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional manifold \( {X}^{n - 1} \) . By (6.3.3), the metric cone must be flat and \( {X}^{n - 1} \) is isometric to a quotient of the round sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{n - 1} \) by fixed point free isometries in the standard metric. To show \( \widetilde{M} \) is isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) , we only need to verify that \( {X}^{n - 1} \) is simply connected.

Let \( \varphi \) be the Busemann function of \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) with respect to the point \( {x}_{0} \) . Since \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) has nonnegative sectional curvature, it is easy to see that for any small \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there is a \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) such that

\[
\left( {1 - \varepsilon }\right) {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \varphi \left( x\right)  \leq  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  M \smallsetminus  {B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) \) . The strict positivity of the sectional curvature of the manifold \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) implies that the square of the Busemann function is strictly convex (and exhausting). Thus every level set \( {\varphi }^{-1}\left( a\right) \) , with \( a > \inf \{ \varphi \left( x\right)  \mid  x \in  M\} \) , of the Busemann function \( \varphi \) is diffeomorphic to the \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -sphere \( {\mathbb{S}}^{n - 1} \) . In particular, \( {\varphi }^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {a,\frac{3}{2}a}\right\rbrack  \right) \) is simply connected for \( a > \inf \{ \varphi \left( x\right)  \mid  x \in  M\} \) since \( n \geq  3 \) .

Consider an annulus portion \( \left\lbrack  {1,2}\right\rbrack   \times  {X}^{n - 1} \) of the metric cone \( \widetilde{M} = {\mathbb{R}}_{ + }{ \times  }_{r}{X}^{n - 1} \) . It is the limit of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) , where

\[
{M}_{k} = \left\{  {x \in  M\left| {\;\frac{1}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }} \leq  {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \frac{2}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right. }\right\}  .
\]

It is clear that

\[
{\varphi }^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {\frac{1}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }},\frac{2\left( {1 - \varepsilon }\right) }{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right\rbrack  \right)  \subset  {M}_{k} \subset  {\varphi }^{-1}\left( \left\lbrack  {\frac{1 - \varepsilon }{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }},\frac{2}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right\rbrack  \right)
\]

for \( k \) large enough. Thus any closed loop in \( \left\{  \frac{3}{2}\right\}   \times  {X}^{n - 1} \) can be shrunk to a point by a homotopy in \( \left\lbrack  {1,2}\right\rbrack   \times  {X}^{n - 1} \) . This shows that \( {X}^{n - 1} \) is simply connected. Hence we have proven that the metric cone \( \left( {\widetilde{M},\widetilde{g}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{0}}\right) \) is isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . Consequently,

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow   + \infty }}\frac{{\operatorname{Vol}}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{r}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right)  \smallsetminus  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},\frac{\sigma r}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}}\right) }\right) }{{\left( \frac{r}{\sqrt{R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{0}}\right) }}\right) }^{n}} = {\alpha }_{n}\left( {1 - {\sigma }^{n}}\right)
\]

for any \( r > 0 \) and \( 0 < \sigma  < 1 \) , where \( {\alpha }_{n} \) is the volume of the unit ball in the Euclidean space \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . Finally, by combining with the monotonicity of the Bishop-Gromov volume comparison, we conclude that the manifold \( \left( {M,{g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) is flat and isometric to \( {\mathbb{R}}^{n} \) . This contradicts the assumption.

Therefore, we have proved the lemma. Ⓡ

Finally we would like to include an alternative simpler argument, inspired by Ni [98], for the above Case 2 and Case 3 to avoid the use of the gap theorem, holonomy groups, and asymptotic cone structure.

Alternative Proof for Case 2 and Case 3. Let us consider the situation of \( 0 \leq \; A <  + \infty \) in the above proof. Observe that \( {\nu }_{M}\left( t\right) \) is nonincreasing in time \( t \) by using Lemma 3.4.1(ii) and the fact that the metric is shrinking in \( t \) . Suppose \( {\nu }_{M}\left( {t}_{0}\right)  > 0 \) , then the solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed for \( t \leq  {t}_{0} \) for some uniform \( \kappa  > 0 \) . By combining with Theorem 6.2.1, there exist a sequence of points \( {q}_{k} \) and a sequence of times \( {t}_{k} \rightarrow   - \infty \) such that the scalings of \( {g}_{ij}\left( {\cdot , t}\right) \) around \( {q}_{k} \) with factor \( {\left| {t}_{k}\right| }^{-1} \) and with the times \( {t}_{k} \) shifting to the new time zero converge to a nonflat gradient shrinking soliton \( \bar{M} \) in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology. This gradient soliton also has maximal volume growth (i.e. \( {\nu }_{\bar{M}}\left( t\right)  > 0 \) ) and satisfies the Li-Yau-Hamilton estimate (Corollary 2.5.5). If the curvature of the shrinking soliton \( \bar{M} \) at the time -1 is bounded, then we see from the proof of Theorem 6.2.2 that by using the equations (6.2.24)-(6.2.26), the scalar curvature has a positive lower bound everywhere on \( \bar{M} \) at the time -1 . In particular, this implies the asymptotic scalar curvature ratio \( A = \infty \) for the soliton at the time -1 , which reduces to Case 1 and arrives at a contradiction by the dimension reduction argument. On the other hand, if the scalar curvature is unbounded, then by Lemma 6.1.4, the Li-Yau-Hamilton estimate (Corollary 2.5.5) and Lemma 6.1.2, we can do the same dimension reduction as in Case 1 to arrive at a contradiction also. 0

knowledge_statements.title: Fine versus Coarse Ricci-Flow Estimates
knowledge_statements.statement_title: Fine versus Coarse Ricci-Flow Estimates
knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
1.1. The distinction between fine and coarse estimates. It is useful to distinguish between what we may call fine estimates with what we may call coarse estimates. Since we apply these terminologies in a casual way, we describe our distinction between them in terms of examples. Examples of fine estimates in the theory of Ricci flow are curvature pinching estimates, Harnack-type estimates, entropy formulas, and monotonicity formulas. We may decree that an aspect of the fineness of an estimate is its sensitivity to perturbation. \( {}^{1} \) Although the matrix and trace Harnack estimates for the Ricci flow are known assuming nonnegative curvature operator in dimensions 2 and above, so far no substantial improvements (i.e., perturbations) seem to be known for dimensions 3 and above (in dimension 2 there is a trace Harnack estimate for arbitrary solutions on closed surfaces). On the other hand, one may think of the Hamilton-Ivey curvature estimate as a perturbation of the 'nonnegative sectional curvature is preserved' estimate in dimension 3. In this sense Harnack-type estimates appear finer than curvature pinching estimates although an analogy exists between them via the space-time approach. \( {}^{2} \) A further comment is that curvature pinching estimates in dimension 3 may be thought of as (large) perturbations of the 'nonnegative sectional (or Ricci) curvature is preserved' estimate.

Another aspect of the fineness of an estimate is how sharp it is; in general, finer estimates are sharper. A classical sharp example in Riemannian geometry is the Bishop-Gromov volume comparison theorem. In the Ricci flow, the matrix Harnack estimate is sharp (i.e., equality is attained in certain directions) on expanding gradient Ricci solitons. Moreover, for the corresponding Harnack estimate for ancient solutions we have that equality is attained on steady gradient Ricci solitons. Strikingly, Perelman has proved sharp monotonicity formulas for complete solutions of the Ricci flow on both closed and noncompact manifolds (without curvature sign restrictions). These estimates are sharp, as are monotonicity formulas in geometric flows in general.

On the other hand, in deriving coarse estimates, the ability to successfully apply the maximum principle to the evolution equations of the relevant quantities does not depend in a sensitive way on the constants in these quantities. For this reason we consider the global and local derivative of curvature estimates to be coarse estimates. Perhaps for the same reason derivative estimates hold for a number of different geometric evolution equations besides the Ricci flow including the heat equation on Riemannian manifolds and the mean curvature flow.

---

\( {}^{1} \) That is, the finer the estimate, the more difficult it is to perturb.

\( {}^{2} \) However, the reader may argue that a Harnack estimate in dimension \( n \) corresponds to a curvature estimate in dimension \( n + 1 \) since time adds a dimension, so that the apparent increase in fineness really corresponds to an increase in dimension.

---

The fineness or coarseness of an estimate may not be related to its relative importance to the study of a geometric flow; however, it may be related to its geometric significance. We venture to say that, in general, finer estimates are positively correlated to more geometrically significant estimates. An example of what we mean by this is that in many monotonicity formulas, the equality case, i.e., the case where the geometric invariant is constant under the flow, is characterized as occurring if and only if the solution is self-similar.
