knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
Consider any sequence of three-dimensional ancient \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solutions and marking points \( \left( {{x}_{k},0}\right) \) with \( R\left( {{x}_{k},0}\right)  = 1 \) . By Theorem 6.4.3(i), the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality and Hamilton's compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), we can extract a \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) converging subsequence such that the limit \( \left( {\bar{M},{\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) , with \( - \infty  < t \leq  0 \) , is an ancient solution to the Ricci flow with nonnegative curvature operator and \( {\kappa }_{{0}^{ - }} \) noncollapsed on all scales. Since any ancient \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -solution satisfies the Li-Yau-Hamilton inequality, it implies that the scalar curvature \( \bar{R}\left( {x, t}\right) \) of the limit \( \left( {\bar{M},{\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) is pointwise nondecreasing in time. Thus it remains to show that the limit solution has bounded curvature at \( t = 0 \) .

Obviously we may assume the limiting manifold \( \bar{M} \) is noncompact. By pulling back the limiting solution to its orientable cover, we can assume that the limiting manifold \( \bar{M} \) is orientable. We now argue by contradiction. Suppose the scalar curvature \( \bar{R} \) of the limit at \( t = 0 \) is unbounded.

By applying Lemma 6.1.4, we can choose a sequence of points \( {x}_{j} \in  \bar{M}, j = \; 1,2,\ldots \) , divergent to infinity such that the scalar curvature \( \bar{R} \) of the limit satisfies

\[
\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)  \geq  j\text{ and }\bar{R}\left( {x,0}\right)  \leq  4\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)
\]

for all \( j = 1,2,\ldots \) , and \( x \in  {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{j}, j/\sqrt{\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) }}\right) \) . Then from the fact that the limiting scalar curvature \( \bar{R}\left( {x, t}\right) \) is pointwise nondecreasing in time, we have

(6.4.20)

\[
\bar{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)
\]

for all \( j = 1,2,\ldots , x \in  {B}_{0}\left( {{x}_{j}, j/\sqrt{\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) }}\right) \) and \( t \leq  0 \) . By combining with Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5) and the \( {\kappa }_{0} \) -noncollapsing, we know that a subsequence of the rescaled solutions

\[
\left( {\bar{M},\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) {\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t/\bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right) }\right) ,{x}_{j}}\right) ,\;j = 1,2,\ldots ,
\]

converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a nonflat smooth solution of the Ricci flow. Then Proposition 6.1.2 implies that the new limit at the new time \( \{ t = 0\} \) must split off a line. By pulling back the new limit to its universal cover and applying Hamilton's strong maximum principle, we deduce that the pull-back of the new limit on the universal cover splits off a line for all time \( t \leq  0 \) . Thus by combining with Theorem 6.2.2 and the argument in the proof of Lemma 6.4.1, we further deduce that the new limit is either the round cylinder \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) or the round \( {\mathbb{{RP}}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Since \( \bar{M} \) is orientable, the new limit must be \( {\mathbb{S}}^{2} \times  \mathbb{R} \) . Moreover, since \( \left( {\bar{M},{\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x,0}\right) }\right) \) has nonnegative curvature operator and the points \( \left\{  {x}_{j}\right\} \) are going to infinity and \( \bar{R}\left( {{x}_{j},0}\right)  \rightarrow   + \infty \) , this gives a contradiction to Proposition 6.1.1. So we have proved that the limit \( \left( {\bar{M},{\bar{g}}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right) \) has uniformly bounded curvature. \( \square \)

knowledge_statements.statement_title: Canonical Neighborhood Theorem for Ricci Flow from PIC Metrics
knowledge_statements.statement_latex: (cf. G. Perelman [33, Th. 12.1]). Let \( \left( {M,{g}_{0}}\right) \) be a compact manifold with positive isotropic curvature of dimension \( n \geq  {12} \) , which does not contain any nontrivial incompressible \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional space forms. Let \( g\left( t\right) , t \in  \lbrack 0, T) \) , denote the solution to the Ricci flow with initial metric \( {g}_{0} \) . Given a small number \( \widetilde{\varepsilon } > 0 \) and a large number \( {A}_{0} \) , we can find a positive number \( \widehat{r} \) with the following property: If \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) is a point in space-time with \( Q \mathrel{\text{ := }} \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {\widehat{r}}^{-2} \) , then the parabolic neighborhood \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},{A}_{0}{Q}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \times \; \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {A}_{0}{Q}^{-1},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) is, after scaling by the factor \( Q,\widetilde{\varepsilon } \) -close to the corresponding subset of an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution satisfying \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \varnothing \mathrm{{id}} \in \) PIC.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
The proof of Theorem 7.2 is an adaptation of Perelman's work [33]. (See also [12], where the four-dimensional case is treated.) By Corollary 1.3, the flow \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) has \( \left( {f,\theta }\right) \) -pinched curvature for some function \( f \) satisfying \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{s \rightarrow  \infty }}\frac{f\left( s\right) }{s} \; = 0 \) and some constant \( \theta  > 0 \) . Let us fix a small number \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , and let \( {C}_{1} = {C}_{1}\left( {n,\theta ,\varepsilon }\right) \) and \( {C}_{2} = {C}_{2}\left( {n,\theta ,\varepsilon }\right) \) denote the constants in Corollary 6.22. It suffices to prove the assertion when \( {A}_{0} \geq  8{C}_{1} \) and \( \widetilde{\varepsilon } \) is much smaller than \( \varepsilon \) . To do that, we argue by contradiction. If the assertion is false, then we can find a sequence of points \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) in space-time with the following properties:

(i) \( {Q}_{j} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {j}^{2} \) .

(ii) After dilating by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) , the parabolic neighborhood

\[
{B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{A}_{0}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{j} - {A}_{0}{Q}_{j}^{-1},{t}_{j}}\right\rbrack
\]

is not \( \widetilde{\varepsilon } \) -close to the corresponding subset of any ancient \( \kappa \) -solution satisfying \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \varnothing \mathrm{{id}} \in \) PIC.

By a point-picking argument, we can arrange that \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the following condition:

(iii) If \( \left( {\widetilde{x},\widetilde{t}}\right) \) is a point in space-time such that \( \widetilde{t} \leq  {t}_{j} \) and \( \widetilde{Q} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \operatorname{scal}\left( {\widetilde{x},\widetilde{t}}\right)  \geq  4{Q}_{j} \) , then the parabolic neighborhood \( {B}_{g\left( \widetilde{t}\right) }\left( {\widetilde{x},{A}_{0}{\widetilde{Q}}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {\widetilde{t} - {A}_{0}{\widetilde{Q}}^{-1},\widetilde{t}}\right\rbrack \) is, after dilating by the factor \( \widetilde{Q},\widetilde{\varepsilon } \) -close to the corresponding subset of an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution satisfying \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \varnothing \mathrm{{id}} \in \) PIC.

Our strategy is to rescale the flow \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) around the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) . We will show that the rescaled flows converge to an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution satisfying \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \oslash \) id \( \in \) PIC. To that end, we proceed in several steps:

Step 1: We first establish a pointwise curvature derivative estimate. By Corollary 6.20, we can find a large constant \( \eta \) , depending only on \( n \) and \( \theta \) , such that \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  \eta {\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  \eta {\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) on every ancient \( \kappa \) -solution. Using property (iii) above, we conclude that \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) for each point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in space-time satisfying \( t \leq  {t}_{j} \) and \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  4{Q}_{j} \) .

Step 2: We next prove bounds for the higher order covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor. Suppose that \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) is a point in space-time satisfying \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {x, t}\right)  + {Q}_{j} \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) . The pointwise curvature derivative estimate in Step 1 implies that \( \operatorname{scal} \leq  8{r}_{0}^{-2} \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},\frac{{r}_{0}}{100\eta }, - \frac{{r}_{0}^{2}}{100\eta }}\right) \) . Using Shi’s interior derivative estimates, we conclude \( \left| {{D}^{m}R}\right|  \leq  C\left( {n, m,\eta }\right) {r}_{0}^{-m - 2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) .

Step 3: We next prove a long-range curvature estimate. Given any \( \rho  > 0 \) , we define

\[
\mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) }}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{t}_{j}}\right) .
\]

Here, we allow the possibility that \( \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  = \infty \) . The pointwise curvature derivative estimate in Step 1 implies that \( \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  \leq  8 \) for \( 0 < \rho  < \frac{1}{100\eta } \) .

We claim that \( \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \) for all \( \rho  > 0 \) . Suppose this is false. Let

\[
{\rho }^{ * } = \sup \{ \rho  \geq  0 : \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \}  < \infty .
\]

Clearly, \( {\rho }^{ * } \geq  \frac{1}{100\eta } \) . By definition of \( {\rho }^{ * } \) , we have an upper bound for the curvature in the geodesic ball \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) for each \( \rho  < {\rho }^{ * } \) . By Step 2, we obtain bounds for the covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor in the geodesic ball \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) for each \( \rho  < {\rho }^{ * } \) . Moreover, Perelman’s noncollapsing estimate gives a lower bound for the volume. We rescale around \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) and pass to the limit as \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) . In the limit, we obtain an incomplete manifold \( \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) that is weakly PIC2 (cf. [31, Th. 5.6]).

By definition of \( {\rho }^{ * } \) , we can find a sequence of points \( {y}_{j} \) such that

\[
{\rho }_{j} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {Q}_{j}^{\frac{1}{2}}{d}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{y}_{j}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }^{ * }\;\text{ and }\;{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty .
\]

For each \( j \) , we can find a unit speed geodesic \( {\gamma }_{j} : \left\lbrack  {0,{\rho }_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) such that \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( 0\right)  = {x}_{j} \) and \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {{\rho }_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  = {y}_{j} \) . Let \( {\gamma }_{\infty } : \left\lbrack  {0,{\rho }^{ * }}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) denote the limit of \( {\gamma }_{j} \) . Using the pointwise curvature derivative estimate in Step 1, we obtain

\[
{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {{\gamma }_{\infty }\left( s\right) }\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {s{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {\left( \eta \left( {\rho }^{ * } - s\right) \right) }^{-2} \geq  {100}
\]

if \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {{\rho }^{ * } - \frac{1}{100\eta },{\rho }^{ * }}\right) \) .

Let us consider a real number \( \bar{s} \in  \left\lbrack  {{\rho }^{ * } - \frac{1}{100\eta },{\rho }^{ * }}\right) \) such that \( 8{C}_{1}\eta \left( {{\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}}\right)  \leq  \bar{s} \) . We claim that \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) lies at the center of a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ). Indeed, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, it follows from property (iii) and Corollary 6.22 that the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck; or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap; or a closed manifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) ; or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -quotient neck. Furthermore, the Canonical Neighborhood is contained in a geodesic ball around \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) of radius \( 2{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , and the scalar curvature is at most \( 2{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) at each point in the Canonical Neighborhood. Since \( \mathbb{M}\left( \bar{s}\right)  < \infty \) , we obtain

\[
\mathop{\lim }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  = \infty ;
\]

consequently, \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  4{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Hence, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood does not contain the point \( {y}_{j} \) . We next observe that

\[
8{C}_{1}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}{\left( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  8{C}_{1}\eta \left( {{\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}}\right)  \leq  \bar{s}.
\]

This implies \( 4{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Hence, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood does not contain the point \( {x}_{j} \) . In particular, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) cannot be a closed manifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) . Moreover, if the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) is a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap, then the geodesic \( {\gamma }_{j} \) must enter and exit this \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap, but this is impossible since \( {\gamma }_{j} \) minimizes length. Finally, if the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) is a quotient neck, then Theorem A. 1 in [6] implies that \( M \) contains a nontrivial incompressible \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional space form, contrary to our assumption. To summarize, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ), then the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck. In particular, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ), then we have \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  C\left( n\right) \varepsilon {\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) .

Passing to the limit as \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) , we conclude that \( \left| {D{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}}\right|  \leq  C\left( n\right) \varepsilon {\operatorname{scal}}_{{q}^{\infty }}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at the point \( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \) . Integrating this estimate along \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) gives \( {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {{\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) }\right)  \geq \; {\left( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \left( {\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}\right) \right) }^{-2} \) . Moreover, since \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies at the center of a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck for \( j \) sufficiently large, the point \( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \) must lie on a \( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) .

As in [33, §12.1], there is a sequence of rescalings that converges to a piece of a nonflat metric cone in the limit. Using the pointwise curvature derivative estimate established in Step 1, we can extend the metric backwards in time. This gives a locally defined solution to the Ricci flow that is weakly PIC2 and that, at the final time, is a piece of nonflat metric cone. This contradicts Proposition 6.5.

Step 4: We now rescale the manifold \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) around the point \( {x}_{j} \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) . By Step 3, we have uniform bounds for the curvature at bounded distance. Using the curvature derivative estimate in Step 1 together with Shi's interior derivative estimates, we conclude that the covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor are bounded at bounded distance. Combining this with Perelman's noncollapsing estimate, we conclude that (after passing to a subsequence) the rescaled manifolds converge in the Cheeger-Gromov sense to a complete smooth limit manifold \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) . Since \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) has \( \left( {f,\theta }\right) \) -pinched curvature, the curvature tensor of \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) is weakly PIC2 and satisfies \( R - \; \theta \) scalid \( \oslash \) id \( \in \) PIC. Using property (iii) and Corollary 6.22, we conclude that every point in \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) with scalar curvature greater than 4 has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck; or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap; or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -quotient neck. Note that the last possibility cannot occur; indeed, if \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) contains a quotient neck, then \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) contains a quotient neck for \( j \) sufficiently large, and Theorem A.1 in [6] then implies that \( M \) contains a nontrivial incompressible \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional space form, contrary to our assumption.

We claim that the limit manifold \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) has bounded curvature. Indeed, if there is a sequence of points in \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) with curvature going to infinity, then \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) contains a sequence of necks with radii converging to 0, contradicting Proposition 6.9. Thus, \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) has bounded curvature.

Step 5: We now extend the limit \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time. By Step 4, the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) is bounded from above by a constant \( \Lambda  > 4 \) . Using the pointwise curvature derivative estimate in Step 1, we conclude that

\[
\mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{\left( {x, t}\right)  \in  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{j} - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1},{t}_{j}}\right\rbrack  }}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {2\Lambda }
\]

for each \( A > 1 \) . Hence, if we put \( {\tau }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }}  - \frac{1}{200\eta \Lambda } \) , then we can extend \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time to a complete solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) of the Ricci flow that is defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfies \( {\Lambda }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  {2\Lambda } \) . In the next step, we put \( {\tau }_{2} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\tau }_{1} - \frac{1}{{200n}{\Lambda }_{1}} \) . Using the pointwise curvature derivative estimate in Step 1, we can extend the solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack \) , backwards in time to a solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{2},0}\right\rbrack \) . Moreover, \( {\Lambda }_{2} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \; \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{2},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  2{\Lambda }_{1} \) . Continuing this process, we can extend the solution backwards in time to the interval \( \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m},0}\right\rbrack \) , where \( {\tau }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{200\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} \) and \( {\Lambda }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m} \) .

Let \( {\tau }^{ * } = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\tau }_{m} \leq   - \frac{1}{200\eta \Lambda } \) . Using a standard diagonal sequence argument, we obtain a complete, smooth limit flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined on the interval \( \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) and that has bounded curvature for each \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) . Since \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) has \( \left( {f,\theta }\right) \) -pinched curvature, the curvature tensor of the limit flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is weakly PIC2 and satisfies \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \varnothing \) id \( \in \) PIC.

Step 6: We claim that \( {\tau }^{ * } =  - \infty \) . To prove this, we argue by contradiction. Suppose \( {\tau }^{ * } >  - \infty \) . Clearly, \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {\tau }_{m + 1}}\right)  = 0 \) , hence \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\Lambda }_{m} = \infty \) .

By the Harnack inequality (cf. Theorem 6.1 above), the function \( t \mapsto \; \left( {t - {\tau }^{ * }}\right) {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\left( x\right) \) is monotone increasing at each point \( x \in  {M}^{\infty } \) . Since \( {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\left( x\right)  \leq  \Lambda \) for all \( x \in  {M}^{\infty } \) , we obtain

\[
{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\left( x\right)  \leq  \frac{-{\tau }^{ * }}{t - {\tau }^{ * }}\Lambda
\]

for all \( x \in  {M}^{\infty } \) and all \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) . Using Lemma 8.3(b) in [33], we conclude that

\[
0 \leq   - \frac{d}{dt}{d}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  C\left( n\right) \sqrt{\frac{-{\tau }^{ * }}{t - {\tau }^{ * }}\Lambda }
\]

for all \( x, y \in  {M}^{\infty } \) and all \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) . Integrating over \( t \) gives

\[
{d}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  {d}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\left( {x, y}\right)  \leq  {d}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\left( {x, y}\right)  + C\left( n\right) \left( {-{\tau }^{ * }}\right) \sqrt{\Lambda }
\]

for all \( x, y \in  {M}^{\infty } \) and all \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) .

By the maximum principle,

\[
\mathop{\inf }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  \mathop{\inf }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( 0\right) } \leq  1
\]

for all \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) . Hence, we can find a point \( {y}_{\infty } \in  {M}^{\infty } \) such that \( {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\left( {y}_{\infty }\right) \; \leq  4 \) for \( t = {\tau }^{ * } + \frac{1}{1000\eta \Lambda } \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) . Using the pointwise curvature derivative estimate in Step 1, we obtain \( {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\left( {y}_{\infty }\right)  \leq  8 \) for all \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },{\tau }^{ * } + \frac{1}{1000\eta \Lambda }}\right\rbrack \) . In particular, \( {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) }\left( {y}_{\infty }\right)  \leq  8 \) if \( m \) is sufficiently large. Arguing as in Step 3, we can show that

\[
\mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{{B}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) \left( {{y}_{\infty }, A}\right) }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) } < \infty
\]

for every \( A > 1 \) .

Consequently, a subsequence of the manifolds \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) ,{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) converges in the Cheeger-Gromov sense to a complete, smooth limit. If this limit manifold has unbounded curvature, then (by property (iii) above) it contains a sequence of necks with radii converging to 0 , contradicting Proposition 6.9. Therefore, a subsequence of the manifolds \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) ,{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) converges in the Cheeger-Gromov sense to a complete, smooth limit with bounded curvature. Consequently, we can find a constant \( {\Lambda }^{ * } > \Lambda \) (independent of \( A \) ) such that

\[
\mathop{\liminf }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{{B}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) }{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) } \leq  {\Lambda }^{ * }
\]

for every \( A > 1 \) . Using the distance estimate, we obtain \( {B}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\left( {{y}_{\infty }, A}\right)  \subset \; {B}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) }\left( {{y}_{\infty }, A + C\left( n\right) \left( {-{\tau }^{ * }}\right) \sqrt{\Lambda }}\right) \) . Putting these facts together, we conclude that

\[
\mathop{\liminf }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{{B}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( 0\right) }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) }{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) } \leq  {\Lambda }^{ * }
\]

for every \( A > 1 \) . Hence, for each \( A > 1 \) , we can find a large integer \( m \) (depending on \( A \) ) such that \( {\tau }_{m} \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },{\tau }^{ * } + \frac{1}{{1000\eta }{\Lambda }^{ * }}}\right\rbrack \) and

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{{B}_{g}\infty \left( 0\right) }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {{\tau }_{m}, A}\right) }{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( {\tau }_{m}\right) } \leq  2{\Lambda }^{ * }.
\]

Using the pointwise derivative estimate in Step 1, we obtain

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },{\tau }^{ * } + \frac{1}{{1000\eta }{\Lambda }^{ * }}}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{{B}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( 0\right) }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  4{\Lambda }^{ * }
\]

for every \( A > 1 \) . Since \( {\Lambda }^{ * } \) is independent of \( A \) , we conclude that

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },{\tau }^{ * } + \frac{1}{{1000\eta }{\Lambda }^{ * }}}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( t\right)  \leq  4{\Lambda }^{ * }.
\]

Therefore, the flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) , has bounded curvature. This contradicts the fact that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\Lambda }_{m} = \infty \) . Thus, \( {\tau }^{ * } =  - \infty \) .

To summarize, if we dilate the flow \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) around the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) , then (after passing to a subsequence), the rescaled flows converge in the Cheeger-Gromov sense to an ancient \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) , \( t \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) , satisfying \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \oslash \) id \( \in \) PIC. Here, \( \kappa \) depends only on the initial data. This contradicts statement (ii). This completes the proof of Theorem 7.2.

Then we can find positive numbers \( \widehat{r} \) and \( \widehat{\delta } \) with the following property: Suppose that we have a Ricci flow with surgery with parameters \( \varepsilon ,\widehat{r},\widehat{\delta }, h \) that is defined on some interval \( \lbrack 0, T) \) . Moreover, suppose that \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) is an arbitrary point in space-time satisfying \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {\left( 2\widehat{r}\right) }^{-2} \) . Then there exists a neighborhood \( B \) of \( {x}_{0} \) such that

\[
{B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},{\left( 2{C}_{1}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {x}_{0},{t}_{0}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \subset  B \subset  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},2{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {x}_{0},{t}_{0}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)
\]

and

\[
{\left( 2{C}_{2}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \leq  \operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{t}_{0}}\right)  \leq  2{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  B \) . Moreover, \( B \) is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck (in the sense of [35]) with center at \( {x}_{0} \) or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap. Finally, we have \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq \; {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) .

We argue by contradiction. Suppose that the assertion is false. Then we can find a sequence of Ricci flows with surgery \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) and a sequence of points \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) in space-time with the following properties:

(i) The flow \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) is defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{j}}\right) \) and has surgery parameters \( \varepsilon ,{\widehat{r}}_{j},{h}_{j},{\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \) , where \( {\widehat{r}}_{j} \leq  \frac{1}{j} \) and \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \leq  \min \left\{  {\widetilde{\widetilde{\delta }}\left( {\widehat{r}}_{j}\right) ,\frac{1}{j}}\right\} \) . Here, \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( \cdot \right) \) is the function introduced in Proposition 10.9.

(ii) \( {Q}_{j} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {\left( 2{\widehat{r}}_{j}\right) }^{-2} \) .

(iii) The point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) does not satisfy the conclusion of Theorem 10.10.

Condition (iii) means that at least one of the following statements is true:

- There does not exist a neighborhood \( B \) of \( {x}_{j} \) with the property that \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{\left( 2{C}_{1}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  \subset  B \subset  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},2{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) and \( {\left( 2{C}_{2}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \leq  \operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{t}_{j}}\right)  \leq  2{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) for all \( x \in  B \) , and such that \( B \) is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck (in the sense of [35]) with center at \( {x}_{j} \) or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap.

- \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  > {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) .

- \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  > {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) at \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) .

We will proceed in several steps:

Step 1: By Definition 10.1, we have \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {4\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq \; {4\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) for each point \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in space-time satisfying \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {x, t}\right)  \geq  4{Q}_{j} \) . Moreover, by Proposition 10.9, the flow \( {\mathcal{M}}^{\left( j\right) } \) is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales less than \( \varepsilon \) for some uniform constant \( \kappa \) that may depend on the initial data, but it is independent of \( j \) .

Step 2: Suppose that \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) is a point in space-time satisfying \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \; + {Q}_{j} \leq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) . The pointwise curvature derivative estimate implies that scal \( \leq \; 8{r}_{0}^{-2} \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0},\frac{{r}_{0}}{100\eta }, - \frac{{r}_{0}^{2}}{100\eta }}\right) \) . Using Proposition 10.4, we conclude that \( \left| {{D}^{m}R}\right|  \leq  C\left( {n, m,\eta }\right) {r}_{0}^{-m - 2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Moreover, Proposition 10.9 implies \( {\operatorname{vol}}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{B}_{g\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\left( {{x}_{0},{r}_{0}}\right) }\right)  \geq  \kappa {r}_{0}^{n} \) for some uniform constant \( \kappa \) that is independent of \( j \) .

Step 3: We next prove a long-range curvature estimate. Given any \( \rho  > 0 \) , we put

\[
\mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  = \mathop{\limsup }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{x \in  {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) }}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {x,{t}_{j}}\right) .
\]

The pointwise curvature derivative estimate implies that \( \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  \leq  {16} \) for \( 0 < \; \rho  < \frac{1}{100\eta }. \)

We claim that \( \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \) for all \( \rho  > 0 \) . Suppose this is false. Let

\[
{\rho }^{ * } = \sup \{ \rho  \geq  0 : \mathbb{M}\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \}  < \infty .
\]

By definition of \( {\rho }^{ * } \) , we have an upper bound for the curvature in the geodesic ball \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) for each \( \rho  < {\rho }^{ * } \) . Using the results in Step 2, we obtain bounds for all the covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor in the geodesic ball \( {B}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},\rho {Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) for each \( \rho  < {\rho }^{ * } \) . Moreover, the noncollapsing estimate in Step 2 gives a lower bound for the volume. We rescale around \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) and pass to the limit as \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) . In the limit, we obtain an incomplete manifold \( \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) that is weakly PIC2 (cf. [31, Th. 5.6]).

By definition of \( {\rho }^{ * } \) , there exists a sequence of points \( {y}_{j} \) such that

\[
{\rho }_{j} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {Q}_{j}^{\frac{1}{2}}{d}_{g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\left( {{x}_{j},{y}_{j}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }^{ * }\;\text{ and }\;{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty .
\]

Let \( {\gamma }_{j} : \left\lbrack  {0,{\rho }_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) be a unit-speed geodesic such that \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( 0\right)  = {x}_{j} \) and \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {{\rho }_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right)  = {y}_{j} \) , and let \( {\gamma }_{\infty } : \left\lbrack  {0,{\rho }^{ * }}\right)  \rightarrow  \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) denote the limit of \( {\gamma }_{j} \) . Using the estimate \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {4\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) we obtain for \( s \in  \left\lbrack  {{\rho }^{ * } - \frac{1}{100\eta },{\rho }^{ * }}\right) \) ,

\[
{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {{\gamma }_{\infty }\left( s\right) }\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {s{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {\left( 2\eta \left( {\rho }^{ * } - s\right) \right) }^{-2} \geq  {100}.
\]

Let us consider a real number \( \bar{s} \in  \left\lbrack  {{\rho }^{ * } - \frac{1}{100\eta },{\rho }^{ * }}\right) \) such that \( {64}{C}_{1}\eta \left( {{\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}}\right)  \leq  \bar{s} \) . We claim that \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) lies at the center of a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ). Indeed, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood Assumption implies that the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap. Furthermore, the Canonical Neighborhood is contained in a geodesic ball around \( {\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) of radius \( 8{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) , and the scalar curvature is at most \( 8{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) at each point in the Canonical Neighborhood. Since \( \mathbb{M}\left( \bar{s}\right)  < \infty \) , we obtain \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{j \rightarrow  \infty }}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-1}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  = \infty \) ; consequently, \( \operatorname{scal}\left( {{y}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right)  \geq  {16}{C}_{2}\operatorname{scal}\left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Hence, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood does not contain the point \( {y}_{j} \) . We next observe that \( {32}{C}_{1}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}{\left( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  {64}{C}_{1}\eta \left( {{\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}}\right)  \leq  \bar{s} \) . This implies \( {16}{C}_{1}\operatorname{scal}{\left( {\gamma }_{j}\left( \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}\right) ,{t}_{j}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  \bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Hence, if \( j \) is sufficiently large, then the Canonical Neighborhood does not contain the point \( {x}_{j} \) . If the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) is a \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap, then the geodesic \( {\gamma }_{j} \) must enter and exit this \( {4\varepsilon } \) -cap, but this is impossible since \( {\gamma }_{j} \) minimizes length. To summarize, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ), then the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck. In particular, if \( j \) is sufficiently large (depending on \( \bar{s} \) ), then we have \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  C\left( n\right) \varepsilon {\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at the point \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) . \)

Passing to the limit as \( j \rightarrow  \infty \) , we conclude that \( \left| {D{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}}\right|  \leq  C\left( n\right) \varepsilon {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) at the point \( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \) . Integrating this estimate along \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) gives \( {\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }}\left( {{\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) }\right)  \geq \; {\left( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \left( {\rho }^{ * } - \bar{s}\right) \right) }^{-2} \) . Moreover, since \( \left( {{\gamma }_{j}\left( {\bar{s}{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies at the center of a strong \( {4\varepsilon } \) -neck for \( j \) sufficiently large, the point \( {\gamma }_{\infty }\left( \bar{s}\right) \) must lie on a strong \( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {{B}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) .

As in \( \left\lbrack  {{33},§{12.1}}\right\rbrack \) , there is a sequence of rescalings that converges to a piece of a nonflat metric cone in the limit. Let us fix a point on this metric cone. In view of the preceding discussion, this point must lie on a strong \( C\left( n\right) \varepsilon \) -neck. This gives a locally defined solution to the Ricci flow that is weakly PIC2 and that, at the final time, is a piece of nonflat metric cone. This contradicts Proposition 6.5.

Step 4: We now dilate the manifold \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) around the point \( {x}_{j} \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) . By Step 3, we have uniform bounds for the curvature at bounded distance. Using the results in Step 2, we obtain bounds for all the covariant derivatives of the curvature tensor at bounded distance. Using these estimates together with the noncollapsing estimate in Step 2, we conclude that the rescaled manifolds converge in the Cheeger-Gromov sense to a complete limit manifold \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) . Since \( \left( {M, g\left( {t}_{j}\right) }\right) \) has \( \left( {f,\theta }\right) \) -pinched curvature, the curvature tensor of \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) is weakly PIC2 and satisfies \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \varnothing \mathrm{{id}} \in \) PIC. Using the Canonical Neighborhood Assumption, we conclude that every point in \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) with scalar curvature greater than 4 has a neighborhood that is either a strong \( {8\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {8\varepsilon } \) -cap.

We claim that \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) has bounded curvature. Indeed, if there is a sequence of points in \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) with curvature going to infinity, then \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) contains a sequence of necks with radii converging to 0 , contradicting Proposition 6.9. This shows that \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) has bounded curvature.

Step 5: We now extend the limit \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time. By Step 4, the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) is bounded from above by a constant \( \Lambda  > 4 \) . We claim that, given any \( A > 1 \) , the parabolic neighborhood

\[
P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right)
\]

is free of surgeries if \( j \) is sufficiently large. To prove this, fix \( A > 1 \) and suppose that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) contains points modified by surgery. Let \( {s}_{j} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }}\right\rbrack \) be the largest number such that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is free of surgeries. The pointwise curvature derivative estimate gives

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{\left. P\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1}\right) \right) }\operatorname{scal} \leq  {2\Lambda }{Q}_{j}
\]

if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Since the scalar curvature is greater than \( \frac{1}{2}{h}_{j}^{-2} \) at each point modified by surgery, we deduce that \( \frac{1}{2}{h}_{j}^{-2} \leq  {2\Lambda }{Q}_{j} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. In particular, \( {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1} \leq  \frac{1}{10\eta }{h}_{j}^{2} \) if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Since \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \rightarrow  0 \) ,

Proposition 10.5 implies that the parabolic neighborhood

\[
P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - {s}_{j}{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right)
\]

is, after dilating by the factor \( {h}_{j} \) , arbitrarily close to a piece of the standard solution when \( j \) is sufficiently large. Using Corollary 9.3, we conclude that \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap when \( j \) is sufficiently large. If \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on an \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, then this neck is actually a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, since we are assuming that each \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \) -neck on which we perform surgery has a large backward parabolic neighborhood that is free of surgeries (cf. Definition 10.1). Moreover, Corollary 9.3 implies that \( \left| {D\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . Therefore, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of Theorem 10.10, and this contradicts statement (iii). Thus, given any \( A > 1 \) , the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda }{Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is free of surgeries if \( j \) is sufficiently large.

Let \( {\tau }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }}  - \frac{1}{200\eta \Lambda } \) . In view of the preceding discussion, we may extend \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time to a complete solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfies \( {\Lambda }_{1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  {2\Lambda } \) .

We now repeat this process. Suppose that we can extend \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }}\right) \) backwards in time to a complete solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m},0}\right\rbrack \) , and satisfies \( {\Lambda }_{m} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } < \infty \) . Let \( {\tau }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{200\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} \) . We claim that we can extend the solution \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) backward to the interval \( \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack \) , and \( {\Lambda }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m} \) .

Indeed, if this is not possible, then there exists a number \( A > 1 \) with the property that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{100\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) contains points modified by surgery for \( j \) sufficiently large. Let \( {s}_{j} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{1}{{100\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}}}\right\rbrack \) be the largest number such that \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is free of surgeries. The pointwise curvature derivative estimate gives

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{\left. P\left( {x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}\right) \right) }\operatorname{scal} \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m}{Q}_{j}
\]

if \( j \) is sufficiently large. Let us choose \( {\alpha }_{m} \in  \left\lbrack  {0,\frac{n - 1}{2}}\right) \) so that \( \frac{{\alpha }_{m}}{{K}_{\text{ stnd }}\left( {1 - \frac{2{\alpha }_{m}}{n - 1}}\right) } \geq \; 8{\Lambda }_{m}\left( {\frac{1}{{100\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} - {\tau }_{m}}\right) \) . If \( \left( {{s}_{j} - {\tau }_{m}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1} \geq  {\alpha }_{m}{h}_{j}^{2} \) for \( j \) sufficiently large, then Proposition 10.5 together with the lower bound for the scalar curvature on the standard solution (cf. Theorem 9.1) gives

\[
\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) }}\operatorname{scal} \geq  \frac{1}{2{K}_{\text{ stnd }}\left( {1 - \frac{2{\alpha }_{m}}{n - 1}}\right) }{h}_{j}^{-2}
\]

\[
\geq  \frac{{\alpha }_{m}}{2{K}_{\text{ stnd }}\left( {1 - \frac{2{\alpha }_{m}}{n - 1}}\right) }{\left( {s}_{j} - {\tau }_{m}\right) }^{-1}{Q}_{j}
\]

\[
\geq  4{\Lambda }_{m}{Q}_{j}
\]

for \( j \) sufficiently large, which is impossible. Consequently, \( \left( {{s}_{j} - {\tau }_{m}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1} \leq  {\alpha }_{m}{h}_{j}^{2} \) for \( j \) sufficiently large. Since \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \rightarrow  0 \) , Proposition 10.5 implies that the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}, A{Q}_{j}^{-\frac{1}{2}},\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {s}_{j}}\right) {Q}_{j}^{-1}}\right) \) is, after dilating by the factor \( {h}_{j} \) , arbitrarily close to a piece of the standard solution when \( j \) is sufficiently large. Using Corollary 9.3, we conclude that \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap when \( j \) is sufficiently large. If \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) lies on an \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, then this neck is actually a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck, since we are assuming that each \( {\widehat{\delta }}_{j} \) -neck on which we perform surgery has a large backward parabolic neighborhood that is free of surgeries (cf. Definition 10.1). Moreover, Corollary 9.3 implies that \( \left| {D\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\text{ scal }}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . Therefore, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of Theorem 10.10, and this contradicts statement (iii). Thus, we may extend the flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) backward to the interval \( \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack \) , where \( {\tau }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} {\tau }_{m} - \frac{1}{{200\eta }{\Lambda }_{m}} \) , and we have \( {\Lambda }_{m + 1} \mathrel{\text{ := }} \mathop{\sup }\limits_{{t \in  \left\lbrack  {{\tau }_{m + 1},0}\right\rbrack  }}\mathop{\sup }\limits_{{M}^{\infty }}{\operatorname{scal}}_{{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) } \leq  2{\Lambda }_{m}. \)

Let \( {\tau }^{ * } = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\tau }_{m} \leq   - \frac{1}{100\eta \Lambda } \) . Using a standard diagonal sequence argument, we obtain a complete, smooth limit flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) that is defined on the interval \( \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) and that has bounded curvature for each \( t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) .

Step 6: We next show that \( {\tau }^{ * } =  - \infty \) . Indeed, if \( {\tau }^{ * } >  - \infty \) , it follows that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}\left( {{\tau }_{m} - {\tau }_{m + 1}}\right)  = 0 \) , hence \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\Lambda }_{m} = \infty \) . Arguing as in Step 6 in the proof of Theorem 7.2, we can show that the limit flow \( \left( {{M}^{\infty },{g}^{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) , t \in  \left( {{\tau }^{ * },0}\right\rbrack \) has bounded curvature. This contradicts the fact that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{m \rightarrow  \infty }}{\Lambda }_{m} = \infty \) . Thus, \( {\tau }^{ * } =  - \infty \) . Hence, if we dilate the flow \( \left( {M, g\left( t\right) }\right) \) around the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) by the factor \( {Q}_{j} \) , then (after passing to a subsequence) the rescaled flows converge to an ancient solution that is complete, has bounded curvature, is weakly PIC2, and satisfies \( R - \theta \) scalid \( \oslash \) id \( \in \) PIC. By Proposition 10.9, the limiting ancient solution is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed for some \( \kappa  > 0 \) that depends only on the initial data. By Corollary 6.22, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck with center at \( {x}_{j} \) ; or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap; or a closed manifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) ; or a quotient neck. Recall that we have discarded all connected components that are diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) (see Definition 10.1). Hence, the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) cannot be a closed manifold diffeomorphic to \( {S}^{n}/\Gamma \) . If the Canonical Neighborhood of \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) is a quotient neck, then Theorem A. 1 in [6] implies that the underlying manifold contains a nontrivial incompressible \( \left( {n - 1}\right) \) -dimensional space form, contrary to our assumption. Consequently, the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) has a Canonical Neighborhood that is either a strong \( {2\varepsilon } \) -neck with center at \( {x}_{j} \) or a \( {2\varepsilon } \) -cap. Finally, Corollary 6.20 implies that \( \left| {D\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\operatorname{scal}}^{\frac{3}{2}} \) and \( \left| {\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\mathrm{{scal}}}\right|  \leq  {2\eta }{\mathrm{{scal}}}^{2} \) at the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) . In summary, we have shown that the point \( \left( {{x}_{j},{t}_{j}}\right) \) satisfies the conclusion of Theorem 10.10. This contradicts statement (iii). This completes the proof of Theorem 10.10.

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
(Justification of the canonical neighborhood assumption). Given any small \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there exist decreasing sequences \( 0 < {\widetilde{r}}_{j} < \varepsilon ,{\kappa }_{j} > 0 \) , and \( 0 < {\widetilde{\delta }}_{j} < {\varepsilon }^{2}, j = 1,2,\cdots \) , with the following property. Define the positive function \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) \) on \( \lbrack 0, + \infty ) \) by \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right)  = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{j} \) for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {j - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, j{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) \) . Suppose there is a surgically modified solution, defined on \( \lbrack 0, T) \) with \( T <  + \infty \) , to the Ricci flow which satisfies the following:

(1) it starts on a compact orientable three-manifold with normalized initial metric, and

(2) it has only a finite number of surgeries such that each surgery at a time \( t \in  \left( {0, T}\right) \) is a \( \delta \left( t\right) \) -cutoff surgery with

\[
0 < \delta \left( t\right)  \leq  \min \{ \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) ,\bar{\delta }\left( t\right) \} .
\]

Then on each time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\left( {j - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, j{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack  \bigcap \lbrack 0, T), j = 1,2,\cdots \) , the solution satisfies the \( {\kappa }_{j} \) -noncollapsing condition on all scales less than \( \varepsilon \) and the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) with \( r = {\widetilde{r}}_{j} \) .

Here and in the following, we call a (three-dimensional) surgically modified solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) ,0 \leq  t < T,\kappa \) -noncollapsed at \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) on the scales less than \( \rho \) (for some \( \kappa  > 0,\rho  > 0 \) ) if it satisfies the following property: whenever \( r < \rho \) and

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {r}^{-2}
\]

for all those \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}, r, - {r}^{2}}\right)  = \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {B}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) ,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {r}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , for which the solution is defined, we have

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) }\right)  \geq  \kappa {r}^{3}.
\]

The proof of the proposition is by induction: having constructed our sequences for \( 1 \leq  j \leq  m \) , we make one more step, defining \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m + 1} \) , \( {\kappa }_{m + 1},{\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) , and redefining \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) . In view of the previous lemma, we only need to define \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m + 1} \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) .

In Theorem 7.1.1 we have obtained the canonical neighborhood structure for smooth solutions. When adapting the arguments in the proof of Theorem 7.1.1 to the present surgical solutions, we will encounter the new difficulty of how to take a limit for the surgically modified solutions. The idea to overcome the difficulty consists of two parts. The first part, due to Perelman [104], is to choose \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) small enough to push the surgical regions to infinity in space. (This is the reason why we need to redefine \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) .) The second part is to show that solutions are smooth on some small, but uniform, time intervals (on compact subsets) so that we can apply Hamilton's compactness theorem, since we only have curvature bounds; otherwise Shi's interior derivative estimate may not be applicable. In fact, the second part is more crucial. That is just concerned with the question of whether the surgery times accumulate or not. Our argument will use the canonical neighborhood characterization of the standard solution in Lemma 7.3.5.

We now start to prove the proposition by contradiction. Suppose for sequence of positive numbers \( {r}^{\alpha } \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) , satisfying \( {r}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  0 \) as \( \alpha  \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  \frac{1}{\alpha  \cdot  \beta }\left( { \rightarrow  0}\right) \) , there exist sequences of solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) to the Ricci flow with surgery, where each of them has only a finite number of cutoff surgeries and has a compact orientable normalized three-manifold as initial data, so that the following two assertions hold:

(i) each \( \delta \) -cutoff at a time \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) satisfies \( \delta  \leq  {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) ; and

(ii) the solutions satisfy the statement of the proposition on \( \left\lbrack  {0, m{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) , but violate the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) on \( \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) .

For each solution \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) , we choose \( \bar{t} \) (depending on \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) ) to be the nearly first time for which the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) is violated. More precisely, we choose \( \bar{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) so that the canonical neighborhood assumption with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) and with accuracy parameter \( \varepsilon \) is violated at some \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , however the canonical neighborhood assumption with accuracy parameter \( {2\varepsilon } \) holds on \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . After passing to subsequences, we may assume each \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) is less than the \( \widetilde{\delta } \) in Lemma 7.4.2 with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) when \( \alpha \) is fixed. Then by Lemma 7.4.2 we have uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing on all scales less than \( \varepsilon \) on \( \left\lbrack  {0,\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) with some \( \kappa  > 0 \) independent of \( \alpha ,\beta \) .

Slightly abusing notation, we will often drop the indices \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) .

Let \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) be the rescaled solutions around \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with factors \( R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \left( { \geq  {r}^{-2} \rightarrow   + \infty }\right) \) and shift the times \( \bar{t} \) to zero. We hope to take a limit of the rescaled solutions for subsequences of \( \alpha ,\beta  \rightarrow  \infty \) and show the limit is an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution, which will give the desired contradiction. We divide our arguments into the following six steps.

Step 1. Let \( \left( {y,\widehat{t}}\right) \) be a point on the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) with \( \widetilde{R}\left( {y,\widehat{t}}\right)  \leq  A \) (for some \( A \geq  1 \) ) and \( \widehat{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {-\left( {\bar{t} - \left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) ,0}\right\rbrack \) . Then we have estimate

(7.4.14)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10A}
\]

for those \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {y,\widehat{t},\frac{1}{2}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-1}}\right)  \triangleq \; \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {y,\frac{1}{2}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {\widehat{t} - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-1},\widehat{t}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , for which the rescaled solution is defined.

Indeed, as in the first step of the proof of Theorem 7.1.1, this follows directly from the gradient estimates (7.3.4) in the canonical neighborhood assumption with parameter \( {2\varepsilon } \) .

Step 2. In this step, we will prove three time extension results.

Assertion 1. For arbitrarily fixed \( \alpha ,0 < A <  + \infty ,1 \leq  C <  + \infty \) and \( 0 \leq  B < \frac{1}{2}{\varepsilon }^{2}{\left( {r}^{\alpha }\right) }^{-2} - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{C}^{-1} \) , there is a \( {\beta }_{0} = {\beta }_{0}\left( {\varepsilon , A, B, C}\right) \) (independent of \( \alpha \) ) such that if \( \beta  \geq  {\beta }_{0} \) and the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) on the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) is defined on a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack \) with \( 0 \leq  b \leq  B \) and the scalar curvature satisfies

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C,\;\text{ on }{\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-b,0}\right\rbrack  ,
\]

then the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) on the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) is also defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-b - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{C}^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) .

Before giving the proof, we make a simple observation: once a space point in the Ricci flow with surgery is removed by surgery at some time, then it never appears for later time; if a space point at some time \( t \) cannot be defined before the time \( t \) , then either the point lies in a gluing cap of the surgery at time \( t \) or the time \( t \) is the initial time of the Ricci flow.

Proof of Assertion 1. Firstly we claim that there exists \( {\beta }_{0} = {\beta }_{0}\left( {\varepsilon , A, B, C}\right) \) such that when \( \beta  \geq  {\beta }_{0} \) , the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) on the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) can be defined before the time \( - b \) (i.e., there are no surgeries interfering in \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-b - {\epsilon }^{\prime }, - b}\right\rbrack \) for some \( \left. {{\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0}\right) \) .

We argue by contradiction. Suppose not, then there is some point \( \widetilde{x} \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) such that the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) at \( \widetilde{x} \) cannot be defined before the time \( - b \) . By the above observation, there is a surgery at the time \( - b \) such that the point \( \widetilde{x} \) lies in the instant gluing cap.

Let \( \widetilde{h}\left( { = R{\left( \bar{x},\bar{t}\right) }^{\frac{1}{2}}h}\right) \) be the cut-off radius at the time \( - b \) for the rescaled solution. Clearly, there is a universal constant \( D \) such that \( {D}^{-1}\widetilde{h} \leq  \widetilde{R}{\left( \widetilde{x}, - b\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \leq  D\widetilde{h} \) .

Now, by taking convergent subsequences from the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) , we see that the limit solution is defined smoothly on a space-time open subset of \( {M}_{\infty } \times \; ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) containing \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) . By Step 4, we see that the limiting metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , - {t}_{\max }}\right) \) at time \( - {t}_{\max } \) has bounded curvature. Then by combining with the canonical neighborhood assumption of accuracy \( {2\varepsilon } \) , we conclude that the curvature of the limit is uniformly bounded on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) . So we have excluded the possibility (1).

Hence we have proved a subsequence of the rescaled solutions converges to an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution.

Finally by combining with the canonical neighborhood theorem (Theorem 6.4.6), we see that \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) has a canonical neighborhood with parameter \( \varepsilon \) , which is a contradiction. Therefore we have completed the proof of the proposition. 0

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
Proof of Theorem 5.2.1. Let \( M \) be a compact three-manifold with positive Ricci curvature and let the metric evolve by the Ricci flow. By Lemma 5.2.4 we know that there exists a positive constant \( \beta  > 0 \) such that

\[
{R}_{ij} \geq  {\beta R}{g}_{ij}
\]

for all \( t \geq  0 \) as long as the solution exists. The scalar curvature evolves by

\[
\frac{\partial R}{\partial t} = {\Delta R} + 2{\left| {R}_{ij}\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
\geq  {\Delta R} + \frac{2}{3}{R}^{2}
\]

which implies, by the maximum principle, that the scalar curvature remains positive and tends to +0 in finite time.

We now use a blow up argument as in Section 4.3 to get the following gradient estimate.

CLAIM. For any \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there exists a positive constant \( {C}_{\varepsilon } <  + \infty \) such that for any time \( \tau  \geq  0 \) , we have

\[
\mathop{\max }\limits_{{t \leq  \tau }}\mathop{\max }\limits_{{x \in  M}}\left| {\nabla {Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  \varepsilon \mathop{\max }\limits_{{t \leq  \tau }}\mathop{\max }\limits_{{x \in  M}}{\left| Rm\left( x, t\right) \right| }^{\frac{3}{2}} + {C}_{\varepsilon }.
\]

We argue by contradiction. Suppose the above gradient estimate fails for some fixed \( {\varepsilon }_{0} > 0 \) . Pick a sequence \( {C}_{j} \rightarrow   + \infty \) , and pick points \( {x}_{j} \in  M \) and times \( {\tau }_{j} \) such that

\[
\left| {\nabla \operatorname{Rm}\left( {{x}_{j},{\tau }_{j}}\right) }\right|  \geq  {\varepsilon }_{0}\mathop{\max }\limits_{{t \leq  {\tau }_{j}}}\mathop{\max }\limits_{{x \in  M}}{\left| \operatorname{Rm}\left( x, t\right) \right| }^{\frac{3}{2}} + {C}_{j},\;j = 1,2,\ldots
\]

Choose \( {x}_{j} \) to be the origin, and pull the metric back to a small ball on the tangent space \( {T}_{{x}_{j}}M \) of radius \( {r}_{j} \) proportional to the reciprocal of the square root of the maximum curvature up to time \( {\tau }_{j} \) (i.e., \( \mathop{\max }\limits_{{t \leq  {\tau }_{j}}}\mathop{\max }\limits_{{x \in  M}}\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right| \) ). Clearly the maximum curvatures go to infinity by Shi's derivative estimate of curvature (Theorem 1.4.1). Dilate the metrics so that the maximum curvature

\[
\mathop{\max }\limits_{{t \leq  {\tau }_{j}}}\mathop{\max }\limits_{{x \in  M}}\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|
\]

becomes 1 and translate time so that \( {\tau }_{j} \) becomes the time 0 . By Theorem 4.1.5, we can take a (local) limit. The limit metric satisfies

\[
\left| {\nabla \operatorname{Rm}\left( {0,0}\right) }\right|  \geq  {\varepsilon }_{0} > 0.
\]

However the pinching estimate in Proposition 5.2.5 tells us the limit metric has

\[
{R}_{ij} - \frac{1}{3}R{g}_{ij} \equiv  0.
\]

By using the contracted second Bianchi identity

\[
\frac{1}{2}{\nabla }_{i}R = {\nabla }^{j}{R}_{ij} = {\nabla }^{j}\left( {{R}_{ij} - \frac{1}{3}R{g}_{ij}}\right)  + \frac{1}{3}{\nabla }_{i}R,
\]

we get

\[
{\nabla }_{i}R \equiv  0\;\text{ and then }\;{\nabla }_{i}{R}_{jk} \equiv  0.
\]

For a three-manifold, this in turn implies

\[
\nabla {Rm} = 0
\]

which is a contradiction. Hence we have proved the gradient estimate claimed.

We can now show that the solution to the Ricci flow becomes round as the time \( t \) tends to the maximal time \( T \) . We have seen that the scalar curvature goes to infinity in finite time. Pick a sequence of points \( {x}_{j} \in  M \) and times \( {\tau }_{j} \) where the curvature at \( {x}_{j} \) is as large as it has been anywhere for \( 0 \leq  t \leq  {\tau }_{j} \) and \( {\tau }_{j} \) tends to the maximal time. Since \( \left| {\nabla {Rm}}\right| \) is very small compared to \( \left| {{Rm}\left( {{x}_{j},{\tau }_{j}}\right) }\right| \) by the above gradient estimate and \( \left| {{R}_{ij} - \frac{1}{3}R{g}_{ij}}\right| \) is also very small compared to \( \left| {{Rm}\left( {{x}_{j},{\tau }_{j}}\right) }\right| \) by Proposition 5.2.5, the curvature is nearly constant and positive in a large ball around \( {x}_{j} \) at the time \( {\tau }_{j} \) . But then the Bonnet-Myers’ theorem tells us this is the whole manifold. For \( j \) large enough, the sectional curvature of the solution at the time \( {\tau }_{j} \) is sufficiently pinched. Then it follows from the Klingenberg injectivity radius estimate (see Section 4.2) that the injectivity radius of the metric at time \( {\tau }_{j} \) is bounded from below by \( c/\sqrt{\left| \operatorname{Rm}\left( {x}_{j},{\tau }_{j}\right) \right| } \) for some positive constant \( c \) independent of \( j \) . Dilate the metrics so that the maximum curvature \( \left| {{Rm}\left( {{x}_{j},{\tau }_{j}}\right) }\right|  = \mathop{\max }\limits_{{t \leq  {\tau }_{j}}}\mathop{\max }\limits_{{x \in  M}}\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right| \) becomes 1 and shift the time \( {\tau }_{j} \) to the new time 0 . Then we can apply Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5) to take a limit. By the pinching estimate in Proposition 5.2.5, we know that the limit has positive constant curvature which is either the round \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) or a metric quotient of the round \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) . Consequently, the compact three-manifold \( M \) is diffeomorphic to the round \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) or a metric quotient of the round \( {\mathbb{S}}^{3} \) . 0

(Shi [114]). There exist constants \( {C}_{m}, m = 1,2,\ldots \) , such that if the curvature of a complete solution to Ricci flow is bounded by

\[
\left| {R}_{ijkl}\right|  \leq  M
\]

up to time \( t \) with \( 0 < t \leq  \frac{1}{M} \) , then the covariant derivative of the curvature is bounded by

\[
\left| {\nabla {R}_{ijkl}}\right|  \leq  {C}_{1}M/\sqrt{t}
\]

and the \( {m}^{th} \) covariant derivative of the curvature is bounded by

\[
\left| {{\nabla }^{m}{R}_{ijkl}}\right|  \leq  {C}_{m}M/{t}^{\frac{m}{2}}.
\]

Here the norms are taken with respect to the evolving metric.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
We shall only give the proof for the compact case. The noncompact case can be deduced from the next local derivative estimate theorem. Let us denote the curvature tensor by \( {Rm} \) and denote by \( A * B \) any tensor product of two tensors \( A \) and \( B \) when we do not need the precise expression. We have from Proposition 1.3.1 that

(1.4.1)

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{Rm} = {\Delta Rm} + {Rm} * {Rm}.
\]

Since

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\Gamma }_{jk}^{i} = \frac{1}{2}{g}^{il}\left\{  {{\nabla }_{j}\frac{\partial {g}_{kl}}{\partial t} + {\nabla }_{k}\frac{\partial {g}_{jl}}{\partial t} - {\nabla }_{l}\frac{\partial {g}_{jk}}{\partial t}}\right\}
\]

\[
= \nabla {Rm},
\]

it follows that

(1.4.2)

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}\left( {\nabla {Rm}}\right)  = \Delta \left( {\nabla {Rm}}\right)  + {Rm} * \left( {\nabla {Rm}}\right) .
\]

Thus

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| Rm\right| }^{2} \leq  \Delta {\left| Rm\right| }^{2} - 2{\left| \nabla Rm\right| }^{2} + C{\left| Rm\right| }^{3}
\]

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| \nabla Rm\right| }^{2} \leq  \Delta {\left| \nabla Rm\right| }^{2} - 2{\left| {\nabla }^{2}Rm\right| }^{2} + C\left| {Rm}\right|  \cdot  {\left| \nabla Rm\right| }^{2},
\]

for some constant \( C \) depending only on the dimension \( n \) .

Let \( A > 0 \) be a constant (to be determined) and set

\[
F = t{\left| \nabla Rm\right| }^{2} + A{\left| Rm\right| }^{2}.
\]

We compute

\[
\frac{\partial F}{\partial t} = {\left| \nabla Rm\right| }^{2} + t\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| \nabla Rm\right| }^{2} + A\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| Rm\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
\leq  \Delta \left( {t{\left| \nabla Rm\right| }^{2} + A{\left| Rm\right| }^{2}}\right)  + {\left| \nabla Rm\right| }^{2}\left( {1 + {tC}\left| {Rm}\right|  - {2A}}\right)  + {CA}{\left| Rm\right| }^{3}.
\]

Taking \( A \geq  C + 1 \) , we get

\[
\frac{\partial F}{\partial t} \leq  {\Delta F} + \bar{C}{M}^{3}
\]

for some constant \( \bar{C} \) depending only on the dimension \( n \) . We then obtain

\[
F \leq  F\left( 0\right)  + \bar{C}{M}^{3}t \leq  \left( {A + \bar{C}}\right) {M}^{2},
\]

and then

\[
{\left| \nabla Rm\right| }^{2} \leq  \left( {A + \bar{C}}\right) {M}^{2}/t
\]

The general case follows in the same way. If we have bounds

\[
\left| {{\nabla }^{k}{Rm}}\right|  \leq  {C}_{k}M/{t}^{\frac{k}{2}},
\]

we know from (1.4.1) and (1.4.2) that

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| {\nabla }^{k}Rm\right| }^{2} \leq  \Delta {\left| {\nabla }^{k}Rm\right| }^{2} - 2{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} + \frac{C{M}^{3}}{{t}^{k}},
\]

and

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} \leq  \Delta {\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} - 2{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 2}Rm\right| }^{2} + {CM}{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} + \frac{C{M}^{3}}{{t}^{k + 1}}.
\]

Let \( {A}_{k} > 0 \) be a constant (to be determined) and set

\[
{F}_{k} = {t}^{k + 2}{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} + {A}_{k}{t}^{k + 1}{\left| {\nabla }^{k}Rm\right| }^{2}.
\]

Then

\[
\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{F}_{k} = \left( {k + 2}\right) {t}^{k + 1}{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} + {t}^{k + 2}\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
+ {A}_{k}\left( {k + 1}\right) {t}^{k}{\left| {\nabla }^{k}Rm\right| }^{2} + {A}_{k}{t}^{k + 1}\frac{\partial }{\partial t}{\left| {\nabla }^{k}Rm\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
\leq  \left( {k + 2}\right) {t}^{k + 1}{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
+ {t}^{k + 2}\left\lbrack  {\Delta {\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} - 2{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 2}Rm\right| }^{2} + {CM}{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} + \frac{C{M}^{3}}{{t}^{k + 1}}}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
+ {A}_{k}\left( {k + 1}\right) {t}^{k}{\left| {\nabla }^{k}Rm\right| }^{2}
\]

\[
+ {A}_{k}{t}^{k + 1}\left\lbrack  {\Delta {\left| {\nabla }^{k}Rm\right| }^{2} - 2{\left| {\nabla }^{k + 1}Rm\right| }^{2} + \frac{C{M}^{3}}{{t}^{k}}}\right\rbrack
\]

\[
\leq  \Delta {F}_{k} + {C}_{k + 1}{M}^{2}
\]

for some positive constant \( {C}_{k + 1} \) , by choosing \( {A}_{k} \) large enough. This implies that

\[
\left| {{\nabla }^{k + 1}{Rm}}\right|  \leq  \frac{{C}_{k + 1}M}{{t}^{\frac{k + 1}{2}}}.
\]

The above derivative estimate is a somewhat standard Bernstein estimate in PDEs. By using a cutoff argument, we will derive the following local version, which is called Shi's derivative estimate. The following proof is adapted from Hamilton [63].
