knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
The proof of the first statement is by contradiction. Fix \( \rho  > 0 \) and \( \delta  > 0 \) and suppose that there is no \( 0 < h \leq  \min \left( {\rho  \cdot  \delta ,\rho /{2C}}\right) \) as required. Then there is a sequence of generalized Ricci flows \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) defined for \( 0 \leq  t < {T}_{n} < \infty \) satisfying Assumptions 11.18 and points \( {x}_{n} \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) with \( \mathbf{t}\left( {x}_{n}\right)  = {T}_{n} \) contained in \( {2\epsilon } \) -horns \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) in \( {\Omega }_{n} \) with boundary contained in \( {\left( {\Omega }_{n}\right) }_{\rho /{2C}} \) with \( {Q}_{n} = R\left( {x}_{n}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) but such that no \( {x}_{n} \) is the center of a strong \( \delta \) -neck in \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) . Form the maximal extensions, \( \left( {{\widehat{\mathcal{M}}}_{n},{\widehat{G}}_{n}}\right) \) , to time \( T \) of the \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) .

CLAIM 11.32. The sequence \( \left( {{\widehat{\mathcal{M}}}_{n},{\widehat{G}}_{n},{x}_{n}}\right) \) satisfies the five hypotheses of Theorem 11.1.

Proof. By our assumptions, hypotheses (1) and (3) of Theorem 11.1 hold for this sequence. Also, we are assuming that any point \( y \in  {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) with \( R\left( y\right)  \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. Since \( R\left( {x}_{n}\right)  = \; {Q}_{n} \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) this means that for all \( n \) sufficiently large, any point \( y \in  {\widehat{\mathcal{M}}}_{n} \) with \( R\left( y\right)  \geq  R\left( {x}_{n}\right) \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. This establishes hypothesis (2) in the statement of Theorem 11.1.

Next, we have:

CLAIM 11.33. For any \( A < \infty \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the ball \( B\left( {{x}_{n},0, A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2}}\right) \) is contained in the \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) and has compact closure in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) .

Proof. Any point \( z \in  \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) has scalar curvature at most \( {16}{C}^{2}{\rho }^{-2} \) and there is a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( z \) . This means that for all \( y \) with \( {d}_{{G}_{n}}\left( {z, y}\right)  < {\epsilon }^{-1}\rho /{2C} \) we have \( R\left( y\right)  \leq  {32}{C}^{2}{\rho }^{-2} \) . Hence, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( {d}_{{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n}, z}\right)  > {\epsilon }^{-1}\rho /{2C} \) , and thus \( {d}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n}, z}\right)  > {Q}_{n}^{1/2}{\epsilon }^{-1}\rho /{2C} \) . This implies that, given \( A < \infty \) , for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( z \notin  {B}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n},0, A}\right) \) . Since this is true for all \( z \in  \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) , it follows that for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( {B}_{{Q}_{n},{G}_{n}}\left( {{x}_{n},0, A}\right)  \subset  {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) . Next, we must show that, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, this ball has compact closure. That is to say, we must show that for every \( A \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large the distance from \( {x}_{n} \) to the end of the horn \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) is greater than \( A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2} \) . If not, then since the curvature at the end of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) goes to infinity for each \( n \) , this sequence would violate Theorem 10.2.

Because \( B\left( {{x}_{n},0, A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2}}\right) \) is contained in a \( {2\epsilon } \) -horn, it is \( \kappa \) -non-collapsed on scales \( \leq  r \) for a universal \( \kappa  > 0 \) and \( r > 0 \) . Also, because every point in the horn is the center of a strong \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck, for every \( n \) sufficiently large and every \( y \in  B\left( {{x}_{n},0, A{Q}_{n}^{-1/2}}\right) \) the flow is defined on an interval through \( y \) defined for backward time \( R{\left( y\right) }^{-1} \) .

This completes the proof that all the hypotheses of Theorem 11.1 hold and establishes Claim 11.32.

We form a new sequence of generalized Ricci flows from the \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) by translating by \( - {T}_{n} \) , so that the final time-slice is at \( {\mathbf{t}}_{n} = 0 \) , where \( {\mathbf{t}}_{n} \) is the time function for \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) .

Theorem 11.1 implies that, after passing to a subsequence, there is a limit flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) ,\left( {{x}_{\infty },0}\right) }\right) , t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack  ) \) defined for some \( {t}_{0} > 0 \) for the sequence \( \left( {{Q}_{n}{\widehat{\mathcal{M}}}_{n},{Q}_{n}{\widehat{G}}_{n},{x}_{n}}\right) \) . Because of the curvature pinching toward positive assumption, by Theorem 5.33, the limit Ricci flow has non-negative sectional curvature. Of course, \( R\left( {x}_{\infty }\right)  = 1 \) so that the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is non-flat.

CLAIM 11.34. \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) is isometric to the product \( \left( {{S}^{2}, h}\right)  \times  \left( {\mathbb{R}, d{s}^{2}}\right) \) , where \( h \) is a metric of non-negative curvature on \( {S}^{2} \) and \( d{s}^{2} \) is the usual Euclidean metric on the real line.

Proof. Because of the fact that the \( \left( {{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{G}_{n}}\right) \) have curvature pinched toward positive, and since \( {Q}_{n} \) tend to \( \infty \) as \( n \) tends to infinity, it follows that the geometric limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) has non-negative curvature. In \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) take a minimizing geodesic ray \( {\alpha }_{n} \) from \( {x}_{n} \) to the end of \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) and a minimizing geodesic \( {\beta }_{n} \) from \( {x}_{n} \) to \( \partial {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) . As we have seen, the lengths of both \( {\alpha }_{n} \) and \( {\beta }_{n} \) tend to \( \infty \) as \( n \rightarrow  \infty \) . By passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the \( {\alpha }_{n} \) converge to a minimizing geodesic ray \( \alpha \) in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) and that the \( {\beta }_{n} \) converge to a minimizing geodesic ray \( \beta \) in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) . Since, for all \( n \) , the union of \( {\alpha }_{n} \) and \( {\beta }_{n} \) forms a piecewise smooth ray in \( {\mathcal{H}}_{n} \) meeting the central 2-sphere of a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{n} \) in a single point and at this point crossing from one side of this 2-sphere to the other, the union of \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) forms a proper, piecewise smooth map of \( \mathbb{R} \) to \( {M}_{\infty } \) that meets the central 2-sphere of a \( {2\epsilon } \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{\infty } \) in a single point and crosses from one side to the other at the point. This means that \( {M}_{\infty } \) has at least two ends. Since \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }}\right) \) has non-negative curvature, according to Theorem 2.13, this implies that \( {M}_{\infty } \) is a product of a surface with \( \mathbb{R} \) . Since \( M \) has nonnegative curvature, the surface has non-negative curvature. Since \( M \) has positive curvature at least at one point, the surface is diffeomorphic to the 2-sphere.

According to Theorem 11.1, after passing to a subsequence there is a limit flow defined on some interval of the form \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) for \( {t}_{0} > 0 \) . Suppose that, after passing to a subsequence there is a limit flow defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T,0}\right\rbrack \) for some \( 0 < T < \infty \) . It follows that for any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-T,0}\right\rbrack \) , the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is of non-negative curvature and has two ends. Again by Theorem 2.13, this implies that for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-T,0}\right\rbrack \) the Riemannian manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is a Riemannian product of a metric of non-negative curvature on \( {S}^{2} \) with \( \mathbb{R} \) . Thus, by Corollary 4.19 the Ricci flow is a product of a Ricci flow \( \left( {{S}^{2}, h\left( t\right) }\right) \) with the trivial flow on \( \left( {\mathbb{R}, d{s}^{2}}\right) \) . It now follows from Corollary 4.14 that for every \( t \in  ( - T,0\rbrack \) the curvature of \( {g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) \) on \( {S}^{2} \) is positive.

Let \( {M}_{n} \) be the zero time-slice of \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) . Since \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) is the geometric limit of the \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( 0\right) ,{x}_{n}}\right) \) , there is an exhaustive sequence \( {x}_{\infty } \in \; {V}_{1} \subset  {V}_{2} \subset  \cdots \) of open subsets of \( {M}_{\infty } \) with compact closure and embeddings \( {\varphi }_{n} : {V}_{n} \rightarrow  {M}_{n} \) sending \( {x}_{\infty } \) to \( {x}_{n} \) such that \( {\varphi }_{n}^{ * }\left( {{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( 0\right) }\right) \) converges in the \( {C}^{\infty } \) -topology, uniformly on compact sets, to \( {g}_{\infty } \) .

CLAIM 11.35. For any \( z \in  {M}_{\infty } \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( z \in  {V}_{n} \) , so that \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) \) is defined. Furthermore, for all \( n \) sufficiently large, there is a backward flow line through \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) \) in the generalized Ricci flow \( \left( {{Q}_{n}{\mathcal{M}}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}\right) \) defined on the interval \( \left( {-T - \left( {{R}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}^{-1}\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) ,0}\right) /2}\right) ,0}\right) \) . The scalar curvature is bounded above on this entire flow line by \( R\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) ,0}\right) \) .

Proof. Of course, for any compact subset \( K \subset  {M}_{\infty } \) and any \( {t}^{\prime } < T \) for all \( n \) sufficiently large, \( K \subset  {V}_{n} \) , and there is an embedding \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack   \subset \; {Q}_{n}{\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) compatible with time and the vector field. The map \( {\varphi }_{n} \) defines a map \( {Q}_{n}^{-1}{\varphi }_{n} : K \times  \left\lbrack  {-{Q}_{n}^{-1}{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack   \rightarrow  {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) . Since the scalar curvature of the limit is positive, and hence bounded away from zero on the compact set \( K \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) and since \( {Q}_{n} \rightarrow  \infty \) as \( n \) tends to infinity, the following is true: For any compact subset \( K \subset  M \) and any \( {t}^{\prime } < T \) , for all \( n \) sufficiently large, the scalar curvature of \( {G}_{n} \) on the image \( {Q}_{n}^{-1}{\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{Q}_{n}^{-1}{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) is greater than \( {r}_{0}^{-2} \) , and hence for all \( n \) sufficiently large, every point in \( {Q}_{n}^{-1}{\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times \; \left\lbrack  {-{Q}_{n}^{-1}{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood in \( {\mathcal{M}}_{n} \) . Since having a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood is invariant under rescaling, it follows that for all \( n \) sufficiently large, every point of \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood.

Next we claim that, for all \( n \) sufficiently large and for any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , the point \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck. We have already seen that for all \( n \) sufficiently large \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) has a strong \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -canonical neighborhood. Of course, since \( {M}_{\infty } \) is non-compact, for \( n \) sufficiently large, the canonical neighborhood of \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) must either be a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap or a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck. We shall rule out the possibility of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap, at least for all \( n \) sufficiently large.

To do this, take \( K \) to be a neighborhood of \( \left( {z,0}\right) \) in the limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) with the topology of \( {S}^{2} \times  I \) and with the metric being the product of a positively curved metric on \( {S}^{2} \) with the Euclidean metric on \( I \) . We take \( K \) to be sufficiently large to contain the \( {2C} \) -ball centered at \( \left( {z,0}\right) \) . Because the limit flow is the product of a positively curved flow on \( {S}^{2} \) with the trivial flow on \( \mathbb{R} \) , the flow is distance decreasing. Thus, for every \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) the subman-ifold \( K \times  \{ t\} \) contains the ball in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) centered at \( \left( {z, t}\right) \) of radius \( {2C} \) . For every \( n \) sufficiently large, consider the submanifolds \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) of \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) \) . Since the metrics \( {\varphi }_{n}^{ * }{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) \) are converging uniformly for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) to the product flow on \( K \) , for all \( n \) sufficiently large and any \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , this submanifold contains the \( C \) -ball centered at \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) in \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) \) . Furthermore, the maximal curvature two-plane at any point of \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) is almost tangent to the \( {S}^{2} \) -direction of \( K \) . Hence, by Lemma A. 2 the central 2-sphere of any \( \epsilon \) -neck contained \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) is almost parallel to the \( {S}^{2} \) -factors in the product structure on \( K \) at every point. This implies that the central 2-sphere of any such \( \epsilon \) -neck is isotopic to the \( {S}^{2} \) -factor of \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) . Suppose that \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) is contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap \( \mathcal{C} \) . Then \( \mathcal{C} \) is contained in \( {\varphi }_{n}\left( K\right)  \times  \{ t\} \) . Consider the \( \epsilon \) -neck \( N \subset  \mathcal{C} \) that is the complement of the core of \( \mathcal{C} \) . Its central 2-sphere, \( \sum \) , is isotopic in \( K \) to the 2-sphere factor of \( K \) , but this is absurd since \( \sum \) bounds a 3-ball in the \( \mathcal{C} \) . This contradiction shows that for all \( n \) sufficiently large and all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , it is not possible for \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) to be contained in the core of a \( \left( {C,\epsilon }\right) \) -cap. The only other possibility is that for all \( n \) sufficiently large and all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) the point \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck in \( \left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) \) .

Fix \( n \) sufficiently large. Since, for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , the point \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right) \) is the center of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck, it follows from Definition 9.78 that for all \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) we have \( R\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , t}\right)  \leq  R\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) ,0}\right) \) (this follows from the fact that the partial derivative in the time-direction of the scalar curvature of a strong \( \epsilon \) -neck of scale one is positive and bounded away from 0 \( ) \) . It also follows from Definition 9.78 that the flow near \( \left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( z\right) , - {t}^{\prime }}\right) \) extends backwards to time

\[
- {t}^{\prime } - {R}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}^{-1}\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( {z,{t}^{\prime }}\right) }\right)  <  - {t}^{\prime } - {R}_{{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}}^{-1}\left( {{\varphi }_{n}\left( {z,0}\right) }\right) ,
\]

with the same inequality for scalar curvature holding for all \( t \) in this extended interval. Applying this for \( {t}^{\prime } < T \) but sufficiently close to \( T \) establishes the last statement in the claim, and completes the proof of the claim.

Let \( {Q}_{0} \) be the upper bound of the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( 0\right) }\right) \) . By the previous claim, \( {Q}_{0} \) is also an upper bound for the curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( {-{t}^{\prime }}\right) }\right) \) for any \( {t}^{\prime } < T \) . Applying Theorem 11.1 to the flows

\[
\left( {{M}_{n},{Q}_{n}{G}_{n}\left( t\right) }\right) , - {t}^{\prime } - {Q}_{0}^{-1}/2 < t \leq   - {t}^{\prime },
\]

we conclude that there is \( {t}_{0} \) depending only on the bound of the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{g}_{\infty }\left( {-{t}^{\prime }}\right) }\right) \) , and hence depending only on \( {Q}_{0} \) , such that, after passing to a subsequence the limit flow exists for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime } - {t}_{0}, - {t}^{\prime }}\right\rbrack \) . Since the limit flow already exists on \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , we conclude that, for this further subsequence, the limit flow exists on \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}^{\prime } - {t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) . Now apply this with \( {t}^{\prime } = T - {t}_{0}/2 \) . This proves that if, after passing to a subsequence, there is a limit flow defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T,0}\right\rbrack \) , then, after passing to a further subsequence there is a limit flow defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T - {t}_{0}/2,0}\right\rbrack \) where \( {t}_{0} \) depends only on \( {Q}_{0} \) , and in particular, is independent of \( T \) . Repeating this argument with \( T + \left( {{t}_{0}/2}\right) \) replacing \( T \) , we pass to a further subsequence so that the limit flow is defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T - {t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) . Repeating this inductively, we can find a sequence of subsequences so that for the \( n \) subsequence the limit flow is defined on \( \left\lbrack  {-T - n{t}_{0},0}\right\rbrack \) . Taking a diagonal subsequence produces a subsequence for which the limit is defined on \( ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) .

The limit flow is the product of a flow on \( {S}^{2} \) of positive curvature defined for \( t \in  ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) and the trivial flow on \( \mathbb{R} \) . Now, invoking Hamilton’s result (Corollary 9.50), we see that the ancient solution of positive curvature on \( {S}^{2} \) must be a shrinking round \( {S}^{2} \) . This means that the limit flow is the product of the shrinking round \( {S}^{2} \) with \( \mathbb{R} \) , and implies that for all \( n \) sufficiently large there is a strong \( \delta \) -neck centered at \( {x}_{n} \) . This contradiction proves the existence of \( h \) as required.

Now let us establish the last statement in Theorem 11.31. The subset of \( \mathcal{H} \) consisting of all \( z \in  \mathcal{H} \) with \( R\left( z\right)  \leq  {\rho }^{-2} \) is compact (since \( R \) is a proper function), and disjoint from any \( \delta \) -neck of scale \( h \) since \( h < \rho /{2C} \) . On the other hand, for any point \( z \in  \mathcal{H} \) with \( R\left( z\right)  \leq  {\rho }^{-2} \) take a minimal geodesic from \( z \) to the end of \( \mathcal{H} \) . There must be a point \( y \) on this geodesic with \( R\left( y\right)  = {h}^{-2} \) . The \( \delta \) -neck centered at \( y \) is disjoint from \( z \) (since \( h < \rho /{2C} \) ) and hence this neck separates \( z \) from the end of \( \mathcal{H} \) . It now follows easily that there is a point \( y \in  \mathcal{H} \) with \( R\left( y\right)  = {h}^{-2} \) and such that the central 2-sphere of the \( \delta \) -neck centered at \( y \) divides \( \mathcal{H} \) into two pieces with the non-compact piece disjoint from \( {\Omega }_{\rho } \) .

(Justification of the canonical neighborhood assumption). Given any small \( \varepsilon  > 0 \) , there exist decreasing sequences \( 0 < {\widetilde{r}}_{j} < \varepsilon ,{\kappa }_{j} > 0 \) , and \( 0 < {\widetilde{\delta }}_{j} < {\varepsilon }^{2}, j = 1,2,\cdots \) , with the following property. Define the positive function \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) \) on \( \lbrack 0, + \infty ) \) by \( \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right)  = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{j} \) for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {j - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, j{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) \) . Suppose there is a surgically modified solution, defined on \( \lbrack 0, T) \) with \( T <  + \infty \) , to the Ricci flow which satisfies the following:

(1) it starts on a compact orientable three-manifold with normalized initial metric, and

(2) it has only a finite number of surgeries such that each surgery at a time \( t \in  \left( {0, T}\right) \) is a \( \delta \left( t\right) \) -cutoff surgery with

\[
0 < \delta \left( t\right)  \leq  \min \{ \widetilde{\delta }\left( t\right) ,\bar{\delta }\left( t\right) \} .
\]

Then on each time interval \( \left\lbrack  {\left( {j - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}, j{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack  \bigcap \lbrack 0, T), j = 1,2,\cdots \) , the solution satisfies the \( {\kappa }_{j} \) -noncollapsing condition on all scales less than \( \varepsilon \) and the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) with \( r = {\widetilde{r}}_{j} \) .

Here and in the following, we call a (three-dimensional) surgically modified solution \( {g}_{ij}\left( t\right) ,0 \leq  t < T,\kappa \) -noncollapsed at \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) on the scales less than \( \rho \) (for some \( \kappa  > 0,\rho  > 0 \) ) if it satisfies the following property: whenever \( r < \rho \) and

\[
\left| {{Rm}\left( {x, t}\right) }\right|  \leq  {r}^{-2}
\]

for all those \( \left( {x, t}\right)  \in  P\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}, r, - {r}^{2}}\right)  = \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {B}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) ,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - {r}^{2},{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , for which the solution is defined, we have

\[
{\operatorname{Vol}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{B}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {{x}_{0}, r}\right) }\right)  \geq  \kappa {r}^{3}.
\]

The proof of the proposition is by induction: having constructed our sequences for \( 1 \leq  j \leq  m \) , we make one more step, defining \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m + 1} \) , \( {\kappa }_{m + 1},{\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) , and redefining \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) . In view of the previous lemma, we only need to define \( {\widetilde{r}}_{m + 1} \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) .

In Theorem 7.1.1 we have obtained the canonical neighborhood structure for smooth solutions. When adapting the arguments in the proof of Theorem 7.1.1 to the present surgical solutions, we will encounter the new difficulty of how to take a limit for the surgically modified solutions. The idea to overcome the difficulty consists of two parts. The first part, due to Perelman [104], is to choose \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) small enough to push the surgical regions to infinity in space. (This is the reason why we need to redefine \( {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m} = {\widetilde{\delta }}_{m + 1} \) .) The second part is to show that solutions are smooth on some small, but uniform, time intervals (on compact subsets) so that we can apply Hamilton's compactness theorem, since we only have curvature bounds; otherwise Shi's interior derivative estimate may not be applicable. In fact, the second part is more crucial. That is just concerned with the question of whether the surgery times accumulate or not. Our argument will use the canonical neighborhood characterization of the standard solution in Lemma 7.3.5.

We now start to prove the proposition by contradiction. Suppose for sequence of positive numbers \( {r}^{\alpha } \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) , satisfying \( {r}^{\alpha } \rightarrow  0 \) as \( \alpha  \rightarrow  \infty \) and \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \leq  \frac{1}{\alpha  \cdot  \beta }\left( { \rightarrow  0}\right) \) , there exist sequences of solutions \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) to the Ricci flow with surgery, where each of them has only a finite number of cutoff surgeries and has a compact orientable normalized three-manifold as initial data, so that the following two assertions hold:

(i) each \( \delta \) -cutoff at a time \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {\left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) satisfies \( \delta  \leq  {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) ; and

(ii) the solutions satisfy the statement of the proposition on \( \left\lbrack  {0, m{\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) , but violate the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) on \( \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) .

For each solution \( {g}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) , we choose \( \bar{t} \) (depending on \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) ) to be the nearly first time for which the canonical neighborhood assumption (with accuracy \( \varepsilon \) ) is violated. More precisely, we choose \( \bar{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\left( {m + 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right\rbrack \) so that the canonical neighborhood assumption with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) and with accuracy parameter \( \varepsilon \) is violated at some \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) , however the canonical neighborhood assumption with accuracy parameter \( {2\varepsilon } \) holds on \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {m{\varepsilon }^{2},\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) . After passing to subsequences, we may assume each \( {\widetilde{\delta }}^{\alpha \beta } \) is less than the \( \widetilde{\delta } \) in Lemma 7.4.2 with \( r = {r}^{\alpha } \) when \( \alpha \) is fixed. Then by Lemma 7.4.2 we have uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing on all scales less than \( \varepsilon \) on \( \left\lbrack  {0,\bar{t}}\right\rbrack \) with some \( \kappa  > 0 \) independent of \( \alpha ,\beta \) .

Slightly abusing notation, we will often drop the indices \( \alpha \) and \( \beta \) .

Let \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) be the rescaled solutions around \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with factors \( R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \left( { \geq  {r}^{-2} \rightarrow   + \infty }\right) \) and shift the times \( \bar{t} \) to zero. We hope to take a limit of the rescaled solutions for subsequences of \( \alpha ,\beta  \rightarrow  \infty \) and show the limit is an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution, which will give the desired contradiction. We divide our arguments into the following six steps.

Step 1. Let \( \left( {y,\widehat{t}}\right) \) be a point on the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) with \( \widetilde{R}\left( {y,\widehat{t}}\right)  \leq  A \) (for some \( A \geq  1 \) ) and \( \widehat{t} \in  \left\lbrack  {-\left( {\bar{t} - \left( {m - 1}\right) {\varepsilon }^{2}}\right) R\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) ,0}\right\rbrack \) . Then we have estimate

(7.4.14)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10A}
\]

for those \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in the parabolic neighborhood \( P\left( {y,\widehat{t},\frac{1}{2}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-\frac{1}{2}}, - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-1}}\right)  \triangleq \; \left\{  {\left( {{x}^{\prime },{t}^{\prime }}\right)  \mid  {x}^{\prime } \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}^{\prime }}\left( {y,\frac{1}{2}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) ,{t}^{\prime } \in  \left\lbrack  {\widehat{t} - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}{A}^{-1},\widehat{t}}\right\rbrack  }\right\} \) , for which the rescaled solution is defined.

Indeed, as in the first step of the proof of Theorem 7.1.1, this follows directly from the gradient estimates (7.3.4) in the canonical neighborhood assumption with parameter \( {2\varepsilon } \) .

Step 2. In this step, we will prove three time extension results.

Assertion 1. Before giving the proof, we make a simple observation: once a space point in the Ricci flow with surgery is removed by surgery at some time, then it never appears for later time; if a space point at some time \( t \) cannot be defined before the time \( t \) , then either the point lies in a gluing cap of the surgery at time \( t \) or the time \( t \) is the initial time of the Ricci flow.

Firstly we claim that there exists \( {\beta }_{0} = {\beta }_{0}\left( {\varepsilon , A, B, C}\right) \) such that when \( \beta  \geq  {\beta }_{0} \) , the rescaled solution \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\alpha \beta } \) on the ball \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) can be defined before the time \( - b \) (i.e., there are no surgeries interfering in \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {-b - {\epsilon }^{\prime }, - b}\right\rbrack \) for some \( \left. {{\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0}\right) \) .

\[

CLAIM 1. For any \( 0 < \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) with \( \rho \) near \( {\rho }_{0} \) , by applying Assertion 3 as before, we get that the rescaled solutions on the balls \( {B}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},\rho }\right) \) are defined on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - \frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}M{\left( \rho \right) }^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) for all large \( k \) . By Step 1 and Shi’s derivative estimate, we further know that the covariant derivatives and higher order derivatives of the curvatures on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},\rho  - \frac{\left( {\rho }_{0} - \rho \right) }{2}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - \frac{1}{32}{\eta }^{-1}M{\left( \rho \right) }^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) are also uniformly bounded. Then by the uniform \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing property and Hamilton’s compactness theorem (Theorem 4.1.5), after passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the marked sequence \( \left( {{\widetilde{B}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{y}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}}\left( {\cdot ,{t}_{k}}\right) ,{y}_{k}}\right) \) converges in the \( {C}_{loc}^{\infty } \) topology to a marked (noncomplete) manifold \( \left( {{B}_{\infty },{\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty },{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) and the geodesic segments \( {\gamma }_{k} \) converge to a geodesic segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {B}_{\infty } \) emanating from \( {y}_{\infty } \) .

Clearly, the limit also has nonnegative sectional curvature by the pinching assumption. Then by repeating the same argument as in the proof of Assertion 4 (i) in the rest, we derive a contradiction with Hamilton's strong maximum principle. This proves Assertion 5.

We then apply the second estimate of (7.4.17) and Assertion 5 to conclude that for any large constant \( 0 < A <  + \infty \) , there is a positive constant \( C\left( A\right) \) such that for any small \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) , the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) satisfy

(7.4.18)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C\left( A\right)
\]

for all \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime },0}\right\rbrack \) , and for all sufficiently large \( k \) . Then by applying Assertion 1 in Step 2, we conclude that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) on the geodesic balls \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) are also defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime } - }\right. \; \left. {\frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) for all sufficiently large \( k \) . Furthermore, by the gradient estimates as in Step 1, we have

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10C}\left( A\right)
\]

for \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } + {\epsilon }^{\prime } - \frac{1}{8}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) . Since \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } > 0 \) is arbitrarily small and the positive constant \( C\left( A\right) \) is independent of \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \) , we conclude that the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) on \( {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) are defined on the extended time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - }\right. \; \left. {\frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) and satisfy

(7.4.19)

\[
\widetilde{R}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  {10C}\left( A\right) ,
\]

for \( x \in  {\widetilde{B}}_{0}\left( {\bar{x}, A}\right) \) and \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max } - \frac{1}{16}{\eta }^{-1}C{\left( A\right) }^{-1},0}\right\rbrack \) , and for all sufficiently large \( k \) .

Now, by taking convergent subsequences from the rescaled solutions \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{{\alpha }_{k}{\beta }_{k}} \) , we see that the limit solution is defined smoothly on a space-time open subset of \( {M}_{\infty } \times \; ( - \infty ,0\rbrack \) containing \( {M}_{\infty } \times  \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) . By Step 4, we see that the limiting metric \( {\widetilde{g}}_{ij}^{\infty }\left( {\cdot , - {t}_{\max }}\right) \) at time \( - {t}_{\max } \) has bounded curvature. Then by combining with the canonical neighborhood assumption of accuracy \( {2\varepsilon } \) , we conclude that the curvature of the limit is uniformly bounded on the time interval \( \left\lbrack  {-{t}_{\max },0}\right\rbrack \) . So we have excluded the possibility (1).

Hence we have proved a subsequence of the rescaled solutions converges to an orientable ancient \( \kappa \) -solution.

Finally by combining with the canonical neighborhood theorem (Theorem 6.4.6), we see that \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) has a canonical neighborhood with parameter \( \varepsilon \) , which is a contradiction. Therefore we have completed the proof of the proposition. 0

knowledge_statements.statement_latex: (cf. Theorem I.12.1) Given \( \epsilon ,\kappa ,\sigma  > 0 \) and a function \( \Phi \) as above, one can find \( {r}_{0} > 0 \) with the following property. Let \( g\left( \cdot \right) \) be a Ricci flow solution on a three-manifold \( M \) , defined for \( 0 \leq  t \leq  T \) with \( T \geq  1 \) . We suppose that for each \( t, g\left( t\right) \) is complete, and the sectional curvature is bounded on compact time intervals. Suppose that the Ricci flow has \( \Phi \) -almost nonnegative curvature and is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales less than \( \sigma \) . Then for any point \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{0} \geq  1 \) and \( Q = R\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right)  \geq  {r}_{0}^{-2} \) , the solution in \( \left\{  {\left( {x, t}\right)  : {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{0}}^{2}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  < {\left( \epsilon Q\right) }^{-1},{t}_{0} - {\left( \epsilon Q\right) }^{-1} \leq  t \leq  {t}_{0}}\right\} \) is, after scaling by the factor \( Q \) , \( \epsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of a \( \kappa \) -solution.

knowledge_statements.proof_latex:
We give a proof which differs in some points from the proof in [51] but which has the same ingredients. We first outline the argument.

Suppose that the theorem is false. Then for some \( \epsilon ,\kappa ,\sigma  > 0 \) , we have a sequence of such \( \Phi \) -nonnegatively curved 3-dimensional Ricci flows \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) defined on intervals \( \left\lbrack  {0,{T}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) , and sequences \( {r}_{k} \rightarrow  0,{\widehat{x}}_{k} \in  {M}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k} \geq  1 \) such that \( {M}_{k} \) is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales \( < \sigma \) and \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right)  \geq  {r}_{k}^{-2} \) , but the \( {Q}_{k} \) -rescaled solution in \( {B}_{{\left( \epsilon {Q}_{k}\right) }^{-1/2}}\left( {\widehat{x}}_{k}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {{\widehat{t}}_{k} - {\left( \epsilon {Q}_{k}\right) }^{-1},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) is not \( \epsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of any \( \kappa \) -solution.

We note that if the statement were false for \( \epsilon \) then it would also be false for any smaller \( \epsilon \) . Because of this, somewhat paradoxically, we will begin the argument with a given \( \epsilon \) but will allow ourselves to make \( \epsilon \) small enough later so that the argument works. To be clear, we will eventually get a contradiction using a fixed (small) value of \( \epsilon \) , but as the proof goes along we will impose some upper bounds on this value in order for the proof to work. (If we tried to list all of the constraints at the beginning of the argument then they would look unmotivated.)

The goal is to get a contradiction based on the "bad" points \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) . In a sense, the method of proof of Theorem 52.7 is an induction on the curvature scale. For example, if we were to make the additional assumption in the theorem that \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  R\left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) for all \( x \in  M \) and \( t \leq  {t}_{0} \) then the theorem would be very easy to prove. We would just take a convergent subsequence of the rescaled solutions, based at \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) , to get a \( \kappa \) -solution; this would give a contradiction. This simple argument can be considered to be the first step in a proof by induction on curvature scale. In the proof of Theorem 52.7 one effectively proves the result at a given curvature scale inductively by assuming that the result is true at higher curvature scales.

The actual proof consists of four steps. Step 1 consists of replacing the sequence \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) by another sequence of "bad" points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) which have the property that points near \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) with distinctly higher scalar curvature are "good" points. It then suffices to get a contradiction based on the existence of the sequence \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) .

In steps 2-4 one uses the points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) to build up a \( \kappa \) -solution, whose existence then contradicts the "badness" of the points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . More precisely, let \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) be the result of rescaling \( {g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) \) by \( R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . We will show that the sequence of pointed flows \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) accumulates on a \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) , thereby obtaining a contradiction.

In step 2 one takes a pointed limit of the manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{k},{x}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) in order to construct what will become the final time slice of the \( \kappa \) -solution, \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) . In order to take this limit, it is necessary to show that the manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{k},{x}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) have uniformly bounded curvature on distance balls of a fixed radius. If this were not true then for some radius, a subsequence of the manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{k},{x}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) would have curvatures that asymptotically blowup on the ball of that radius. One shows that geometrically, the curvature blowup is due to the asymptotic formation of a cone-like point at the blowup radius. Doing a further rescaling at this cone-like point, one obtains a Ricci flow solution that ends on a part of a nonflat metric cone. This gives a contradiction as in the case \( 0 < \mathcal{R} < \infty \) of Theorem 41.2.

Thus one can construct the pointed limit \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) . The goal now is to show that \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) is the final time slice of a \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) . In step 3 one shows that \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) extends backward to a Ricci flow solution on some time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - \Delta ,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , and that the time slices have bounded nonnegative curvature. In step 4 one shows that the Ricci flow solution can be extended all the way to time \( \left( {-\infty ,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , thereby constructing a \( \kappa \) -solution

Step 1: Adjusting the choice of basepoints.

We first modify the points \( \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) slightly in time to points \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) so that in the given Ricci flow solution, there are no other "bad" points with much larger scalar curvature in a earlier time interval whose length is large compared to \( R{\left( {x}_{k},{t}_{k}\right) }^{-1} \) . (The phrase "nearly the smallest curvature \( Q \) " in [51, Proof of Theorem 12.1] should read "nearly the largest curvature \( Q \) ". This is clear from the sentence in parentheses that follows.) The proof of the next lemma is by pointpicking, as in Appendix H.

Lemma 52.9. We can find \( {H}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty ,{x}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) , and \( {t}_{k} \geq  \frac{1}{2} \) such that \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) , and for all \( k \) the conclusion of Theorem 52.7 fails at \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) , but holds for any \( \left( {y, t}\right)  \in \; {M}_{k} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - {H}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) for which \( R\left( {y, t}\right)  \geq  {2R}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) .

Proof. Choose \( {H}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) such that \( {H}_{k}{\left( R\left( {\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}\right) \right) }^{-1} \leq  \frac{1}{10} \) for all \( k \) . For each \( k \) , initially set \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  = \left( {{\widehat{x}}_{k},{\widehat{t}}_{k}}\right) \) . Put \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) and look for a point in \( {M}_{k} \times  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - {H}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1},{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) at which Theorem 52.7 fails, and the scalar curvature is at least \( {2R}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . If such a point exists, replace \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) by this point; otherwise do nothing. Repeat this until the second alternative occurs. This process must terminate with a new choice of \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) satisfying the lemma.

Hereafter we use this modified sequence \( \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . Let \( \left( {{M}_{k},\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) be the result of rescaling \( {g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) \) by \( {Q}_{k} = R\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) . We use \( {\bar{R}}_{k} \) to denote its scalar curvature; in particular, \( {\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  = 1 \) . Note that the rescaled time interval of Lemma 52.9 has duration \( {H}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) ; this is what we want in order to try to extract an ancient solution.

Step 2: For every \( \rho  < \infty \) , the scalar curvature \( {\bar{R}}_{k} \) is uniformly bounded on the \( \rho \) -balls \( B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) (the argument for this is essentially equivalent to [51, Pf. of Claim 2 of Theorem I.12.1]). Before proceeding, we need some bounds which come from our choice of basepoints, and the derivative bounds inherited (by approximation) from \( \kappa \) -solutions.

Lemma 52.10. There is a constant \( C = C\left( \kappa \right) \) so that for any \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) in a Ricci flow solution, if \( R\left( {x, t}\right)  > 0 \) and the solution in \( {B}_{t}\left( {x,{\left( \epsilon R\left( x, t\right) \right) }^{-1/2}}\right)  \times  \left\lbrack  {t - {\left( \epsilon R\left( x, t\right) \right) }^{-1}, t}\right\rbrack \) is \( \epsilon \) -close to a corresponding subset of a \( \kappa \) -solution then \( \left| {\nabla {R}^{-1/2}}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C \) and \( \left| {{\partial }_{t}{R}^{-1}}\right| \left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  C \) .

Proof. This follows from the compactness in Theorem 46.1.

Note that the same value of \( C \) in Lemma 52.10 also works for smaller \( \epsilon \) .

Lemma 52.11. (cf. Claim 1 of I.12.1) For each \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{k} - \frac{1}{2}{H}_{k}{Q}_{k}^{-1} \leq  \bar{t} \leq  {t}_{k} \) , we have \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4{\bar{Q}}_{k} \) whenever \( \bar{t} - c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  c{\bar{Q}}_{k}^{-1/2} \) , where \( {\bar{Q}}_{k} = {Q}_{k} + \left| {{R}_{k}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) }\right| \) and \( c = c\left( \kappa \right)  > 0 \) is a small constant.

Proof. If \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  2{Q}_{k} \) then there is nothing to show. If \( {R}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  > 2{Q}_{k} \) , consider a spacetime curve \( \gamma \) that goes linearly from \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to \( \left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) , and then goes from \( \left( {x,\bar{t}}\right) \) to \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) along a minimizing geodesic. If there is a point on \( \gamma \) with curvature \( 2{Q}_{k} \) , let \( p \) be the nearest such point to \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) . If not, put \( p = \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) . From the conclusion of Lemma 52.9, we can apply Lemma 52.10 along \( \gamma \) from \( \left( {x, t}\right) \) to \( p \) . The claim follows from integrating the ensuing derivative bounds along \( \gamma \) .

Lemma 52.12. In terms of the rescaled solution \( {\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) \) , for each \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) \) with \( {t}_{k} - \frac{1}{2}{H}_{k} \leq  \bar{t} \leq  {t}_{k} \) , we have \( {\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  4{\widetilde{Q}}_{k} \) whenever \( \bar{t} - c{\widetilde{Q}}_{k}^{-1} \leq  t \leq  \bar{t} \) and \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{\bar{t}}\left( {x,\bar{x}}\right)  \leq  c{\widetilde{Q}}_{k}^{-1/2} \) , where \( {\widetilde{Q}}_{k} = 1 + \left| {{\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right) }\right| . \)

Proof. This is just the rescaled version of Lemma 52.11.

For all \( \rho  \geq  0 \) , put

(52.13)

\[
D\left( \rho \right)  = \sup \left\{  {{\bar{R}}_{k}\left( {x,{t}_{k}}\right)  \mid  k \geq  1, x \in  B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) }\right\}  ,
\]

and let \( {\rho }_{0} \) be the supremum of the \( \rho \) ’s for which \( D\left( \rho \right)  < \infty \) . Note that \( {\rho }_{0} > 0 \) , in view of Lemma 52.12 (taking \( \left( {\bar{x},\bar{t}}\right)  = \left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) ). Suppose that \( {\rho }_{0} < \infty \) . After passing to a subsequence if necessary, we can find a sequence \( {y}_{k} \in  {M}_{k} \) with \( {\operatorname{dist}}_{{t}_{k}}\left( {{x}_{k},{y}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} \) and \( \bar{R}\left( {{y}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) . Let \( {\eta }_{k} \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) be a minimizing geodesic segment from \( {x}_{k} \) to \( {y}_{k} \) . Let \( {z}_{k} \in  {\eta }_{k} \) be the point on \( {\eta }_{k} \) closest to \( {y}_{k} \) at which \( \bar{R}\left( {{z}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right)  = 2 \) , and let \( {\gamma }_{k} \) be the subsegment of \( {\eta }_{k} \) running from \( {y}_{k} \) to \( {z}_{k} \) . By Lemma 52.12 the length of \( {\gamma }_{k} \) is bounded away from zero independent of \( k \) . Due to the \( \Phi \) -pinching (see (52.4)), for all \( \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) , we have a uniform bound on \( \left| \mathrm{{Rm}}\right| \) on the balls \( B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) . The injectivity radius is also controlled in \( B\left( {{x}_{k},\rho }\right) \) , in view of the curvature bounds and the \( \kappa \) -noncollapsing. Therefore after passing to a subsequence, we can assume that the pointed sequence \( \left( {B\left( {{x}_{k},{\rho }_{0}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) converges in the pointed Gromov-Hausdorff topology (i.e. for all \( \rho  < {\rho }_{0} \) we have the usual Gromov-Hausdorff convergence) to a pointed \( {C}^{1} \) -Riemannian manifold \( \left( {Z,{\bar{g}}_{\infty },{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) , the segments \( {\eta }_{k} \) converge to a segment (missing an endpoint) \( {\eta }_{\infty } \subset  Z \) emanating from \( {x}_{\infty } \) , and \( {\gamma }_{k} \) converges to \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \subset  {\eta }_{\infty } \) . Let \( \bar{Z} \) denote the completion of \( \left( {Z,{\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) , and \( {y}_{\infty } \in  \bar{Z} \) the limit point of \( {\eta }_{\infty } \) . Note that by Lemma 52.9 and part 4 of Corollary 42.1, the Riemannian structure near \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) may be chosen to be many times differentiable. (Alternatively, this follows from Lemma 52.12 and the Shi estimates of Appendix D.) In particular the scalar curvature \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty } \) is defined, differentiable, and satisfies the bound in Lemma 52.10 near \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) .

Lemma 52.14. 1. There is a function \( c : \left( {0,\infty }\right)  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) depending only on \( \kappa \) , with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}c\left( t\right)  = \; \infty \) , such that if \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) then \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) d{\left( {y}_{\infty }, w\right) }^{2} > c\left( \epsilon \right) \) .

2. There is a function \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } : \left( {0,\infty }\right)  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \cup  \{ \infty \} \) depending only on \( \kappa \) , with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}{\epsilon }^{\prime }\left( t\right)  = 0 \) , such that if \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) and \( d\left( {{y}_{\infty }, w}\right) \) is sufficiently small then the pointed manifold \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( 2{\epsilon }^{\prime }\left( \epsilon \right) \) -close to a round cylinder in the \( {C}^{2} \) topology.

Proof. It follows from Lemma 52.9 that for all \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) , the pointed Riemannian manifold \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( {2\epsilon } \) -close to (a time slice of) a pointed \( \kappa \) -solution. From the definition of pointed closeness, there is an embedded region around \( w \) , large on the scale defined by \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) \) , which is close to the corresponding subset of a pointed \( \kappa \) -solution. This gives a lower bound on the distance \( {\rho }_{0} - d\left( {w,{x}_{\infty }}\right) \) to the point of curvature blowup, thereby proving part 1 of the lemma.

We know that \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( {2\epsilon } \) -close to a pointed \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {N,\star , h\left( t\right) }\right) \) in the pointed \( {C}^{2} \) -topology. By Lemma 52.10, we know \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) \) tends to \( \infty \) as \( d\left( {w,{x}_{\infty }}\right)  \rightarrow  {\rho }_{0} \) , for \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) . In particular, \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {d}^{2}\left( {w,{x}_{\infty }}\right)  \rightarrow  \infty \) . From part 1 above, we can choose \( \epsilon \) small enough in order to make \( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {d}^{2}\left( {w,{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) large enough to apply Proposition 49.1. Hence the pointed manifold \( \left( {N,\star , R\left( \star \right) h\left( t\right) }\right) \) is \( {\epsilon }^{\prime \prime }\left( \epsilon \right) \) -close to a round cylinder, where \( {\epsilon }^{\prime \prime } : \left( {0,\infty }\right)  \rightarrow  \mathbb{R} \) is a function with \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{t \rightarrow  0}}{\epsilon }^{\prime \prime }\left( t\right)  = 0 \) . The lemma follows.

Note that the function \( {\epsilon }^{\prime } \) in Lemma 52.14 is independent of the particular manifold \( Z \) that arises in our proof.

From part 2 of Lemma 52.14, if \( \epsilon \) is small and \( w \in  {\gamma }_{\infty } \) is sufficiently close to \( {y}_{\infty } \) then \( \left( {Z, w,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is \( {C}^{2} \) -close to a round cylinder. The cross-section of the cylinder has diameter approximately \( \pi {\left( {\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( w\right) /2\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \) . If we form the union of the balls \( B\left( {w,{2\pi }{\left( {R}_{\infty }\left( w\right) /2\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) , as \( w \) ranges over such points in \( {\gamma }_{\infty } \) , then we obtain a connected Riemannian manifold \( W \) . By adding in the point \( {y}_{\infty } \) , we get a metric space \( \bar{W} \) which is locally complete, and geodesic near \( {y}_{\infty } \) . As the original manifolds \( {M}_{k} \) had \( \Phi \) -almost nonnegative curvature, it follows from Lemma 52.5 that \( W \) is nonnegatively curved. Furthermore, \( {y}_{\infty } \) cannot be an interior point of any geodesic segment in \( \bar{W} \) , since such a geodesic would have to pass through a cylindrical region near \( {y}_{\infty } \) twice. The usual proof of the Toponogov triangle comparison inequality now applies near \( {y}_{\infty } \) since minimizers remain in the smooth nonnegatively curved part of \( \bar{W} \) . Then \( \bar{W} \) has nonnegative curvature in the Alexandrov sense.

This implies that blowups of \( \left( {\bar{W},{y}_{\infty }}\right) \) converge to the tangent cone \( {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{W} \) . As \( \bar{W} \) is three-dimensional, so is \( {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{W} \) [12, Corollary 7.11]. It will be \( {C}^{2} \) -smooth away from the vertex and nowhere flat, by part 2 of Lemma 52.14. Pick \( z \in  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{W} \) such that \( d\left( {z,{y}_{\infty }}\right)  = 1 \) . Then for any \( \delta  < \frac{1}{2} \) , the ball \( B\left( {z,\delta }\right)  \subset  {C}_{{y}_{\infty }}\bar{W} \) is the Gromov-Hausdorff limit of a sequence of rescaled balls \( B\left( {{\widehat{z}}_{k},{\widehat{r}}_{k}}\right)  \subset  \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) where \( {\widehat{r}}_{k} \rightarrow  0 \) , whose center points \( \left( {{\widehat{z}}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) \) satisfy the conclusions of Theorem 52.7. Applying Lemma 52.12 and Appendix B, if \( \delta  = \delta \left( \kappa \right) \) is taken small enough then we get the curvature bounds needed to extract a limiting Ricci flow solution whose time zero slice is isometric to \( B\left( {z,\delta }\right) \) . Now we can apply the reasoning from the \( 0 < \mathcal{R} < \infty \) case of Theorem 41.2 to get a contradiction. This completes step 2.

Step 3: The sequence of pointed flows \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) ,\left( {{x}_{k},{t}_{k}}\right) }\right) \) accumulates on a pointed Ricci flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) ,\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) which is defined on a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) with \( {t}^{\prime } < {t}_{0} \) . By step 2, we know that the scalar curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) at \( y \in  {M}_{k} \) is bounded by a function of the distance from \( y \) to \( {x}_{k} \) . Lemma 52.12 extends this curvature control to a backward parabolic neighborhood centered at \( y \) whose radius depends only on \( d\left( {y,{x}_{k}}\right) \) . Thus we can conclude, using \( \Phi \) -pinching (52.4) and Shi’s estimates (Appendix D), that all derivatives of the curvature \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) }\right) \) are controlled as a function of the distance from \( {x}_{k} \) , which means that the sequence of pointed manifolds \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( {t}_{k}\right) ,{x}_{k}}\right) \) accumulates to a smooth manifold \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) .

From Lemma 52.5, \( {M}_{\infty } \) has nonnegative sectional curvature. We claim that \( {M}_{\infty } \) has bounded curvature. If not then there is a sequence of points \( {q}_{k} \in  {M}_{\infty } \) so that \( \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{k \rightarrow  \infty }}\bar{R}\left( {q}_{k}\right)  = \; \infty \) and \( \bar{R}\left( q\right)  \leq  2\bar{R}\left( {q}_{k}\right) \) for \( q \in  B\left( {{y}_{k},{A}_{k}\bar{R}{\left( {q}_{k}\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}}}\right) \) , where \( {A}_{k} \rightarrow  \infty \) ; compare [33, Lemma 22.2]. Lemma 52.9 implies that for large \( k \) , a rescaled neighborhood of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{q}_{k}}\right) \) is \( \epsilon \) -close to the corresponding subset of a time slice of a \( \kappa \) -solution. As in the proof of Theorem 46.1, we obtain a sequence of neck-like regions in \( {M}_{\infty } \) with smaller and smaller cross-sections, which contradicts the existence of the Sharafutdinov retraction.

By Lemma 52.12 again, we now get curvature control on \( \left( {{M}_{k},{\bar{g}}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) for a time interval \( \left\lbrack  {{t}_{k} - \Delta ,{t}_{k}}\right\rbrack \) for some \( \Delta  > 0 \) , and hence we can extract a subsequence which converges to a pointed Ricci flow \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) ,{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) defined for \( t \in  \left\lbrack  {{t}_{0} - \Delta ,{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , which has nonnegative curvature and bounded curvature on compact time intervals.

Step 4: Getting an ancient solution. Let \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) be the maximal time interval on which we can extract a limiting solution \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) with bounded curvature on compact time intervals. Suppose that \( {t}^{\prime } >  - \infty \) . By Lemma 52.12 the maximum of the scalar curvature on the time slice \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) must tend to infinity as \( t \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime } \) . From the trace Harnack inequality, \( {R}_{t} + \frac{R}{t - {t}^{\prime }} \geq  0 \) , and so

(52.15)

\[
{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( {x, t}\right)  \leq  Q\frac{{t}_{0} - {t}^{\prime }}{t - {t}^{\prime }},
\]

where \( Q \) is the maximum of the scalar curvature on \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) . Combining this with Corollary 27.16, we get

(52.16)

\[
\frac{d}{dt}{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  \geq  \text{ const. }\sqrt{Q\frac{{t}_{0} - {t}^{\prime }}{t - {t}^{\prime }}}.
\]

Since the right hand side is integrable on \( \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , and using the fact that distances are nonincreasing in time (since \( \mathrm{{Rm}} \geq  0 \) ), it follows that there is a constant \( C \) such that

(52.17)

\[
\left| {{d}_{t}\left( {x, y}\right)  - {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x, y}\right) }\right|  < C
\]

for all \( x, y \in  {M}_{\infty }, t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) .

If \( {M}_{\infty } \) is compact then by (52.17) the diameter of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) is bounded independent of \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) . Since the minimum of the scalar curvature is increasing in time, it is also bounded independent of \( t \) . Now the argument in Step 2 shows that the curvature is bounded everywhere independent of \( t \) . (We can apply the argument of Step 2 to the time- \( t \) slice because the main ingredient was Lemma 52.9, which holds for rescaled time \( t \) .)

We may therefore assume \( {M}_{\infty } \) is noncompact. To be consistent with the notation of I.12.1, we now relabel the basepoint \( \left( {{x}_{\infty },{t}_{0}}\right) \) as \( \left( {{x}_{0},{t}_{0}}\right) \) . Since nonnegatively curved manifolds are asymptotically conical (see Appendix G), there is a constant \( D \) such that if \( y \in  {M}_{\infty } \) , and \( {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {y,{x}_{0}}\right)  > D \) , then there is a point \( x \in  {M}_{\infty } \) such that

(52.18)

\[
{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x, y}\right)  = {d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {y,{x}_{0}}\right) \;\text{ and }\;{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {x,{x}_{0}}\right)  \geq  \frac{3}{2}{d}_{{t}_{0}}\left( {y,{x}_{0}}\right) ;
\]

by (52.17) the same conditions hold at all times \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) , up to error \( C \) . If for some such \( y \) , and some \( t \in  \left( {{t}^{\prime },{t}_{0}}\right\rbrack \) the scalar curvature were large, then \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },\left( {y, t}\right) ,{\bar{R}}_{\infty }\left( {y, t}\right) {\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) would be \( {2\epsilon } \) -close to a \( \kappa \) -solution \( \left( {N, h\left( \cdot \right) ,\left( {z,{t}_{0}}\right) }\right) \) . When \( \epsilon \) is small we could use Proposition 49.1 to see that \( y \) lies in a neck region \( U \) in \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( t\right) }\right) \) of diameter \( \approx  R{\left( y, t\right) }^{-\frac{1}{2}} \ll  1 \) .

We claim that \( U \) separates \( {x}_{0} \) from \( x \) in the sense that \( {x}_{0} \) and \( x \) belong to disjoint components of \( {M}_{\infty } - U \) , where \( {x}_{0}, y \) , and \( x \) satisfy (52.18). To see this, we recall that if \( {M}_{\infty } \) has more than one end then it splits isometrically, in which case the claim is clear. If \( {M}_{\infty } \) has one end then we consider an exhaustion of \( {M}_{\infty } \) by totally convex compact sets \( {C}_{t} \) as in Section 46. One of the sets \( {C}_{t} \) will have boundary consisting of an approximate 2-sphere cross-section in the neck region \( U \) , giving the separation.

(For another argument, suppose that \( U \) does not separate \( {x}_{0} \) from \( x \) . Since \( {\widetilde{Z}}_{y}\left( {{x}_{0}, x}\right)  > \frac{\pi }{2} \) (from Proposition 49.1), the segments \( \overline{y{x}_{0}} \) and \( \overline{yx} \) must exit \( U \) by different ends. If \( {x}_{0} \) and \( x \) can be joined by a curve avoiding \( U \) then there is a nonzero element of \( {\mathrm{H}}^{1}\left( {{M}_{\infty },\mathbb{Z}}\right) \) . The corresponding infinite cyclic cover of \( {M}_{\infty } \) will then isometrically split off a line and its quotient \( {M}_{\infty } \) will be compact, which is a contradiction. We thank one of the referees for this argument.)

Obviously, at time \( {t}_{0} \) the set \( U \) still separates \( {x}_{0} \) from \( x \) . Since \( {\bar{g}}_{\infty } \) has nonnegative curvature, we have \( {\operatorname{diam}}_{{t}_{0}}\left( U\right)  \leq  {\operatorname{diam}}_{t}\left( U\right)  \ll  1 \) . Since \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }\left( {t}_{0}\right) }\right) \) has bounded geometry, there cannot be topologically separating subsets of arbitrarily small diameter. Thus there must be a uniform upper bound on \( R\left( {y, t}\right) \) and the curvature of \( \left( {{M}_{\infty },{\bar{g}}_{\infty }}\right) \) is uniformly bounded (in space and time) outside a set of uniformly bounded diameter. Repeating the reasoning from Step 2, we get uniform bounds everywhere. This contradicts our assumption that the curvature blows up as \( t \rightarrow  {t}^{\prime } \) .

It remains to show that the ancient solution is a \( \kappa \) -solution. The only remaining point is to show that it is \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed at all scales. This follows from the fact that the original Ricci flow solutions \( \left( {{M}_{k},{g}_{k}\left( \cdot \right) }\right) \) were \( \kappa \) -noncollapsed on scales less than the fixed number \( \sigma \) .

knowledge_statements.statement_latex:
Let \( M \) be an \( n \) -dimensional complete noncompact Riemannian manifold. Suppose \( {g}_{ij}\left( {x, t}\right) , x \in  M \) and \( t \in  \left( {-\infty , T}\right) \) with \( T > 0 \) , is a nonflat ancient solution of the Ricci flow with nonnegative curvature operator and bounded curvature. Then the asymptotic volume ratio of the solution metric satisfies

\[
{\nu }_{M}\left( t\right)  = \mathop{\lim }\limits_{{r \rightarrow   + \infty }}\frac{{\operatorname{Vol}}_{t}\left( {{B}_{t}\left( {O, r}\right) }\right) }{{r}^{n}} = 0
\]

for each \( t \in  \left( {-\infty , T}\right) \) .
